  17. Limits

At a glance

  • Today has two layers you can work with: your wiring, which stays (work with it), and today’s conditions, which pass (work around them).
  • Check your state before a hard talk. Weather, the three states, the stress tank and the battery are different words for the same thing; “One state, many words” below shows how they line up.
  • If a feeling is hard to name, start with the body. For many people that is the normal way in, and it has a name: alexithymia.
  • Your needs and limits are information. Plan what settles you on a calm day, and say what helps in one short sentence.
  • Different isn’t wrong. A mix-up between two different minds runs both ways (the double empathy problem), so both of you adjust a little.

Sunday, 7:50pm

A friend asks, “Are you okay?” You say, “Fine.” The truth is you can’t tell whether you’re fine, tired or quietly bothered, and you couldn’t explain it to yourself, let alone to them.

Everything in this part is about you, and it is for you. Nothing is ever filled in about someone else, nothing is a test, and nothing you try needs to be shared. This part is about today: how you are built, what kind of day you are having and what you can say about both.

Where this fits: the five big ideas

The whole program rests on five big ideas. Each one starts inside you and then shows up between you and other people. This part mostly teaches “Read your state first” and “Tune how you send and receive,” with help from “See the whole load” and “Fix the setup, not the person.” (Borrowed from neurobiology, psychology and philosophy.)

  • In you: Check your state and know your wiring before you judge a reaction. Count the hidden effort, like masking (hiding or toning down how you naturally are, to fit in) or holding an old alarm down, as real load.
  • Between you and others: Change the setup, not the person. Tell people what helps, tune how you send and receive, and treat a mismatch as tuning, not a moral failing.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxlayersqzToday is made of two layers you can work with

A reaction has three layers: wiring, patterns life taught you and today’s conditions. Then (page 20) covered the middle layer, the patterns. This part is about the other two.

LayerWhat it isThe move
Your wiringTemperament, pace, sensory makeup, how you process words and feelings. It stays.Work with it: written plans, quiet time after work, a heads-up before changes, a visible calendar
Today’s conditionsSleep, stress, hunger, the load you’re carrying, the room, the time of day. They pass.Work around it: eat first, sleep on it, say “low-battery day,” move the talk to tomorrow

Conditions amplify the other layers. A mild wiring need (“I prefer a heads-up”) becomes a hard limit when you’re exhausted, and an old alarm that stays quiet on good days can go off at full volume on bad ones. Because conditions change fastest, they are the easiest layer to adjust, and the first place to look.

A lot of frustration comes from using the wrong move. Trying to force your wiring to change tends to wear you out. Treating a bad day as your permanent self makes a passing storm feel like the climate. A kind rule of thumb: change the conditions today, work with the wiring always, and work on the patterns over time.

The full guide, with a sorting table of common reactions, is Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself-in-depth). It also covers working on it, with it and around it (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself-in-depth#work) in more detail.

Why the two layers need different moves

Wiring is the climate and conditions are the weather. You dress for the climate every day, and you check the weather each morning. Expecting your climate to change wears you out, and treating a stormy afternoon as your climate makes you think less of yourself than you should.

In different relationships

  • Two partners on different shifts: Ruby works nights and Ottilie works days. Their worst arguments happen at 7am, when Ruby is ending a twelve-hour shift and Ottilie is starting her day. Neither is an angry person. They move anything important to Saturday lunch, when both are rested. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).
  • A grandparent minding grandchildren: A grandfather who loves his grandchildren finds himself short-tempered by four o’clock on minding days. His wiring likes quiet. His conditions are a long day and no lunch break. A sandwich at noon and a half-hour of cartoons at three change the whole afternoon. See Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “If I’m tired, my feelings don’t count.” They count. Tiredness turns the volume up; it doesn’t make the feeling false. Look at it again once rested.
  • “My wiring is an excuse.” Wiring explains, and a good setup is your part. “I need a heads-up” comes with “and I’ll tell you early when plans don’t suit me.”

If you’re the only one doing this: Change your own conditions first: sleep, food, when you raise things. You don’t need anyone’s agreement to eat before a hard talk.

Research note: In lab studies, people who have missed a night’s sleep show stronger reactions to upsetting images, and studies of couples have linked a poor night’s sleep with more conflict the next day. Temperament research describes lasting differences in things like sensitivity and pace from early childhood. This book’s idea: the “work with it, work around it” moves.

Your wiring, and how you like to be spoken to

Wiring isn’t a flaw to fix. It is the lasting part of how you take in the world: your temperament, your sensory makeup, your pace, and how you handle words and feelings. You can understand it and plan around it, through routines, tools and a better setup.

Two free pages help you put it into words:

  • How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) asks a few short questions and gives you a four-letter Wave Code. Pace is Quick Spark or Slow Simmer, lens is Forest or Trees, sending is Direct or Nuanced, and receiving is Explicit or Attuned. It is a fun way to describe your preferences, not a test that measures you, and everyone uses both ends of each line sometimes. The wiring step is optional, it is self-identified, and it isn’t a diagnosis.
  • The “How to talk to me” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) turns how you actually take in words into one page: what helps, what silence means for you, how a request is best phrased. A card is a simple note, not a label, and not permission to criticize. It tells someone how to send a request so it gets through. It doesn’t make them responsible for managing you, and it doesn’t mean you have to be available no matter how you feel.

When you share either one, pick a calm moment and offer it as information: “I wrote this so you don’t have to guess. Would you read it?” Invite theirs, and put the two side by side. The places where you differ are not problems. They are the best places for a short talk. Update yours when life changes, because what you need changes too.

Why it helps to describe your wiring

Most mix-ups between kind people come from mismatched settings, not from bad intent. When you can say how you take in words, other people stop guessing, and you stop being misread. A description you write yourself is also kinder than a label someone else gives you.

Professor Puddles

Describing your wiring is a kindness to the people around you: it saves them guessing. The one-page card puts it in your own words, ready to share or to keep.

Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

In different relationships

  • Roommates: One roommate says what they mean in a single line. The other reads short messages as cross. After swapping “How to talk to me” cards, the first adds a smiley face to notes, and the second stops reading tone into them. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).
  • A parent and a grown-up son: She likes long talks with every detail. He likes the headline first. On calls, he asks, “Headline or the whole story?” and she laughs and gives him the headline first.
  • Business partners: One is a Quick Spark who decides in the meeting. The other is a Slow Simmer who decides overnight. They agree that big decisions always get a night’s sleep.

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “My Wave Code says I’m Direct, so people should cope.” A code describes a preference. It doesn’t excuse unkindness, and it goes both ways.
  • Handing over a card in the middle of a fight. Share it on a calm day, as information, and invite theirs.

If you’re the only one doing this: Write your card anyway, and use it yourself: it helps you notice what you need before a hard day. You can share one line of it when the moment is right.

If someone uses what you shared to control or mock you, that isn’t a communication mix-up.

Research note: Well-studied personality research uses five broad traits (often called the Big Five), measured on scales rather than types. Type-based quizzes are less reliable as measurement. The Wave Code is not a personality test. This book’s idea: the Wave Code and the “How to talk to me” card, as conversation starters.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxstateqzKnow your load and your state before you speak

Every conversation passes through your own state first. Chapter III (page 205), in Part Two, is the whole chapter on this, with leftover stress and this-moment stress (page 207), the three everyday states (page 209), the stress-tank score (page 210) and why a full tank means “later,” not “never.” (page 216) This part does not repeat them. It adds the habit of taking a reading on your own, on ordinary days, so that it is familiar by the time you need it.

  • My weather today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a one-minute reading of your own conditions in weather words.
  • How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), five quick questions about what you’re already carrying.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxstatexwordsqzOne state, many words

The book and its tools use several everyday pictures for one thing: how much room you have today. If you take words literally, they can look like five different measures. They aren’t. They are five ways of describing the same state, and you only ever need one of them.

The pictureWhere you meet itWhat it saysWhich way is heavier
The three states (Part Three calls them the ladder)Part Three, Chapter 2; the ladder check on the siteCalm and connected · revved up · running on emptyFurther along the list
My weather today: the skyThe one-minute self-checkClear · gusty · fogged in: the same three states in sky wordsFogged in
My weather today: the pressureThe same checkLight · building · heavy: how much you were already carrying. Behind the forecast sits a rough tally from 0 to 100 that you only see if you ask for the numbers.Heavier, or a higher tally
The stress tank (also called the load)How much are you carrying?; Part Two, Chapter IIIFive answers from 0 to 4, added up and divided by 20: a score from 0 to 1A higher score
The batteryThe self path, Step 1; everyday speech (“a low-battery day”)The energy you have left: the other side of the tankA lower battery

So one person at four o’clock can be gusty, revved up, at 0.55 on the stress tank and on a low battery, and all four describe the same afternoon. Two more words sit beside these. Flooded isn’t a fourth state: it means so wound up that listening stops working for a while, at the far end of revved up. Leftover stress is the part of the tank you brought in from earlier, before this moment started. Use whichever words suit you. Plain words are enough; the tank score is only there for people who like numbers, and the book never asks you to track them all.

Because a reading is quick, it is easy to do a few mornings in a row. Patterns tend to show within a week. A tank that has stayed full for a long time can start to feel normal, and “I’m fine” can come to mean “I stopped noticing,” as Chapter III (page 216) describes.

Why a reading on ordinary days helps

A reading you have practiced on calm days is there when you need it on a hard one. And a reading over a week shows patterns a single day can’t, like the fact that every Thursday is gusty.

Tidbit

Checking your weather on a boring day totally counts. Ordinary days are how you find out what normal looks like for you.

Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

In different relationships

  • A long-distance couple: Both take a one-word weather reading before their evening call. “Fogged in” means a light, short call. “Clear” means time for the big topics. See Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).
  • A caregiver and a partner with an illness: The caregiver notices his readings have been gusty or fogged in for three weeks. That tells him he needs a real break, not just a better attitude. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) and Caregivers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “A reading is a mood score for others to judge.” It is for you. Share it only if it helps.
  • “If my tank is full, I can’t talk at all.” A full tank means later, not never. Name a time and keep it.

If you’re the only one doing this: A reading only needs you. You don’t have to share it, and it still changes what you decide to say and when.

Research note: Studies on “affect labeling” (Matthew Lieberman and colleagues, 2007) found that putting a feeling into words reduced activity in the brain’s alarm areas in the lab. Lisa Feldman Barrett’s work on “emotional granularity” suggests people who can describe feelings in finer detail tend to cope with them better. Both are early, lab-based findings, not proof that a word cures a feeling.

Where is this feeling coming from? A four-step self-check

When a feeling is bigger than you expected, here is a short way to work it out. It works best once the first wave has passed a little.

  1. Name it. A word or two is enough, even a rough one: “tight and annoyed,” “flat,” “jumpy.” If words are hard to find, that’s common. Start with the body instead: where do you feel it?
  2. Is it about now, or does it feel older? Ask whether this is the size of the moment. A small thing that brings a big feeling often has something left over in it, either from earlier today or from much longer ago.
  3. Which layer is it? Wiring (“this always bothers me”), a pattern (“this reminds me of something”) or conditions (“I’d probably shrug this off after a good night’s sleep”). Usually it is a mix, so pick the biggest part.
  4. What does it need? Food, rest or space. A heads-up or a written plan. A fact check, or a slower try at a new response. Sometimes it needs a real conversation, later, when you’re both settled.

Feelings often reach the body before they reach words. A hot face and fast breathing, tight shoulders, or a heavy, foggy feeling are everyday clues about your state. Everyone’s are a little different, and they are not a medical reading of anything.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxhardxtoxnameqzWhen feelings are hard to name

For some people, “What are you feeling?” is a hard question most of the time, not just on bad days. They notice a racing heart or a heavy stomach but can’t tell whether it is worry, anger, hunger or excitement. Or they simply draw a blank, and “Fine” is the honest answer to a question they can’t answer. Psychologists call this alexithymia, from the Greek for “no words for feelings.” The psychiatrist Peter Sifneos named it in the 1970s.

  • It is a trait, not an illness. Like most traits it runs from a little to a lot. It is not a diagnosis, and you don’t need a name for it to use anything here.
  • It is common, and more common in some people. A review that pooled 15 studies found high alexithymia in about half of the autistic people studied, compared with about 1 in 20 people in the comparison groups. Plenty of people who are not autistic have it too, and plenty of autistic people don’t.
  • It is often about the body’s signals. Sensing what is going on inside your body, such as a fast heart, a tight throat or hunger, is called interoception. When those signals are faint, or hard to tell apart, the feeling behind them is harder to name. Part Three, Chapter 1 (page 310) explains how feelings start in the body.
  • It isn’t a lack of feeling, or of caring. The feelings are there; the words come slowly, or not at all. Someone with alexithymia can love deeply and still answer “I don’t know” when asked how they feel.

What helps:

  • Start with the body and the facts. “Tight chest, short night, skipped lunch” is a useful reading on its own.
  • Choose between two, not from fifty. “More tired or more annoyed? Space or company?”
  • Use a picture or a number instead of a feeling word. The sky words in My weather today, the three states, or “about a 6 out of 10” all work.
  • Give it time. Many people can name a feeling an hour or a day later. “I’ll tell you tomorrow” is a real answer.
  • Write it, or type it. For some people, words come more easily on a screen or on paper than out loud.

If someone close to you finds feelings hard to name: ask either-or questions, take “I don’t know” as true rather than as a brush-off, and ask what would help rather than what they feel. “Do you want company or quiet?” is easier to answer than “How are you feeling about it?”

Why four small steps beat one big question

“What’s wrong with me?” has no useful answer. Four small questions each do have one. They slow you down just enough for the thinking part of you to catch up with the feeling part.

In different relationships

  • Friends: A friend cancels lunch for the second time. Name it: hurt, a bit rejected. Now or older? Older; you were often left out at school. Layer: pattern. Need: a fact check. You reply, “No worries. Is everything okay with you?” and learn her child has been ill. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • A foster caregiver: A foster child shouts, “You’re not my real mom!” Name it: stung. Now or older? Mostly now, and tired. Need: to stay steady and talk later. The caregiver says, “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere.” See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Doing the check at the peak of a feeling. Let the first wave pass. Breathe, walk, drink water, then ask.
  • “I couldn’t name it, so I failed.” Start with the body. “Tight chest” is a perfectly good first answer.

If you’re the only one doing this: All four steps happen inside you. Nobody else has to do anything for them to work.

Research note: Peter Sifneos (1973) coined the word alexithymia in a small clinical study. Elizabeth Kinnaird and colleagues (2019) pooled 15 studies and found high alexithymia in about half of autistic participants and about 5% of comparison participants, measured mostly by questionnaires people fill out about themselves. That is a reason to start with the body or a simple choice of words, not a sign the check isn’t for you. This book’s idea: the four-step self-check.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxsettleqzPlan what settles you on a calm day

The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) is a plan for heated moments that you make while you are calm. On an ordinary day, write down what tends to set you off and where you feel it first. Pick two calming steps. Agree with yourself on one sentence to say when you step away: how you feel, how long, and when you’ll be back. In the moment, you just follow the plan.

The kit is for you, never for them. One person uses it about themselves, and it is never something to hand to the other person. Your line always includes a time you’ll return, so a break is never mistaken for walking out. Chapter III (page 216) says how to check your tank again and go back.

Why you plan it while calm

In a heated moment, the part of you that plans is the part that goes offline first. A plan made on a calm day is like a note left by a wiser you. In the moment, you only have to follow it.

Professor Puddles

A plan written while you’re calm is a note from your steadier self. The Calm-Down Kit gives it a shape: what helps, what doesn’t, and one sentence to say when you need a pause.

Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

In different relationships

  • Separated co-parents: A mom knows handover days make her tense. Her kit: a short walk before the handover, a scripted “Thanks, see you Sunday,” and ten minutes with her sister afterward. See Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).
  • A teen and a parent: A fourteen-year-old and his dad each make their own kit. Both agree that “I need ten minutes” means ten minutes, not “I’m leaving.”
  • Coworkers: A nurse keeps one line ready for a heated shift: “Let me check that and come back to you in five minutes.”

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Using your kit as a weapon: “Go and use your calm-down plan.” The kit is only ever for yourself.
  • Stepping away without a return time. Always add when you’ll be back, and come back on time.

If you’re the only one doing this: Make your own kit. It works whether or not anyone else has one, and it makes the moment safer for both of you.

If someone blocks you from leaving a heated room, or punishes you for stepping away, that is about safety, not technique.

Research note: Research on “implementation intentions” (Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran) found that deciding ahead what you’ll do in a given situation helps people follow through. John Gottman’s work with couples describes “flooding,” when the body is too stirred up to listen, and suggests breaks long enough for the body to settle, often twenty minutes or more.

Your needs, what matters to you, and what’s fair to you

A need is information. “I do better with a heads-up,” “I need an hour of quiet after work,” “I can’t take on another job this week.” These are facts about you, not demands and not complaints. Said kindly and early, they let other people plan, instead of guessing and getting it wrong.

It helps to know them before you’re asked. Knowing what matters to you (quiet, time with family, being on time, honesty, rest) also helps you tell a real limit from a passing mood. A limit that is fair to you can be stated without a fight, in three parts:

  1. What is true for you. “I’m low on battery this week.”
  2. What you can do. “I can do the groceries.”
  3. What you can offer instead, and when. “Could we look at the school forms on Sunday?”
What you notice in yourselfA kind way to say it
You like to know plans ahead“A text a few hours before really helps me. It isn’t about you.”
You’re low today“I’m low on battery. Can we talk about this tomorrow at eight?”
You’re at your limit on a job“I can’t take that one on this week. I can do this one instead.”
You need time to think“Let me think and come back to you tonight.”

Two workpapers help. Who did what (Part B) (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01-in-depth) has ready-made, kind ways to say no. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) turns a raw reaction into a fact, a feeling and an ask before you say or send anything.

This is also where the book’s later chapters meet this part. Chapter II (page 168) asks whether the way you share the work can last, and what you have left is part of that answer. Chapter IV (page 238) asks what “fair” means to each of you. Both are easier to talk about when you already know your own side, and a limit that is fair to you is not a score against anyone else.

Why needs said early go further

A need said early and plainly gives other people a chance to plan. A need held in until it bursts out tends to arrive as a complaint, and gets heard as one.

In different relationships

  • Three partners at home: Ren needs Sunday mornings alone. Said as a fact (“Sunday mornings are my reset”) it fits into the week. Before, it came out as snapping. See More than two partners at home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).
  • An adult child and an elderly parent: A son who visits his mother every day says, “I can come four days a week, and I’ll call on the other three.” It is honest, and it keeps him going for years instead of months.

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “A limit is a punishment.” A limit is a fact about your capacity. Say it warmly and offer what you can.
  • Saying a need as a complaint about the other person. “You never give me notice” becomes “A heads-up helps me.”

Words you could use: “This is true for me right now: ___. I can ___. Could we ___ instead?”

If you’re the only one doing this: You can state a need even if the other person doesn’t state theirs. Just be ready to hear theirs when they do.

Research note: Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication teaches saying an observation, a feeling, a need and a request. It is a widely used practice framework rather than a well-tested therapy. Assertiveness, saying what you want clearly while respecting others, has long been taught in skills training. This book’s idea: the three-part limit.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxdifferentqzBeing wired differently is not being wrong

Some people take in words, noise, change and feelings differently from what most social customs were designed around. That includes people who are autistic, have ADHD, are dyslexic or are highly sensitive, and many who are not sure. Nothing about that makes someone wrong. A setup that doesn’t suit you is a setup problem, so the question is how to build one that does.

  • It often has a hidden cost. Holding an old alarm down, masking, rehearsing what to say, or getting through a loud room all use real energy. This book counts it as part of your load, even when nobody sees it.
  • A mix-up usually runs both ways. When two differently wired people misread each other, each is decoding with a receiver built for their own kind of signal. The next section explains this. On the site, Wired Differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently-in-depth) is a full guide to fourteen kinds of wiring.
  • Don’t label anyone. This includes you. You can describe what helps without a name for it, and a name is not needed to use anything here.

The same goes the other way. When you meet someone else’s difference, ask “What was that like for you?” and let them answer. Never fill out a “How to talk to me” card or a Wave Code for another person. That would turn a reflection tool into a way of watching someone.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxdoublexempathyqzA mix-up runs both ways: the double empathy problem

For a long time, research described autistic people as short on empathy or “social skills,” as if every misunderstanding between an autistic and a non-autistic person was the autistic person’s doing. In 2012 the autistic researcher Damian Milton gave a name to a different view: the double empathy problem. Empathy, he argued, runs in two directions. When two people have very different ways of communicating and of making sense of the world, each finds the other hard to read. The non-autistic person struggles to read the autistic person just as much as the other way around. It is noticed less, because most social customs were built around the non-autistic way.

There is some evidence for it. In a 2020 study, Catherine Crompton and colleagues passed a story along chains of eight people. Chains made up only of autistic people passed on as much detail as chains made up only of non-autistic people. Mixed chains lost detail faster, and the people in them reported feeling less at ease with each other. It is one careful study of one task, so it is a strong hint rather than the last word.

What it changes in practice:

  • Nobody is the broken one. In a mix-up between different minds, ask “Where did we lose each other?” rather than “What’s wrong with you?” or “What’s wrong with me?”
  • Both people adjust, a little each. The direct speaker adds a softener when it matters. The hint-reader asks “Did you mean exactly that?” before deciding what it meant.
  • Easy company is information. Many autistic people find talking with other autistic people easier. That isn’t a lack of social skill; it is a shared way of talking.
  • The idea reaches further. The same two-way gap shows up between cultures, generations, or a fast talker and a slow thinker. Part Two, Chapter I (page 148) calls this being out of tune: nobody has to be wrong.

Why “different, not wrong” matters

If you believe your wiring is a defect, you spend energy hiding it. If you see it as a difference, you can spend that energy on a setup that works. The same goes for the people around you.

In different relationships

  • A parent and a child with ADHD: A dad who has ADHD himself realizes his daughter isn’t ignoring him; she needs one instruction at a time. He tries one instruction, then a thumbs up. See When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids).
  • An autistic friend and a non-autistic friend: One friend says exactly what she means. The other hears hints in everything. They agree: “If I want something, I’ll ask it straight. You can take what I say at face value.”

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “If I need adjustments, I’m being difficult.” Glasses aren’t difficult. Neither is a quiet room.
  • Deciding someone else is “probably autistic.” Ask what helps them instead. Labels are theirs to choose.

If you’re the only one doing this: You can build your own setup without anyone else changing: headphones, written lists, a quiet half hour.

Research note: The “double empathy problem,” described by Damian Milton in 2012, suggests that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run both ways. Studies of autistic adults (for example, Laura Hull and colleagues, 2017) describe “camouflaging,” or masking, as tiring and linked with stress. Elaine Aron’s research on “sensory processing sensitivity” describes people who take in their surroundings more deeply.

Explain yourself without over-sharing

You never owe anyone your history. Share the part that helps them help you, and keep the rest. Three short sentences cover most moments:

  • “This is how I’m wired. It won’t change, but here’s what helps.”
  • “This is an old alarm. I’m working on it, and here’s what helps in the moment.”
  • “Today’s a low-battery day.”

Offer them as information, not as rules, and ask about theirs. When you want a bit more, Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself-in-depth#explain) has scripts and a guide to how much to share. And when someone else shares, ask questions, not labels (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself-in-depth#others).

Why less can be more

A short, clear sentence about what helps is easier to remember than a long story about why. It also protects you: your history is yours to share when you choose, with people who have earned it.

In different relationships

  • Coming out at work: A woman who has just come out to her family isn’t ready to share at work yet. When a colleague asks why she seems tired, she says, “It’s been a big month at home. I’m okay, thanks for asking.” See Coming out as an adult (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-out).
  • An interfaith couple at a family dinner: A husband who doesn’t drink for religious reasons says to his in-laws, “I don’t drink, but I’d love a lemonade.” No lecture needed. See Two faiths or cultures (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “Being open means telling everything.” Being open means being honest about what you share, not sharing it all.
  • Explaining as a way to win. “It’s how I’m wired” starts a conversation. It doesn’t end one.

If you’re the only one doing this: Your sentences are yours to use whether or not anyone else explains themselves.

Research note: Research on self-disclosure, going back to Irwin Altman and Dalmas Taylor in the 1970s, describes closeness growing through gradual, two-way sharing. That fits the advice here: share a little, see how it is received, and share more with people who respond with care.

A worked example: the surprise dinner, replayed

Friday, 6:40pm. Alex says, “Surprise! I booked us dinner with my cousins tonight.” They meant it as a gift. Sam feels their chest tighten and hears themselves say “Great” in a flat voice.

Without the tools: Sam goes to the dinner, stays quiet and gets through it. Alex senses something is wrong and asks. Sam says, “It’s nothing,” and thinks, “What’s wrong with me?” Both end the evening unsure what happened.

With the tools: The next morning, Sam takes a minute. Name it: tight, a bit cornered. Now or older? Bigger than the moment. Which layer? Mostly wiring, a need to know plans ahead, plus a long week. What does it need? A heads-up next time, and a rested Sam. That evening Sam says, “Thank you for thinking of me. I do better with a heads-up, it’s how I’m wired. Would a text a few hours before work for both of us?” Alex says, “Easy. I didn’t know.” They try it, and agree to look again at the end of the month.

Two more worked examples

The roommate and the vacuum. Tomás comes home after a twelve-hour shift and his roommate is vacuuming. He snaps, “Seriously, now?” Later, he runs the four steps. Name it: raw, prickly. Now or older? Mostly now. Layer: conditions (exhausted) and wiring (noise always bothers him). Need: quiet when he first gets in. He says, “Sorry I snapped. After long shifts I need half an hour of quiet. Could the vacuum wait until seven?” His roommate says yes, and asks him to text when he is on his way home.

A grandmother and the phone. Agnes, 72, feels hurt that her grandson only sends short texts. She takes a reading. Layer: mostly wiring; she likes voices, he likes typing. She says, “I love hearing your voice. Could we have a ten-minute call on Sundays? Texts are lovely the rest of the week.” He agrees, and starts sending her voice notes too.

zqaxselfx2xnowxxcontrolqzYour circle of control, and matching energy

Every moment has three rings. In the middle is what you control: your words, your effort, your tone, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. Around it is what you can influence but not decide: you can ask, explain, invite and offer, and the other person still chooses. Outside is what isn’t yours at all: their mood, their past, their pace, whether they agree. Most exhaustion comes from pouring energy into the outer ring.

In your hands

  • What you say, and how and when you say it
  • Doing your own jobs well
  • Saying yes, no or “not today”
  • Resting before you’re empty
  • Asking clearly for what would help

Theirs to decide

  • How your words land
  • Whether they change
  • How fast they calm down
  • What they think of you
  • Whether they say yes

Your energy is a budget

Your battery only holds so much (How much are you carrying? reads the other side of it, your stress tank). Signs you’re over-giving: quiet resentment, a silent scorecard, feeling invisible, being tired before the day starts. Those aren’t character flaws. They’re a budget running in the red.

How to match energy, kindly

  1. Notice. “I’m usually the one who plans, texts first or apologizes.”
  2. Name it once, without blame. “I’ve noticed I’m often the one who starts our plans. I’d love it if you started the next one.”
  3. Adjust your side. Give the effort that’s being given: a warm reply to a warm message, a lighter touch where little comes back.
  4. See what comes back. Some people step up once there’s space. Some don’t, and that’s information too.

Matching energy means matching care and effort, never volume or meanness. If someone gets loud, you don’t have to get loud. If someone is going through something, you match their capacity, not their output, and you can choose to give more for a season, as long as it’s a choice and something refills you. With children and anyone who depends on you, you give what they need.

Words you could use: “I want to keep showing up for this, and I need it to go both ways.” “I can do my part. That one is yours.” “I’m low today, so I’m keeping my energy for the essentials.”

Why the circle helps

When you sort a worry into “mine” or “not mine,” you stop spending energy where it can’t do anything. That energy comes back to you for the things you can change.

In different relationships

  • A business partner: You can make sure your half of the accounts is clear and on time. You can’t make your partner do theirs. You ask once, put it in writing, and then decide what you will do if it doesn’t happen.
  • A parent of a teen: You can’t make your sixteen-year-old talk. You can be in the kitchen at the same time every evening with a snack and no questions. Many teens talk more when no one is asking.
  • Friends: You notice you always start the chat. You reply warmly but stop starting for a month. See Always the one reaching out? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends#reaching-out)

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “Not my circle” means “not my problem.” You can still care, offer and ask. You just stop trying to decide for them.
  • Matching energy as a cold tally. It is balance over time. In a hard season, you match capacity, not output.

If you’re the only one doing this: This section is, by its nature, something you do alone. Your circle is the part only you can act on.

Research note: The split between what is and isn’t up to us comes from the Stoic teacher Epictetus. Equity theory, from J. Stacy Adams in the 1960s and applied to close relationships by Elaine Hatfield (then Walster) and colleagues in the 1970s, found that people tend to feel uneasy when a relationship feels unbalanced either way. Studies of family caregivers generally link having practical and emotional support with lower strain.

You, in all your relationships

Your wiring and your weather come with you into every room. Here is where they tend to show up.

  • With yourself first: Noticing “I’m low today” before you decide “I’m failing,” and planning your week to suit how you’re built.
  • With a partner, or partners: A heads-up, a quiet hour, and a better time for big talks. In a home with more than two partners, each person’s wiring adds to the mix. See More than two partners at home.
  • With friends: How you like to keep in touch, and how much you can give right now. See Friends.
  • With family: Visits that run long, noise, old roles and big gatherings. A rest planned ahead turns a retreat into a plan. See For grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children).
  • At work: An agenda ahead, a minute before you answer, a written follow-up.
  • With roommates: Light, noise and quiet time. See Sharing a room.
  • On different hours: Sleep at odd times is still sleep. See Different hours.
  • On your own: No one to adjust around but you, which is a chance to build a week that truly fits. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

To find help for your own situation, see help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship). If you guide others, see For counselors, coaches and group leaders (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors).

In the individual program

This part goes with Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the individual program: check your battery, get to know your wiring, plan what settles you, and find words for what you feel.

Your next step: Step 1: check your battery (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · Step 2: your wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path#wiring) · Step 4: what settles you (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path#settle) · Step 5: find the words (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path#words) · The whole book on knowing yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-know-yourself)

Where the thirteen fields meet in this part

This part draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (the About page, spreadloveandacceptance.com/about, lists them all). Here is what each one brings, and which of the five big ideas it serves.

FieldWhat it brings hereBig idea
PsychologyHow you take words in and send them out, and what helps you feel understood.Tune how you send and receive
NeurobiologyYour nervous system’s state comes before your words, and wiring is part of how you are built. Both are things to understand, not things to be ashamed of.Read your state first
PhilosophyWhat Is Up to Us: your honesty, your ask and your tone are yours, and the other person’s answer is theirs.Tune how you send and receive
Behavioral scienceSmall routines, tried on calm days, are the ones that survive a hard one: a one-minute reading, and a sentence you keep ready.Read your state first
Holistic therapiesBody first, words second. Decide on a calm day what settles you, and treat that as care, not as an extra.Read your state first
EconomicsCapacity again: managing yourself costs attention and energy that nobody sees, and a limit is a true statement about a limited supply.See the whole load

How they connect

The word in brackets is the root the two fields share; the polymath page explains all seven. From the most obvious connection to the most abstract:

  • Obvious: Psychology + Holistic therapies (state and setting). Calm the body before the conversation. Words land better, and come out better, once the body has settled. This holds up “Read your state first.”
  • Hidden: Behavioral science + Neurobiology (limited capacity). A tired body makes good habits harder, so the habits in this book are tiny. They have to survive the worst day of the week, which is why you practice them on a calm one. This holds up “Read your state first.”
  • Abstract: Philosophy + Neurobiology (state and setting). If getting revved up or shutting down is a body doing its job, it isn’t a character flaw. That changes what blame means, including the blame you aim at yourself. This holds up “Fix the setup, not the person.”

The body tells you what state you’re in, and the story you tell about it decides what you do next.

Connect any two fields yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath) · Ask Professor Puddles how all thirteen connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask)

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, “This is just how I am” becomes a way to end every conversation. Or self-knowledge turns into self-criticism: a long list of what’s wrong with you. Or someone uses a label as a weapon (“You’re obviously just anxious”) and calls it understanding.

When it goes right, you take your own reading, quietly, and say one clear sentence about what helps. You ask about theirs. Over a few weeks you both learn what each of you needs, and you start to allow for it before the hard moment, not in the middle of it.

Questions people often ask

Isn’t focusing on myself selfish?

Every conversation runs through your own state first. Knowing it makes you easier to talk with and easier to hear. The other person’s side matters just as much, and the chapters after Part One are about that.

Do I need a diagnosis to use any of this?

No. Nothing here needs one and nothing here gives one. The wiring step in How you connect is self-identified.

What if I can’t tell what I’m feeling?

That is common, and some people are wired that way (see When feelings are hard to name, above). Start with the body, or with a choice between two simple words, like “more tired or more annoyed? Space or company?” My weather today uses weather words for the same reason.

Can I use this to understand someone else?

Not as a verdict. You can ask, gently, what something was like for them, and then let them answer. A guess about someone else’s wiring often turns into a judgment of them. The tools are for filling in about yourself.

What if the people around me don’t care how I’m wired?

You can still build your own setup and say one clear sentence about what helps. Some people need to hear it more than once.

Where can I talk this through?

Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly chat host, can help you work out where a feeling came from before you decide what to say.

Limits

  • This part is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis, a test or treatment, and it can’t tell you what you or anyone else has.
  • The layers are a thinking tool, not a scientific category system. Real people are messier, and the layers overlap.
  • A Wave Code is a fun description of preferences, not a test that measures you. Everyone uses both ends of every line sometimes.
  • Fill things in about yourself only. Never sort, score or label another person, and never use what you learned about yourself to win a point.
  • Research notes in this chapter describe well-known findings in plain words, and say where the evidence is limited. Notes marked “This book’s idea” are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.
  • “That’s just how I am” explains a reaction. It doesn’t excuse it, and it doesn’t replace a kind repair.
  • These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private.

What to remember

  • Today is made of two layers you can work with.
  • Check your weather before you speak.
  • Plan what settles you on a calm day.
  • Being wired differently is not being wrong.
  • Do your part, and only your part.

Part One · Next

Know yourself: next, shaping who you are becoming

You aren’t finished, and some of who you become is up to you. This chapter is about choosing a direction and building small steps that still work on a tired day.

In this chapter

  1. Where this fits: the five big ideas
  2. Start with what matters to you
  3. Pick one small goal, in plain words
  4. Name what gets in the way
  5. Make the step tiny, and repeatable
  6. Decide ahead with a simple if-then
  7. Ask for support, as information
  8. Look back kindly once a month
  9. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan
  10. A worked example: the walk that kept slipping
  11. Plan inside your circle, and budget your energy
  12. You, in all your relationships
  13. In the individual program
  14. Where the thirteen fields meet in this part
  15. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  16. Questions people often ask
  17. Limits

At a glance

  • Start with what matters to you, in two or three plain words, then pick one small goal you can do.
  • Make the step tiny and decide ahead: “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.”
  • Ask for support as information, and look back kindly once a month.
  • A missed day is information about the plan, not a verdict on you. Change the plan.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend your energy where it comes back.

Wednesday, 9:10pm

You meant to start walking after dinner. You meant to last week, too. Tonight you’re tired, the shoes are by the door, and you tell yourself you’ll begin on Monday.

Everything in this part is for you. Nothing is graded, nothing is shared unless you choose to, and every step can be made smaller or put down. It follows Then (where your lens came from) and Now (your wiring, your weather and your words), and it asks one question: given who you are, what would you like to grow toward?

Where this fits: the five big ideas

The whole program rests on five big ideas. This part mostly teaches “Fix the setup, not the person” and “Notice the quiet incentives,” with help from “Read your state first.”

  • In you: Treat your own routines as a setup you can adjust, not a character test. Notice the defaults and cues that steer you, and let the easy path be the one you want. Pick the step for the energy you really have.
  • Between you and others: Say what you’re trying and what would help, as information. Let people’s answers be theirs, and fix the setup, not the person.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxmattersqzStart with what matters to you

A goal built on someone else’s idea of success is hard to keep up, because nothing in you is pulling toward it. Before you pick anything, ask: what do I want my days to be like? Write two or three plain words, like calm, close to my family, steady, creative, useful, rested. They are a direction, not a score. You can’t finish “calm,” and you can’t fail at it. You can only lean toward it.

  • Look at what fills you and what drains you. How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) and Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) can help you notice. A value you keep wanting and keep skipping is worth a look in its own right.
  • Borrowed goals feel heavy. If a goal comes with “I should” and a face (a parent, a boss, a feed), look for the thing under it you do want, and aim at that.
  • Values can sit side by side. “Close to my family” and “time alone” are both allowed. Part of the work is making room for both.

Why values come before goals

A value is a direction you can walk in every day. A goal is one stop along the way. When a goal slips, a value is still there, so you don’t lose the whole plan with one bad week.

In different relationships

  • A couple whose children have left home: After twenty-six years of school runs, Moira and Clive each write two words. Moira: “useful, outdoors.” Clive: “calm, curious.” They stop arguing about how to spend Saturdays and plan one morning for each. See Kids grown and gone (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest).
  • Someone coming out in midlife: Dominic’s old goals were built around what his parents expected. His two new words, “honest” and “close,” lead to different goals: fewer late nights at work, more dinners with friends who know him. See Coming out as an adult (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-out).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “My values should match my partner’s.” They can differ. Shared plans can make room for both.
  • Picking the values you think you should have. Notice what you actually reach for when nobody is watching.

If you’re the only one doing this: Values are personal by definition. You can choose yours without asking anyone.

Research note: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, developed by Steven Hayes and colleagues, uses values as a direction rather than a finish line, and has a growing body of research. Self-determination theory (Edward Deci and Richard Ryan) found that goals people choose for their own reasons tend to be kept up longer than goals driven by pressure or guilt.

Pick one small goal, in plain words

Just one, to begin with. Say it as something you will do, not something you hope will happen: “Walk for ten minutes after dinner,” not “get healthier.” The difference matters because your own actions are up to you. How other people respond, and how things turn out in the end, are not.

  • Describe the action, not the result. “Send one note to a friend on Sundays” is yours. “Have more friends” is a hope.
  • Keep it kind and honest. “Be the calm one” can hide a rule that you aren’t allowed to be upset. Ask whether the goal leaves room for you to be a person.
  • One at a time. Attention is limited, so one small goal that sticks beats five big ones that all wobble. Add a second when the first feels ordinary.

Why an action beats a hope

A hope depends on things you can’t control. An action depends on you. Writing a goal as an action also makes it clear when you have done it, which is quietly encouraging.

In different relationships

  • Students in the dorms: A first-year student wants “to get on better with my roommate.” As an action: “Ask her once a week if anything in the apartment is bothering her.” See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).
  • Two partners and money: “Stop fighting about money” is a hope. “Bring the bank statement to our Sunday check-in” is an action. See Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).
  • A team leader: “Be a better boss” becomes “Thank one person by name each Friday.”

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Five goals at once. Pick one. Add a second when the first feels ordinary.
  • A goal that is secretly a rule about feelings. “Never get annoyed” isn’t an action. “Take a breath before I answer” is.

If you’re the only one doing this: Your action is yours. It doesn’t need anyone’s agreement to start.

Research note: Goal-setting research by Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that specific goals usually lead to better performance than vague ones like “do your best.” Later work suggests that for new or complex skills, goals about learning and doing tend to help more than goals about results.

Name what gets in the way

When a step keeps slipping, the useful question is not “what’s wrong with me?” but “what is in the way?” Use what you learned in Then (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-1-then) and Now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now). It is usually one of three things:

  • Your wiring. A plan that ignores how you’re built was built for someone else. If you hate mornings, a six a.m. plan is a poor fit, however good the goal.
  • An old rule. “Rest has to be earned.” “Don’t make a fuss.” Rules from growing up can quietly veto a step you chose. Notice the rule, then decide whether you still want it.
  • Today’s conditions. A tired evening, a hard week, a house full of noise. These change, and the plan can change with them.

Then change the arrangement, never yourself: move the step to the morning, put the shoes by the bed, shorten it to two minutes. That is “Fix the setup, not the person,” applied to you.

Why “what’s in the way” is the kind question

“What’s wrong with me?” makes you the problem. “What’s in the way?” makes the setup the problem, and setups can be changed today.

In different relationships

  • A shift worker: Dwayne’s schedule changes every week, so “every evening” never works. He ties his run to “my first day off” instead, and it sticks. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).
  • A parent of a child with ADHD: A mom keeps planning calm mornings that fall apart. The setup: shoes, bags and coats are in three rooms. One hook by the door changes the morning. See When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Blaming willpower. Willpower is the least reliable part of any plan. Change the setup first.
  • Missing the old rule. If a step keeps slipping for no clear reason, ask whether some old rule is quietly saying no.

If you’re the only one doing this: You can change your own setup alone: where things are, when you do them, how big the step is.

Research note: Research by Wendy Wood and others suggests that much everyday behavior is driven by habits cued by our surroundings, not by moment-to-moment decisions. That is why changing the surroundings often works better than trying harder.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxtinyqzMake the step tiny, and repeatable

Small enough to survive your worst week. “Put my shoes on” counts, and it often leads to the walk. Two ideas help:

  • Tie it to something you already do. After brushing my teeth. After the kettle clicks. After I sit down for lunch. An existing habit is a handle for a new one.
  • Small and often beats big and rare. This is the same idea as the 90-second daily check-in in Chapter I (page 155) of Part Two. Start in 10 minutes (spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes) shows how small a whole path can be.

Make the helpful thing the easy thing, too. Put the book on the pillow, the water on the desk, the phone in another room. These small defaults do quiet work, which is “Notice the quiet incentives” on your side.

Why tiny works

A tiny step survives bad weeks, and a habit that survives bad weeks is the one that lasts. Tiny steps also leave room to grow: two minutes often turns into ten on a good day.

Tidbit

Tiny steps count, even the wobbly ones. If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.

Tool: Calm games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

In different relationships

  • On your own after a breakup: Aoife wants to rebuild her social life. Her tiny step: one message to one friend every Sunday. Six weeks later she has three regular coffee dates. See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).
  • A grandparent and a grandchild far away: A grandfather wants to be closer to his granddaughter who lives abroad. Tiny step: one photo and one line every Friday. See Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “Tiny doesn’t count.” Tiny is how big things start, and it is often all a hard week allows.
  • Growing the step too fast. Grow it only when the small version feels ordinary.

If you’re the only one doing this: Tiny steps are yours alone. Nobody else needs to notice them for them to work.

Research note: A study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues (2010) followed people forming a new daily habit. On average it took about two months for the habit to feel automatic, with a very wide range from person to person, and missing a single day did not undo progress. BJ Fogg’s “Tiny Habits” is a popular method built on starting very small; it is a practical approach rather than a tested treatment.

Decide ahead with a simple if-then

“If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.” Deciding ahead means one less decision on a tired day. It is the same idea as the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11), which you make while you are calm so that you don’t have to invent it in the middle of a hard moment.

  • Write it in the plain form: “If ___, then I ___.” Pick a cue you’ll definitely meet, and an action you’ll definitely be able to do.
  • Plan for the bad day, too: “If I’m too tired to walk, then I stretch for two minutes.” A smaller backup keeps the habit alive.
  • If a plan isn’t working, that’s information about the plan. Change the cue, the size or the time. Don’t change your opinion of yourself.

Why deciding ahead helps

Every decision costs a little energy. An if-then makes the decision once, on a good day, so a tired you only has to follow it.

In different relationships

  • Separated co-parents: Before handovers, Tanya’s if-then is: “If I pull up outside, then I take three slow breaths before I open the door.” Her son notices she seems calmer. See Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).
  • An interfaith family: “If a vacation invitation comes in, then we talk about it together before either of us says yes.” It ends a year of double-booked festivals. See Two faiths or cultures (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • A cue that doesn’t happen every day. Choose one that does: the kettle, the front door, brushing your teeth.
  • No backup plan. Add a smaller version for bad days: “If I’m too tired, then I stretch for two minutes.”

If you’re the only one doing this: An if-then lives in your head. You can set one up today without telling anyone.

Research note: A large review of many studies by Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran (2006) found that if-then plans, which they called implementation intentions, helped people follow through on goals, on average, by a meaningful amount.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxsupportqzAsk for support, as information

Tell one person what you’re trying and what would help: “I’m trying to walk after dinner. Could you ask me about it on Sunday?” It isn’t a demand, they can say no, and you don’t need their agreement to start.

  • Say what you want, not what they did wrong. “Could you not mention the snacks?” works better than a speech.
  • Let their answer be theirs. If they say not now, you’ve learned something, and you can ask someone else or do it alone.

Why a specific ask works better

A vague “I’m trying to be healthier” leaves people unsure what to do. A specific ask (“Could you ask me on Sunday?”) gives them an easy yes or an easy no, and either answer is useful.

In different relationships

  • A caregiver for a partner after a stroke: Maria asks her brother, “Could you sit with Bernard on Thursday afternoons so I can swim?” He says yes to every other Thursday, which is still a lot. See When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).
  • Coworkers: A new manager asks a trusted colleague, “If I talk over people in meetings, could you give me a nod?”
  • Kinship caregivers: A grandmother raising her grandson asks the school for a short weekly note, so she isn’t guessing about homework. See Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Announcing a goal to everyone. Ask one person for one specific thing instead.
  • Treating a “no” as rejection. A no is information about their week, not your worth.

Words you could use: “I’m trying ___. Would you be up for ___? It’s fine to say no.”

If you’re the only one doing this: You don’t need support to start. If nobody can help right now, your tiny step and your if-then still work.

If a partner or family member uses your goal to watch, check or control you, for example your food, money or phone, that isn’t support.

Research note: Studies by Peter Gollwitzer and colleagues (2009) found that publicly announcing some kinds of goals, ones about who you want to be, sometimes made people put in less effort, as if the announcement itself felt like progress. A specific request for help is different from an announcement.

zqaxselfx3xnextxxlookxbackqzLook back kindly once a month

This mirrors Chapter V, the monthly look-back (page 271) in Part Two, pointed at yourself. Once a month, take ten minutes with a cup of tea and ask three questions:

  1. What went well? Even something small. Name it.
  2. What kept slipping? Without blame. Just notice.
  3. Was the gap in the plan, in how much I have right now, or just a one-off week? A plan gap is fixed by changing the plan. A low-energy season is fixed by shrinking the step. A one-off week needs nothing at all.

Then choose what to try next month. You don’t add up old misses, and you don’t carry a score from one month to the next. The look-back fixes the arrangement, never the person.

Why monthly, and why kindly

A month is long enough to see a pattern and short enough to change course before a small problem grows. Kindness keeps you coming back to the look-back. A look-back that feels like a trial gets skipped.

Professor Puddles

Your monthly look is the solo version of the look-back in Chapter V. Borrow its questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

In different relationships

  • Roommates: Two roommates each do their own look-back, then share one line: “The trash went well; the bathroom kept slipping.” They swap who owns the bathroom.
  • A parent and a teenager: A sixteen-year-old and her mom each look back on their own goals once a month over hot chocolate. It is never about grading each other.

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Counting misses from last month. Each month starts fresh.
  • Only looking at what went wrong. Start with what went well. It shows what to keep.

If you’re the only one doing this: You can look back on your own goals alone, and it still works.

Research note: A review of many studies by Benjamin Harkin and colleagues (2016) found that keeping track of progress helps people reach their goals, especially when it is written down. Research by Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis (2014) found that people are more likely to start goals at “fresh starts” like a new week or a new month, which is one reason the first of the month works well.

Kindness to yourself is part of the plan

A plan that needs you to be harsh with yourself is built on what Buddhist teachers call a “second arrow”: first something happens (you skip a day), then you add a story about what it means (you’re hopeless). The story is the part you can leave out.

  • A missed day is information. It tells you something about the setup.
  • Rest is part of the plan, not a prize for finishing. Small repeated acts work like rhythms, and rhythms include quiet.
  • You can shrink a goal, change it or drop it. Nothing here is required, and you can stop any time.
  • Be as fair to yourself as you would be to a friend who told you the same thing.

Why kindness works better than a stick

Harshness can feel like it should work, but it mostly makes people hide their misses, including from themselves. Kindness keeps the facts in view, which is what a good plan needs.

Sugarfoot

When a step slips, talk to yourself the way you’d talk to a friend who tried. Then pick the smallest next step. If the kind words won’t come, Professor Puddles is good at finding them.

Tool: Ask Professor Puddles spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask

In different relationships

  • A teenager and a grandmother: A sixteen-year-old misses three nights of studying and says, “I’m useless.” His grandmother asks, “What would you tell your best friend?” He shrinks the goal to twenty minutes.
  • Two partners: One partner has a goal to drink less. On a slip, the other says, “One night isn’t the whole plan. What would help next time?” not “You promised.”

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • “Being kind to myself means letting myself off.” It means telling yourself the truth gently, then choosing the next step.
  • Kindness only after success. Kindness matters most after a miss.

If you’re the only one doing this: Your inner voice is the one relationship nobody else can change for you. It is a good place to practice.

Research note: Kristin Neff’s research describes self-compassion as treating yourself as you would a friend. A 2012 study by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen found that people encouraged to be self-compassionate after a failure were more motivated to improve, not less.

A worked example: the walk that kept slipping

Asha wants to feel stronger. What matters: steady and outdoors. One small goal: walk for ten minutes after dinner. After a week she has walked once. Instead of deciding she’s lazy, she asks what got in the way.

Wiring: evenings are her lowest energy. Old rule: “I don’t get to rest until the kitchen is done.” Conditions: a long week. She changes the arrangement: shoes by the front door, the walk moves to just after she gets home, and the if-then is “If I turn the key in the door, then I put my shoes back on and walk to the corner.” She tells her sister, who agrees to ask on Sunday. On the first of the month she looks back: four walks, two skipped weeks, one clear lesson. Nothing went wrong. She knows which part of the setup to change.

Two more worked examples

The handover. Tanya and her ex share their son, and handovers on Sunday evenings keep turning tense. What matters: calm and kind. One goal: be steady at handovers. What’s in the way: a long Sunday, and an old rule that says “stand your ground.” Tiny step and if-then: “If I pull up outside, then I take three breaths and say only ‘Thanks, see you Friday.’” She asks a friend to text her afterward. At the end of the month: three calm handovers out of four. She keeps the plan.

The coworker who never speaks up. Tunde, a junior engineer, wants to share ideas in meetings. What’s in the way: wiring (he thinks best on paper) and an old rule (“children should be seen and not heard”). Tiny step: read the agenda the day before and write one comment. If-then: “If the meeting reaches my topic, then I read my note.” His manager starts asking him first, because his notes are good.

Plan inside your circle, and budget your energy

Goals stall for a simple reason: they quietly depend on someone else. “My partner will help more” is a hope. “I’ll ask once, kindly, on Sunday, and suggest one job” is a plan, because every part of it is yours to do. Rewrite each goal until the next step is something you can do whatever anyone else decides.

Outside your circle

  • “They’ll appreciate me more.”
  • “We won’t argue about money.”
  • “My boss will notice my work.”

Inside your circle

  • “I’ll name one thing I’d love thanks for, once.”
  • “I’ll bring the budget to a calm Sunday check-in.”
  • “I’ll send a short weekly note of what I finished.”

Budget your energy like it matters, because it does

Make a quick list of what drains you and what refills you. Then plan your week so the refills come first, not last. Spend more energy on the people and plans that give back: the friend who calls you too, the project that leaves you proud, the habit that leaves you lighter. Spend less on what only takes. That is matching energy with energy, and it’s how a plan survives a hard month.

It isn’t a reason to drop anyone in a rough season. When someone close to you can’t give right now, you match their capacity, and you choose, on purpose, to carry a little more for a while. The monthly look-back is a good time to ask: is this still a choice, and is anything refilling me?

Why a goal inside your circle is a stronger goal

A goal that depends on someone else can be ruined by them. A goal inside your circle can only be ruined by you not doing it, and you can always shrink it.

In different relationships

  • Adult siblings after a rift: “My brother will forgive me” is outside your circle. “I’ll write him one short, honest letter and not chase a reply” is inside. See Reaching out (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) and I’m not ready (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts#not-ready).
  • A home with more than two partners: “They’ll all agree on a chore schedule” is a hope. “I’ll bring a draft to Sunday’s house meeting” is a plan. See More than two partners at home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).

Mix-ups, and how to fix them

  • Rewriting other people into your plan. “I’ll ask” is yours. “They’ll say yes” isn’t.
  • Treating energy-matching as revenge. It is about protecting your battery, not making a point.

If you’re the only one doing this: This whole section is about what you can do alone. Start there.

Research note: The Stoic teacher Epictetus taught that some things are up to us and some aren’t. Stress researchers Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman described coping as a mix of acting on the parts of a problem you can change and finding ways to live with the parts you can’t. Susan Nolen-Hoeksema’s research linked going over and over a problem (rumination) with more distress.

Try this: take your one small goal and check each step. If a step needs someone else to change, rewrite it as something you can do. Then add one refill to your week before the first hard task.

You, in all your relationships

A goal for yourself almost always touches other people. These are the places it tends to show up.

  • With yourself first: Rest, health, a hobby you dropped, a kinder inner voice. These are goals too, and often the ones everything else rests on.
  • With a partner, or partners: One small habit you offer, not one you demand. See Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) and More than two partners at home.
  • With friends: One message a week, one plan a month. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • With family: A regular call, a visit you can keep up, or a first step after years apart. See Family rifts and For grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children).
  • At work: One comment per meeting, one clear handover note, one “no” said kindly.
  • With money: One small habit you can keep yourself. See Money together.
  • After time apart: Coming home means new routines for everyone. See Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home).
  • On your own: A week built around what fills you up. See On my own.

To find help for your own situation, see help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship). If you guide others, see For counselors, coaches and group leaders (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors).

In the individual program

This part goes with the end of the individual program: a gentle first week, then the Individual package, which turns your workpapers into a report written just for you.

Your next step: A gentle first week (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) · The Individual package and your report (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path#package) · All six steps (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path#steps) · The whole book on knowing yourself (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-know-yourself)

Where the thirteen fields meet in this part

This part draws on 6 of the author’s thirteen fields (the About page, spreadloveandacceptance.com/about, lists them all). Here is what each one brings, and which of the five big ideas it serves.

FieldWhat it brings hereBig idea
Behavioral scienceHabits beat willpower, especially when you’re tired. Cues and defaults steer us more than intentions do.Notice the quiet incentives
PsychologyWhat matters to you, and what you tell yourself when a day goes wrong.Tune how you send and receive
PhilosophyWhat Is Up to Us: your actions are, results aren’t. Aristotle’s idea that we become what we repeatedly do.Tune how you send and receive
BusinessA small, regular review catches problems while they are small.Fix the setup, not the person
EconomicsAttention is limited, so one small goal beats five big ones.See the whole load
Holistic therapiesSmall repeated acts are rhythms, and rest is part of the rhythm.Read your state first

How they connect

From the most obvious connection to the most abstract:

  • Obvious: Behavioral science + Economics. Your attention is a limited budget, and cues and defaults decide where it goes. Spend it on one small step and arrange things so that step is the easy one.
  • Hidden: Business + Holistic therapies. A short regular review and a regular rest have the same job: they catch drift early and keep the rhythm gentle.
  • Abstract: Philosophy + Behavioral science. Aristotle thought we become what we repeatedly do. Character, like a habit, is built by small acts, not by one big decision. And what is up to us is the act, not the outcome.

The polymath way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath) · Ask Professor Puddles how all thirteen connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask)

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, a goal turns into a stick: a big target, a streak you’re afraid to break, a tally of every miss. Or the plan ignores how you’re built, so every day feels like failing at someone else’s plan. Or you ask someone for support and then treat their reply as a verdict.

When it goes right, you have two plain words for what matters, one small step that fits your energy, an if-then for the evenings you don’t feel like it, and a kind look-back each month. You change the setup when something slips, and you keep your opinion of yourself out of it.

Questions people often ask

Isn’t this just self-improvement with a gentler voice?

It has a different starting point. Self-improvement often begins with what’s wrong with you. This begins with who you are (Then and Now) and asks what you’d like to lean toward. Nothing needs fixing about you. The arrangement can change.

What if I don’t know what matters to me?

That’s common, and it can change with seasons. Start with what you notice yourself wanting more of, or what you envy in a quiet way. Two plain words are enough, and you can swap them any time.

How do I keep going when motivation drops?

Plan for it. Shrink the step, use the if-then, and treat low motivation as information about the day, not about you. Often the right move is to do the two-minute version.

What if my goal involves other people?

Aim your goal at your own actions (“I will ask once, calmly”) and let the other person’s response be theirs. If it is a goal you share, the chapters after Part One are about doing it together.

What if my goal is about leaving a relationship?

That is a big decision, and it deserves care and support.

Where can I talk this through?

Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly chat host, can help you turn a vague wish into one small step.

Limits

  • This part is general education. It isn’t therapy or coaching, and it can’t promise any result.
  • If a goal ever starts to feel like a weight, shrink it or put it down. Nothing here is required.
  • Nothing you write needs to be shared. Keep your notes private if you like.
  • Research notes in this chapter describe well-known findings in plain words, and say where the evidence is limited. Notes marked “This book’s idea” are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Try this: Write two plain words for what matters to you right now. Write one small goal as something you will do, the tiniest first step, and one if-then: “If ___, then I ___.” Put a ten-minute look-back on the calendar for a month from now.

What to remember

  • Start with what matters to you.
  • Name what gets in the way.
  • Decide ahead with a simple if-then.
  • Look back kindly once a month.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.
