Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry, whether you’re on your own, at home, with friends or at work.

In this chapter

  1. How this chapter is built: three lenses
  2. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  3. Feelings start in the body
  4. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  5. More words, better tools
  6. Feelings come in layers
  7. Feelings rise and pass like waves; moods are weather
  8. Feelings spread between people
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. When feelings weren’t talked about
  11. Putting it together
  12. Worked examples
  13. Exercises
  14. Questions people often ask
  15. Limits
  16. More for your situation

At a glance

  • A feeling is a signal, not a verdict. It says “something here matters to me.” It doesn’t say what to do.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often comes before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • Feeling it isn’t doing it. You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • My weather today and the daily check-in (Part One, Now, page 48; Part Two, Chapter I, page 139) ask for one word about how you are. Naming a feeling turns its volume down a little, and a daily word catches feelings while they are still small. Big idea: read your state first.
  • Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) asks for a feeling, not a verdict. “I felt let down” is easier to hear than “you never care.” Big idea: tune how you send and receive.

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager: “Got a minute tomorrow?” Your stomach drops. By the time you get home you have snapped at the cat, skipped dinner and replayed every mistake from the last month. Nobody has said anything bad. Your body heard “trouble” before you had a single clear thought.

Part Three of this book is about how people work. Not just couples, and not just homes: you on your own, your family, your friends, the people you work with and the strangers you pass. It starts with feelings, because almost everything else runs through them. How we talk, how we judge each other, how we cope with stress and how we heal all depend on what we feel and what we do with it.

The aim is education first and self-help second. Each section explains how something works, then offers a few things to try. You can read one section and stop.

How this chapter is built: three lenses

Each idea is looked at in three ways, then brought together:

  • Psychology: what researchers have found, named honestly, with a note where the evidence is thin, mixed or debated.
  • Philosophy: what thinkers and traditions have said about the same question, in plain paraphrase. People were thinking hard about feelings long before anyone had a brain scanner.
  • Through an autistic lens: how the idea can look from an autistic point of view. This is a perspective, not a list of problems. Autistic people often notice things about feelings that everyone can learn from: the value of saying things plainly, the role of the senses, and how much a predictable day matters. Not every autistic person is the same, and nothing here is a way to diagnose anyone.

Where something is this book’s idea rather than established research, it says so.

A feeling is a signal, not a verdict

A feeling is a fast message about something that matters to you. It arrives before careful thought because, for most of human history, speed kept people alive. You didn’t have time to reason about the rustle in the grass. You had time to feel afraid and move.

Each common feeling has a rough job. Fear points at possible danger. Anger points at something in the way, or something that seems unfair. Sadness points at a loss. Disgust points at something to keep out. Guilt points at a rule you think you broke. Joy and interest point at things worth moving toward. These are rough sketches, not laws, and the same feeling can do several jobs.

A signal can be right about the theme and wrong about the details. A smoke alarm is right that there is smoke. It can’t tell burned toast from a house fire. Feelings are like that. Jealousy can be right that a friendship matters to you and wrong that your friend is leaving.

Psychology

Charles Darwin’s The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) treated emotions as useful, inherited reactions shared with other animals. Later, Nico Frijda described emotions as “action readiness”: a feeling gets the body ready to do something, such as approach, avoid, fight or freeze. Many modern “appraisal” theories, including work by Richard Lazarus and Klaus Scherer, say an emotion starts with a fast, often unconscious judgment about whether something matters to your goals.

Norbert Schwarz and Gerald Clore (1983) showed something about feelings as information. People phoned on sunny days rated their lives as more satisfying than people phoned on rainy days, unless the interviewer first mentioned the weather. Once people noticed where their mood came from, they stopped using it as information about their life. Later, much larger studies found the weather effect on life satisfaction to be very small, so treat this as an illustration of the idea rather than a strong finding. The idea itself, that we use our feelings as evidence, is widely accepted.

Researchers still disagree about exactly what an emotion is. That debate comes up again in the next section.

Philosophy

The Chinese philosopher Mencius argued that people are born with “sprouts” of goodness. His example: anyone who suddenly saw a small child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and concern, before any thought of reward or reputation. For Mencius, that feeling is a signal of what we care about, and it can be grown.

The Stoics of ancient Greece and Rome were more suspicious of strong emotions, which they saw as mistaken judgments. Yet even they described “first movements”: the involuntary jolt, the flush or the start, that happens before we agree with it. Seneca wrote that even the wisest person feels these. What matters, for the Stoics, is whether we then agree with the story the jolt tells.

In our own time, Martha Nussbaum has argued that emotions are a kind of judgment about what is important to our lives. Grief, on this view, is not a malfunction. It is how we register that someone mattered.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe feelings arriving differently: sometimes later, sometimes all at once, sometimes as body sensations before they have a name. A feeling may be strong and still hard to read. Treating a feeling as a signal to check, rather than a verdict to obey, fits this well. It invites the question “What is this about?” instead of the demand “Explain yourself.”

Autistic people are also often told their feelings are wrong for the situation: too big, too small, or about the “wrong” thing, like a change of routine or a sound. Seen as signals, those feelings make sense. Distress at a sudden change is a signal that predictability matters to that person’s nervous system. It deserves to be taken seriously, not argued away.

Thoughts you could try: “This is a signal that something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

zqaxunderstandingx1xfeelingsxxbodyqzFeelings start in the body

Very often, the body moves first: a racing heart, a hot face, a lump in the throat, a heavy chest, a churning stomach. The brain then works out what those sensations mean, using what is going on around you and what you have learned. That is why hunger can feel like irritation, a hangover can feel like dread, and a near miss in traffic can leave you snappy for an hour.

Psychology

In 1884 the psychologist and philosopher William James asked a famous question: do we run because we are afraid, or are we afraid because we run? He argued that the feeling of an emotion is, in large part, our sense of the body’s changes. Carl Lange made a similar argument around the same time. Their view was challenged by Walter Cannon and others, who pointed out that different emotions can share very similar body states.

In 1962, Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer proposed that an emotion has two parts: body arousal, plus a label we give it based on the situation. Their famous experiment has not replicated well, but the broad idea lives on. Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron’s 1974 “wobbly bridge” study suggested that people can mistake the arousal of fear for attraction. It too is debated, and is best treated as an interesting example.

Today, the study of interoception, the sense of what is happening inside your body, is a growing field. Bud Craig and others have described how signals from the heart, gut and lungs reach brain areas such as the insula. Lisa Feldman Barrett’s theory of constructed emotion goes further. It says the brain is always predicting what the body needs, and builds emotions by making sense of body sensations with concepts it has learned. Others, in the tradition of Paul Ekman, argue for a small set of more built-in basic emotions. In a well-known study, Ekman and Friesen (1971) found that people in a remote community in Papua New Guinea, who had seen little Western media, mostly matched short emotion stories to the same facial expressions that Western people chose. The debate is real and unfinished. What both sides accept is that body and feeling are tightly linked.

Philosophy

Baruch Spinoza, writing in the 1600s, refused to split mind and body into two separate things. For him, an “affect” was a change in the body’s power to act, and at the same time the idea of that change. A feeling, on this view, is the body and the mind telling the same story.

Buddhist teaching on mindfulness lists “feelings” (in Pali, vedanā) as one of four foundations to pay attention to. Here “feeling” means the basic tone of an experience, pleasant, unpleasant or neither, noticed in the body before any story is added. The practice is simply to notice that tone, moment by moment.

Through an autistic lens

Interoception varies from person to person, and many autistic people describe it as working differently for them. Some notice hunger, thirst, pain or a racing heart very strongly. Others barely notice them until they are extreme. Research on interoception in autistic people, including work by Sarah Garfinkel, Rebecca Brewer and colleagues, has produced mixed findings, and it seems to vary a lot from person to person. If the body’s signals are muted or hard to read, a feeling may seem to arrive “out of nowhere.” If they are very loud, ordinary sensations can feel overwhelming.

Sensory load matters too. A bright, noisy supermarket can fill the body with alarm that then looks like an emotion, such as irritability or panic, when it is really sensory overload. A practical lesson for everyone: before deciding what a feeling means, check the body and the surroundings. Is it loud? Bright? Am I hungry, cold, in pain, tired?

Thoughts you could try: “Where is this in my body?” “What’s around me right now: noise, light, crowds?” “When did I last eat, drink or rest?”

zqaxunderstandingx1xfeelingsxxnamingqzNaming a feeling helps you hold it

A feeling without a name can feel like weather that fills the whole sky. Putting it into words gives it edges. Once it has edges, you can look at it, tell someone about it, and decide what to do.

Psychology

Matthew Lieberman and colleagues (2007) found that when people labeled the emotion in a picture of an angry or scared face, activity in the amygdala, a brain area involved in alarm, went down compared with other tasks. They called this affect labeling. A later review by Jared Torre and Lieberman (2018) gathered evidence that naming feelings can work as a quiet form of emotion regulation, often without people realizing it is helping. In one study, led by Katharina Kircanski with Lieberman and Michelle Craske (2012), people afraid of spiders who described their fear in words while near a spider later showed less body arousal than people who had tried to talk themselves out of the fear.

James Pennebaker’s research on expressive writing, from the 1980s onward, found that writing about difficult experiences for short sessions was linked with small benefits for some people. The effects are modest and vary, and writing about very raw trauma alone isn’t right for everyone.

A note on limits: most of these studies are done in labs, with pictures and short tasks. Naming isn’t magic, and it doesn’t make a feeling vanish. It tends to make a feeling a little more manageable.

Philosophy

Spinoza made a claim that sounds very modern. He argued that a feeling which overwhelms us loses some of its grip once we form a clear and distinct idea of it. Understanding a feeling, for him, was a kind of freedom.

Many traditions use naming in practice. Some meditation teachers suggest “noting”: quietly naming what is present, such as “worry, worry” or “hearing, hearing,” then letting it go. The aim is not to argue with the feeling, but to see it clearly.

Through an autistic lens

Alexithymia means finding it hard to identify and describe your own feelings. It is not a diagnosis, and it is found in many people, autistic or not. Reviews have found it is much more common among autistic people than in the general population, though far from universal. Geoffrey Bird and Richard Cook’s “alexithymia hypothesis” (2013) suggests that some differences in recognizing emotions, which used to be blamed on autism itself, may be better explained by alexithymia.

So “just name it” isn’t always simple. But naming can take many forms. A number (“I’m at a seven”), a color, a traffic light, a body description (“my chest is tight and my hands are buzzy”), a written note, or a chart of feeling words to point at are all real names. Writing can be easier than speaking. Taking time can be easier than answering on the spot. Many autistic people find that precise, concrete descriptions work better than broad labels, and that is a strength, not a workaround.

Words you could use: “I think what I’m feeling is…” “I don’t have the word yet, but my body feels like…” “I’m at about a six out of ten.”

Professor Puddles

If the words won’t come, weather words often will. Pick “foggy” or “stormy” and start from there.

Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

More words, better tools

“Bad,” “stressed” and “fine” cover a huge range of feelings. Splitting them into finer words is like having more than one tool in the box. “Disappointed” suggests talking about hopes. “Overwhelmed” suggests taking something off the pile. “Lonely” suggests reaching out. “Ashamed” suggests self-kindness. The finer the word, the clearer the next step.

Psychology

Lisa Feldman Barrett and colleagues call this emotional granularity, or emotion differentiation. In studies where people rated their feelings several times a day, those who used finer distinctions for negative feelings tended to have more ways of coping with them. A review by Todd Kashdan, Barrett and Patrick McKnight (2015) linked low granularity with a range of difficulties, such as more binge drinking or more aggression after being hurt, in some studies. Most of this research is correlational, so it can’t prove that learning more words causes better coping. Early studies trying to teach granularity are promising but small.

Philosophy

The ancient Stoics built detailed lists of emotions. They grouped them into four families, roughly distress, fear, craving and delight, and then divided each family into many kinds, such as envy, pity, grief and worry under distress. Their aim was to understand each passion well enough to see the judgment inside it.

Aristotle took a different view of what to do with feelings, but he also valued precision. He argued that good character means feeling the right thing, toward the right person, to the right degree, at the right time. You can only aim that precisely if you can tell your feelings apart.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people have a very precise, detailed way of describing inner experience, even if standard emotion words don’t fit well. “I feel like the volume on everything has been turned up” or “I’m at forty percent battery” can be more exact than “I’m stressed.” That is granularity, just in a different vocabulary.

Shared, agreed words help everyone. A family or team can agree a small set of words or numbers and what each one means: “Amber means I can talk but I need it short.” Explicit, literal agreements like this reduce guessing, which is one of the biggest sources of misunderstanding between people who are wired differently.

Words you could use: “It’s less angry and more let down.” “I’m not sad exactly, I’m lonely.” “Can we agree what ‘I’m fine’ means between us?”

Feelings come in layers

The feeling on top isn’t always the first one that came. Anger often sits on top of hurt or fear, because anger feels stronger and less exposed. Irritation can sit on top of tiredness. Numbness can sit on top of something too big to feel all at once.

We also have feelings about our feelings. Being ashamed of crying. Scared of our own anger. Guilty for feeling relief. These second-layer feelings can hurt more than the first, and they often come from what we were taught growing up about which feelings were allowed.

Psychology

Leslie Greenberg’s emotion-focused therapy distinguishes primary emotions (the first, direct response, such as sadness at a loss) from secondary emotions (reactions to that first feeling, or covers for it, such as anger that hides hurt). In that approach, getting to the primary feeling is often what helps.

John Gottman, Lynn Katz and Carole Hooven (1996) studied what they called parents’ meta-emotion philosophy: how parents feel and think about emotions themselves. Parents who saw a child’s sadness or anger as a chance to connect and teach, rather than something to dismiss, tended to have children who later handled feelings more easily. See helping kids name big feelings (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents).

Research on thought suppression, starting with Daniel Wegner’s “white bear” studies (1987), found that trying hard not to think of something can make it come back more. Acceptance-based approaches, such as acceptance and commitment therapy, build on the idea that making room for a feeling often makes it easier to live with than fighting it.

Philosophy

A Buddhist teaching called the Second Arrow (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth) says that when we are hurt, we are struck by one arrow. Then we often shoot a second arrow at ourselves: blame, worry, “why does this always happen to me?” The first arrow may be unavoidable. The second is the one we can learn to put down.

Friedrich Nietzsche, in a very different spirit, warned that feelings we are not allowed to express don’t disappear. He described how resentment, pushed down, can turn into something bitter that shapes a whole outlook. You don’t have to share his wider philosophy to find the warning useful.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people have spent years being told that their reactions were “too much,” or adjusting their faces and voices to seem fine. This is often called masking. Over time, it can add a heavy second layer to every feeling: not just “I’m overwhelmed,” but “I’m not allowed to be overwhelmed.” Naming that second layer, and letting the first feeling be valid, can be a big relief.

Anxiety about a possible meltdown can also become its own layer, making overload more likely. Plans made on a calm day (where to go, what to say, what helps) can take some of the fear out of the second layer. That idea is useful for anyone who dreads their own big feelings.

Thoughts you could try: “What might be under this?” “I’m allowed to feel this. I don’t need a second arrow.”

Feelings rise and pass like waves; moods are weather

An emotion usually has a shape: it rises, peaks and settles. If you keep feeding it with the same thoughts, it can keep going. If you let it run its course without adding to it, it often fades sooner than you expect.

Moods are different. They are longer, lower-level states that color everything, often without a clear cause. A low mood makes neutral things look negative. A good mood makes the same things look fine. Many big decisions get made in moods, not facts.

Psychology

Philippe Verduyn and colleagues asked people how long their emotions lasted. Durations varied hugely. Sadness tended to last longest, and feelings like surprise, fear and shame were among the shortest. Emotions linked to something important, and emotions people kept thinking about (rumination), lasted longer. This supports a practical idea: going over and over something can keep a feeling going.

“Urge surfing,” from G. Alan Marlatt’s work on relapse prevention, teaches people to notice an urge rise and fall like a wave without acting on it. Mindfulness-based approaches use similar ideas. The evidence for mindfulness is real but more modest than its popularity suggests, and it doesn’t suit everyone.

Recovery groups often use the word HALT: hungry, angry, lonely, tired. It isn’t a research tool, but it names four states that make every feeling louder.

Philosophy

Impermanence (in Pali, anicca) is a core Buddhist teaching: everything that arises passes away, including every feeling. The Greek philosopher Heraclitus made a similar point with his image of a river you can’t step into twice. Marcus Aurelius, the Stoic emperor, often reminded himself in his private notebook how quickly things change and pass. None of these thinkers meant that feelings don’t matter. They meant that no feeling is the final word.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people find that feelings, especially after overload, take longer to settle, and that switching from one emotional state to another is hard, much as switching tasks can be. Recovery may need quiet, time alone, a familiar activity or a special interest, rather than more talking. Pressure to “be over it” can make it last longer.

Routines can help here. A predictable day lowers the background load, so waves are smaller and pass more easily. That is true for many people, autistic or not.

Thoughts you could try: “This is a wave. It will peak and pass.” “Is this about now, or is a mood coloring everything?” “No big decisions at the top of a wave.”

Feelings spread between people

We catch each other’s feelings: a tense voice tightens our chest, a laugh makes us smile. This is part of how people bond and stay in step. It also means stress can move through a home, a classroom or a team without anyone saying a word. Caring about someone’s feeling doesn’t mean you have to feel all of it.

Psychology

Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson described emotional contagion in the early 1990s: people tend to mimic each other’s faces, voices and postures, and that mimicry can shift their own feelings. Studies of moods spreading through social networks, such as work by Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler, are interesting but debated, because it is hard to separate catching a feeling from simply sharing the same surroundings.

Psychologists also separate empathy (feeling with someone) from compassion (caring about their suffering and wanting to help). Research by Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki suggests that compassion training may protect people from distress better than practicing empathic feeling alone. This matters for anyone who supports others, which is the subject of a later chapter.

Philosophy

David Hume compared people to strings tuned alike: when one moves, the others move with it. Adam Smith, in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), described sympathy as our ability to imagine ourselves into another person’s situation, and argued it was central to moral life. Both saw shared feeling as the glue of society, not a weakness.

Through an autistic lens

There is an old stereotype that autistic people lack empathy. Many autistic people describe the opposite: absorbing others’ feelings so strongly that it becomes overwhelming. Others say they may not read a feeling from a face or a tone, but care deeply once they know. Both are forms of caring. The double empathy problem, described by Damian Milton (2012), points out that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run in both directions. Non-autistic people often misread autistic feelings too.

A useful lesson for everyone: saying a feeling plainly (“I’m worried, not angry”) works better than hoping it is caught correctly. Contagion is fast but not precise. Words are slower and clearer.

Thoughts you could try: “Is this mine, or did I pick it up?” “I can stand beside their storm without standing in it.”

Tidbit

Good moods are catching too. Tail wags definitely are. Want a small way to share one?

Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it

Every feeling comes with an urge. Anger wants to push. Fear wants to run or check. Shame wants to hide. Sadness wants to withdraw. The feeling itself isn’t chosen. What you do with the urge is more open, especially with practice and a calm-day plan.

There are two common traps. One is pushing feelings down so hard that they leak out sideways later. The other is acting on every urge right away, which can hurt people and leave you with regrets. The path between them is: let the feeling be there, name it, and then choose the action.

Psychology

James Gross’s process model (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions) describes points where people can shape an emotion: choosing or changing the situation, shifting attention, rethinking what it means (reappraisal), or changing how they respond. Gross and Oliver John (2003) found that people who habitually used reappraisal tended to do better on well-being measures than people who habitually hid their feelings (suppression). Later work found the costs of suppression vary between cultures, so “always express” is not a universal rule.

Brad Bushman (2002) found that hitting a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered you tended to increase anger and aggression, not release it. “Venting” in that sense doesn’t seem to drain anger. Calming the body, waiting, and then talking about it tends to work better.

Philosophy

Seneca, in On Anger, argued that the best remedy for anger is delay: give the first wave time to pass before you act. Aristotle, as above, thought anger could be right, if it was felt toward the right person, for the right reason, in the right amount. Put together, they offer a balanced idea: some anger is fair, and waiting helps you find out which kind this is.

Through an autistic lens

A meltdown is not a choice or a tantrum. It is an involuntary response to overwhelm, and so is a shutdown, which can look like going quiet or “switching off.” Neither is the same as acting on an urge. They are what happens when the nervous system has had too much. What helps is less input, fewer demands and more time, not reasoning or consequences in the moment.

Many autistic people also use actions that settle the body, such as rocking, flapping, humming, pacing or holding something with a good texture. This is often called stimming. It is a healthy way of doing something with a feeling, and it deserves respect, not correction. For everyone, the lesson is that there are many safe actions between “hold it in” and “let it out on someone.”

Words you could use: “I’m feeling a lot. I’m going to take ten minutes before I reply.” “I’m not ignoring you. I’m letting this settle so I answer well.”

They never excuse harm. “I was angry” is a reason to look at your anger, not a reason someone else has to live in fear.

When feelings weren’t talked about

Many people grew up in homes where feelings were private. “Don’t make a fuss.” “Big boys don’t cry.” “We just got on with it.” This is especially common for men, for older generations, and in some families and cultures, where keeping feelings to yourself is a sign of strength, dignity or respect. If that is you, nothing in this chapter is a criticism. You learned a way of living that made sense where you were. The question is only whether it still helps you now, especially in hard times such as illness or bereavement.

Psychology

Psychologists use the word alexithymia for difficulty identifying and describing one’s own feelings. In a review of 41 samples, Levant and colleagues (2009) found that men scored slightly higher than women on average, but the difference was small: there was far more overlap than difference. Ronald Levant has argued that much of this is learned, because many boys were taught to hide vulnerable feelings like sadness and fear, and he called the pattern “normative male alexithymia.” Culture plays a part too. In a study across 23 countries, Matsumoto, Yoo and Nakagawa (2008) found that people in cultures that placed more value on social order and hierarchy tended to report holding their feelings in more. So holding back is partly a habit a whole community shares, not just a personal quirk.

Care is not only spoken. Many people show love mainly through practical help: fixing, driving, cooking, providing, turning up. That is real care, and the people around them often know it. Words can be added to it slowly. Short, plain sentences are enough, and writing can be easier than speaking. An early experiment by Pennebaker and Beall (1986), in which students wrote privately about difficult experiences, started decades of research on writing as a way to work through feelings, and many people find writing easier than talking.

Philosophy

Many traditions have valued emotional restraint. In the Confucian Analects, Confucius praises an old poem for being joyful without excess and sorrowful without harm: feeling fully, but in proportion. The Stoics, too, admired steadiness. Neither tradition asked people to feel nothing. They asked people to hold their feelings well. Aristotle, writing about friendship, said a true friend wishes good things for the other for the other’s own sake, and acts on it. On that view, much quiet, practical care is friendship at its best.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people also show care mainly by doing: solving a problem, sharing useful information, remembering exact details. Some also find feelings hard to name (see Naming a feeling). An adult who was never told they were autistic may have spent a lifetime being called “cold” when they were feeling a great deal, without the words for it. Whatever the reason, the same tools help: body words, numbers, plain short sentences, and writing instead of speaking.

Words you could use, for yourself: “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

Words you could use, for someone like this: “I know you show it by doing. I see it, and thank you.” “You don’t have to say much. I’m here.”

Putting it together

Here is the whole chapter as one short sequence. It is this book’s idea, a way of joining the research above into something easy to remember, not a tested method:

  1. Notice the body. Where is it? Hot, tight, heavy, buzzing? Check the basics: hungry, tired, in pain, overloaded?
  2. Name it, roughly. A word, a number, a color. A guess is fine.
  3. Look underneath. Is there another feeling under this one? Am I adding a second arrow?
  4. Ask what it’s pointing at. What matters to me here? Is the signal about the fire, or the toast?
  5. Choose the next action. Wait, move, ask, explain, rest or reach out. Not every feeling needs an action at all.

The three lenses agree more than they differ. Psychology says feelings are fast, bodily, partly constructed signals that become easier to handle when named. Philosophy, from Mencius and the Stoics to Spinoza and the Buddhist teachers, says feelings tell us what we value, that understanding them gives us some freedom, and that none of them is permanent. The autistic lens adds that people sense and express feelings in different ways, that the senses and predictability matter, and that being plain and explicit about feelings helps everyone.

Worked examples

On your own: the Sunday evening dread

Bettina lives alone and feels a heavy dread every Sunday evening. She used to call it “I hate my life.” Using the sequence, she notices a tight throat and restless legs; names it as “dread, about a six”; looks underneath and finds loneliness as well as worry about Monday; and sees that it points at two things: a hard week ahead, and an empty weekend behind. Her actions: lay out Monday’s first task on Sunday afternoon, and set aside time with a friend each Sunday. The dread is smaller, and it no longer says “my life.” See On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Partners: the anger that was fear

Rhodri gets angry whenever Tamsin drives fast. They argue about speed limits. One evening, calm, Rhodri says: “I think under the anger I’m scared. My cousin was in a crash.” Tamsin slows down without being asked twice. The argument was never about rules. It was about a fear that had been wearing anger’s coat.

Parent and child: naming, not fixing

Seven-year-old Kian sobs because his tower fell. His mom’s first urge is “It’s only blocks.” Instead she says, “You’re so disappointed. You worked hard on that.” He nods, cries a little longer, and rebuilds it. She didn’t fix anything. She gave the feeling a name and a place. See For parents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents#feelings).

Coworkers: contagion in a team

A small team notices that Monday meetings always feel tense. They try one change: anyone can start by giving a number from one to five for how they are, with no explanation needed. When the manager says “two today, nothing to do with any of you,” the team stops reading her apartment face as disapproval. Feelings spread less when they are named. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).

Autistic and non-autistic roommates

Riya, who is autistic, goes silent and leaves the room when the kitchen gets loud during a party. Her roommate Finn reads it as sulking and feels hurt. Later they agree a plain signal: Riya says or texts “too loud, back soon,” and Finn knows it is about noise, not him. Riya feels less pressure to hide her overload, and Finn feels less rejected. Both were reading each other carefully, just differently. See Neurodivergent relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

Friends: the second arrow

After a friend forgets her birthday, Mabel feels hurt, then ashamed of being hurt (“it’s childish to care”). The shame makes her go quiet, which the friend notices and worries about. When Mabel drops the second arrow and simply says “I was a bit hurt you forgot,” her friend apologizes and they make a plan. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).

Exercises

  1. Three body check-ins a day. At three set times, such as breakfast, lunch and dinner, ask: “What does my body feel like?” Write one line. After a week, look for patterns.
  2. One finer word. Each time you notice “bad,” “stressed” or “fine,” find one more exact word. Keep a list of the words that fit you best.
  3. Your own scale. Make a five-point scale for yourself, in words, numbers or colors, with what each point feels like in your body and what helps at that point. Share it with one person if you like.
  4. Under the top layer. Next time you feel angry or irritated, ask, “Is there hurt, fear or tiredness underneath?” Write the answer down, even if you share it with nobody.
  5. Wait before acting. Choose one urge you often act on too fast, such as a sharp text or a quick yes. For one week, wait ten minutes first and notice what changes.
  6. A family or team feeling word list. Agree three to five shared words or numbers and exactly what they mean, so nobody has to guess.

Sugarfoot

Big feelings are easier to ride when you’ve already planned what helps. Make the plan on a quiet day.

Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

Questions people often ask

Isn’t it self-indulgent to focus on feelings?

Not really. Feelings drive what people do, whether we look at them or not. Understanding them usually makes people kinder and more careful with each other, not more self-absorbed.

What if I truly can’t tell what I feel?

Start with the body and with simple scales. “Something unpleasant, about a seven, in my chest” is a good answer. Some people always find naming hard, and that is a difference to work with, not a failure.

Should I always say what I feel?

No. Naming it to yourself is almost always useful. Saying it to others depends on the person, the setting and your safety. You get to choose what to share.

Can I change what I feel?

Not directly, in the moment. You can change things around a feeling: your situation, your attention, how you read what happened, and your body’s state. Over time, those changes often change the feelings too.

My partner says my feelings are “wrong.” Are they?

A feeling can be based on a misunderstanding, and it is fair to check the facts together. But a feeling itself isn’t right or wrong. If someone regularly tells you that what you feel, see or remember isn’t real, and you start to doubt yourself, take that seriously.

Are feelings the same in every culture?

Not exactly. Some feelings seem common across many cultures, but cultures differ in which feelings they name, which ones they encourage showing, and what the body language looks like. That is another reason to ask rather than assume.

Limits

Big feelings are part of life.

This chapter is general education, not diagnosis or therapy.

What to remember

  • A feeling is a signal that something matters to you. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often arrives before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they’re flooded, and which kinds of rest actually put something back.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  9. Sleep and stress feed each other
  10. Putting it together
  11. Worked examples
  12. Exercises
  13. Questions people often ask
  14. Limits
  15. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Stress is your body getting ready for a demand. A little helps. Too much, for too long, wears you down.
  • Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty. Each one changes how you think and hear.
  • Flooded means offline. When stress is very high, listening and careful thinking get much harder. Pause, settle, then come back.
  • Rest is a skill. Different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • How much are you carrying? and the stress tank (Part Two, Chapter III, page 205) work because stress adds up from many small loads. A full tank makes small things feel big, so you check the tank before you judge the moment. Big idea: read your state first.
  • The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 48) settles the body before any words, because a flooded body can’t think or listen. Its “come back at a set time” rule stops a pause looking like walking out.
  • The setup score (Part Two, Chapter II, page 168) counts stress as well as hours, because a split that looks fair on paper can still leave one person running on empty.

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late, the kids can’t find a shoe, and your phone buzzes with a work message. Your partner says, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself snap, “I’m not your secretary!” A second later you think, “Where did that come from?” It came from a body that was already full.

Chapter 1 looked at feelings: fast signals about what matters. This chapter looks at the system that carries them, your nervous system, and what happens to it under pressure. Stress explains a lot of behavior that otherwise looks like bad character: the snap, the shutdown, the friend who cancels, the colleague who can’t take in a simple point. Understanding it makes people, including you, easier to forgive and easier to help.

As in every chapter of Part Three, each idea is looked at through three lenses: psychology (named research, with its limits), philosophy (thinkers and traditions, in plain paraphrase) and an autistic lens (a perspective, not a deficit; not every autistic person is the same, and nothing here diagnoses anyone), with an ADHD lens where it matters most. Then the chapter pulls it together, with worked examples, exercises and questions. Where something is this book’s idea, it says so.

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxreadyqzStress is your body getting ready

When something needs dealing with, the body prepares. Stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol rise. The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, blood moves to the big muscles, digestion slows and attention narrows onto the problem. In short bursts this is useful. It is why you can catch a falling child, give a speech or hit a deadline.

The same system becomes a problem when it stays switched on. A zebra that escapes a lion calms down quickly. Humans can keep the alarm running for weeks by worrying about the lion, remembering the lion, and checking their phone for messages about the lion.

Psychology

Walter Cannon described the “fight or flight” response in the early twentieth century. Hans Selye, from the 1930s, described a general pattern of response to stress, which he saw as moving from alarm, to resistance, to exhaustion if the stress went on. Later researchers added freeze to fight and flight, and Shelley Taylor and colleagues (2000) proposed “tend and befriend”: under stress, many people, perhaps especially women, also move to protect others and seek company. Robert Sapolsky’s book Why Zebras Don’t Get Ulcers made the point about humans keeping stress going with thought and memory, which is the picture used above.

Researchers generally agree that short-term stress responses are adaptive and that long-lasting, unrelieved stress is linked with poorer physical and mental health. The details, such as exactly how much and through which pathways, are still being studied.

Philosophy

The ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus is often misread as recommending luxury. In fact he aimed at ataraxia, a calm freedom from disturbance, and thought the way there was through simple pleasures, friendship and letting go of needless fears. For him, a good life wasn’t free of all effort. It was free of unnecessary alarm.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, the alarm can be set off by things others barely notice: a buzzing light, a scratchy label, an unexpected change of plan, a room full of overlapping voices. The body’s response is just as real as if the trigger were a lion. Calling it “overreacting” misses the point. The nervous system is reacting to a real load, even if that load is invisible to someone else. Taking the trigger seriously, and lowering it where you can, is often the quickest way to calm.

Thoughts you could try: “My body is getting ready. That’s its job.” “The emergency is over. I can show my body it’s over.”

Stress depends on what you have to meet it

Stress isn’t simply “a lot happening.” It grows when a demand looks bigger than what you have to meet it: time, energy, money, sleep, skills, information or help. Change either side and the stress changes. That is why support can shrink stress without changing the task, and why a small task can feel impossible on an empty day.

Psychology

Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman’s appraisal model (1984) is still one of the most influential accounts. In a first appraisal, you judge whether something matters and whether it threatens you. In a second, you judge whether you can cope. Stress comes from the balance between the two. Work psychology has a similar idea, the job demands-resources model from Arnold Bakker and Evangelia Demerouti: high demands are more manageable when resources such as control, support and feedback are high.

Researchers including Jim Blascovich and Wendy Berry Mendes distinguish a challenge state (I can meet this) from a threat state (this may be too much). Studies by Jeremy Jamieson and colleagues suggest that telling people their racing heart can help them perform may shift them toward a challenge state and, in some studies, improve performance. These effects are real but not huge, and they don’t remove real overload.

You may also have heard of the Yerkes-Dodson law, which says performance rises with arousal up to a point and then falls. The original 1908 study was on mice. The idea that “a bit of pressure helps, too much hurts” is a useful rough picture, not a precise law.

Philosophy

The Stoic teacher Epictetus taught that people are disturbed not by things themselves, but by their judgments about things. He also taught the dichotomy of control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth): some things are up to us (our judgments, our choices) and some are not (other people, the weather, the past). Peace comes from putting effort where it can make a difference.

Read fairly, this isn’t “it’s all in your head.” Epictetus had been enslaved, and knew real hardship. The point is that how we read a situation is one of the few levers we always have, alongside changing the situation where we can.

Through an autistic lens

Many demands are invisible. Processing spoken words in a noisy room, filtering out background sounds, tracking unwritten social rules and keeping up a “normal” face all take energy. For many autistic people, those background demands are high every day, so less is left for everything else.

Uncertainty is a demand too. Research has linked intolerance of uncertainty with anxiety in many people, and it seems especially important for many autistic people. A clear plan, a heads-up about changes, and knowing exactly what is expected are resources: they reduce the demand side directly. Christine Miserandino’s “spoon theory” (2003), written about living with lupus and now used widely by disabled and neurodivergent people, puts it simply: each person starts the day with a certain number of spoons, and every task costs some.

Words you could use: “It’s not the task. I don’t have much left today.” “Could you tell me the plan ahead of time? It helps me a lot.”

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxladderqzThe ladder: three everyday states

This book uses three plain words for how your body is running, on what it calls the Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks):

  • Calm and connected: breathing is easy, you can think and listen, and hard things can be heard.
  • Revved up: tense and fast. Small things feel urgent or personal. Pace speeds up and tone sharpens.
  • Running on empty: flat and slow. Words are harder to find and replies get short.

Everyone moves up and down this ladder many times a day. The ladder is this book’s idea: everyday words to help you guess your state, not a medical model or a measurement.

Psychology

The three words are loosely inspired by Stephen Porges’s polyvagal theory (1994 onward), which links calm social engagement, fight-or-flight and shutdown to different parts of the nervous system. It is popular in therapy, but many of its physiological and evolutionary claims are disputed by other researchers, including Paul Grossman. That is why this book uses the words only as everyday labels.

A related idea with fewer claims is the window of tolerance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress), a phrase from psychiatrist Dan Siegel (1999). Inside the window, you can handle feelings and think. Above it (hyperarousal) you are flooded and reactive. Below it (hypoarousal) you are numb or shut down. It is used as a map, not a lab finding.

Philosophy

A well-known Buddhist story tells of a monk named Sona, who had been a musician. He was pushing himself so hard in practice that he was ready to give up. The Buddha asked him whether a lute plays well when its strings are too tight, or too loose. Neither, said Sona: only when they are tuned just right. Practice, the Buddha said, is the same. Aristotle’s idea of virtue as a middle point between too much and too little makes a similar point. The aim isn’t zero tension. It is the right tension for the moment.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe two ends of the ladder that others may not see clearly. At the top, a meltdown: an involuntary loss of control when overwhelm is too great. At the bottom, a shutdown: going quiet, losing speech, being unable to move or respond. A shutdown can look calm from the outside. It isn’t. Treating a quiet, frozen person as “fine” can push them further down.

There is also a long-term version of running on empty. Autistic burnout, described by Dora Raymaker and colleagues (2020) from autistic adults’ own accounts, involves long-lasting exhaustion, loss of skills and lower tolerance for sensory input, often after long periods of masking and overload. It is different from work burnout, though they can overlap, and it needs real rest and fewer demands, not more effort.

Words you could use: “I’m revved up. Give me ten minutes.” “I’m running on empty. Can this wait until the morning?” “I’ve gone quiet because I’m overloaded, not because I’m angry.”

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxfloodingqzWhen you’re flooded, thinking goes offline

At high stress, the body goes into full alarm. Careful thinking, listening, holding two ideas at once and seeing the other side all get much harder. Many people call this being flooded. You may say things you don’t mean, repeat the same point, freeze, or just want to escape. It isn’t a failure of character. It is a body that needs to come down before the talk can go anywhere good.

Psychology

John Gottman’s research on couples described flooding (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships): during conflict, some partners became so physically aroused, with a fast heart rate and stress hormones, that they could no longer take in what was said. His work suggested taking a real break, often at least twenty minutes, and doing something soothing rather than rehearsing the argument. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten (2009) reviewed evidence that high stress weakens the functioning of the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain most involved in planning and flexible thinking, while strengthening more habitual responses. Popular phrases like “amygdala hijack,” from Daniel Goleman, are simpler than the science but point at the same thing.

Philosophy

Plato, in the Phaedrus, pictured the soul as a charioteer driving two horses, one calm and one wild. When the wild horse bolts, the charioteer can’t steer until it slows. Seneca’s advice for anger was simple: delay. Give the first rush time to pass before you speak or act. Both describe what flooding feels like from the inside, centuries before anyone measured a heart rate.

Through an autistic lens

For someone in a meltdown, questions, explanations, eye contact, touch and even kind words can add to the load. What usually helps is less: less talk, less light, less noise, fewer people, and more time. Afterward, many autistic people find it easier to talk about what happened in writing, or side by side rather than face to face. This is good advice for anyone who has been flooded: come back to the topic when calm, in the format that works for you.

Meltdowns are also not manipulation or a tantrum. They are not aimed at anyone. Responding with consequences or arguments in the moment tends to make things worse. Planning on a calm day, together, tends to make them less frequent.

Words you could use: “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?” “I’ll come back to this. I need it quiet for a bit.”

A pause has a time to come back. Days of silence used to punish someone are something else, and a different problem from stress.

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxloadqzStress adds up, like a tank filling

Stress from different places pours into the same tank. A bad night’s sleep, a hard meeting, a crowded train, a money worry and a sharp text all add up. By evening, a tiny thing tips it over. The last drop gets the blame, but the tank was nearly full already.

Psychology

Bruce McEwen and Eliot Stellar (1993) introduced the idea of allostatic load: the wear and tear on the body from repeated or long-lasting stress responses. In a classic study, Allen Kanner, Richard Lazarus and colleagues (1981) found that everyday hassles were related to health symptoms at least as strongly as major life events. Small things count.

Stress also spills over. Rena Repetti’s studies of air traffic controllers (1989) found that after high-workload days, they tended to be more withdrawn with their families. Niall Bolger and colleagues found stress could also cross from one partner to the other. Sleep matters too: research from Matthew Walker’s lab (2007) found that after a night without sleep, the brain’s alarm center reacted much more strongly to upsetting pictures. Part Two’s Chapter III (page 206) turns this into a simple self-check.

Philosophy

There is a well-known Zen story about a professor who visits a teacher to learn about Zen, then talks without pause about his own ideas. The teacher pours him tea and keeps pouring as the cup overflows. “Like this cup,” he says, “you are full. How can I show you anything until you empty it?” The story is about opinions, but it fits stress too: a full cup can’t take in even something good.

Seneca described a habit, borrowed from the philosopher Sextius, of reviewing each day at bedtime: what went well, what went badly, what to do differently. Done gently, an evening review is a way of emptying the cup before sleep rather than carrying it into tomorrow.

Through an autistic lens

Masking, the effort of hiding autistic traits to fit in, fills the tank fast. Laura Hull and colleagues (2017) described how autistic adults experience this “camouflaging”: many said it was exhausting and left them drained afterward. Many parents of autistic children notice that a child who seemed fine at school falls apart as soon as they get home. Some parents call this “after-school restraint collapse.” It isn’t a research term, but it describes the tank well: the child held it together all day, and home is the safe place to let it out.

The lesson for everyone: when someone falls apart over something small, ask what filled the tank, not why they’re making a fuss about the last drop.

Through an ADHD lens

Life with ADHD often adds a hidden layer to the tank: the constant effort of keeping track, the cost of lost keys and missed messages, and the low hum of worry about what you might have forgotten. So the tank can be fairly full before the day has properly started. Strong feelings can also be harder to bring back down once they rise: a review by Shaw and colleagues (2014) found this is common in ADHD at every age. Moving the remembering out of your head (a shared list, alarms with labels, one place for keys) empties part of the tank every day. Planning hard conversations for a time of day when your focus and energy are usually better helps too.

Words you could use: “My tank was full before you said a word. That wasn’t about you.” “You don’t have to explain. Want a quiet hour first?”

Professor Puddles

Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long shower of rain. I would know. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

Settle the body first

You can’t argue a body out of alarm. You can help it come down, and the thinking tends to follow. Things that often help include slow breathing with long out-breaths, moving (a walk, stairs, shaking out your arms), cold water on the face, steady pressure, a familiar sound, and leaving a loud or crowded space. Different things work for different people, and what works on one day may not on another.

Psychology

A systematic review by Andrea Zaccaro and colleagues (2018) found that slow breathing, around six breaths a minute, was linked with signs of relaxation and calmer mood, though many studies were small. A 2023 study led by Melis Yilmaz Balban found that a few minutes a day of breathing with long out-breaths improved mood a little more than mindfulness meditation over a month; it was one study, and the differences were modest. Physical activity has a large body of research behind it for mood and stress. Progressive muscle relaxation, developed by Edmund Jacobson in the early twentieth century, teaches people to tense and release muscle groups. Dialectical behavior therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan, includes quick body-based skills such as changing temperature and intense exercise for moments of very high distress.

None of these is a cure-all. Their value is practical: they give you something to do with your body when your mind is too loud to think.

Philosophy

The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught breathing as a way of coming home to the present moment: breathing in, knowing you are breathing in; breathing out, knowing you are breathing out. He meant it as a practice anyone could use, washing dishes or walking, not only on a cushion. Taoist writing, such as the Tao Te Ching, often praises softness and stillness, like water that finds its level, over force.

Through an autistic lens

Some popular calming advice doesn’t suit everyone. For some autistic people, and others who are very aware or unaware of their body’s signals, focusing on the breath can increase anxiety rather than reduce it. Alternatives that often help include deep pressure (a weighted blanket, a firm hug if wanted, lying under cushions), rhythmic movement such as rocking or swinging, stimming, chewing, humming, a special interest, or simply cutting input with headphones, sunglasses or a dim room. Research on some of these, such as weighted blankets, is still limited, but many people find them helpful, and they are safe to try.

The underlying lesson is universal: there is no single right way to settle. The right way is the one that works for your body. Find yours on a calm day.

Thoughts you could try: “Body first, words second.” “What has helped me settle before? Can I do one of those now?”

Tidbit

Tidbit’s favorite: a breathing game where the flowers open as you breathe out slowly. Body first, words second.

Tool: Cool-down corner: breathing game spreadloveandacceptance.com/night-garden

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxrestqzRest isn’t one thing

Being off work isn’t the same as recovering. Scrolling may feel like rest while keeping your brain busy. Socializing may restore one person and drain another. Real recovery comes in different kinds, and different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest.

Psychology

Sabine Sonnentag and Charlotte Fritz (2007) described four recovery experiences linked with feeling restored after work: psychological detachment (switching off from work in your head), relaxation, mastery (doing something absorbing or challenging that you enjoy, like learning a skill) and control (choosing how you spend your own time). Sleep is the foundation under all of them; a large body of research links poor sleep with worse mood and stronger stress reactions. Rachel and Stephen Kaplan’s attention restoration theory (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/calm) suggests time in nature can help tired attention recover, though effect sizes vary.

The idea that introverts are drained by socializing and extraverts energized is popular but simpler than the evidence. Studies that track people through the day, such as work by Sointu Leikas and Ville-Juhani Ilmarinen (2017), have found many people feel good during social time and more tired a few hours later. Your own experience is the best guide.

Philosophy

The Jewish philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel, in The Sabbath (1951), described the weekly day of rest as something like a sanctuary built in time rather than space: a day not for producing, but for being. The Catholic philosopher Josef Pieper argued in Leisure: The Basis of Culture (1948) that true leisure isn’t just a break to make us better workers. It is an open, receptive state that makes room for wonder. Bertrand Russell, in his essay “In Praise of Idleness” (1932), argued that a society working less would be happier and kinder. Across very different traditions, rest is treated as part of a good life, not a reward for finishing it.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe monotropism: attention that tends to go deep into a few things at a time (explained in full in Chapter 9, page 510). For many autistic people, time spent deep in a special interest is one of the most restoring kinds of rest: a state of flow, not an escape. Interrupting it can be costly, so planned transitions help.

Other common forms of autistic rest include time alone, a predictable routine, low-sensory spaces, and being with someone without having to talk (sometimes called parallel play, even for adults). None of these is antisocial. They are ways of refilling the tank, and many non-autistic people need them too.

Words you could use: “I need quiet rest tonight, not people rest. It’s not about you.” “Can we be in the same room, but not talk for a bit?”

Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared

Nervous systems affect each other. A calm voice, a steady presence or a familiar person nearby can help someone else settle. A tense, rushed person can unsettle a whole room. Saying your state out loud helps others read you right, and sharing stress well is a skill: it lets someone stand beside you without making them carry it all.

Psychology

In a well-known study, James Coan, Hillary Schaefer and Richard Davidson (2006) found that women facing the threat of a mild electric shock showed less threat-related brain activity when holding their husband’s hand, especially in happier marriages. It was a small study, but it fits a wider body of research on co-regulation: people, from infancy onward, help each other’s bodies settle. Edward Tronick’s “still face” studies (1970s onward) showed how quickly babies become distressed when a parent’s face goes blank and unresponsive, and how they recover when connection returns.

Guy Bodenmann’s research on dyadic coping found that couples who tell each other about their stress and help each other cope tend to be more satisfied. It applies well beyond couples: friends, families and teams also cope better together than alone.

Philosophy

The Southern African idea of Ubuntu is often summed up in a Nguni saying usually translated as “a person is a person through other persons.” It holds that we become ourselves through our relationships, so care is shared, not private. Epicurus, too, ranked friendship among the greatest sources of a calm and happy life.

Through an autistic lens

Co-regulation doesn’t have to mean talking, eye contact or hugs. For many autistic people, the most calming presence is a quiet one: someone nearby, doing their own thing, not asking questions. Touch can be soothing for some and overwhelming for others, so ask. Clear, explicit signals for state, such as a color, a number or a card on the fridge, can replace guessing for everyone in a home or team.

Going off alone to settle is also a form of regulation, not rejection. Agreeing on this ahead of time (“If I go to my room, I’m resetting, not upset with you”) can save a lot of hurt on both sides. It is the double empathy idea again: both people are reading carefully, in different ways, and plain words close the gap.

Words you could use: “I’m stressed, and it’s not about you.” “Do you want help, company or space?” “If I go quiet tonight, I’m resetting, not upset.”

zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxsleepqzSleep and stress feed each other

Stress and sleep run in a loop. A worried mind and a revved-up body make it harder to fall asleep and stay asleep. A short or broken night then lowers the threshold for stress the next day: small things feel bigger, and patience runs out sooner. Seeing the loop is the first step to loosening it.

Psychology

In a brain-imaging study, Yoo and colleagues (2007) found that after a night without sleep, the amygdala (part of the brain’s alarm system) reacted more strongly to negative pictures and was less connected to the front of the brain, which helps keep reactions in proportion. Sleep also shapes how people get along. In a daily study, Gordon and Chen (2014) found that people reported more conflict with their partner after nights of poor sleep, and that conflicts were resolved best when both partners had slept well. In experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept an approaching person at a greater distance and felt lonelier; the researchers also reported that rested people who briefly watched them felt lonelier themselves. These are mostly studies of one bad night or short periods; long-term sleep problems are more complicated, and effective help exists.

Practical points follow from this. Avoid hard conversations when either person is exhausted (“Can we talk after we’ve slept?”). Notice when a bad mood might be a bad night. And treat a wind-down routine (the same few calm steps before bed, in the same order) as part of stress care, not a luxury. See sleep and mood (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#sleep-and-mood) in the library.

Philosophy

In Shakespeare’s Macbeth, sleep is the thing “that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care”: the mender of a mind worn ragged by worry. Many traditions treat rest at night as part of a good life, not a reward for finishing everything. The Stoic habit of reviewing the day each evening, then setting it down, was partly a way of not carrying the day into the night.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic and ADHD people describe long-standing sleep difficulties: a mind that won’t switch off, a body clock that runs later than other people’s, or a bedroom that is too bright, noisy or scratchy to settle in. Sensory changes (blackout blinds, earplugs, the right bedding, a weighted blanket for those who like pressure) can matter as much as any routine. A predictable wind-down can help too.

Words you could use: “I slept badly. If I’m short today, that’s why, and it’s not about you.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

Sugarfoot

Rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of soft music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it close.

Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

Putting it together

Here is the chapter as a short sequence. It is this book’s idea, a way of joining the ideas above, not a tested method:

  1. Check the called. Calm, revved up or running on empty? Flooded?
  2. Check the tank. How full was I before this? What filled it?
  3. Settle the body first. Use something you know works for you.
  4. Look at both sides of the balance. What is being asked of me, and what could add to what I have: time, help, information, rest?
  5. Say your state. One sentence, so the people around you don’t have to guess.
  6. Plan real recovery. Match the rest to the kind of tired.

The three lenses agree on the big picture. Psychology shows that stress is a body-and-mind response shaped by how we read demands and resources, that it adds up, and that it narrows thinking at the top of the curve. Philosophy, from Epictetus and the Buddha to Heschel and Ubuntu, says the aim isn’t to remove all tension, but to tune it, to put effort where it counts, to rest as part of a good life, and to carry hard things together. The autistic lens adds that many demands are invisible, that predictability and sensory comfort are real resources, that shutdown is not calm, and that there are many valid ways to settle and rest.

Worked examples

On your own: the Sunday scroll

Liam spends every Sunday on the couch scrolling and still feels exhausted on Monday. Using the recovery types, he sees he gets almost no detachment (work emails on his phone), no mastery and no real relaxation. He moves work email off his phone for weekends and starts an hour of guitar on Sunday afternoons. Mondays feel lighter. Nothing about his job changed. His recovery did.

Partners: the snap at the door

Paula comes home from long shifts and snaps at Jonty’s first question. They agree a twenty-minute landing time: no questions, no news, just a drink and a shower. Then they check in. Jonty stops taking the snap personally, and Paula stops snapping. See Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

Parent and autistic child: after school

Every day, ten-year-old Benji melts down within half an hour of getting home. His dad used to ask about his day right away. Now there is a quiet snack, headphones and Lego for forty minutes, with no questions. The meltdowns become rarer. Benji talks about his day later, when he is ready, often at bedtime. See Neurodivergent families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

Coworkers: the flooded meeting

In a project review, Naomi’s voice speeds up and she starts repeating herself. Her colleague notices and says, “Let’s take ten and come back in half an hour.” After a coffee and a walk, Naomi hears the feedback and agrees with most of it. Pushing on would have cost them both an afternoon. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).

Friends: the canceled plan

Tash has canceled on Megan three times. Megan is hurt and nearly gives up. Then she sends: “No pressure at all. Would a short walk be easier than dinner?” Tash replies that she has been running on empty for weeks caring for her mom, and a walk sounds perfect. Lowering the demand kept the friendship. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) and Caregivers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

Roommates: the tank and the dishes

Gabe and Cal used to argue about dishes every Thursday. They realize Thursday is the day both have the longest work hours. They move the dishes job to Saturday morning. The dishes didn’t change. The tank did. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

Exercises

  1. Find your flood signs. Think back to the last time you said something you regretted. What did your body feel like just before? Write down two or three signs to watch for.
  2. Map a day’s tank. At bedtime, list what filled your tank today, including small things like noise, waiting or hunger, and what emptied it.
  3. Build a settle list. On a calm day, list three things that help your body come down, and three that make it worse. Keep it somewhere easy to find, or build it into the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11).
  4. Match your rest. For one week, before resting, ask: body-tired, brain-tired, people-tired or feelings-tired? Choose a rest that matches, and notice the difference.
  5. Agree a pause. With someone you live or work with, agree a pause word and that the person who pauses names a time to come back.
  6. Say your state. For three days, tell one person your state each evening in one sentence, and ask theirs.

Questions people often ask

Is some stress good for you?

Short, manageable stress that you recover from can help you rise to a challenge and grow. The problem is stress that is too big, too constant, or with no recovery.

How do I know if I’m burned out or just tired?

Ordinary tiredness lifts after good rest. Burnout tends to last, even after a vacation, and often comes with feeling detached, cynical or ineffective.

My partner always needs to “take space.” Is that avoiding me?

Not necessarily. Many people genuinely need time to come down before they can talk well. The fair version is: take the space, and say when you’ll come back. If space is used to punish, or a promised return never comes, talk about that pattern. One wants to talk now, one needs space (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) has more.

Breathing exercises make me more anxious. Is something wrong with me?

No. That is a common experience. Try movement, pressure, cold water, music or reducing input instead. There is no single right way to settle.

Can I help someone who is in a meltdown or shutdown?

Usually by doing less: lower the noise and light, stop asking questions, keep others away, stay nearby if they want that, and wait. Talk about it later, if they want to, in a way that suits them.

Isn’t this just making excuses for bad behavior?

Understanding why someone snapped isn’t the same as saying it was fine. Stress explains behavior; it doesn’t excuse harm. The point is to reduce the conditions that make harm more likely, and to repair when it happens.

Limits

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis.

How we see each other: perception, bias, and the stories we tell

Why two people can watch the same moment and come away with two different stories, and how to see others, and yourself, a little more fairly.
