Part Three · Chapter 5

Attachment, trust and belonging

Why we need each other, how the bonds we had early on shape what we expect today, and how trust and belonging are built and lost and built again, one small moment at a time.

In this chapter

  1. Belonging is a basic need
  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect
  3. Patterns, not boxes
  4. Trust is built in small moments
  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body
  6. Fitting in isn’t belonging
  7. Rebuilding broken trust
  8. Building connection from where you are
  9. Putting it together
  10. Worked examples
  11. Exercises
  12. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  13. Helping someone else with belonging
  14. Questions people often ask
  15. Limits

At a glance

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger, not a flaw.
  • Early bonds set expectations, not a sentence. What we learned about being cared for can soften and change.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small. One friendly exchange, one kept promise, one kind word to yourself.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) works because trust is built from small promises kept. A named owner turns a vague hope (“someone will do it”) into a promise others can rely on. Big idea: fix the setup, not the person.
  • The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, page 271) is “not a review of either person.” Feeling safe with someone is what lets people say what went wrong without bracing for blame.

Sunday, 9:30pm

Kai sent a long message to a friend at lunchtime. It’s been read, but there’s no reply. By evening, Kai has gone from “she’s busy” to “she’s annoyed with me” to “nobody really likes me.” The friend, meanwhile, is at her nephew’s birthday, phone in a coat pocket. One silence, two very different nights.

Why can one unanswered message ruin an evening? Why do some people reach for closeness when they’re scared, while others pull away? Why does trust take years to build and moments to break? This chapter is about the deep human need to belong: where it comes from, how it shapes the way we love and work and live together, and what helps when it hurts.

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses. Psychology tells us what researchers have found, and where the evidence is limited. Philosophy shows how thinkers from many traditions have understood the same questions. Through an autistic lens looks at each idea from the point of view of autistic people. It is a perspective, not a diagnosis, and it often shows that “normal” ways of belonging are only one way among several.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxbelongingqzBelonging is a basic need

We are not built to be alone. For most of human history, being cut off from the group was dangerous. It makes sense, then, that being left out still feels alarming, and that connection feels like relief. Loneliness is not a character flaw. It is a signal, like hunger or thirst, pointing at a need.

Psychology

Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary (1995) reviewed a large body of research and argued that the “need to belong” is a fundamental human motivation: people need frequent, pleasant contact with a few others, inside relationships that feel stable and caring. John Cacioppo, who studied loneliness for decades, described it as a biological alarm, like hunger, that tells us our social connections are running low.

Connection also matters for health. A large review by Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy Smith and Bradley Layton (2010) found that people with stronger social relationships were more likely to survive over the years the studies followed them. Studies like these show links, not proof that one causes the other, but the pattern is strong and has been found many times. Research on exclusion by Kipling Williams and colleagues (2000) found that even being left out of a simple online ball-tossing game by strangers lowered people’s mood and sense of belonging. We are sensitive to exclusion, even when it shouldn’t matter.

Philosophy

Aristotle described human beings as naturally social and political animals. In the Politics, he suggested that someone who truly needs no community would have to be either a beast or a god. Many African philosophies express a related idea through ubuntu, often summed up in a Nguni saying usually translated as “a person is a person through other persons.” On this view, we don’t first become ourselves and then join others. We become ourselves through others.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people need belonging too, though it may look different. Some prefer a few deep friendships to a wide circle. Some connect best through shared interests, or by being in the same room doing different things (“parallel company”). Social time can use a lot of energy, so needing to recharge alone is not the same as not wanting people. A common myth says autistic people don’t want connection. Many autistic adults describe the opposite: wanting it very much, and being hurt by repeated exclusion. Loneliness, here, is often about a lack of acceptance, not a lack of desire.

Thoughts you could try: “My loneliness is a signal, not a verdict.” “I can want people and also need time alone.”

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxattachmentqzEarly bonds teach us what to expect

From our earliest days, we learn from the people who care for us. Do they come when I cry? Can I explore and come back? Is it safe to need someone? The answers become quiet expectations we carry into later relationships: a kind of map of how people tend to respond.

Psychology

The psychiatrist John Bowlby developed attachment theory from the 1950s onward. He argued that babies are born with a drive to stay close to a caregiver, who serves as a safe haven when they’re frightened and a secure base from which to explore. Mary Ainsworth studied this in her “Strange Situation” research, watching how toddlers reacted when a parent left a room and came back. She described secure patterns, where children were upset but easily comforted, and insecure ones, where children clung anxiously or seemed not to seek comfort. Later, Mary Main and Judith Solomon (1990) added a “disorganized” pattern seen when children seemed frightened or confused about the caregiver.

Attachment theory is one of the best-studied ideas in psychology, but it has limits. Much of the early research came from Western, middle-class families. Researchers such as Heidi Keller have pointed out that in many cultures children are raised by several caregivers, and “good” care looks different. Early patterns also predict later relationships only moderately. They are an influence, not a destiny.

Philosophy

Philosophers in the tradition known as the ethics of care, such as Nel Noddings, Virginia Held and Eva Feder Kittay, start from a fact many older theories ignored: every human being begins life completely dependent on others, and most of us will be dependent again, through illness or old age. Kittay reminds us that everyone is “some mother’s child,” cared for by someone. On this view, dependence isn’t a weakness to grow out of. It’s the ground of human life, and caring well for each other is one of the most important things we do.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic children form deep attachments to their caregivers. A review by Anna Rutgers and colleagues (2004) found that in the studies using the Strange Situation, about half of the autistic children were securely attached to their parents. On average they were secure less often than other children, but that difference disappeared among children without an additional intellectual disability. Attachment may simply be shown differently: a child may seek comfort through a favorite object, a routine or a parent’s familiar presence, rather than through hugs or eye contact. Tests built around typical behaviors can miss this. For autistic adults looking back, it can help to know that feeling “different” as a child, or misunderstood, can shape expectations as much as how loving a family was. Both can be true at once.

Words you could use: (to a child) “Whenever you need me, I’ll come.” (to yourself) “I learned to expect this as a child. I can learn something new now.”

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxpatternsqzPatterns, not boxes

As adults, we bring our maps into friendships, partnerships and even work. Under stress, some of us reach harder for closeness and reassurance. Some of us pull back and handle things alone. Most of us do a mix, depending on the person and the day.

Psychology

Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) suggested that adult romantic relationships draw on the same attachment system as childhood bonds. Later research, such as work by Kelly Brennan, Catherine Clark and Shaver (1998), found that adult attachment is best described along two dimensions: anxiety (worry about being rejected or left) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness and depending on others). Studies by R. Chris Fraley and colleagues suggest these are scales, not separate types: people sit somewhere along each one, rather than fitting neatly into “anxious,” “avoidant” or “secure.”

These patterns can change. Researchers talk about “earned security”: adults who had difficult early relationships but became more secure through supportive relationships, therapy or reflection. When an anxious and an avoidant pattern meet, a common cycle forms: one pursues, the other withdraws, and each move makes the other’s stronger. See When one talks and one goes quiet (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw).

Philosophy

Arthur Schopenhauer told a parable about porcupines on a cold day. They huddle together for warmth, but their quills prick each other, so they move apart, get cold, and come together again, until they find a distance where they are warm enough and hurt little. Every relationship is a search for that distance, and two people’s comfortable distances may differ. See The porcupines (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth) in the site’s stories from philosophy.

It is worth noting that Buddhist teaching about “attachment” means something different from attachment theory. In Buddhism, the problem is clinging: grasping at things to stay the same when everything changes. That is not the same as loving someone or depending on them. You can love deeply while holding the relationship with open hands.

Through an autistic lens

It is easy to misread autistic behavior as attachment insecurity. Repeated checking (“Are we still meeting at six?”) may come from a need for certainty and clear plans, not fear of being left. Going quiet after a busy day may be recovering from sensory or social overload, not avoiding closeness. Before applying a label, it helps to ask what the behavior is for. A partner who says “I need certainty about plans” or “I need a quiet hour to recharge” is giving useful information, not showing an insecure style. See Intolerance of uncertainty (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring) in the library.

Words you could use: “When I go quiet, I’m recharging, not leaving. I’ll come back by eight.” “When I check plans, I’m not doubting you. Certainty just helps me relax.”

Trust is built in small moments

Trust is the belief that someone will act with care toward you, especially when you’re vulnerable. It isn’t usually built by grand gestures, but by small, ordinary moments that add up: a promise kept, a message answered, a secret held.

Psychology

John Rempel, John Holmes and Mark Zanna (1985) described trust in close relationships as growing in stages: first predictability (I can tell what you’ll do), then dependability (I can rely on you), and finally faith (I feel secure in your care, even when I can’t be sure). John Gottman’s research describes “bids for connection”: small reaches like a comment, a question or a touch. Partners who more often “turned toward” these bids, rather than away from them, tended to stay together and feel happier. Gottman calls the small choices “sliding door moments”: each one is tiny, but together they build trust or wear it down. See Bids for connection (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships) and Turning toward (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward).

At work, Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety (1999) found that teams learned and improved more when people felt safe to admit mistakes and speak up. That kind of trust is built the same way: by how leaders and teammates respond, again and again, to small risks.

Philosophy

The philosopher Annette Baier (1986) described trust as accepting that we are vulnerable to someone else’s goodwill. When we trust, we let someone hold something we care about, and we rely on them not to harm it. That’s why betrayal hurts so much: it isn’t just a broken plan, it’s a misused vulnerability. Onora O’Neill, in her 2002 Reith Lectures, argued that the goal shouldn’t be simply “more trust.” It should be trust placed wisely, in people and institutions that show themselves to be trustworthy. The question isn’t “Do I trust?” but “Is this person showing they can be trusted?”

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, trust is closely tied to honesty and predictability. Saying what you mean and doing what you said can matter more than warmth of manner. Vague promises (“We’ll see,” “Maybe later”) can feel unsettling, while clear ones (“I’ll call on Thursday at seven”) build security. Many autistic people are also very honest, sometimes to their own cost, and can find it hard to understand white lies or hidden agendas. Being trustworthy to an autistic friend, partner or colleague often simply means being clear, being consistent, and telling the truth kindly.

This book’s idea: “Say it, do it, show it”: say what you’ll do, do it, and if you can’t, show where it’s at before the deadline. That last step, flagging early, builds as much trust as doing the thing.

Words you could use: “I’m going to be late with this. Here’s where it’s at, and here’s when you’ll have it.” “I’ll call you on Thursday at seven.”

Professor Puddles

Trust grows in small moments that repeat. This workpaper helps you notice the little rituals you already have, and keep them going.

Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxsafexhavenqzFeeling safe with someone calms the body

When we’re stressed, the presence of someone we trust can calm our body as well as our mind. This is one of the deepest gifts of close relationships, and it’s something we can offer others too.

Psychology

In a well-known study, James Coan, Hillary Schaefer and Richard Davidson (2006) asked married women to lie in a brain scanner while facing the threat of a mild electric shock. When they held their husband’s hand, brain areas linked to threat responded less than when they held a stranger’s hand or no hand, and the effect was stronger for women in happier marriages. It was a small study, but it fits a wider idea Coan calls social baseline theory: our brains expect to have trusted others nearby, and they work harder when we’re alone.

Researchers also describe co-regulation: people settling each other’s stress through voice, presence and touch. It starts between parents and babies and continues all through life. One calm person can help a whole room calm down. See Co-regulation (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) in the library.

Philosophy

The ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus thought friendship was one of the greatest goods of a happy life. He made a striking point: we don’t so much need our friends’ help as the confidence that their help is there if we need it. That’s the secure base in a single thought. Knowing someone will come is often enough to let us face hard things alone.

Through an autistic lens

Co-regulation looks different for different people. For some autistic people, a hug when they’re overwhelmed is the last thing that helps; touch, eye contact or talking can add to an overload. A quiet, calm person nearby, dimmer lights, fewer words, or simply sending a message (“I’m here when you’re ready”) can be the safe haven instead. “Body doubling,” doing tasks alongside someone, is another form of company many autistic and ADHD people find steadying. The question is never “What would help me?” but “What helps you?”

Words you could use: “Do you want company, quiet, or both?” “Would a hug help, or would you rather I just sat here?”

Sugarfoot

Everyone feels cared for in their own way. A “What feels like care” card lets you say, in a few lines, what feels like care to you.

Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxgroupsqzFitting in isn’t belonging

We belong to more than one person. We belong to families, friendship groups, teams, faiths, neighborhoods, online communities. Groups can give us identity, support and purpose. They can also pressure us to hide who we are.

Psychology

Henri Tajfel and John Turner’s social identity theory (1979) describes how part of our sense of self comes from the groups we belong to, and how easily we favor “us” over “them,” even when groups are formed on trivial grounds. That can bring warmth and loyalty, and also exclusion. The researcher Brené Brown, drawing on her interview studies, made a distinction many people find useful: fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted, while belonging means being accepted as you are. Her research is qualitative rather than experimental, but the distinction rings true for many.

Edmondson’s psychological safety research shows that groups where people can speak up, ask questions and admit mistakes tend to work better and learn more. Belonging, in this sense, isn’t only a nice feeling. It helps groups think.

Philosophy

The ubuntu tradition sees community as the setting in which people become fully human, but it also asks a lot of communities: to include, to share, and to repair harm rather than cast people out. Many religious and philosophical traditions hold a similar tension between belonging to a group and staying true to yourself. Simone Weil, in The Need for Roots (1949), argued that having roots in a community is one of the most important and least recognized needs of the human soul.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe masking or camouflaging: hiding autistic traits to fit in, such as forcing eye contact, rehearsing small talk or suppressing stimming. Research by Laura Hull and colleagues (2017) and others has found that long-term masking is often exhausting and linked with poorer well-being. In other words, fitting in can come at a real cost. By contrast, studies of autistic people spending time with other autistic people, such as interviews by Catherine Crompton and colleagues (2020), describe a sense of ease, of not having to translate. Belonging, for anyone, grows where it’s safe to stop pretending. Groups can help by making differences normal: offering quiet spaces, written agendas and several ways to take part. See Masking (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring#masking) and neurodiversity at work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).

Words you could use: “Is there a way to join in that suits you better?” “You don’t have to do small talk with me.”

Rebuilding broken trust

Trust can break in big ways (an affair, a betrayed secret, a lie about money) or through a slow pile-up of small let-downs. Either way, it rarely comes back with one conversation. It returns, if it returns, through words that are matched by actions over time.

Psychology

Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount (2016) studied which parts of an apology people found most effective. Acknowledging responsibility came first, followed by an offer to repair the harm. Explaining, expressing regret and promising to change helped less on their own. Research on forgiveness, by Everett Worthington and others, distinguishes forgiveness (letting go of resentment, which can happen inside one person) from reconciliation (rebuilding the relationship, which needs both people and safety). You can forgive without trusting again.

Couple therapists, including the Gottmans, describe rebuilding trust after a serious betrayal in stages: taking full responsibility, rebuilding understanding, and then slowly restoring closeness. Evidence for specific programs is still limited, but most approaches agree on one thing: the person who broke trust carries the work of being consistent, and the person who was hurt sets the pace.

Philosophy

The Jewish tradition of teshuvah, often translated as “return” or “repentance,” describes a path of recognizing the harm, feeling real regret, putting things right with the person hurt, and changing. The medieval philosopher Maimonides wrote that complete teshuvah is shown when a person faces the same situation again and chooses differently. That is a useful test for any apology: not how sorry it sounds, but what happens next time.

Through an autistic lens

Explicit, specific repair often works best: “Here’s exactly what I did. Here’s exactly what I’ll do differently. Here’s how you’ll know.” Vague apologies (“Sorry if you were upset”) can feel especially hollow to someone who values honesty. Some autistic people find it easier to apologize, or to receive an apology, in writing, with time to process. On the other side, an autistic person who has been hurt may need to know precisely what will change before they can trust again. That isn’t unforgiving. It’s needing the information that makes trust possible.

Words you could use: “I did this. It hurt you. Here’s what I’ll do from now on. Take all the time you need.” See How to apologize so it counts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages).

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxbuildingqzBuilding connection from where you are

If you feel alone, advice like “put yourself out there” can feel impossible. But connection isn’t one big leap. It grows from small, repeated contact, and some of the smallest forms of contact matter more than we think.

Psychology

Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder (2014) asked commuters to talk to a stranger on their train or to sit in silence. People expected talking to be unpleasant, but those who talked reported a more positive journey. Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn (2014) found that people who had a brief friendly exchange with a barista felt more connected and in a better mood than those who kept it purely efficient. These “weak ties” (acquaintances, neighbors, regulars) add up to a real sense of belonging. See Weak ties (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection).

Friendships take time. Jeffrey Hall (2019) found that moving from acquaintance to friend, and from friend to close friend, takes many hours spent together. That’s encouraging in a way: if you don’t have close friends yet, it may simply be that you haven’t yet had the hours, not that something is wrong with you.

Philosophy

Aristotle described three kinds of friendship: those based on usefulness, those based on pleasure, and those based on caring about each other’s good character. He thought the third kind was rarest and best, and that it takes time; people must, as he put it, eat salt together. But he didn’t dismiss the other two. Friendly colleagues and fun acquaintances are real goods too. See Aristotle on friendship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth#friendship).

Through an autistic lens

Connection doesn’t have to come from parties or small talk. Many autistic people find their people through shared interests: a hobby group, a game, an online forum, a volunteer role. Sharing a deep interest (“info-dumping”) is, for many autistic people, a way of offering friendship. Online friendships are real friendships. Autistic-led communities, which have grown since the early 1990s, have given many people their first experience of being understood without translating. If mainstream social life has felt hard, it may be that you haven’t yet found the right setting, not that you can’t connect.

This book’s idea: The “three circles” check: once a week, notice one contact in each circle: someone close, someone friendly, and someone you barely know. If one circle is empty, make it your small step for next week.

Words you could use: “I’d love to hear more about that.” “Would you like to come along next week?” “I’m better at messaging than calling. Can we keep in touch that way?”

Tidbit

One small hello is a great start. Want an idea? There’s a tool that picks one for you.

Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Putting it together

Belonging is a need, not a luxury. We learn our first lessons about it from the people who cared for us, and those lessons become maps we carry into later life. Under stress, our maps may tell us to reach harder or to pull away. Trust grows from small moments, kept promises and turning toward each other. Feeling safe with someone calms the body. Groups can offer belonging, or only ask us to fit in. And when trust breaks, it can sometimes be rebuilt, slowly, with actions that match words.

A few threads run through all of it:

  • Your patterns made sense once. Reaching harder, or pulling away, were ways of coping. You can keep what helps and update what doesn’t.
  • Small and steady beats big and rare. Trust and belonging are built from ordinary moments.
  • Ask what it’s for. Before labeling someone’s behavior, ask what it does for them: reassurance, rest, certainty, safety.
  • Belonging, not fitting in. Look for places where you, and others, can stop pretending.
  • Trust should go to people who show themselves trustworthy.

Worked examples

On your own: the unanswered message

Back to Kai. Kai notices the spiral: “busy” to “annoyed” to “nobody likes me.” Kai recognizes the old map (“people leave if I’m too much”) and tries a different reading: “She’s probably busy. I can check tomorrow.” Kai texts a different friend about a movie and goes to bed. The next morning, the first friend replies: “Sorry! Nephew’s party. Loved your message.”

Partners: the pursue-withdraw dance

When Sara is worried, she wants to talk. When Ade is worried, he goes quiet. Each reaction makes the other stronger. They learn to name it: “I’m pursuing.” “I’m withdrawing.” Ade agrees to say when he’ll come back. Sara agrees to wait. Over months, the dance gets shorter. See When one talks and one goes quiet.

Parent and child: the new school

Seven-year-old Noor is clingy at school pickup after a move. Her dad resists the urge to say “Don’t be silly.” He says, “New places feel scary. I’ll be right here at three.” He’s there at three every day. By week three, she runs in. A secure base makes exploring possible.

Coworkers: the new manager

A new manager wants to build trust fast. Instead of a big speech, she does three small things: she answers every message within a day, she says “I don’t know, let me find out” when she doesn’t know, and she thanks people for raising problems. Six months later, her team brings her issues early. See At work.

Friends: the friend who always cancels

Elliot feels hurt when his friend cancels a third time. Instead of drifting, he asks: “Is something making it hard to meet? I miss you.” His friend admits she’s exhausted from caring for her mom. They switch to short walks near her home. The friendship survives. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).

Teenagers: left out of the group chat

Ezra is 16. On Saturday he sees a photo: his three closest friends at the movies. Then he realizes there is a group chat he isn’t in. His stomach drops, and for the rest of the day he feels sick and stupid. That reaction isn’t an overreaction. In a brain-scan study by Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams (2003), being left out of a simple online ball game raised activity in a brain area also involved in the distress of physical pain. And in online studies by Williams and colleagues (2000), being ignored even by strangers on a screen lowered people’s sense of belonging.

His first urge is to post something sharp under the photo. He doesn’t. He waits until Monday and messages the one friend he is closest to: “Saw the movie theater pic. Kind of bummed not to be asked. Did I do something?” The answer surprises him: “No! You’ve been at football every weekend, we thought you’d say no.” That part was a misunderstanding, and it gets fixed. Another part isn’t. One of the three has been drifting for months, and that friendship is quietly ending. That is a real loss too, and it’s allowed to hurt.

Words you could use, as a teenager: “Kind of bummed not to be asked. Did something happen?” “I’d like to come next time, even if I can’t always make it.” “I miss how we used to be. Are we okay?”

Not every friendship lasts, and many change most between 13 and 18. If being left out is happening on purpose, again and again, or comes with put-downs, that is being picked on, not drifting apart. Chapter 17 (page 714) has more on group chats and being picked on.

Roommates and community: the newcomer

A student from overseas, Lin, feels invisible in her shared house. A roommate starts a Sunday “everyone brings one thing” dinner. Lin brings dumplings and teaches two roommates to fold them. Belonging grew from one shared, repeated ritual.

An autistic adult finding their people

For years, Lowri masked at work and felt lonely at parties. She joins an online group about trains, her lifelong interest, then a local meetup. “It’s the first time I haven’t had to translate myself,” she says. She still finds parties hard. She no longer thinks the problem is her.

Exercises

  1. Your safe base. Write about one person who was a safe base for you at any age. What did they do? Is there anyone you could be that person for?
  2. Your pattern under stress. Think of the last time you felt unsure of someone. Did you reach out, pull back, or both? What were you hoping would happen?
  3. Turn toward three bids. For a week, notice small reaches from others (a comment, a look, a message) and turn toward three of them each day.
  4. Keep three small promises. Make three small, specific promises this week, and keep them. Notice how it feels.
  5. The three circles. Each week, have one contact with someone close, someone friendly and someone you barely know. (This book’s idea)
  6. Where can you be yourself? List the places and people where you can stop pretending. How could you spend more time there?
  7. Ask what helps. Ask one person you care about: “When you’re stressed, what helps most: company, quiet, words, or something else?”

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, an old map takes over. One person reaches harder for reassurance; the other feels crowded and pulls further away. Small let-downs are never named, so trust wears thin without anyone noticing. In groups, people mask and hide mistakes. Loneliness grows quietly, and each person decides the problem is them.

When it goes right, people notice their patterns and say them out loud. Promises are small and kept. When trust slips, it’s repaired early and specifically. Groups make room for different ways of joining in. Someone who feels lonely takes one small step, and someone else notices and opens the door a little wider.

Helping someone else with belonging

If someone you care about feels lonely, left out or unable to trust, the most useful things are often the quietest. Be reliable: turn up when you said, reply when you can, and say when you can’t. Keep inviting without pressure, because people who feel on the edge may need several invitations before they can say yes. Listen to their experience of loneliness before offering solutions, and resist the urge to label them (“you’re so avoidant”). In groups, notice who is on the edge and make one small opening for them: ask their view, sit next to them, explain the in-jokes.

Words you could use: “I’m glad you told me.” “No pressure at all, but there’s a seat for you on Friday.”

Questions people often ask

Can my attachment style really change?

Yes. Research on “earned security” shows that people who started with insecure patterns can become more secure, especially through steady relationships, reflection and sometimes therapy. Change is usually gradual.

Should I take an attachment style quiz?

Quizzes can be a starting point for reflection, but they’re snapshots, and many online ones aren’t based on research. Use them for curiosity, not as a label. Remember that patterns vary between relationships.

My partner is very jealous. Is that just anxious attachment?

Feeling insecure is human, and so is asking for reassurance, or for something out of care for the relationship. That is not control. But checking your phone without agreement, controlling who you see or punishing you for time apart isn’t explained away by attachment. Those take away your freedom, and that is control.

I’m autistic and I don’t want lots of friends. Is something wrong?

No. Many people, autistic or not, are content with a few close connections. What matters is whether your need for connection is met in a way that suits you, not how many people you know.

How long does it take to rebuild trust?

There’s no set time. It depends on how deep the hurt was, how consistent the other person is, and your own pace. If you feel pressured to “be over it,” that pressure is itself worth talking about.

Can you feel lonely even with people around you?

Yes, and it’s very common. Loneliness is about the gap between the connection you have and the connection you need, not the number of people nearby. You can feel lonely in a busy office, a full family home or a long relationship, often because you don’t feel truly seen. Naming that gently to one person (“I’ve been feeling a bit far from you lately”) is often the first step back.

What if I’ve never felt like I belong anywhere?

That is painful, and more common than people say. It may help to look for smaller, interest-based groups. And it’s worth remembering: not having found your place yet is not proof that there isn’t one.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education. It isn’t therapy, and attachment ideas shouldn’t be used to diagnose yourself or anyone else.
  • Much attachment research comes from particular cultures and family types. Caring well looks different around the world.

The library’s relationships and connection pages have more on each idea.

What to remember

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger.
  • Early bonds set expectations that can change. What we learned about being cared for can soften over time.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small, with one friendly exchange or one kept promise.

Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change that fits who you want to be
  8. Supporting change in others
  9. Putting it together
  10. Worked examples
  11. Exercises
  12. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  13. Helping someone else change
  14. Questions people often ask
  15. Limits

At a glance

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • Small and set up beats big and willpower. Make the first step tiny and change the setup around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day is information about the plan, not proof about you.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it. You can’t force it.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • One small step a week (the six-week program; Part One, Next, page 81) works because change that lasts starts smaller than feels useful, and an if-then plan does the deciding ahead of time.
  • The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 168; Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) change the setup instead of asking for more willpower. Habits follow cues and easy paths. Big ideas: fix the setup, not the person and notice the quiet incentives.
  • What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, page 271) treats a repeat as information, not failure, because slips are a normal part of change.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work. The sneakers are by the door. But the phone is in your hand, and somehow it’s 7:40 and you’re scrolling with cold coffee. By evening, a quiet voice says: “See? You never stick to anything.” That voice is wrong. You aren’t weak. You’ve met a habit.

Almost everyone has something they’d like to change: a habit, a reaction, a way of speaking to the people they love. And almost everyone has found that wanting to change is not the same as changing. This chapter explains why, drawing on what researchers have learned about habits and motivation, and then turns to what actually helps.

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses. Psychology tells us what researchers have found, and where findings are weaker than popular books suggest. Philosophy shows how thinkers have wrestled with habit, willpower and character for thousands of years. Through an autistic lens looks at change from the point of view of autistic people, for whom routines often matter deeply. Where it matters most, an ADHD lens does the same for people with ADHD. It is a perspective, not a diagnosis, and it sheds light on how everyone experiences change.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Change is hard for good reasons

Our brains are built to save effort. Anything we do often in the same situation gradually becomes automatic, so we can do it without thinking and save our attention for something else. That’s a gift: imagine having to decide, every morning, how to brush your teeth. It’s also why change is hard. The old way is fast, easy and familiar. The new way is slow and takes effort, every time, until it isn’t new anymore.

Psychology

Wendy Wood and colleagues (2002) asked people to keep diaries of what they did and thought throughout the day. Roughly four in ten everyday actions were done almost daily, in the same place, often while people were thinking about something else. Much of daily life, in other words, runs on habit. Neuroscientists such as Ann Graybiel have described how repeated actions get “chunked” in brain circuits so that a whole sequence can run from a single trigger.

Other forces protect the status quo too. William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser (1988) described a status quo bias: people tend to stick with the current option, even when a change would serve them better. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky’s research on loss aversion suggests losses tend to feel bigger than equal gains, so what we’d give up by changing can loom larger than what we’d gain. None of this means change is impossible. It means difficulty is normal, not a sign of weak character.

Philosophy

Aristotle argued in the Nicomachean Ethics that character is built through habit: we become fair by doing fair things, and brave by doing brave things. Virtue, for him, was a settled disposition formed by practice, not a feeling or a one-off decision. (The popular line “We are what we repeatedly do” sums up his view well, but it was written by the historian Will Durant, not by Aristotle.) The hopeful side of his view is that if habits made us, new habits can remake us.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people rely on routines to make the world predictable and manageable. Routines reduce the number of decisions, lower uncertainty and save energy for everything else. From the outside, this is sometimes called “rigidity.” From the inside, it’s often regulation: a routine is a way of staying steady. Unexpected change can cost a great deal of energy and cause real distress. This lens is useful for everyone: change always costs something, and some people pay more. Respecting that cost, with warning, explanation and time to adjust, is not indulgence. It’s good sense.

Thoughts you could try: “This is hard because it’s a habit, not because I’m weak.” “Change costs me energy. I’ll plan for that.”

Habits run on cues

Most habits follow a simple pattern: a cue (a time, a place, a feeling, a person, or the action just before) sets off a routine, and some reward, often small and quick, keeps it going. Over time, the cue alone is enough. That’s why you can find yourself doing something before you’ve decided to.

Psychology

David Neal, Wendy Wood and colleagues (2011) gave people popcorn at a movie theater, some of it fresh and some a week old. People who habitually ate popcorn at the movies ate about as much of the stale popcorn as the fresh, while others ate less of the stale. In a meeting room, without the movie theater cues, the habitual eaters ate less stale popcorn too. The setting was driving the behavior more than the taste. Research like this suggests that habits are triggered by context, and that changing the context can loosen them.

The “cue, routine, reward” loop was popularized by the journalist Charles Duhigg. It’s a helpful simplification of a more complex research picture, but the core idea, that context triggers habits, is well supported. See Habits and cues (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation).

Philosophy

The philosopher and psychologist William James wrote a famous chapter on “Habit” in his Principles of Psychology (1890). He called habit the great flywheel of society, keeping people in their grooves. His advice for building a new habit was to start with as strong a commitment as possible and never allow an exception until the habit was rooted. Modern research has softened that last point: missing once seems to matter less than he feared (see Slips). But his central insight holds: habits are the scaffolding of a life, so it is worth choosing them on purpose.

Through an autistic lens

Explicit cues can be very helpful: a visual schedule, a timer, an alarm with a label, a note on the door. Many autistic people describe deep, single-track focus (monotropism; see Chapter 9, page 510). Deep focus is a strength, and it can make switching from one task to another harder. Some also describe autistic inertia: difficulty starting, stopping or changing activity, even when they want to. A clear, gentle cue to leave the “tunnel,” with time to finish, often works better than a sudden demand. See Monotropism (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring) and Autistic inertia (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring#autistic-inertia).

Thoughts you could try: “What happened just before I did that?” “What was it giving me: comfort, relief, a break?”

Start smaller than feels useful

When we decide to change, we often aim big: run every day, never shout, clear the whole house. Big goals feel inspiring, but they need a good day to do, and most days aren’t good days. Tiny steps are easy enough to do even when you’re tired. That’s what lets them repeat, and repetition is what builds a habit.

Psychology

Phillippa Lally and colleagues (2010) followed people trying to build a new daily habit. On average it took about two months for the behavior to feel automatic, with a very wide range from person to person, from a few weeks to most of a year. Simpler behaviors became automatic faster. Peter Gollwitzer’s research on implementation intentions (1999), plans in the form “When X happens, I will do Y,” found that people who made such plans were more likely to act on their goals. A review by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran (2006) found the effect was reliable across many studies. See If-then plans (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation#implementation-intentions).

The behavior scientist B. J. Fogg popularized “tiny habits,” attaching a very small action to an existing routine. It fits well with the research above, though the tiny-habits method itself has been studied less formally.

Philosophy

The Tao Te Ching, traditionally attributed to Laozi, says that a tree you can barely reach around grows from a tiny shoot, and a journey of a thousand miles begins beneath your feet. Big things are made of small ones. The Japanese idea of kaizen, continuous small improvement, brought a similar idea into modern workplaces. Neither asks for heroic leaps. Both trust the steady accumulation of small steps.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people find vague goals (“be healthier,” “keep your room tidy”) hard to act on, because it isn’t clear what to actually do. Concrete, specific steps (“put the books on the shelf,” “drink one glass of water after brushing teeth”) are clearer for everyone. Changing one thing at a time also helps, because each change uses energy. For ADHD minds, which often run on interest and urgency, making a tiny step more interesting (music, a game, doing it with someone) can matter as much as making it small.

This book’s idea: The “tired-day version”: for any change, decide the smallest version you can still do on your worst day. One push-up. One sentence in the journal. One kind word. On hard days, the tired-day version counts in full.

Words you could use: “After I make my coffee, I’ll...” “What’s the tired-day version of this?”

Change the setup, not just your willpower

We tend to believe change is a battle of willpower. But willpower is unreliable: it fades when we’re tired, hungry, stressed or unwell, which is exactly when old habits are strongest. Our surroundings, on the other hand, are there every day. Shaping them is one of the most effective things we can do.

Psychology

Roy Baumeister’s theory of “ego depletion” (1998) suggested that self-control works like a muscle that tires with use. It was very influential, but a large replication project led by Martin Hagger (2016), run across many labs, found an effect close to zero. The idea is now debated. Meanwhile, research by Wilhelm Hofmann and colleagues (2012) found that people who score high on self-control seem to report fewer temptations in daily life, perhaps because they set up their lives to avoid them, rather than resisting more often.

Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein’s work on “nudges” (2008) showed how small changes in how choices are presented, such as which option is the default or which food is placed first, can shift behavior. Wood’s habit research points the same way: add a little friction to the old habit (put it out of reach, add a step) and remove friction from the new one (put it in sight, get it ready).

Philosophy

In Homer’s Odyssey, Ulysses wants to hear the Sirens’ song without steering his ship onto the rocks. He doesn’t trust his willpower. Instead, he has his crew tie him to the mast and plug their own ears with wax. The philosopher Jon Elster (1979) used this story to explore precommitment: wise people sometimes bind their future selves, knowing their in-the-moment selves will be weak. That isn’t failure. It’s knowing yourself.

Through an autistic lens

The setup includes the sensory environment: light, noise, textures, smells, clutter. A habit that keeps failing might be failing because the space is overwhelming, not because the person isn’t trying. Lowering demands, reducing noise or changing lighting can make room for new habits. This fits a broader principle that runs through this book: fix the setup, not the person. It’s fairer, and it usually works better.

Through an ADHD lens

Plans that run on willpower and memory tend to fail first for people with ADHD, which is why changing the setup matters even more. What tends to help: make the cue impossible to miss (the trash bag hung on the door handle, an alarm with a label, not just a beep); do the step the moment the cue appears, before anything else catches your attention; make the reward come now, not next month (music while you clean, a tick on the fridge); and expect novelty to wear off, so swap the method every few weeks rather than blaming yourself. Doing a boring job alongside someone else, even on a video call, helps many people start. For lighter ways to use the book’s chore tools, see Chapter 9 (page 521).

Words you could use: “What could we change about the setup so this gets easier?” “Let’s make the right thing the easy thing.”

Professor Puddles

Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

Being in two minds is normal

Most of us are in two minds about our habits. We want to change, and we also don’t, because the old habit does something for us. Recognizing both sides isn’t weakness. It’s honest. And it often unlocks change better than pushing harder against ourselves.

Psychology

William Miller and Stephen Rollnick developed motivational interviewing, a way of talking about change that treats mixed feelings (ambivalence) as normal. Rather than arguing for change, which tends to make people argue back, the helper draws out the person’s own reasons. It has good evidence for some areas, such as reducing drinking, and more mixed evidence for others. James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente’s stages of change model (from the early 1980s) describes moving from not thinking about change, to considering it, to preparing, acting and maintaining. The model is widely used, but researchers have questioned whether people really move through neat stages. It’s best seen as a rough map. See Stages of change (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation#stages-of-change).

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan’s self-determination theory suggests that change lasts longer when people feel autonomy (it’s my choice), competence (I can do this) and relatedness (I’m connected to others). Pressure tends to undermine all three. See Self-determination theory (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation#self-determination-theory).

Philosophy

Ancient Greek philosophers debated akrasia, or weakness of will: knowing what’s best and doing something else. In Plato’s Protagoras, Socrates argues that nobody knowingly chooses what’s worse, so apparent weakness must be a kind of ignorance. Aristotle disagreed, saying people really can know better and still act against it, swept along by desire. Augustine, in his Confessions, admitted praying, as a young man, to be made good, but not yet. Being in two minds is an old and deeply human experience.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people, and many non-autistic people, find that pressure to change triggers strong resistance or anxiety, even for changes they want. Some describe intense anxiety around demands. Offering choices, explaining the reason for a change, and letting the person shape it all help. Autonomy isn’t a nice extra here. It’s often the thing that makes change possible at all.

Thoughts you could try: “What does the old habit give me?” “What would make this change worth it to me?”

zqaxunderstandingx6xchangexxslipsqzSlips are part of change

Almost no one changes in a straight line. People slip, restart, slip again and gradually slip less. The slip itself is rarely the problem. The thought that follows it often is: “I’ve ruined it, so I might as well give up.”

Psychology

In Lally’s habit study, missing a single day didn’t meaningfully set back progress. Alan Marlatt and Judith Gordon’s work on relapse prevention (1985) described the abstinence violation effect: after breaking a rule, people often feel guilt and a sense of total failure, which makes a full relapse more likely. Dieting researchers have described a similar “what-the-hell” effect: one cookie becomes the whole package because the day is “ruined.”

Kindness helps. Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012) found that people encouraged to think about a past mistake with self-compassion were more motivated to improve and to avoid repeating it than those encouraged simply to boost their self-esteem. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off the hook. It makes it easier to look honestly at what went wrong. See Self-compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection).

Philosophy

The Stoic philosopher Seneca described reviewing each day before sleep: what did I do well, where did I fall short, what will I do differently? He described doing it gently, more like a fair judge than a harsh one, pardoning himself this time and resolving to do better. Meditation traditions teach something similar: when your mind wanders, you notice and return to the breath without scolding. The return, not the wandering, is the practice.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic adults describe autistic burnout, a period of deep exhaustion after long stretches of stress and masking, in which skills and routines that usually work can temporarily slip. Research led by Dora Raymaker (2020) helped describe it. In burnout, slipping isn’t failure. It’s a sign the system needs rest. A plan for change should include low-energy versions and permission to pause. All-or-nothing thinking also catches many people; planning in advance what “partly” looks like can help.

Thoughts you could try: “A slip is a moment, not a verdict.” “What made today harder? What can I plan for next time?”

Tidbit

A slip is a stumble, not a fall. Shake it off and try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts makes practicing more fun.

Tool: Calm games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

Change that fits who you want to be

Changes made only because someone else wants them, or out of shame, tend to be fragile. Changes that connect to what we care about, and to the kind of person we want to be, have deeper roots. Each small action becomes a piece of evidence: “I’m someone who does this.”

Psychology

Daryl Bem’s self-perception theory (1972) suggested that we partly learn who we are by watching what we do, much as we would learn about someone else. Do something a few times, and you start to see yourself as that kind of person. Christopher Bryan and colleagues (2011) found that asking people about “being a voter” rather than “voting” increased turnout in their studies, though later attempts to repeat it had mixed results. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, developed by Steven Hayes and colleagues, puts values at the center: choosing actions that move toward what matters to you, even when they’re uncomfortable. See Values (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation#values).

Philosophy

Jean-Paul Sartre argued that “existence precedes essence”: we aren’t born with a fixed nature but make ourselves through our choices. That can feel daunting, and freeing. The Confucian philosopher Xunzi compared self-cultivation to straightening wood with steam and a frame: our raw nature is shaped by practice, ritual and learning. Both views agree: who you are is not fixed. You are, in part, what you keep choosing.

Through an autistic lens

Change should never mean trying to become less yourself. For many autistic people, the most meaningful change is the reverse: unmasking, letting themselves stim, saying no to draining social events, and building a life that fits their mind. That is real change too. A good test for any change is: does this help me live more as myself, or does it ask me to hide? Changes that fit who you are tend to last. Changes that require constant pretending tend to cost too much.

Thoughts you could try: “This matters to me because...” “Does this change help me be more myself, or less?”

Supporting change in others

Many of us want other people to change: a partner who’s always late, a parent who drinks too much, a teenager glued to a screen, a colleague who never replies. It is natural, and often well meant. But other people’s change belongs to them. We can influence it, support it and ask for what we need. We can’t make it happen.

Psychology

Research on “social control” in relationships, such as by Megan Lewis and Karen Rook (1999), found that when partners try to control each other’s health habits, it can sometimes lead to change, but it often comes with resentment and distress. Niall Bolger and colleagues (2000) found that support was sometimes most helpful when the person receiving it hardly noticed it, perhaps because it didn’t make them feel less capable. Stephen Drigotas and colleagues (1999) described the Michelangelo phenomenon: partners who see and affirm the best in each other help each other grow toward their ideal selves. See The Michelangelo effect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships).

In couples research, Andrew Christensen and Neil Jacobson developed acceptance-based approaches, finding that when partners stop fighting every difference and accept some as part of who the other person is, some change often follows more easily. See Acceptance and change (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict).

Philosophy

The Stoic teacher Epictetus began his handbook by dividing the world into what is up to us (our own judgments, choices and actions) and what is not (other people’s choices, among many other things). Peace, he said, comes from focusing on the first. That doesn’t mean not caring about others. It means putting your effort where it can actually work: in what you say, what you ask for, and what you do. See What’s up to us (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth).

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people often experience change imposed by others: a new office layout, a changed plan, a different teacher, a rearranged kitchen. Those changes can be hard, not because of stubbornness, but because the predictability that helped them cope has been taken away. Giving advance notice, explaining why, involving the person in the decision and allowing time to adjust makes a big difference. In shared homes and workplaces, this is good practice for everyone.

This book’s idea: “Ask, offer, notice”: ask what would help, offer one concrete thing, and notice small steps out loud. It’s a simple way to support without taking over.

Words you could use: “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. Thank you.”

Sugarfoot

You can’t make anyone change, but you can ask kindly. A clear request is easier to say yes to than a complaint.

Tool: Small wins: Flip it spreadloveandacceptance.com/small-wins

Putting it together

Change is hard because habits are efficient, the old way is easy, and losses loom large. Habits run on cues, so understanding your cues lets you plan for them. Small steps beat big leaps because they’re repeatable. Shaping your setup works better than relying on willpower. Mixed feelings are normal, and listening to them helps. Slips are part of the path, and kindness helps you restart. Change lasts longer when it connects to who you want to be. And other people’s change belongs to them, though you can support it.

A simple plan that brings it together:

  1. Pick one change that matters to you.
  2. Find the cue: when, where, after what.
  3. Make it tiny: “After I ___, I will ___.”
  4. Tweak the setup to make it easier.
  5. Plan the tired-day version and the kind sentence for slips.
  6. Connect it to a value: “because I care about...”
  7. Look back after a few weeks, kindly, and adjust.

The book’s Part One chapter Know yourself, next (page 88) and the self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) turn this into worksheets.

Worked examples

On your own: the morning walk

Back to the scrolling morning. Instead of “walk 30 minutes before work,” the plan becomes: “After I make my coffee, I put my sneakers on.” The phone charges in the hall overnight. The tired-day version is a walk to the end of the street. After two weeks, the walk is usually 20 minutes. On bad days it’s the end of the street, and that counts.

Partners: the evening phones

Nesrin wants her partner to spend less time on his phone in the evenings. Nagging hasn’t worked. She asks instead: “I miss talking in the evenings. Could we try something together?” They agree on a basket for both phones from nine, one evening a week to start. She notices out loud when it works. It’s a shared change, not a demand. See Gaming, phones and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together).

Parent and child: the bedtime routine

A family with an autistic seven-year-old needs a new bedtime after a move. They make a picture chart of each step, give a ten-minute warning before bath time, and keep the same order every night. The change is explained in advance, and the child picks which pajamas go on the chart. Within two weeks, bedtime is calmer. See Neurodivergent relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

Coworkers: the meeting habit

A team keeps forgetting who agreed to do what. Instead of “be more organized,” they add one tiny habit: the last two minutes of every meeting are “who does what by when,” written in the shared notes. It’s a setup change, not a personality change, and it works. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).

Friends: moving more together

Two friends both want to exercise more and both keep canceling the gym. They swap to a Saturday walk with coffee at the end. The friendship is the reward. Six months later, it’s the most reliable part of their week.

Roommates: the dishes

Four students argue about dishes. They try a schedule, which fails. Then they try a setup change: each person gets one plate, one bowl, one mug, and the rest go in a cupboard. The pile disappears. Nobody had to become a different person.

Big life change: a new baby

After their baby arrives, a couple’s old routines collapse. Instead of mourning them, they treat it as a fresh start: one tiny ritual each (a two-minute check-in at the evening feed, a walk with the stroller on Sundays). Researchers have noticed that fresh starts, like new years, birthdays and big changes, can be good moments to begin new habits. See New parents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/new-parent).

Exercises

  1. Map a habit. For three days, note the cue, routine and reward each time a habit you’d like to change happens.
  2. Shrink it. Take a change you want and shrink it until it takes two minutes. Write it as “After I ___, I will ___.”
  3. One setup change. Change one thing in your surroundings today to make the new habit easier or the old one harder.
  4. Two lists. Write “What I like about how things are” and “What I’d like about changing.” Read both kindly.
  5. Plan for slips. Write the kind sentence you’ll say to yourself after a slip, and the one small step you’ll take to restart.
  6. The tired-day version. For your change, decide the smallest version you’ll do on your worst day. (This book’s idea)
  7. Ask, offer, notice. If you’re hoping someone else will change, try one week of asking what would help, offering one concrete thing, and noticing small steps out loud.

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, someone sets a big goal on a hopeful Sunday. It needs a perfect day, so it slips on Wednesday. The slip feels like proof of weakness, so they give up until the next fresh start. If others are involved, there’s nagging, resentment and digging in. Nothing in the setup changed, so nothing much else does.

When it goes right, someone picks one small change tied to something they care about. They plan for the cue, adjust the setup and decide on a tired-day version. When they slip, they say something kind and start again the next day. The people around them notice small steps and help with the setup. Months later, the change isn’t something they do. It’s part of how they live.

Helping someone else change

If you want to support someone through a change, the research and traditions above point the same way. Start by asking rather than advising: “Would ideas help, or would you rather think out loud?” Help them find their own reasons, because change built on someone else’s reasons rarely lasts. Offer practical help with the setup, such as a ride, a shared calendar, a quieter evening or fewer snacks in the house, which often does more than encouragement. Notice small steps out loud and say little about the gaps. When they slip, respond the way you’d hope someone would respond to you: “That’s okay. Tomorrow’s another go.” And look after yourself. Caring about someone’s change doesn’t mean carrying it, and you can set limits on what you’ll live with while still being kind.

Words you could use: “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days in a row. That’s not nothing.”

Questions people often ask

How long does it really take to form a habit?

There’s no single answer. In Lally’s study the average was around two months, with a huge range. Simpler habits form faster. The “21 days” figure often quoted doesn’t come from habit research.

Is willpower a myth?

Not exactly, but it’s less reliable than we think, and the idea that it runs out like fuel is now debated. Shaping your setup tends to work better than relying on willpower.

What if I’ve tried to change many times and always failed?

That’s very common, and it doesn’t mean you can’t change. It may mean the plan was too big, the setup didn’t change, or there’s something underneath, like stress, exhaustion or a health issue, that needs attention first.

How do I get my partner (or parent, or child) to change?

You can’t make them, but you can say clearly what you need, ask what would help, make changes together, and notice their small steps. If a behavior is harmful to you, you can also decide what you’ll do if it doesn’t change. Saying calmly what you will do is a boundary, not a threat.

I’m autistic and change is very hard for me. Is something wrong with me?

No. Many autistic people find change costly, because routines help them stay regulated. You can still change things that matter to you, often more easily with warning, clear steps, one change at a time, and support. And you don’t have to change things that are working for you just because others do them differently.

Should I tell people about my goal?

It depends. Telling a supportive person who’ll encourage you can help. Telling people who’ll nag or judge may not. Choose who you tell, and what you’d like from them.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education about how habits and change tend to work. It isn’t treatment for addiction, eating difficulties, or mental health conditions.
  • Some popular ideas about habits are stronger in books than in research. We’ve tried to say where findings are mixed or debated.

The library’s motivation and habits page has more on each idea.

What to remember

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.
