Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. How to read this chapter
  2. Worth that doesn’t have to be earned
  3. Guilt, shame and repair
  4. How shame works in the body
  5. The critic and the soothing system
  6. What self-compassion is, and isn’t
  7. Comparison and steady self-worth
  8. Two common shields: perfectionism and people-pleasing
  9. Owning it, repairing it, letting it rest
  10. How worth is given and learned
  11. Putting it together
  12. Your part, and only your part
  13. Worked examples
  14. Exercises
  15. Questions people often ask
  16. Limits

At a glance

  • Your worth isn’t a score. It doesn’t rise and fall with each day’s results.
  • Guilt and shame are different. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.” Guilt is easier to put right.
  • Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off. Being kind to yourself after a mistake makes it easier to own it and grow.
  • Worth is something we can give. How we treat each other teaches people what they are worth.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • “Writing it down isn’t keeping score” (the Preface to Part Two, page 108) and “It judges the setup, never a person” (Part Two, Chapter II, page 168) matter because shame makes people hide and defend. Tools that measure the setup, not anyone’s worth, keep shame out of the room. Big idea: fix the setup, not the person.
  • “Covering is kind. Say it out loud” (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) is the everyday version of owning a slip without drowning in it.

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong file to the whole team. Someone noticed, fixed it, and said “no worries.” Hours later you are still awake, replaying it. The voice in your head isn’t saying “that was a mistake.” It’s saying “you’re useless. They all know it now.”

Why does one small mistake feel like a verdict on your whole self? Why do some people hear every comment as an attack, while others shrug it off? And why does being kind to yourself sound, to so many of us, like an excuse? This chapter takes those questions slowly.

How to read this chapter

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses, then brings them together:

  • Psychology: what researchers have found, named honestly, with a note where the evidence is thin or debated.
  • Philosophy: what thinkers and traditions have said about the same question, paraphrased fairly. These are ways of seeing, not proof.
  • Through an autistic lens: how the idea can look from an autistic point of view. This is a perspective, not a deficit, and not a rule about any one person. Autistic people differ from each other as much as anyone.

Where something is the book’s own way of putting ideas into practice, rather than established research, it is marked This book’s idea. Nothing here diagnoses anyone.

Worth that doesn’t have to be earned

Self-worth is the background sense that you matter and are acceptable as a person. It’s different from confidence (believing you can do a task) and from pride in something you achieved. Many people never notice their sense of worth until it’s shaken: by a job loss, a breakup, an illness or a public mistake.

Often, without ever deciding it, we tie our worth to conditions. “I’m okay when I’m useful.” “I’m okay when I’m liked.” “I’m okay when I’m thin, top, busy, calm, needed or never a bother.” Each condition works until it doesn’t. Then the drop feels like a drop in the whole self.

Psychology

Carl Rogers, one of the founders of humanistic psychology, wrote in the 1950s about “conditions of worth”: the sense, learned in childhood, that you are only lovable when you behave in certain ways. He argued that people grow best with “unconditional positive regard,” being valued as a person even when their behavior isn’t approved of.

Later research by Jennifer Crocker and Connie Wolfe (2001) described “contingencies of self-worth”: the areas where people stake their self-esteem, such as appearance, approval from others, academic success, or being a good person. Their studies suggest that the more someone’s worth depends on an area, the more their mood and self-esteem swing with each success or setback there. The research doesn’t say you should stop caring about anything. It suggests that worth staked on outcomes you can’t fully control is fragile.

Philosophy

Immanuel Kant drew a line between things that have a price, which can be swapped for something of equal value, and persons, who have dignity, a worth beyond any price. On this view, your worth isn’t something you earn by being useful; it belongs to you because you are a person. You don’t have to agree with all of Kant’s system to find this a steadying idea.

Many religious and spiritual traditions say something similar in their own language: that each person is valued before they do anything at all. The Southern African idea often summed up as ubuntu, roughly “a person is a person through other people,” adds a twist: worth isn’t only a private possession. It is recognized and held between people.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people grow up being corrected for how they naturally move, speak, play and feel: “look at me,” “stop flapping,” “don’t be so blunt,” “why can’t you just…?” Each correction may be well meant. Together they can teach a child a condition of worth: “I’m acceptable when I seem less like myself.”

A study by Eilidh Cage, Jessica Di Monaco and Victoria Newell (2018) found that autistic adults who felt more accepted by others, and who accepted their own autism more, tended to report fewer symptoms of depression. It was one study, measured at one time, so it can’t prove cause. But it fits what many autistic writers say: being accepted as you are is not a luxury; it is protective.

Thoughts you could try: “I can want to do well without needing to do well to matter.” “My worth was here before today, and it’s still here.”

Guilt, shame and repair

Guilt and shame are both “self-conscious” feelings: they come from looking at yourself through someone else’s eyes. But they point in different directions. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

Psychology

Psychologist Helen Block Lewis (1971) first described this difference carefully, from listening to therapy sessions. June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s book Shame and Guilt (2002) summarizes years of studies that followed. In general, people who tend toward guilt are more likely to feel empathy, apologize and try to make things right. People who tend toward shame are more likely to hide, deny, blame others or feel angry.

The limits matter. Some researchers question whether the questionnaires fully separate the two feelings. And shame has different meanings across cultures: in some, a sense of shame is mainly a healthy concern for the group and for one’s family name, not only a private wound. The research is strongest on shame as a global “I am bad” feeling that people can’t see a way out of.

Philosophy

The Chinese philosopher Mencius taught that every person has “sprouts” of goodness, and one of them is a sense of shame at doing wrong. For him, shame wasn’t poison; it was the start of a moral sense, something to grow into good judgment. That is a useful balance to the modern view. A small, specific shame (“I shouldn’t have said that”) can guide us. What hurts is shame that spreads to the whole self and has nowhere to go.

Many ethical traditions build in a path back: confession and forgiveness, making amends, restorative practices in communities. They share a practical idea: a wrong should lead somewhere, toward repair, rather than to a permanent label on a person.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people describe a strong sense of fairness and honesty, and a matching strength of guilt when they think they’ve broken a rule. Others are told they “don’t seem sorry,” because their face or voice doesn’t show remorse in the expected way. Then shame gets added on top: not just “I did something wrong,” but “I’m wrong for how I feel it.” That is the double empathy problem at work: two people reading each other with different maps, and each missing what the other means. Clear, explicit repair helps both sides: “I’m sorry. Here’s exactly what I’ll do differently.”

Thoughts you could try: “Is this guilt, about one thing I did, or shame, about all of me?” “If it’s about one thing, what would make it right?”

How shame works in the body

Shame is fast. Before you have a thought, the body has often already reacted: face hot, eyes down, shoulders curled, a drop in the stomach, an urge to vanish. Some people go blank and can’t think. Others feel a rush of anger.

Psychology

Researchers who study emotions across species have suggested that the shame posture (head down, body smaller, gaze away) resembles the appeasement signals some animals show after losing a status contest. It may have evolved as a way of saying “I’m no threat, don’t throw me out.” That is a theory, but it helps explain why shame feels so urgent: being cast out of the group was once dangerous.

Helen Block Lewis also noticed what she called “shame-rage”: a quick turn from feeling small to lashing out, because anger feels more powerful than shame. Tangney’s research linked shame-proneness with more blaming and anger in conflicts. Psychologist and author Brené Brown, whose research on shame is mostly interview-based rather than experimental, describes the same pattern in everyday life: shame thrives on secrecy and silence, and loses some of its grip when it is spoken to someone who responds with empathy.

Philosophy

The French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre gave a famous example: someone peeping through a keyhole suddenly hears footsteps behind them, and in that instant feels themselves seen as an object, judged and fixed. Shame, for Sartre, is the feeling of being caught in another person’s gaze. That captures why shame makes us want to hide: we want to step out of the gaze.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people find direct eye contact uncomfortable, or say it makes listening harder. Being told to “look at me when I’m talking to you” during a scolding can add shame to shame. Some autistic people also have alexithymia, finding it hard to name feelings, so shame may show up first as a body state (“I feel sick,” “I need to leave”) rather than as a word. Noticing the body sign is a valid way in. A meltdown or shutdown after a shaming moment is not manipulation. It is a nervous system at its limit.

Words you could use: “I think I felt embarrassed and it came out as anger. That wasn’t fair to you.” “I need a few minutes. I’m not ignoring you; I’m overwhelmed.”

zqaxunderstandingx7xworthxxcriticqzThe critic and the soothing system

Most people have an inner voice that comments on what they do. For some, it’s mostly fair. For others, it’s a relentless critic: “idiot,” “you always,” “who do you think you are?”

Psychology

Psychologist Paul Gilbert developed compassion-focused therapy for people with high shame and self-criticism. He describes three broad emotion systems, as a simple model: a threat system (alert, anxious, defensive), a drive system (wanting, striving, achieving) and a soothing system (safe, calm, connected). In his view, harsh self-criticism keeps the threat system switched on, while many people have had little practice in using the soothing system on themselves. The model is a simplification of a complex brain, and research on compassion-focused therapy is still growing, but early trials are encouraging.

It is often noted that the critic has a protective job: to stop you being rejected by getting there first, or to push you to work harder. Seeing it that way can make it easier to talk back to it calmly rather than fight it.

Philosophy

The Stoic Epictetus taught that we are disturbed not by events but by our judgments about them. Applied here: the mistake is an event; “I’m useless” is a judgment, and judgments can be examined. Stoics practiced writing down and questioning their own thoughts each evening. Marcus Aurelius’s private notebook, now called the Meditations, is full of him reminding himself, gently and firmly, to begin again.

Buddhist traditions offer loving-kindness practice (metta), where you wish yourself and others well in simple phrases. It is meant as training, not as a feeling you must already have.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people find vague comfort (“be gentle with yourself”) hard to act on. What does gentle mean, exactly? Concrete, literal versions can work better: “I will eat something, then sit somewhere quiet for ten minutes, then decide.” Others find their inner voice is a recording of years of other people’s corrections. Writing the critic’s words down, word for word, and checking each one against facts can suit a mind that likes precision.

Thoughts you could try: “That’s the critic. It’s trying to protect me. What do I actually need?” “Is that true, or just loud?”

What self-compassion is, and isn’t

Self-compassion means meeting your own pain the way you’d meet a friend’s: with warmth, not attack. It isn’t pretending things are fine, or excusing harm you did.

Psychology

Kristin Neff (2003) defined self-compassion with three parts:

  • Self-kindness instead of harsh judgment.
  • Common humanity: remembering that suffering and failure are part of being human, instead of feeling it’s “only me.”
  • Mindfulness: noticing painful feelings clearly, without ignoring them or being swept away.

In a set of experiments, Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012) found that people encouraged to be self-compassionate after a failure or a moral mistake were more motivated to improve, such as studying longer for a retest, than people encouraged to boost their self-esteem. Many studies link self-compassion with lower anxiety and depression. Most of this research is correlational, and much of it uses one questionnaire, which some researchers have debated. So it’s fair to say: promising and widely studied, not settled.

Philosophy

Neff drew on Buddhist teachings, where compassion for all beings includes yourself. Aristotle offers another angle: he thought a good person is a friend to themselves, someone who wishes themselves well and enjoys their own company, which is different from selfishness. Albert Ellis, who founded rational emotive behavior therapy and thought much like a philosopher, argued for “unconditional self-acceptance”: rate your actions, not your whole self.

Through an autistic lens

For autistic people who have spent years working hard to fit in, self-compassion can include something specific: permission to stop forcing yourself through situations that hurt. Choosing headphones, leaving early, eating the same lunch, or scripting a hard phone call isn’t weakness. It’s meeting your needs. Common humanity can also mean finding your people: autistic communities, online and offline, where your way of being is ordinary.

Thoughts you could try: “This is hard. Other people struggle with this too. What would help me right now?” (These three lines follow Neff’s three parts.)

Sugarfoot

Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first can help.

Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

Comparison and steady self-worth

We work out how we’re doing partly by looking at others. That’s normal. But it makes worth slippery: there will always be someone richer, calmer, more talented or more loved.

Psychology

Leon Festinger’s social comparison theory (1954) proposed that people evaluate themselves by comparing with others, especially when there’s no clear standard. Comparing upward can inspire or deflate; comparing downward can comfort or make us smug.

A major review by Roy Baumeister and colleagues (2003) found that high self-esteem didn’t reliably cause better performance or relationships, and that efforts to simply boost self-esteem didn’t deliver what had been hoped. Kristin Neff and Roos Vonk (2009) found that self-compassion was linked to a steadier sense of self-worth over time, and less dependent on comparison and approval, than self-esteem. Self-esteem asks “am I good enough?” Self-compassion asks “what do I need?”

Philosophy

Jean-Jacques Rousseau distinguished two kinds of self-love. Amour de soi is the natural care for your own well-being. Amour-propre is self-regard that depends on how others see you and how you rank among them. He thought much unhappiness in society came from the second. Many contemplative traditions also warn against measuring yourself by others, and teach gratitude for what is actually in your life.

Through an autistic lens

Comparison can be especially unfair when the yardstick was built for a different kind of mind. An autistic adult who compares their social life to a non-autistic friend’s may be measuring by a standard that doesn’t fit them. Many autistic people describe deep satisfaction from a focused interest, a small number of close friends, or long time alone. Those aren’t lesser versions of someone else’s life. They are a different life, measured by its own needs.

Thoughts you could try: “Is this a fair comparison, or a different race?” “What does a good day look like for me, not for them?”

Two common shields: perfectionism and people-pleasing

When worth feels conditional, people often build a shield. Two of the most common are perfectionism (“if I’m flawless, I can’t be criticized”) and people-pleasing (“if everyone is happy with me, I can’t be rejected”). Both can look like strengths from the outside. Both are often exhausting from the inside.

Psychology

Researchers such as Paul Hewitt and Gordon Flett have studied perfectionism for decades. They distinguish between high standards you set for yourself, which can be healthy, and the sense that others demand perfection from you, or that any mistake means failure. That second kind is the one more consistently linked with anxiety, depression and burnout. A review by Thomas Curran and Andrew Hill (2019) suggested that perfectionism, especially the sense that others expect perfection, has risen among young people in several Western countries since the late 1980s. That finding is based on questionnaires and doesn’t explain why, but it matches what many teachers and parents notice.

People-pleasing isn’t a formal diagnosis. The term describes a pattern: putting others’ wishes first so reliably that your own needs disappear, often driven by fear of conflict or rejection. It overlaps with what researchers call “sociotropy” and with the “fawn” idea used in some writing on trauma, though that word is a description, not a tested category.

Philosophy

The ancient Greeks had a word, hubris, for overreaching pride. Perfectionism can be its quiet cousin: a belief that you, alone among humans, must never fall short. Many traditions treat humility not as thinking less of yourself, but as accepting that you are a limited, ordinary human being, which is a relief as much as a discipline. Japanese aesthetics, through ideas like wabi-sabi, find beauty in what is imperfect and unfinished.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people value precision and get real joy from doing something exactly right. That’s not a problem in itself. It becomes painful when precision turns into a fear that any error will expose you, often after years of being corrected. People-pleasing can also be a form of masking: copying what others want, agreeing to avoid trouble, rehearsing the “right” face. It can work in the short term and cost a great deal of energy over time. Clear, kind boundaries (“I can do Tuesday, not Thursday”) are a way of letting your real self take up a little more space.

Thoughts you could try: “Good enough is good enough for this one.” “Someone being a little disappointed in me is survivable.”

zqaxunderstandingx7xworthxxmistakesqzOwning it, repairing it, letting it rest

When worth feels safe, owning a mistake gets easier. You can look at what happened without feeling that everything you are is on trial.

Psychology

Studies on apology suggest that people value apologies that acknowledge responsibility and offer repair. Over-apologizing, or turning an apology into a long account of how terrible you feel, can shift the focus onto your feelings and leave the other person comforting you. Research linking guilt to repair suggests that a specific, action-focused apology is easier to give, and easier to receive.

After a reasonable repair, rumination (going over and over it) tends to keep distress going without adding anything useful. Studies on rumination, especially Susan Nolen-Hoeksema’s work, link it with longer and deeper low moods.

This book’s idea: a three-part ownership sentence (what I did, its effect, what I’m doing now), followed by a deliberate “letting it rest” step, like closing a file.

Philosophy

Aristotle thought character is built by practice: we become honest by doing honest things, again and again. A single act doesn’t define you; a pattern shapes you, and patterns can change. The Jewish practice of teshuvah, often translated as “return,” describes a path after wrongdoing: recognizing it, making amends, and choosing differently next time. It treats people as able to return, not as fixed.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people find it hard to let a mistake rest, because the mind keeps returning to it in detail. This isn’t self-indulgence. A mind that focuses deeply on one thing at a time (see Chapter 9, page 510) can get pulled into a loop. Concrete closing rituals can help: writing the apology, sending it, then writing “done” and putting the note away. Clear feedback (“Thank you, we’re okay now”) from the other person can help too, so you aren’t left guessing.

Words you could use: “I did this. I can see it affected you like this. Here’s what I’m doing about it.” And afterward: “Are we okay? It helps me to hear it plainly.”

Professor Puddles

Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

How worth is given and learned

Self-worth isn’t built alone. Children learn it from caregivers, teachers and peers. Adults keep learning it from partners, friends, bosses and communities. The good news: this means we can each help others feel they matter.

Psychology

Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck (1998) found that children praised for being “smart” after a task were more likely to avoid challenges and to struggle after setbacks than children praised for their effort. The wider “growth mindset” research has had mixed results when scaled into school programs, so it’s fair not to overstate it. But the basic point is gentle and useful: praise people for what they do and how they try, and show them they are valued even when they fail.

Research on criticism in couples and families, such as John Gottman’s, suggests that criticism aimed at character (“you’re so selfish”) does more harm than a complaint about a specific behavior (“you didn’t call when you said you would”).

Philosophy

The philosopher Axel Honneth argues that people need recognition from others in three forms: love (being cared for), respect (being treated as an equal with rights), and esteem (being valued for what you contribute). When any is denied, people feel the injury as an injury to the self. That fits everyday experience: being ignored at work, overlooked in a family, or treated as less than equal in a community all chip at worth.

Through an autistic lens

For autistic children and adults, being given worth often looks like being believed: believed about sensory pain, about what is hard, about what helps. It looks like adjustments offered without making the person beg for them. It also looks like interest in their interests. Many autistic people say that a parent, teacher or friend who simply listened to them talk about their favorite subject taught them, more than any praise, that they were worth listening to.

Words you could use: “That didn’t go well. You’re still welcome here.” “Tell me more about that. I want to know what you like about it.”

Putting it together

Here is the chapter in one line: your worth is not on trial, so you can look honestly at what you do. When worth depends on scores, every setback becomes shame, and shame makes us hide or attack. When worth is steady, mistakes become guilt-sized: specific, fixable, and finished.

The three lenses meet at a few points:

  • Psychology shows that shame tends to block repair, while guilt and self-compassion tend to help it.
  • Philosophy offers reasons to see worth as given rather than earned: dignity, recognition, friendship with oneself.
  • The autistic lens shows how much shame can come from being judged by someone else’s map, and how much acceptance protects.

This book’s idea: a simple order for hard moments: notice, name, need, next. Notice the body sign. Name it (“that’s shame”). Ask what you need (food, a break, a kind word). Then choose one next step (repair, rest, or let it go).

Your part, and only your part

You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth as a child. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and who you spend your time with. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters, and let one-sided relationships shrink back to what feels fair. That isn’t cold. It protects the part of you that is still learning it’s worth something. Part One covers this in full: your circle of control, and matching energy (page 72).

Worked examples

On your own. Effie, between jobs, spends mornings scrolling old classmates’ news and feeling worse. She notices her condition of worth: “I matter when I’m employed.” She keeps applying, and also writes three lines each evening: one thing she did, one thing she noticed, one way she was kind. On a bad day, “I got dressed” counts.

Partners. Arjun forgets their anniversary dinner booking. His partner is hurt. Arjun’s first reaction is a shame spiral: “I’m a terrible partner.” That makes his partner end up comforting him. Next time, Arjun tries the three-part sentence: “I forgot the booking. You were looking forward to it, and that hurt. I’ve booked Saturday, and I’ve put our dates in my calendar for the year.”

Parent and child. Ten-year-old Archie spills paint across the table and freezes. His mom notices the freeze and says, calmly, “Accidents happen. Let’s get the cloths.” Later she says, “Thanks for helping clean up.” Archie learns that a mistake leads to repair, not exile.

Coworkers. In a team meeting, Trudy’s report has a wrong figure. Her manager says, “Let’s fix the number. Good catch on the trend, though.” Afterward, Trudy writes down the step she missed and adds a check. The team learns that errors can be raised early.

Friends. Ibrahim, who is autistic, told a friend her new haircut “looks shorter on one side.” She was hurt. He hadn’t meant it as criticism; it was a fact he noticed. They talk: she explains she felt self-conscious; he explains he wasn’t judging. They agree that he’ll ask “do you want my opinion?” first, and she’ll know honesty from him is never meant as a dig.

Roommates. Aled keeps forgetting the recycling and feels like the bad roommate. Instead of avoiding the kitchen, Aled suggests a reminder on the fridge and swaps recycling for a job that fits Aled’s schedule better. The problem was the setup, not the person.

Community. At a volunteer group, a new member makes a mistake at the food bank and is mocked. A long-time volunteer says, “I did the same thing my first week. Here’s the trick.” Shame shrinks when someone stands beside you.

Exercises

1. Find your scores

Finish “I feel okay about myself when I…” five times. Circle the ones that depend on things you can’t fully control. For each, write one sentence of worth that doesn’t depend on it: “I matter when I’m not needed.”

2. Guilt or shame?

Think of something you still feel bad about. Write it as shame (“I’m…”), then rewrite it as guilt (“I did…”). Then add one thing that would repair it, or one reason it’s already been repaired.

3. The friend letter

Write a short letter to yourself about a struggle, as if from a wise and kind friend who knows everything about you. Keep it plain and specific. Read it once, out loud if you can.

4. The critic’s script

Write your critic’s most common sentence, word for word. Ask: whose voice does this sound like? Is it true? What would I say to a friend? Write a reply in one sentence, and keep it on your phone.

5. Recognition, given

For one week, tell one person a day something you value about them that isn’t a result: their patience, their humor, their honesty. Notice how it feels to give worth away.

Questions people often ask

Isn’t some shame healthy?

A small, specific sense of shame (“I shouldn’t have said that”) can guide us, as many traditions teach. The kind that harms is global shame, “I am bad,” with no way back. The aim isn’t to feel nothing; it’s to turn shame into something you can act on.

What if I really did something seriously wrong?

Then guilt is fitting, and repair matters. Self-compassion doesn’t erase responsibility. It gives you the steadiness to face it: to apologize properly, accept consequences and change. Shame alone tends to make people avoid all of that.

I’ve tried being kind to myself and it feels fake. Why?

That’s common, especially if you’ve been criticized a lot. Paul Gilbert calls it a “fear of compassion”: kindness can feel unfamiliar or even threatening at first. Start small and concrete: a meal, a rest, one gentler sentence. Feelings often follow actions.

Is self-esteem bad, then?

No. Feeling good about yourself is pleasant and often helpful. The research suggests that chasing it, or needing to be better than others to feel okay, makes it fragile. Self-compassion gives a steadier floor underneath.

How do I help a child with low self-worth?

Separate the child from the behavior, praise effort and kindness, repair after your own mistakes in front of them, and show interest in what they love. If low self-worth is lasting, keep showing up and keep the door open to talk.

I’m autistic (or think I might be). Is my shame about that?

It might be part of it, and only you can say. Many autistic adults describe years of feeling “wrong” before they understood why. Learning about autism, and meeting other autistic people, helps many of them see old shame differently: not “I failed at being normal,” but “I was using the wrong map.” Minds that work differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds) goes further.

What about shame at work, when the culture blames people?

You can practice owning your own part clearly, and treating others’ mistakes as fixable, even if the wider culture doesn’t. If you lead a team, the way you respond to the first mistake someone admits teaches everyone whether it’s safe to speak up. At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) has more.

Can I talk this through with someone first?

Yes. Professor Puddles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask), the site’s chat host, can help you find a kinder sentence.

Limits

  • This chapter teaches ideas. It isn’t therapy, and it can’t tell you what is going on for you.

Research notes for this chapter live in the site’s library: shame and guilt (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions), self-compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection), self-esteem (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation), perfectionism (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/motivation#perfectionism), rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#rumination) and masking (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring). For where an old inner voice may have started, see Part One: where you came from (page 18). For the next chapters, see Loss, grief and big life changes (page 475) and Minds that work differently (page 498).

What to remember

  • Your worth isn’t a score.
  • Shame makes you want to hide.
  • Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.
  • Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.
  • Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

Part Three · Chapter 8

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

In this chapter

  1. How to read this chapter
  2. What grief is, and what counts
  3. Waves, and the swing between loss and life
  4. The grieving body and brain
  5. Ambiguous and unrecognized grief
  6. Grieving styles and families
  7. Continuing bonds
  8. Endings, the in-between, beginnings
  9. Losing a partner in later life
  10. Resilience, support and stuck grief
  11. Guilt, regret and “if only”
  12. Your part, and only your part
  13. Putting it together
  14. Worked examples
  15. Exercises
  16. Questions people often ask
  17. Limits

At a glance

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves, not stages. A good week and then a bad day is normal, not going backward.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that’s healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some griefs stay heavy for a long time. Both are normal.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • Who did what and the setup score (the Preface to Part Two, page 108; Part Two, Chapter II, page 168) help after a death, an illness, a move or a new baby, because a big change quietly moves jobs from one person to another. Looking at the month again lets you share the new load on purpose. Big idea: see the whole load.
  • “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, page 205) fits grief: grief fills the tank, so some talks wait for a better day, with a time named.
  • Where your lens came from (Part One, Then, page 18) looks at older losses that still shape how you react today.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you’re doing fine. Then, in the supermarket, you see the cereal your dad always bought, and you have to leave your cart in the aisle and sit in the car. Nobody around you knows. It feels like day one again.

Every life includes loss. People die, relationships end, bodies change, homes are left, and futures we pictured don’t arrive. Grief is the natural response, and yet many of us learn very little about it until we are in it. This chapter explains what is known about grief and big life changes, what thinkers across history have said, and how loss can look through an autistic lens. Then it turns to what helps.

How to read this chapter

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses, then brings them together:

  • Psychology: what researchers have found, named honestly, with a note where the evidence is thin or debated.
  • Philosophy: what thinkers and traditions have said, paraphrased fairly. Traditions around death are deeply personal; they are offered here with respect, not as a recommendation.
  • Through an autistic lens: how loss and change can look from an autistic point of view. This is a perspective, not a deficit, and not a rule about any one person.

Where something is the book’s own way of putting ideas into practice, it is marked This book’s idea. If you are grieving right now, you don’t need to read it all. Read one section and stop.

What grief is, and what counts

Grief is the whole response to losing something you were attached to: feelings, thoughts, body changes and changes in behavior. It is not a problem to be solved. It is what love and attachment look like when what they were attached to is gone.

Psychology

Attachment researchers, starting with John Bowlby in the mid-twentieth century, saw grief as an extension of the distress we feel when separated from someone we’re bonded to. Bowlby observed that bereaved adults showed searching and yearning much like young children separated from a parent. Seen this way, grief isn’t strange. It’s the attachment system still reaching for someone who can’t be reached.

Loss also comes in many forms. Psychologists studying “life events,” such as Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe (1967), listed divorce, job loss, moving, illness and retirement alongside bereavement as major stressors. Their scale is dated and rough, but the basic point holds: many changes involve losing something, and the mind responds to them as losses.

Philosophy

Saint Augustine, writing in his Confessions about the death of a close friend in his youth, described how everything he looked at reminded him of his friend, and how his hometown became painful to him. He later reflected that he had loved a mortal person as if they would never die. Whatever you make of his religious conclusions, his account is one of the oldest detailed descriptions of grief in Western writing, and it still feels familiar.

Montaigne, after the death of his friend Étienne de La Boétie, wrote that if pressed to say why he loved him, he could only answer: because it was him, because it was me. Grief, on this view, is the shadow of a particular bond that can’t be replaced, which is why “you can always get another dog” or “you’ll find someone else” misses the point.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people may form very strong bonds with particular people, animals, places, objects or routines. The loss of a pet, a trusted teacher, a house, a favorite shop, or a discontinued food can bring grief as deep as other kinds, even if others don’t understand it. A special interest that has to stop (because of illness, cost or a change of circumstances) can be a real loss too. Treating these griefs as real, rather than as overreactions, is a simple kindness.

Thoughts you could try: “This hurts because it mattered to me. That’s enough reason.”

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxwavesqzWaves, and the swing between loss and life

Many people expect grief to move in a straight line, from devastation to recovery. It rarely does. It comes in waves: sudden, strong, then easing, then returning, often set off by a song, a smell, a date or a place.

Psychology

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described five stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance) in On Death and Dying (1969), from her work with people who were dying. The stages became famous, but research on bereaved people hasn’t found that most move through them in order, and Kübler-Ross herself later said they weren’t meant as a neat sequence. They are better treated as some of the feelings people may have, in any order, or not at all.

Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut (1999) proposed the “dual process model.” It describes healthy grieving as moving back and forth between two kinds of focus: loss-oriented (missing the person, crying, remembering) and restoration-oriented (dealing with practical changes, new roles, taking breaks from grief). They suggested this swinging, which they call oscillation, is helpful: too much of either can wear people down. The model is widely used, and research supports parts of it, though it’s a framework rather than a precise prediction.

Philosophy

The Roman Stoic Seneca wrote letters of consolation, including one to a mother named Marcia, still grieving her son years after his death. He accepted that grief is natural, but argued against letting it become a permanent identity, and encouraged her to remember her son with gladness rather than only pain. Some readers find his tone firm; others find it bracing and kind. Either way, the idea that grief and ordinary life can sit side by side is an old one.

In Japanese aesthetics, mono no aware names a gentle awareness that things pass, a sadness that also deepens appreciation. Cherry blossom viewing is often given as an example: the blossoms are loved partly because they fall so soon.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people describe grief that is delayed: they cope practically at first, then feel it strongly weeks or months later when the routine settles. Others describe grief coming out through the body, as exhaustion, sensory overwhelm or shutdown, rather than through tears. A mind that focuses deeply on one thing at a time (see Chapter 9, page 510) may find it hard to switch between “loss” and “life” mode quickly. Having planned, predictable breaks from grief (a set time for a favorite show, a walk on the same route) can make the swing between the two feel safer.

Thoughts you could try: “This is a wave. It came, and it will ease.” “Taking a break from grief is part of grieving.”

The grieving body and brain

Grief isn’t only emotional. It changes sleep, appetite, energy, attention and memory. Some people feel physical pain, like a heavy chest or aching limbs.

Psychology

Neuroscientist and psychologist Mary-Frances O’Connor, in The Grieving Brain (2022), describes grief partly as a learning problem. The brain built a map of the world in which your person (or home, or job) was always there. After a loss, it keeps expecting them, and has to slowly update that map. That may be why it’s so common to reach for the phone to text someone who has died, and why the reality of the loss can hit again and again.

Studies have also linked bereavement with short-term increases in stress hormones, poorer sleep and changes in immune function, and with a higher risk of some health problems, especially in the early months. These are averages across many people, not predictions for you. But they are a good reason to treat sleep, food and medical check-ups as part of grieving, not distractions from it.

Philosophy

C. S. Lewis, in A Grief Observed (1961), written after the death of his wife, noticed how much grief felt like fear: the restlessness, the fluttering in the stomach, the inability to settle. He also described a kind of laziness and invisible blanket between himself and the world. His notebook is valued because it doesn’t tidy grief up. Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) describes how, after her husband died, part of her mind kept acting as if he might come back, keeping his shoes because he would need them. Both writers describe, in their own words, what O’Connor later explained in brain terms.

Through an autistic lens

Grief can lower anyone’s capacity to cope with noise, light, crowds and small talk. For autistic people who already work hard to manage sensory input, a funeral, a busy family home, or a stream of visitors can push them past their limit. Planning a quiet space, ear defenders, a way to leave early, or a role with a clear task (handing out programs, managing the playlist) can make it possible to be present. Some autistic people need very clear information about what happened, in plain words, before their body can begin to settle. Euphemisms like “we lost him” or “she passed” can be confusing, especially for children. Many people who work with grieving children recommend using the words “died” and “dead” with all children for the same reason.

Words you could use: “I want to be at the funeral, and I’ll need a quiet room and a way to leave early. Can you help me plan that?”

Ambiguous and unrecognized grief

Some losses don’t fit the usual shape. There’s no death certificate, no funeral, no casseroles on the doorstep. And yet the grief is real.

Psychology

Family therapist Pauline Boss named “ambiguous loss” (her book of that name came out in 1999). She described two kinds: someone physically gone but psychologically present (a missing person, an estranged family member, a parent who left), and someone physically present but psychologically gone or changed (dementia, serious brain injury, addiction). Ambiguous loss is hard partly because there’s no clear ending to grieve. Boss suggests learning to hold “both/and” thinking: “He is here, and he is gone.”

Kenneth Doka (1989) named “disenfranchised grief”: grief that isn’t openly recognized or supported by others. Examples include the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss, the death of a pet, a loss by suicide or overdose that people avoid talking about, or the death of someone in a relationship others didn’t know about or approve of. Without recognition, people may grieve alone and feel they don’t have the right to.

Philosophy

Rituals in many cultures do something important: they publicly mark a loss, so the community can share it. Jewish mourning practices such as sitting shiva bring people to the mourners’ home for a set time. Mexican Día de Muertos makes space each year to welcome and remember the dead. Where a loss has no ritual, the philosopher’s question becomes a practical one: what would honor this? People can create their own small rituals, and many find that doing so makes the loss feel real and allowed.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people sometimes experience losses others don’t notice: a friendship that ended without explanation, a support worker who left, a school or job where they finally felt understood. Late diagnosis can bring its own ambiguous grief, for the younger self who struggled without knowing why, alongside relief. These griefs deserve recognition too. An explicit ritual, with a clear beginning and end, can help: writing a letter, choosing a day to visit a place, or making a page of memories.

Words you could use: “I know this might not seem like a big loss to others. It is to me, and I’d like you to know.”

Grieving styles and families

People in the same family, grieving the same person, can grieve in very different ways. This is one of the most common sources of hurt after a loss.

Psychology

Terry Martin and Kenneth Doka (2000) described two broad grieving styles on a spectrum. Intuitive grievers tend to feel and express grief through emotion: crying, talking, sharing. Instrumental grievers tend to experience grief more through thinking and doing: solving problems, taking action, staying busy, creating something. Most people are a blend. Neither style is healthier. They noted that the instrumental style is often misread as “not grieving.”

Culture, faith, gender expectations and age shape how grief is shown. Children often grieve in short bursts: sad one minute, playing the next. Some writers on children’s grief describe this as “puddle jumping.” It doesn’t mean they don’t care; it’s how young minds manage big feelings.

Philosophy

Confucian tradition placed great weight on mourning rites for parents, including long periods of observance, partly as a way of expressing gratitude and continuing respect. Other traditions keep grief more private. Comparing them shows that there isn’t one natural way to grieve; there are many forms, and each family blends its own. That can free people from judging each other’s grief by their own family’s rules.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic grief is sometimes misread as coldness: a flat face, a focus on practical details, questions that seem blunt (“What happens to his car?”), or wanting to go to work the next day. These can all be ways of coping with something overwhelming. This is the double empathy problem again: the meaning gets lost between different ways of expressing the same feeling. It runs both ways. An autistic person may also misread a non-autistic relative’s need to talk about feelings as pressure. Saying it plainly helps everyone: “I’m sad. It just doesn’t show on my face.”

Words you could use: “You’re grieving in your way and I’m grieving in mine. Neither of us loves him less.”

Continuing bonds

For much of the twentieth century, a common idea in Western psychology was that healthy grief meant “letting go” and investing in new relationships. Many grieving people never found that fit their experience.

Psychology

Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, in Continuing Bonds (1996), argued that many bereaved people keep an ongoing inner relationship with the person who died, and that this is often healthy. People talk to them, sense their presence, follow their example, keep their belongings, and mark their birthdays. Later research suggests continuing bonds can be comforting or distressing, depending on the person and how the bond is held. Bonds that help a person carry the relationship into a changed life seem helpful. Bonds that keep someone from accepting that the death happened may be harder.

Philosophy

Many traditions honor continuing bonds: ancestor veneration in parts of East Asia and Africa, saints’ days, memorial prayers on anniversaries, and family altars. Philosophers in many times have also written that the dead live on in the lives they shaped, in the habits, values and kindnesses passed on. You don’t need any particular belief about an afterlife to find meaning in carrying someone’s influence forward.

Through an autistic lens

Continuing bonds can fit naturally with autistic strengths: keeping detailed memories, collecting meaningful objects, maintaining a ritual exactly as it was. Continuing a shared routine (the Sunday walk, the same tea) can be grounding. It can also be painful to have routines suddenly lose their partner. Some autistic people find it helps to adapt a routine on purpose (“I’ll still walk on Sundays, and I’ll take his old route”) rather than trying to keep it identical or drop it completely.

Thoughts you could try: “What part of them do I want to carry forward?” “I can change my life and still keep them with me.”

Endings, the in-between, beginnings

Not every loss is a death. Moving, retiring, a new baby, an empty nest, a diagnosis, a breakup, leaving a faith, or coming out can all bring grief, even when the change is wanted.

Psychology

William Bridges, in Transitions (1980), distinguished between change (the outside event) and transition (the inner process of adjusting). He described three phases: an ending (letting go of the old identity or situation), a neutral zone (an unsettled in-between, where the old way is gone but the new one doesn’t feel real yet), and a new beginning. His work comes from coaching and organizational practice, not controlled studies, but many people find it describes their experience well. The neutral zone is often the most uncomfortable, and the most important not to rush.

Research on the transition to parenthood, retirement and migration finds that even welcome changes can bring a drop in well-being for a time, along with loss of routines, roles and relationships.

Philosophy

The Greek philosopher Heraclitus is remembered for the idea that you can’t step into the same river twice, because the river and you are always changing. Buddhist teaching calls this impermanence (anicca), and treats it not as a tragedy but as the nature of things, which, accepted, can bring a certain peace. A well-known Buddhist story tells of Kisa Gotami, a mother who brought her dead child to the Buddha asking for medicine. He asked her to fetch a mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died. She went from door to door and found no such house, and in that search she understood that loss touches every family.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, change itself has a real cost, even when the change is good. Routines, familiar places and predictable people are often how an autistic nervous system stays regulated. A new job, a house move or a new baby can bring a long period of sensory and social overload. That isn’t inflexibility. Planning for transitions helps: visiting the new place first, keeping some routines constant, getting clear information early, and expecting the in-between to be hard. Some autistic people describe needing more recovery time after change than others expect, and burnout can follow a big transition if that time isn’t given.

Words you could use: “This change is good, and it’s also a lot. I need some things to stay the same for a while.”

Professor Puddles

When a change is hard to talk about, writing can come first. This is a quiet place to put the words down, at your own pace, and to send them only if you want to.

Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage or partnership, the loss is everywhere at once: in the empty chair, the second cup you nearly make, his side of the bed, the jobs that were always hers. Many people say the practical side of the first year surprised them as much as the grief did.

The first year

  • The firsts: the first birthday, wedding anniversary, Christmas or Eid, and the anniversary of the death. The days before can be harder than the day itself. Plan something small and kind for each one, even if the plan is to stay in.
  • Belongings: there is no right time to sort clothes and things. Some people do it in the first month; others wait years. You don’t have to do it alone, and you don’t have to do it all at once. One drawer counts.
  • The paperwork: bank accounts, pensions, bills in their name, passwords nobody wrote down. It is tiring and often comes just when you have least energy. Ask one person to sit with you while you do it, and keep a simple list of what is done.
  • The jobs that were theirs: the finances, the yard, the car, remembering birthdays. Learning them is a second loss on top of the first. It is fine to ask family for a hand, to pay someone to do a job, or to let some of them go.
  • The quiet: evenings and weekends are often the hardest. A small routine (a walk at the same time, a weekly call, a class) gives the week some shape.

Grown-up children, from the parent’s side

Your children have lost a parent, and you have lost a partner. It is the same person and a different loss, so you may grieve on different timetables and in different ways. One of you may want to talk about them all the time while another can’t yet. Neither way is wrong.

Many widowed parents also find they are suddenly being checked on: daily calls, questions about eating and sleeping, advice about selling the house. That checking almost always comes from love and fear of losing you too. It isn’t control. It can still feel like being treated as fragile, or as if you can’t run your own life. Saying what helps, and what doesn’t, is kinder than going quiet. A good time to say it is a calm one, and it often helps to start with thanks.

Words you could use: “I love that you check in. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll text you if I need you?” “I’m sad, and that’s normal. If I’m not coping, I promise I’ll tell you.” “I’m not ready to decide about the house. I’ll know when I am.” “Tell me about your dad. I like hearing what you remember.”

And if you are the grown-up child: ask what helps, rather than deciding. “Would you like me to call every day, or is that too much?” leaves your parent in charge of their own life.

Resilience, support and stuck grief

How do most people get through a major loss? And when should we worry?

Psychology

George Bonanno’s research (summarized in his 2004 paper on loss and resilience, and his book The Other Side of Sadness, 2009) found that many bereaved people show resilience: they feel deep sadness, but continue to function and gradually regain a sense of well-being. That doesn’t mean they didn’t love the person, or that they won’t have hard days. It means that coping is the most common outcome, not the exception. Social support, feeling able to express or not express grief as needed, and some flexibility in coping are often linked to better outcomes.

For a smaller group of people, grief stays intense and disabling for a long time. Since 2022, “prolonged grief disorder” has been recognized in both the World Health Organization’s ICD-11 and the American Psychiatric Association’s DSM-5-TR. It describes intense yearning or preoccupation with the person who died, with other symptoms such as feeling part of oneself died, difficulty re-engaging with life, or feeling life is meaningless, lasting well beyond what is expected in the person’s culture and getting in the way of daily life. Including it as a diagnosis was debated, because some feared it might label normal grief. Supporters argue it helps people who are stuck get specific treatment, and there are therapies designed for it.

James Pennebaker’s research on expressive writing (starting in the 1980s) found that writing about upsetting experiences for a few short sessions was linked with modest benefits for some people. Results vary across studies, but it’s a low-cost thing to try.

Philosophy

The Stoic Epictetus advised never saying “I have lost it,” but “I have given it back”: to treat what we love as on loan. Many people find that cold when grieving, and it’s fair to say so. But some find a gentle version helpful: gratitude for the time they had, rather than only pain at its ending. Iris Murdoch, writing about moral attention, suggested that looking justly and lovingly at reality, including painful reality, is itself a kind of goodness. In grief, that might mean letting ourselves see the loss clearly, and also seeing the love clearly.

Through an autistic lens

Support works best when it fits. Many autistic people find “call me anytime” hard to use: it’s vague, and phone calls can be draining. Clear, specific offers work better: “I’ll text on Sunday evenings. Reply with a number from 1 to 5 for how you are, if you like.” If you support an autistic person who is grieving, believe what they tell you about what helps, even if it’s different from what would help you.

Words you could use: “I’d like support, and I find calls hard. Could we text instead?” “It’s been a long time, and it isn’t easing. I want to talk to someone about it.”

Guilt, regret and “if only”

Almost every grieving person asks “what if?” What if I’d called the doctor sooner, visited more, said sorry, noticed the signs? This is so common that it counts as part of grief itself, not a sign that you did something wrong.

Psychologists call these “counterfactual thoughts”: imagining how things might have gone differently. They are the mind’s way of searching for control in a situation that felt out of control. Sometimes there is a real regret to face, and the ideas in Chapter 7 on owning a mistake (page 466) can help: name it, make what repair is possible (a letter, a changed habit, a kindness to someone else), and let it rest. Often, though, “if only” assumes you knew then what you know now. You didn’t. Hindsight makes the road look clearer than it was.

From an autistic point of view, a mind that likes to work things through in detail may replay events many times, looking for the exact point where it went wrong. That can be a way of making sense of things, and it can also become a loop. Setting a time limit (“I’ll go over it for twenty minutes, then do something with my hands”) or writing out the facts once, fully, can help close the loop.

Thoughts you could try: “I’m judging my past self with information they didn’t have.” “I did what I could with what I knew.”

Your part, and only your part

You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people respond to it. You can control small, kind things: what you eat, whether you rest, who you tell, and what you say no to for now. In a hard season, that is enough. Give your energy to people who make the grief lighter, and let anyone who makes it heavier take up less room for a while. Part One covers this in full: your circle of control, and matching energy (page 72).

Putting it together

Grief is love meeting reality. Psychology shows it is common, varied, physical and slow, and that most people find a way to carry it. Philosophy and tradition offer ways to mark it, share it and find meaning alongside it. The autistic lens shows how much grief can be misread when it looks different, and how much change itself can cost.

Some threads run through all three:

  • There is no single right way. Waves, not stages. Doing as well as feeling. Many cultures, many rituals.
  • Bonds can continue. You don’t have to let go to go on.
  • Change is loss, too. Even good change asks something of us, and the in-between is hard.
  • Support helps when it fits. Specific, steady and on the grieving person’s terms.

This book’s idea: a “grief week plan” for heavy seasons: three basics (food, sleep, daylight), one person to check in with, one small ritual, and one thing you’re allowed to say no to.

Worked examples

On your own. After her divorce, Brenda lives alone for the first time in fifteen years. She’s relieved and grieving at once. She notices the hardest time is Sunday evening, when the house used to be busy. She plans one thing for Sunday evenings: a visit with her sister, a class, or a long bath with music. The grief is still there, but Sundays now have a shape.

Partners. Mateo and Lucia lose a pregnancy at eleven weeks. Lucia wants to talk about it; Mateo goes quiet and throws himself into work. Lucia thinks he doesn’t care. When they talk, Mateo explains that he can’t find words and is terrified of making it worse. They agree on a small ritual together, planting a tree, and Lucia also writes to a friend who lost a pregnancy years ago.

Parent and child. Seven-year-old Pippa’s grandmother dies. Her dad uses plain words: “Grandma died. Her body stopped working and it can’t start again.” Pippa plays happily, then cries at bedtime, then asks if she can still have Grandma’s birthday cake recipe. Her dad answers each question simply, and they bake it together.

Friends. When Lyle’s best friend dies, a group of friends set up a monthly dinner on the date. Two years later, they still meet. They don’t always talk about him, but they always toast him.

Coworkers. When a colleague’s husband dies, the team quietly takes over her deadlines for a month. Her manager checks in privately: “Would you prefer we mention it, or not?” She asks them not to make a fuss, but to keep including her in lunch. They do.

Autistic adult. Jamie, who is autistic, loses the café where he has worked happily for eight years when it closes. Friends say he’ll find another job. He’s grieving: the routine, the regulars, the exact way the morning went. He writes a goodbye letter to the café, keeps his apron, and asks for a week before starting to look for work. His support worker helps him visit new places slowly.

Community. After a flood destroys homes in a small town, neighbors grieve houses, photos, gardens and a sense of safety. A local group organizes a memory board where people pin photos of what was lost. It doesn’t replace anything, but it gives the grief a place.

Exercises

1. Your loss map

Draw a circle for a loss you’re carrying. Around it, write the smaller losses that came with it: routines, roles, plans, people, places. Each one may need its own bit of grief.

2. Loss time, life time

For one week, notice when you’re in “loss” mode and when you’re in “getting on with life” mode. If you’re stuck in one, plan a little of the other: a planned time to remember, or a planned break.

3. A letter

Write a letter to who or what you lost. Say what you miss, what you’re grateful for, what you wish you’d said, and what you’ll carry forward. Keep it, share it or burn it, as you choose.

4. Your support list

Write down two people for practical help, two for listening, and one who has been through something like this. Next to each, write how you prefer to be contacted.

5. The transition map

For a big change, write three headings: what ended, what feels unclear now, what is beginning. Add one small thing that could make the in-between easier.

Professor Puddles

If you’d like to think something through privately, you can ask me, at any hour. I can point you to the right page, or to people who can help.

Tool: Ask Professor Puddles spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask

Questions people often ask

How long does grief last?

There’s no set time. The sharpest grief often eases over months, but many people feel waves for years, especially at anniversaries. Most say grief doesn’t disappear; it becomes something they carry more easily.

Is it normal to feel relief?

Yes. After a long illness, a hard relationship or a period of caring, relief is common and doesn’t mean you didn’t love the person. Relief and grief often come together.

Should I take children to the funeral?

It often helps to offer children the choice, after explaining clearly what will happen, and to have a trusted adult with them who can step out if needed. Plain, honest words help more than shielding them completely.

Why am I grieving someone I was estranged from?

Because you may be grieving more than the person: the relationship you hoped for, the chance to repair, or a childhood that wasn’t what you needed. That is ambiguous grief, and it’s real. Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) has more.

I’m autistic and people think I didn’t care. What can I say?

You might say: “I grieve differently. I’m very sad, even though it doesn’t show the way you expect.” If you can, tell people one thing that would help, like “a text is better than a visit.”

What do I say to someone who is grieving?

Simple words are best: “I’m so sorry. I’m thinking of you.” Avoid explaining the loss (“it was meant to be”) or comparing it (“at least…”). Offer something specific, like a meal or a ride, and keep in touch after the first few weeks, when support often fades. Mentioning the person by name, and sharing a memory, is usually welcome. Psychologist Susan Silk and mediator Barry Goldman, in a 2013 newspaper article, offered a simple rule some people find helpful: comfort flows in toward the person closest to the loss, and venting flows out, away from them.

What if it isn’t easing at all?

If after many months the pain isn’t easing at all, daily life feels impossible, you can’t accept that the death happened, or you feel life has no point, please don’t carry that alone. Tell someone you trust how it really is.

Limits

  • This chapter teaches ideas.

The chapter before this one, Self-worth, shame and self-compassion (page 453), may help with the guilt that often comes with grief.

What to remember

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some griefs stay heavy for a long time.

Part Three · Chapter 9

Minds that work differently

How autistic, ADHD, sensory and learning differences work, why none of them is a character flaw, and how people with different minds can meet in the middle.

In this chapter

  1. How to read this chapter
  2. Neurodiversity and disability
  3. Autism and the double empathy problem
  4. ADHD, time and motivation
  5. Senses, overload and needs
  6. Spiky profiles and learning tools
  7. Masking, energy and burnout
  8. Monotropism, flow and transitions
  9. Adjustments that help everyone
  10. Diagnosis, identity and words
  11. Autistic burnout, rest and recovery
  12. Meltdowns and shutdowns
  13. Stimming
  14. Special interests and well-being
  15. Diagnosis later in life
  16. Executive function in daily life
  17. If you have ADHD: the chore tools, made lighter
  18. Demand avoidance, carefully
  19. Face blindness
  20. Non-speaking people and AAC
  21. Disclosure in friendships and dating
