Part Three · Chapter 11

Healing after hurt: repair, forgiveness and old hurts

How hurt heals, why it lingers, how small breaks get mended, what a real apology sounds like, and what forgiveness is and isn’t.

In this chapter

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time
  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts
  3. Telling someone they hurt you
  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it
  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back
  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry
  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises
  8. Going back is a choice
  9. After an affair
  10. If you decide to separate, doing it kindly
  11. Look after the hurt part of you
  12. Putting it together
  13. Worked examples
  14. Exercises
  15. Questions people often ask
  16. Limits

At a glance

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying it doesn’t mean you’re weak. It means it mattered.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks. A real apology names it, owns it and mends it.
  • Forgiveness isn’t going back. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Going back is a choice. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • “Get back in tune before you carry on” and “go back in with a clear sentence” (Part Two, Chapter I, page 139) are repair in small: breaks are normal, and coming back is the skill. Big idea: tune how you send and receive.
  • The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, page 271) includes “look back even when nothing is slipping,” because small hurts repaired early don’t harden into resentment.

Thursday, 2am

It was one sentence, three weeks ago. They’ve probably forgotten it. You haven’t. It plays again, word for word, and you think of all the things you could have said back. You’re tired of carrying it, and you don’t know how to put it down.

This chapter is about what happens after people hurt each other, and how hurt heals. It covers small hurts, like a sharp word or a broken promise, and gives some guidance on bigger ones. It’s written for the person who was hurt and for the person who did the hurting, because most of us are both at different times.

Each idea is looked at through three lenses. Psychology shares what research has found, and says where the evidence is thin. Philosophy brings in thinkers and traditions, from ancient Rome to modern South Africa, retold in plain words rather than quoted. Through an autistic lens offers a perspective from autistic experience: honest about real differences, never a list of deficits, and never a way to diagnose anyone. Then each idea comes back to everyday life. Ideas that are this book’s own are marked This book’s idea.

If that’s your situation, the healing step is safety.

Hurt is real, and healing takes time

A hurt from someone close can feel strangely physical: a punch in the stomach, a lump in the throat. And it can last far longer than the moment that caused it. Understanding why helps you be patient with yourself.

Psychology

Mark Leary and colleagues (1998) studied hurt feelings and found they are closely tied to “relational devaluation”: the sense that someone doesn’t value the relationship, or you, as much as you hoped. That’s why a small comment from a close friend can hurt more than a big insult from a stranger. It isn’t the words; it’s what they seem to say about where you stand.

Brain imaging work by Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman and Kipling Williams (2003) suggested that being left out activates some of the same brain areas as physical pain. Later research has debated how close the overlap really is, so it’s best read as “social pain is real pain” in a loose sense, not as proof that the two are identical.

Emotional memories tend to be stored more strongly than neutral ones, which helps explain why hurts replay. Susan Nolen-Hoeksema’s research on rumination found that going over and over a hurt, without moving toward understanding or action, tends to keep low mood going rather than easing it. Replaying isn’t a character flaw; the mind is trying to solve something. But it often needs a gentler way to finish. See rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions) in the library.

Philosophy

The Roman Stoic Seneca wrote a whole book, On Anger, about how hurt turns to rage. One of his main remedies was delay: wait before you act, because the first rush of feeling exaggerates. The Buddhist image of the second arrow (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth) says something similar: the first arrow is the hurt itself; the second is everything we add by replaying and fighting it.

The 17th-century Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza argued that a painful feeling loses some of its power over us once we form a clear understanding of it. That’s an old version of something psychology has also found: naming and understanding a feeling can soften it (see affect labeling, spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#affect-labeling).

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe processing social events later, sometimes much later. A hurt may not land until hours or days afterward, when there is time and quiet to go back over it. That’s a different timing, not a lack of feeling. It’s also worth knowing for people close to them: “you seemed fine at the time” doesn’t mean the hurt wasn’t real.

Deep, single-track attention (see Chapter 9, page 510) can make replaying a hurt very intense. Some autistic people find it helps to give the loop somewhere to go: writing the event down in order, as facts, then feelings, then questions. Research has also found that autistic children and adults experience bullying and exclusion more often than their peers, so many arrive at adult life carrying a lot of old hurt. That deserves care, not a “just get over it.”

Putting it into everyday life

Name the replay when it comes (“there’s that memory”). Ask what it’s trying to solve. If there is something to do, like a conversation or a limit, plan it. If there isn’t, write it down and set it aside for now. Expect feelings to return on anniversaries and reminders, and treat each return as part of healing, not a step back.

Thoughts you could try: “This hurts because I care where I stand with them. That makes sense.”

Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts.

It can be a relief to learn that close relationships are full of small breaks, and that this isn’t a sign something is wrong. What seems to matter is what happens next.

Psychology

Edward Tronick’s “still face” studies (from 1978) showed how upset babies become when a parent’s face suddenly goes blank, and how quickly they recover when the parent re-engages. Tronick’s later research described ordinary parent and baby play as moving constantly between being in sync, falling out of sync, and repairing. He argued that these everyday repairs teach children that breaks can be mended.

In couples, John Gottman described “repair attempts”: any word or gesture that stops a conflict from escalating, like a joke, a touch or “Can we start again?” In his research, whether repair attempts worked was one of the things linked to how relationships fared. In therapy, Jeremy Safran and Christopher Muran studied “ruptures” between therapist and client; a review by Catherine Eubanks and colleagues (2018) found that repairing these ruptures was linked with better results. Three very different settings, one shared message: breaks are normal, and repair matters.

Philosophy

Kintsugi, a Japanese tradition of mending broken pottery with lacquer mixed with gold, is often used as a picture of repair. The cracks aren’t hidden; they become part of the object’s history. It’s a craft tradition, not a philosophy of relationships, but many people find it a helpful image: a mended bond isn’t a lesser bond.

Confucius is reported in the Analects as saying, in effect, that the real fault is having a fault and not correcting it. The mistake isn’t the break. It’s leaving it unmended.

Through an autistic lens

In mixed autistic and non-autistic relationships, one person may notice a break that the other didn’t register at all. The double empathy idea (Damian Milton, 2012) suggests both sides can miss each other’s signals. So repair works better when it is explicit: “I think something went wrong between us earlier. Did it?” rather than waiting for the other person to pick up hints.

Timing matters too. After a meltdown or shutdown, many autistic people need quiet and recovery before any repair talk; trying to repair too soon can feel like more pressure. A simple “I want to talk about earlier when you’re ready, no rush” leaves the door open. Some people also find repair easier in writing, where there’s time to choose words.

Putting it into everyday life

Go back after small breaks. Keep it short. Name what happened and how you’d like it to be. With children, repair is one of the most powerful things a parent can model. With adults, agree on a phrase that means “let’s restart,” so either of you can use it.

Words you could use: “I want to go back to earlier. I didn’t like how that went, and I care about us.”

Telling someone they hurt you

Many hurts are never mended because the other person doesn’t know about them. Saying so is brave. It also gives the relationship a chance.

Psychology

Sybil Carrère and John Gottman (1999) found that how a conflict conversation starts, gently or harshly, predicted a lot about how it went. Gottman distinguished a complaint (about a specific event) from criticism (about the person’s character). Complaints can be heard; criticism tends to bring defensiveness. Methods like “I-statements” and Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication use the same pattern: what happened, how I felt, what I’d like. There’s good reason to think this helps, though direct trials of exact wordings are limited.

Research on the gap between intent and impact also matters here. People who caused a hurt often see it as smaller and more understandable than the person who was hurt. Roy Baumeister and colleagues (1990) asked people to write about times they had angered someone and times someone had angered them; the stories were told very differently. Knowing this can make it easier to explain, rather than assume the other person already knows.

Philosophy

Aristotle thought anger isn’t always wrong. He wrote that the good person is angry at the right things, with the right people, in the right way, at the right time, and for the right length of time. That’s a high bar, but it’s a useful one: the goal isn’t no anger; it’s anger used well.

The American poet and essayist Audre Lorde, in a 1981 talk on anger, argued that anger in the face of real injustice carries information and energy, and that what matters is turning it toward clear, honest speech rather than swallowing it. Telling someone “that hurt” is a small, personal version of that idea.

Through an autistic lens

Plain, specific statements tend to work best for everyone, and especially between people with different communication styles. Many autistic people say they would much rather be told directly that they hurt someone, and how, than be given hints or a cold shoulder they can’t decode. If you are telling an autistic person they hurt you, be specific: what was said or done, and what you’d like instead.

The other way round, many autistic people have been told they’re “rude” or “hurtful” without being told what they actually did. That is confusing and painful. It’s fair to ask: “Can you tell me exactly what I said that hurt? I want to understand.” And telling someone in writing is a completely valid choice.

Putting it into everyday life

Write your sentence first: what happened, how you felt, what you’d like. Choose a calm time. Say why you’re telling them (“because I want us to be okay”). Then listen to their side, which may surprise you. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps you shape the sentence.

Words you could use: “I need to tell you something that’s been on my mind. When you…, I felt… I’d like… Can we talk about it?”

zqaxunderstandingx11xhealingxxapologyqzA real apology names it, owns it, and mends it

Everyone has heard an apology that made things worse. “I’m sorry you feel that way.” “Sorry, but….” A good apology is a skill, and it can be learned.

Psychology

Roy Lewicki, Beth Polin and Robert Lount (2016) tested six parts of an apology: expressing regret, explaining what went wrong, acknowledging responsibility, saying you’ll do better, offering to repair, and asking for forgiveness. More parts generally worked better, and the two that mattered most were acknowledging responsibility and offering repair. Asking for forgiveness mattered least.

Karina Schumann’s research found that people often hold back on apologies or make them defensive, and that defensive elements, like excuses or blaming the other person, make apologies less effective. Peter Kim, Donald Ferrin and colleagues (2004) found that apologies tend to help more after mistakes of skill (“I got it wrong”) than after breaches of honesty (“I lied”), where actions matter more than words. The site has more in what research says about apologies (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict).

Philosophy

The philosopher Nick Smith, in I Was Wrong (2008), described what he called a “categorical” apology: naming exactly what you did, accepting blame, recognizing the harm and the value that was broken, showing regret, and committing to change and to repair. He argued that many public apologies fall short because they leave out one or more of these.

The Jewish idea of teshuvah, often translated as repentance or “returning,” was set out by the medieval philosopher Moses Maimonides in steps: recognizing the wrong, regretting it, saying it out loud, and resolving not to repeat it. He wrote that the fullest repentance is shown when you face the same situation again and choose differently. He also taught that wrongs against another person need to be put right with that person, not only privately.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people value precise apologies. “Sorry if anything I did upset you” can feel meaningless, or even dishonest, because it doesn’t say what happened. “I interrupted you three times in the meeting, and that wasn’t fair” is clear and believable.

Facial expression and tone can differ in autistic people, and an apology may be judged as “not sincere” because the face doesn’t look sorry enough. That’s a misreading. Words and actions are better evidence than faces. Some autistic people also apologize very often, out of years of being told they got things wrong. If that’s you, it’s worth saving “sorry” for things that were actually your doing, and using “thank you for waiting” instead of “sorry” for the rest.

Putting it into everyday life

Use four parts: what I did, it was mine, how it affected you, what I’ll do now. Leave out “but” and “if.” Don’t ask to be forgiven right away; let the other person have their response. Then keep your word, because that’s what makes the apology real. Apology languages (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) has more.

Words you could use: “I said… That was my doing, not yours. I can see it hurt. From now on I’ll… Is there anything else that would help?”

Professor Puddles

An apology lands best when it’s plain: what happened, that it was yours, and what you’ll do now. Rewind the talk can help you find those words.

Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back

Forgiveness is one of the most misunderstood words in the language. People feel pressured to forgive, or afraid that forgiving means giving in. Separating out what it is, and isn’t, often makes it easier to think about.

Psychology

Researchers usually define forgiveness as a change inside the person who was hurt: less resentment and wish for revenge, and sometimes more goodwill. Michael McCullough and colleagues measured it as a drop in “avoidance” and “revenge” motivations over time. Everett Worthington distinguished “decisional” forgiveness (deciding not to seek revenge) from “emotional” forgiveness (the feelings actually changing), which often comes later.

Robert Enright developed a process model of forgiveness used in therapy, and Worthington developed a shorter method called REACH. A review by Nathaniel Wade, Worthington and colleagues (2014) found that forgiveness programs helped people forgive more than no program, and modestly reduced depression and anxiety. But forgiveness isn’t always good for you. James McNulty’s research (2008, 2011) found that in some marriages, being very forgiving of a partner who kept behaving badly was linked with the bad behavior continuing. Forgiveness works best alongside limits, not instead of them.

Philosophy

Hannah Arendt, in The Human Condition (1958), argued that forgiveness is what makes it possible to live with the fact that actions can’t be undone. Without it, she thought, we would be stuck forever with the consequences of a single deed. She paired it with promising, which helps us live with an unpredictable future. Forgiveness releases the past; promises steady what comes next.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, wrote in No Future Without Forgiveness (1999) that forgiveness doesn’t mean pretending or forgetting, and that it goes together with telling the truth about what happened. The philosopher Martha Nussbaum, in Anger and Forgiveness (2016), questioned forgiveness that works like a transaction, where the wrongdoer must grovel first, and argued for moving on to generosity and to what will make things better. And the writer Jean Améry, a survivor of torture in the Holocaust, defended the right to resentment, as a refusal to let a terrible wrong be smoothed over. These views don’t fully agree, and that’s useful: there is more than one honest way to respond to being wronged.

Many religious traditions have their own teaching on forgiveness, including Christianity, Islam, Judaism and Buddhism, often with great depth. If your faith matters to you, it can be a rich source here; and nobody should use faith to push you to forgive before you’re ready.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, a strong sense of justice is part of who they are. Forgiveness can feel like saying something unfair was fair. Separating the two helps: you can say “that was wrong” clearly and permanently, and still let go of the wish to get even.

Some autistic people also describe very vivid long-term memory for events, which can make it harder to “just forget.” That’s fine: forgiveness has never required forgetting. Nor does it require pretending to feel fine, which for many autistic people is another kind of masking. Honest forgiveness might sound like: “I’m not angry at you anymore. I still remember, and I still need you not to do it again.”

Putting it into everyday life

Write what forgiveness would mean, and what it wouldn’t. Consider decisional forgiveness (“I won’t seek revenge”) as a first step, and let the feelings follow when they’re ready. Keep your limits. And remember that you’re allowed not to forgive yet, or ever, for some things. See forgiveness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict#forgiveness) in the library.

Thoughts you could try: “I can let go of the wish to get even without saying it was okay.”

You can heal even if they never say sorry

Some apologies never come. The person has died, moved on, can’t understand, or won’t. Healing can still happen.

Psychology

James Pennebaker’s research, starting in the 1980s, found that writing about difficult experiences for fifteen to twenty minutes on a few days in a row was linked, on average, with small improvements in well-being and even health. Later reviews, such as one by Joanne Frattaroli (2006), found the effects real but modest, and not for everyone. Writing seems to help most when it moves toward understanding: making a story with a beginning, middle and end.

Crystal Park’s work on meaning-making (2010) describes how people recover after painful events by finding a way to fit what happened into their understanding of life. Leslie Greenberg and colleagues have studied “unfinished business” in emotion-focused therapy, where clients speak to an imagined person they couldn’t speak to in life; studies suggest it can help resolve lingering hurt. See expressive writing (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#expressive-writing) in the library.

Philosophy

Epictetus taught that it isn’t things themselves that disturb us so much as our judgments about them. That can sound cold when someone has truly wronged you, and it doesn’t mean the wrong didn’t matter. But it points to a place where you have some power: the meaning you give to what happened, and the story you tell about yourself afterward.

The French philosopher Paul Ricoeur wrote about “narrative identity”: we understand ourselves partly through the stories we tell about our lives. Healing often involves rewriting a chapter, not erasing it. “The time I was betrayed” can slowly become “the time I learned what I need from people.”

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people find writing an easier way to process than talking, so letters, journals and notes can be especially helpful tools. Writing facts in order first, then feelings, can bring structure to a confusing event.

Because deep focus can turn into long loops, it may help to set limits: fifteen minutes of writing, then a planned switch to something restoring, like a favorite interest, music or time outdoors. Many autistic adults also find that autistic-led communities and peer support help them make sense of past hurts, especially hurts from being misunderstood for years.

Putting it into everyday life

Write an unsent letter. Tell the story to someone safe. Ask, “What do I want this to mean for me now?” If writing makes you feel much worse, stop, and tell someone you trust instead.

Thoughts you could try: “My healing doesn’t need their permission or their understanding.”

Trust comes back in small, kept promises

Trust breaks fast and mends slowly. That isn’t unfair. It’s how trust works: it’s a prediction, and predictions need evidence.

Psychology

John Rempel, John Holmes and Mark Zanna (1985) described trust in close relationships as built from predictability (you can anticipate what they’ll do), dependability (you can count on them when it matters) and faith (a deeper confidence about the future). Predictability and dependability come from repeated experience, which is why small, kept promises matter so much.

Gottman’s later work, in The Science of Trust (2011), argued that trust is built in many small moments where one person chooses to turn toward the other’s needs. For serious breaches like affairs, Donald Baucom, Kristina Coop Gordon and Douglas Snyder developed a couples approach that moves through three stages: dealing with the impact, understanding how it happened, and deciding how to move forward. Early studies were encouraging, though small.

Philosophy

The philosopher Annette Baier (1986) described trust as accepting that you are vulnerable to someone else’s goodwill. That explains why betrayal hurts so much: you lowered your guard, and it was used against you. Rebuilding trust means asking someone to lower it again, which they’re entitled to do slowly.

Onora O’Neill, in her 2002 Reith Lectures, argued that the aim should be trustworthiness, not just trust. We should trust people who show they’re worthy of it, and check the evidence. That’s a fair stance after a hurt: watch what someone does over time.

Through an autistic lens

Predictability is often at the heart of trust for autistic people. Saying what you will do, and then doing it, builds trust. Vague promises (“we should get coffee sometime”) can erode it, especially if taken literally. Many autistic people say they trust people who are consistent and clear, even if they’re not especially warm on the surface.

Some autistic people have learned, painfully, that taking people at their word left them open to being used. If that’s your history, it’s sensible to rebuild trust step by step, with small tests first. That’s not paranoia. It’s O’Neill’s point about checking trustworthiness, applied to your own life.

Putting it into everyday life

If you broke trust: offer openness before you’re asked, keep small promises, and don’t set a deadline for the other person to “be over it.” If you were let down: say what would help you feel safer, and notice whether it happens. Trust can come back, but it comes back by evidence.

Words you could use: “I can’t undo it. I can be someone you can count on from now on, and I know that will take time.”

Going back is a choice.

After a hurt, there are more than two options. You can repair and continue, change the shape of the relationship, take some distance, or end it. Each can be right in different situations.

Psychology

McNulty’s research (above) suggests that forgiving and carrying on as before can backfire when the other person keeps doing harm. Evan Stark’s work on coercive control (2007) describes patterns of controlling, isolating and frightening behavior that are not ordinary conflict, and where couple-based “repair” is not appropriate.

Family estrangement is more common than many people think. Karl Pillemer’s large survey research in the United States, described in Fault Lines (2020), found that many people have cut off contact with a relative, and that some later reconnect. Estrangement isn’t automatically a failure, and reconnection isn’t automatically right; both can be healthy choices. See Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts).

Philosophy

Immanuel Kant argued that we have duties to ourselves as well as to others, including keeping our own dignity. The philosopher Thomas Hill (1973) built on this, arguing that letting yourself be treated as less than an equal can itself be a moral failing, which he called servility. Protecting yourself isn’t selfish. It’s respect for a person who also matters: you.

Arthur Schopenhauer’s parable of the porcupines (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth#porcupines), who huddle for warmth but prick each other when too close, suggests that some relationships work best at a particular distance. Finding that distance isn’t rejection. It can be what makes the relationship possible.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people find limits easiest to keep when they’re stated plainly and in advance: “I won’t lend money again.” “If voices are raised, I will leave the room and come back later.” Clear limits are easier for everyone to understand.

Research suggests some autistic people are more vulnerable to being taken advantage of, often because they are honest and take people at their word. Years of masking and trying to please can also make it hard to say no. If that sounds familiar, written scripts for saying no, and a trusted person to check things with, can help. None of this is a weakness; it’s a reason to build in support.

Putting it into everyday life

Ask: Is it safe? Has the hurt stopped? Do I want this person in my life, and in what shape? If you choose distance, you can still wish them well. If you choose to repair, you can keep limits.

Words you could use: “I’ve forgiven you, and I’m keeping some distance for now. That’s what I need.”

After an affair

Finding out about an affair is one of the most painful things that can happen in a relationship. Many people describe it like a shock: they can’t sleep, replay every detail, swing between rage and numbness, and ask the same questions again and again. That is a normal reaction to a big hurt, not a sign of going mad. The partner who had the affair often feels shame, fear and grief too, and may want to “move on” long before the hurt partner can.

Couples can and do recover from affairs, and some decide to part. Both can be done well. In a small study of six couples by Gordon, Baucom and Snyder (2004), a structured couples therapy that moved through the three stages described in the trust section above (the impact, understanding how it happened, deciding how to move on) left most couples less distressed and the hurt partners more forgiving. It was a small study, so treat it as a hopeful sign, not a promise.

  • If you had the affair: end it clearly and say so. Answer questions honestly, without pushing graphic detail on someone who hasn’t asked for it. Expect the same questions more than once. Trust comes back through kept promises over months, not one big apology, and you can’t set the pace.
  • If you were hurt: you don’t have to decide anything yet. Look after your body: sleep, food, a walk. Choose one or two people to talk to, rather than everyone. Understanding why it happened can help, and understanding is not the same as excusing.
  • Both of you: agree a time and a place for the conversation when it is too hot to have in passing, and a limit on how long it runs. A few agreed weeks can also help you decide whether to try at all.

A made-up example. Hattie finds messages on Benedict’s phone. For three weeks they barely sleep. Benedict ends the affair, tells Hattie he has, and stops asking her to “just get past it.” They agree one evening a week for her questions, so the questions don’t take over every evening. They keep the weekly evening going for six months. A year on, Hattie says it is not the marriage they had, but a more honest one. Other couples, with the same care, decide to part, and that is a real outcome too.

Words you could use: “I need to ask you things, and I need true answers, even when they hurt.” “I know I can’t set how long this takes. I’m not going anywhere while you decide.” “I don’t know yet if I can stay. I need time, and I need you to give it.”

If you decide to separate, doing it kindly

Sometimes the healing step is an ending. Deciding to separate isn’t a failure of effort or of love; sometimes two people have honestly grown in different directions. How you part still matters a great deal, especially to children and to the years of contact that may follow.

  • If one of you is unsure, a few agreed weeks of trying, aimed at deciding rather than fixing, can help you both feel you made the choice with care.
  • Tell children together if you safely can, in simple words, without blame: what is changing, what is staying the same, and that it isn’t their fault. Never ask a child to choose, carry messages or keep secrets between homes. Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) has more.
  • Write decisions down: money, the home, the children’s weeks. Family mediation is often calmer and cheaper than going to court, where it is safe to use.
  • Agree one short sentence for family and friends, so neither of you has to defend yourself at every gathering.
  • Grieve it. Even a kind, mutual ending is a loss. Chapter 8 (page 475) applies here too.

A made-up example. Isla and Magnus have been unhappy for years and finally agree to separate. They sit their two children down together and say, “We’re going to live in two homes. We both love you, that won’t change, and this isn’t because of anything you did.” They agree the children’s weeks between themselves, in writing, and a rule that they never discuss money in front of the children. It is still sad. It is also calmer than the last three years were.

Mediation and joint conversations are not the right tools when one person is afraid.

Look after the hurt part of you

Hurt isn’t only a thought. It’s carried in sleep, appetite, muscles and energy. Healing goes better when the body is looked after too.

Psychology

Kristin Neff’s research on self-compassion describes three parts: kindness toward yourself, remembering that suffering is part of being human, and mindful awareness of your feelings. Mark Leary and colleagues (2007) found that people higher in self-compassion tended to react less harshly to unpleasant events. Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills (1985) described how social support can buffer the effects of stress. Sleep matters too: lack of sleep makes emotional reactions stronger.

George Bonanno’s research (2004) found that many people show resilience after loss or trauma: they have a hard time, but keep functioning and recover more than expected. Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun (1996) described “post-traumatic growth,” positive changes some people report after struggle. But research by Patricia Frazier and others (2009) found that people’s reports of growth didn’t always match measured change. Growth can happen; it isn’t guaranteed, and you’re not failing if it doesn’t.

Philosophy

Buddhist practice includes metta, loving-kindness, which is traditionally offered to yourself as well as to others. Seneca wrote letters of consolation to grieving friends, mixing gentle comfort with reminders that pain eases with time. Epicurus thought that friendship was one of the greatest protections against suffering.

There’s a famous saying, often traced to Nietzsche, that what doesn’t destroy us makes us stronger. Philosophy and research both suggest a gentler version: what doesn’t destroy us sometimes teaches us something, and sometimes just hurts, and both are allowed.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, sensory care is a central part of healing: quiet, dim light, familiar food, soft clothes, a weighted blanket, movement or stimming. These aren’t extras; they help the nervous system settle. After a long period of strain, many autistic adults describe autistic burnout, and research by Dora Raymaker and colleagues (2020), done with autistic co-researchers, found that recovery usually needs real rest and fewer demands, not just a weekend off.

Many therapies can be adapted with clearer language, written summaries, and a predictable structure.

Putting it into everyday life

Pick one act of care each day. Talk to yourself the way you’d talk to a friend. Notice your body’s needs, and meet one of them. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) and the Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) can help in the moment.

Thoughts you could try: “Anyone would be shaken by this. I’m going to look after myself the way I’d look after a friend.”

Putting it together

Hurt is real, and it lingers because something mattered. Breaks happen in every close relationship, and repair is what builds safety. Telling someone they hurt you gives them a chance to mend it. A real apology names what happened, owns it and offers repair. Forgiveness is an inner letting-go that doesn’t require forgetting, excusing or going back. You can heal without the other person. Trust comes back by evidence, in small kept promises. Going back is a choice. And all of it goes better when you look after your body and your heart.

The three lenses fit together. Psychology shows that repair and self-compassion help, and warns that forgiveness without limits can backfire. Philosophy offers many honest responses to wrong, from Arendt’s forgiveness to Améry’s resentment, and reminds us that self-respect is a duty too. The autistic lens asks for clarity: specific apologies, plain limits, explicit repair, and patience with different timing.

This book’s idea: the healing path has four separate doors, and you choose which to open, in any order: understand it (what happened and what it meant), tell it (to them, or to someone safe), release it (let go of revenge, when you’re ready), and decide (repair, reshape, distance or end). You don’t need to go through all four, and nobody else gets to choose for you.

Worked examples

  • Partners after a hurtful remark: In an argument, Gavin mocks Rosie’s family. The next morning he says: “What I said about your mom was cruel and untrue. I was angry and I aimed to hurt. I’m sorry. I won’t bring your family into our arguments again.” Rosie says she needs a day. He gives it, without sulking.
  • Friends after a missed event: Abena didn’t come to her best friend’s birthday, with no message. Her friend says: “I was hurt you didn’t come or text. I’d like to understand.” Abena explains she was overwhelmed and ashamed, and apologizes for not saying anything. They agree that a one-word text, “can’t,” is always better than silence. See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • A parent and a teenager: A mom reads her 15-year-old’s messages without asking. Her son is furious. She apologizes specifically, explains her worry, and agrees a new rule: she will ask before looking, except if she believes he is in danger, and she’ll tell him if she ever does. Trust comes back slowly over the next months. See For teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens).
  • Coworkers: A manager criticizes a colleague in front of the team. The colleague asks for a private conversation: “When I was corrected in front of everyone, I felt embarrassed. I’d like feedback one-to-one.” The manager agrees and apologizes in the next team meeting. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).
  • Adult siblings after a will: Two brothers haven’t spoken since their mother’s will divided things unevenly. One writes: “I miss you more than I care about the money. Could we meet for coffee, and not talk about the will yet?” The other isn’t ready, and says so. The door stays open. See Family rifts.
  • An autistic and a non-autistic friend: After a group dinner, Saffron (autistic) learns that her honest comment about a friend’s cooking stung. She asks exactly what hurt, then says: “I told the truth about the sauce, but I said it in front of everyone. That was the bit that wasn’t kind. Next time I’ll tell you privately.” Her friend says it helps to know her honesty is meant as respect.
  • On your own, after a long-ago hurt: Lennox was bullied at school. Twenty years later, a smell or a sound can still take him back. He writes the story down, reads it to his sister, and starts to see the boy he was with kindness. The bullies never apologized. His healing went ahead anyway.
  • When going back isn’t safe: After a breakup, Lia’s ex keeps messaging, alternating apologies with threats. Here, healing means safety and support, not repair.

Professor Puddles

Trust comes back in small promises that are kept. A short daily check-in gives those promises a regular, gentle place.

Workpaper WP-13: The 90-second daily check-in spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-13

Exercises

1. The three-line message

For a hurt you want to raise, write three lines: what happened (facts only), how you felt (one or two feeling words), what you’d like. Read it aloud. Remove any word that describes the other person’s character.

2. The apology check

Next time you apologize, check for four parts: what I did, it was mine, how it affected you, what I’ll do now. Then check for two things to leave out: “if” and “but.”

3. What forgiveness would and wouldn’t mean

Make two lists for one hurt. “If I forgave, it would mean…” and “It would not mean….” Notice whether forgiving now feels more possible, or whether you need more time. Both are fine.

4. The unsent letter

Write to the person who hurt you, saying everything. Don’t send it. Put it away for a week, then read it and notice what has changed in you. If it stirs up too much, stop, and talk to someone instead.

5. The trust ledger, the kind way

If you’re rebuilding trust, choose one small, specific promise each week, such as “I’ll text if I’m running late.” Keep it. At the end of a month, notice together what has changed. This book’s idea: the point is evidence, not a score.

6. The three questions

For a relationship after a hurt, ask: Is it safe? Has the hurt stopped? Do I want this person in my life, and in what shape? Write your honest answers, and let them guide your next step.

7. One kind act for the hurt part

Each day for a week, do one small act of care for yourself, and say one kind sentence to yourself, like “That was hard, and I’m getting through it.”

Questions people often ask

Do I have to forgive to heal?

No. Many people find forgiveness helps them heal, and many heal without forgiving some things. Healing is about you being able to live well again. Forgiveness is one possible path, not a requirement.

They apologized. Why do I still feel hurt?

An apology opens the door, but feelings take time to catch up, and trust needs evidence. It’s normal to still feel hurt for a while. If you keep feeling hurt because the same thing keeps happening, that’s important information.

How do I apologize when I don’t think I did anything wrong?

Don’t apologize for something you don’t believe was wrong; it won’t sound real. You can say: “I didn’t mean to hurt you, and I can see that I did. Can you help me understand?” Often, after listening, you find a part you can honestly own.

What if I keep apologizing for the same thing?

Then the apology isn’t the problem; the pattern is. Look at what gets in the way of changing. Chapter 6 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change) covers how change works.

Should I tell someone they hurt me if they might get angry?

If you fear anger in the ordinary sense, it may still be worth trying, gently and at a calm time.

Can a relationship be better after a break?

Often, yes. Many people say that a well-repaired break made them trust each other more, because they learned they could get through it. But it isn’t guaranteed, and it isn’t the measure of whether you did it “right.”

How do I help a child heal after being hurt by another child?

Listen first, take it seriously, and help them name what happened and how they felt. Help them plan what to do next time, and tell the school or adults in charge if it continues. Show them repair in your own life, too.

Limits

  • The research here is real but has limits: many studies are small, and many are from Western countries. Treat it as a guide.
  • The philosophers and traditions are retold in plain words, and their ideas are fuller and more debated than a few sentences can show.
  • The autistic lens is a perspective, not a description of every autistic person, and not a way to diagnose anyone.
  • This chapter isn’t therapy.
  • Repair is for relationships where both people are safe.

Next: Chapter 12, Helping others well (page 588). Before: Chapter 10, Values, meaning and a good life (page 534). All chapters are in the contents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/contents).

What to remember

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying a hurt says more about how much it mattered than about any weakness in you.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks, and a real apology names what happened, owns it and offers to mend it.
  • Forgiving and going back are separate choices. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Going back is a choice. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

Part Three · Chapter 12

Helping others well: support without fixing, boundaries, and not burning out

How to help someone without taking over, by asking what they need, listening first, caring without drowning and keeping kind limits, and how to keep going without burning out.

In this chapter

  1. Ask what kind of help they want
  2. Listening is a kind of help
  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power
  4. Care without drowning in their feelings
  5. Your limits make your help last
  6. Notice when you’re running on empty
  7. Don’t wait for someone else to step in
  8. Let other people help you too
  9. Putting it together
  10. Worked examples
  11. Exercises
  12. Questions people often ask
  13. Limits

At a glance

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing it for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last. Caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • One owner per job: sharing the care (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) works because help lasts when it is shared and named. Caregivers burn out when everything is “just helping” and nobody else owns a job. Big idea: see the whole load.
  • How much are you carrying? (Part Two, Chapter III, page 205) helps you notice when you are running on empty before you snap or stop.

Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend is telling you about her awful week. You have five good ideas before she’s finished her first sentence. You share them all. She goes quiet, then says, “Yeah, maybe.” You both hang up feeling a bit worse, and you’re not sure why.

This chapter is about helping other people well. It covers everyday help, like supporting a friend through a bad week, and harder help, like caring for someone who is ill or being there for someone in a very hard place. Its main message is simple: the best help usually starts with asking, listens before it acts, respects the other person’s choices, and comes from a helper who is looking after themselves too.

Each idea is looked at through three lenses. Psychology shares what research has found, and where it’s uncertain. Philosophy brings in thinkers and traditions on care, duty and kindness, retold in plain words, in paraphrase rather than quotation. Through an autistic lens offers a perspective from autistic experience: real differences, described as differences, without stereotypes and without diagnosing anyone. Where it matters most, an ADHD lens does the same. Then each idea comes back to everyday life. Ideas that are this book’s own are marked This book’s idea.

Ask what kind of help they want

“Help” sounds like one thing. It’s actually several, and the mismatch between what’s offered and what’s wanted causes a surprising amount of hurt between people who care about each other.

Psychology

Researchers often sort support into a few kinds. James House (1981) described emotional support (care, comfort), instrumental support (practical help, like money or a ride), informational support (advice, facts) and appraisal support (helping someone make sense of things). Carolyn Cutrona and Daniel Russell proposed an “optimal matching” idea (1990): support helps most when it fits what the situation and the person need. The evidence for exact matching is mixed, but the everyday lesson holds up: the wrong kind of help can feel like not being heard.

Research on advice, including work by Erina MacGeorge and colleagues, suggests that advice tends to be received better when it was asked for, when the person giving it is seen as caring, and when it doesn’t imply the other person is incapable. Unwanted advice can come across as criticism, even when it’s meant as love.

Philosophy

The political philosopher Joan Tronto, in Moral Boundaries (1993), described care as having several phases: noticing that someone needs care, taking responsibility for it, actually giving the care, and then checking how the care was received. That last phase is easy to skip. Asking “did that help?” is part of caring, not an extra.

The disability rights movement popularized the phrase “Nothing about us without us”: decisions about people should involve those people. It began in politics and public policy, but it fits everyday help too. The person being helped is the expert on what they need.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people say that explicit questions are a relief: “Do you want ideas or just to vent?” takes the guesswork out, for both the helper and the person being helped. It’s a clear example of how a practice that suits many autistic people turns out to help almost everyone.

It also works the other way. Some autistic people show support mostly through information and solutions, because that’s how they would want to be helped. When this is misread as cold, it helps to say the intention aloud: “I’m giving you ideas because I care. Tell me if you’d rather I just listen.”

Putting it into everyday life

Ask before helping. Offer a short menu: ideas, listening, practical help, company. Afterward, check how it landed. And if you need help yourself, tell people which kind you’d like; it makes their job much easier.

Words you could use: “Do you want ideas, a listening ear, or a hand with something?” “Was that helpful, or would something else be better?”

Listening is a kind of help

Many helpers feel they haven’t really helped unless they did something. But being truly listened to can change how a person feels, how clearly they think, and what they decide.

Psychology

The psychologist Carl Rogers argued, from the 1940s on, that people tend to grow and find their own way when they experience empathy (being understood), unconditional positive regard (being accepted) and genuineness from the person helping them. Reflective listening, saying back what you heard, comes from his work. Motivational interviewing, developed by William Miller and Stephen Rollnick, names the “righting reflex”: the helper’s urge to fix and correct, which often makes people defend the very thing they’re unsure about.

Research by Guy Itzchakov, Avraham Kluger and colleagues found that people who were listened to well felt less anxious and defensive, and thought about their own views in a more balanced way. Marsha Linehan, who developed dialectical behavior therapy, described levels of validation, from simply paying attention up to communicating that someone’s reaction makes sense given their situation. Validating a feeling doesn’t mean agreeing with every action. The library covers active listening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication) and validation (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#validation-in-conversation).

Philosophy

The French philosopher Simone Weil wrote that real attention to someone who is suffering is rare and precious, a kind of generosity. Iris Murdoch similarly saw attention as the heart of moral life. Both suggest that listening isn’t a lesser form of help. It may be the purest one.

The Jewish philosopher Martin Buber described two ways of relating: “I-It,” where we treat others as objects or problems, and “I-Thou,” where we meet them as whole persons. Listening fully is a way of meeting someone as a “Thou.” The site retells it in I and Thou (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth).

Through an autistic lens

Listening doesn’t have to look a certain way. Many autistic people listen best without eye contact, or while moving, doodling or fidgeting. It can be helpful to say: “I’m listening, even though I’m not looking at you.” For the person being listened to, what matters is being understood, not the look of the listener.

Many autistic people also show they’ve understood by sharing a related experience of their own. This is sometimes misread as making it about themselves, when it’s often meant as “I get it; this happened to me too.” Saying so helps: “I’m telling you this because I think I understand. Tell me more about yours.”

Putting it into everyday life

Listen for longer than feels natural. Sum up what you heard and check it. Name the feeling if you can (“that sounds so frustrating”). Hold your advice until it’s asked for, or ask whether it’s wanted. The Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins) guide has more on tender conversations.

Words you could use: “Let me check I’ve got it. You’re saying… and you feel… Is that right?”

Fixing it for them can take away their power

When someone we love is struggling, taking over can feel like the most loving thing to do. Sometimes it is. But often, helping someone do it themselves is the deeper kind of help.

Psychology

Niall Bolger, Adam Zuckerman and Ronald Kessler (2000) studied couples where one partner was preparing for a very stressful exam. Support that the stressed person noticed was sometimes linked with feeling worse, perhaps because it reminded them they needed help. Support that the partner gave without it being noticed (“invisible support”) was linked with feeling better. This is one study type among many, and visible support is often welcome, but it shows that help can carry a hidden message about competence.

Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) finds that people do better when they feel autonomy: that their choices are their own. Help that supports someone’s own choices tends to work better than help that controls. Research on “overparenting,” such as work by Chris Segrin and colleagues, has linked very hands-on parenting of young adults with lower confidence in coping on their own. In the 1960s, Stephen Karpman described a “drama triangle” of persecutor, victim and rescuer; it’s a model from transactional analysis rather than a tested finding, but many people recognize the rescuer trap in it.

Philosophy

Maimonides, the medieval Jewish philosopher, described eight levels of giving. He placed at the top helping someone become self-sufficient, such as through a loan, a partnership or a job, so they no longer need charity. The highest help, in this view, is the help that leaves someone stronger.

John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), argued that adults should be free to make their own choices about their own lives, even ones others think unwise, as long as they don’t harm others. Immanuel Kant argued that we have a duty to help others, but also a duty to respect them as people who set their own goals. A line often given from the Tao Te Ching says, in spirit, that the best leaders are barely noticed, and when the work is done the people say “we did it ourselves.”

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people have had a lot of help that wasn’t asked for: being spoken for, having decisions made for them, being “managed.” That history makes autonomy especially important. Asking, rather than assuming, is respectful: “Do you want me to make that call, or would you like me to sit with you while you do?”

At the same time, some tasks really are harder for some autistic people, such as phone calls, forms or noisy shops. Practical help with those isn’t taking power away when it’s asked for. The question isn’t “help or no help.” It’s “whose choice is it?” Body doubling, where someone simply works alongside you, is one kind of help many autistic and ADHD people find useful, precisely because it supports rather than replaces.

Putting it into everyday life

Before you act, ask: “Would you like me to do that, or help you do it?” Offer a scaffold rather than a rescue: a checklist, a second pair of eyes, company while they do it. Let people make choices you wouldn’t make, when it’s their life. And if someone asks you to take over something, that’s their choice too.

Thoughts you could try: “The goal is for them to feel more able, not for me to feel more useful.”

Care without drowning in their feelings

Some people feel others’ pain so strongly that helping becomes exhausting. Understanding the difference between empathy and compassion can make caring sustainable.

Psychology

Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki (2014) described two different responses to someone else’s suffering. In “empathic distress,” you feel their pain as if it were yours, which can be overwhelming and make you want to withdraw. In “compassion,” you feel warmth and concern and want to help, from a steadier place. In their brain-imaging studies, the two engaged different networks, and short compassion training seemed to increase positive feelings and reduce distress. These are lab studies, so real life may be messier.

Charles Figley wrote about “compassion fatigue” in helping professions (1995). The psychologist Paul Bloom, in Against Empathy (2016), argued that empathy works like a spotlight: intense, but narrow and biased toward people like us. He argued for what he called rational compassion. Not everyone agrees with Bloom, but the distinction is useful. See empathic distress and compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) in the library.

Philosophy

Buddhist teaching describes four qualities often practiced together: loving-kindness, compassion, joy in others’ happiness, and equanimity. Equanimity isn’t indifference. It’s the steadiness that lets compassion last without being swept away. The four are meant to balance each other.

The Scottish philosopher Adam Smith, in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), noted that we can never directly feel what another person feels; we imagine ourselves in their place. That’s a humble reminder: you don’t need to feel exactly what they feel to care well, and you can’t anyway.

Through an autistic lens

There’s an old stereotype that autistic people lack empathy. Research doesn’t support it as a general rule. Studies distinguish “cognitive empathy” (working out what someone feels) from “affective empathy” (feeling for them). Many autistic people describe strong, even overwhelming, feelings for others, alongside difficulty reading unfamiliar signals. Geoffrey Bird and colleagues (2010) found that lower empathy scores were linked with alexithymia, which some autistic people have and many don’t, rather than with autism itself. And research on the double empathy problem has found that non-autistic people are often poor at reading autistic people, too.

For autistic people who feel others’ distress intensely, the compassion skills here can be especially useful: noticing when empathy tips into overwhelm, and stepping back to steady yourself, perhaps with sensory regulation, before stepping back in.

Putting it into everyday life

Notice when you’re taking on someone’s feelings as your own: you can’t sleep, you feel their dread. Shift toward compassion: “I care about you, and I’m steady.” Build in recovery after heavy conversations. If you work in a helping job, look for supervision or peer support, which many professions offer for exactly this reason.

Thoughts you could try: “This is their pain. I can be warm and steady beside it without making it mine.”

Sugarfoot

Helpers need looking after too. Check your own tank now and then. It only takes a few minutes.

Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

zqaxunderstandingx12xhelpingxxboundariesqzYour limits make your help last

Helping without limits often ends in exhaustion or resentment, and then in not helping at all. Limits are what make long-term care possible.

Psychology

Vicki Helgeson and Heidi Fritz described “unmitigated communion” (1998): focusing on others to the point of neglecting yourself. In their research it was linked with more distress, unlike healthy care for others, which was linked with well-being. The difference wasn’t how much people cared. It was whether they also cared for themselves.

Research on stress and resources, such as Stevan Hobfoll’s conservation of resources theory (1989), suggests that people under strain try to protect their remaining energy, time and support, and that losing resources tends to lead to more losses. That fits a common experience: once a helper is depleted, things fall apart faster. See boundaries (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#boundaries) and saying no (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#saying-no) in the library.

Philosophy

Kant described the duty to help others as an “imperfect” duty: a real duty, but one with room to choose when, how and whom to help. You’re not required to help everyone all the time. That’s not a loophole; it recognizes that you are a person with your own life too.

Aristotle described generosity as a middle path between stinginess and wastefulness: giving the right amount, to the right people, in the right way. Giving everything away until you have nothing isn’t the highest generosity in his view. It’s a different kind of mistake.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people use energy accounting to manage their days. One well-known picture is “spoon theory,” created by Christine Miserandino (2003) to explain life with chronic illness and adopted by many disabled and autistic people: you have a limited number of spoons each day, and each task costs some. Social and sensory demands can cost a lot. Knowing your budget makes limits easier to set and explain.

Plainly stated limits often work best: “I can talk until 8, then I need quiet.” Some autistic people have spent years over-giving in order to be accepted. If that’s you, scripts can help: “I can’t do that, but I can do this.” A clear no is often kinder than a reluctant yes.

Putting it into everyday life

Decide your limits before you’re asked, when you’re calm. Offer a smaller, sustainable version rather than a flat no. Notice resentment: it’s often a sign a limit has been crossed. And remember that a helper who lasts is worth more than one who burns bright and burns out.

Words you could use: “I can’t do every night. I can do Tuesdays, and I’ll be fully there.”

Professor Puddles

Your limits keep your help going for longer. When you need to say “not this time,” Say no kindly helps you find the words, with something to offer instead.

Tool: Say no kindly: make your scripts spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals

Notice when you’re running on empty

Burnout isn’t a personal failing. It’s what tends to happen when demands stay high, resources stay low, and recovery doesn’t come.

Psychology

Christina Maslach’s research describes burnout as three things: exhaustion, cynicism or distance from the people you serve, and a sense of not achieving anything. The World Health Organization includes burnout in its classification of diseases as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. Family caregivers face similar strain. Reviews by Martin Pinquart and Silvia Sörensen (2003) found that caregivers reported more stress and depression than non-caregivers, with dementia care especially hard. Regular breaks, practical help from others and time with people in the same position can ease the load, though effects vary.

The site’s library covers burnout (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) and caregiver strain (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#caregiver-strain). The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) can help you check where you are today.

Philosophy

Seneca, in On the Shortness of Life, argued that people give their time away carelessly and guard their money closely, when time is the more precious of the two. Many religious traditions build rest into life, like the Jewish Sabbath; the rabbi and philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel described it (1951) as a kind of palace built in time: a day when we stop making things and simply live.

Audre Lorde, writing while living with cancer, described caring for herself as an act of survival, not selfishness. It’s often quoted in a shortened form, but the original point was serious: for people carrying heavy loads, rest is part of being able to keep going.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic burnout, as described in research by Dora Raymaker and colleagues (2020) with autistic co-researchers, is a long-lasting exhaustion with loss of skills and lower tolerance for stimulation, often linked to years of masking and life demands that exceed capacity. It overlaps with work burnout but isn’t the same. Many autistic people are also caregivers, including autistic parents of autistic children, which can double the load.

For autistic helpers, protecting recovery time, reducing sensory load and dropping masking where it’s safe can be essential, not optional. Connecting with other autistic caregivers can also help.

Through an ADHD lens

Many helpers with ADHD say yes fast, because helping is interesting, urgent and kind, and only later see how full the week already was. Then the crash comes all at once. A default sentence buys time without saying no: “I’d like to help. Let me check my week and come back to you tonight.” The other side matters too: people with ADHD often need practical help (a reminder, someone to sit with them while they do the forms) and feel ashamed to ask. Asking for that kind of help is a skill, not a failure.

Putting it into everyday life

Check your energy daily. Learn your early warning signs: snapping, numbness, dread, getting ill. Ask for one specific kind of help. Take small breaks before you need big ones. If you’re a caregiver, contact a caregivers’ organization; Caring for someone you love (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers) has more.

Thoughts you could try: “Rest is part of the job. I can’t pour from an empty cup, and I don’t have to.”

Sometimes the person who needs help is in a very dark place. Being with someone who is thinking about ending their life is frightening, and you don’t need to be an expert. If you’re worried, it’s okay to ask plainly, in your own words. A review by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found that asking doesn’t increase suicidal thoughts, and may reduce them. Thomas Joiner’s interpersonal theory of suicide suggests that feeling like a burden and feeling you don’t belong matter a great deal, which is why a sentence like “everyone would be better off without me” deserves a gentle, direct response. Listen without arguing, stay with them, and help them tell someone else they trust. Afterward, look after yourself too, because it’s a lot to carry.

Philosophy

The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas described the face of another person as a call to responsibility: before any theory, the other’s vulnerability asks something of us. In Albert Camus’s novel The Plague, Dr. Rieux keeps working through an epidemic not as a hero but because it’s simply what decency requires. Both point to a plain kind of courage: showing up.

Through an autistic lens

Not every hard moment looks the same. Autistic meltdowns and shutdowns are responses to overload, not tantrums or bad behavior. Helpful responses usually mean less: fewer words, lower light and noise, space, no touching without consent, and time. Asking “Do you want me to stay, or give you space?” and accepting the answer is often the best help.

Don’t wait for someone else to step in

In public, it’s easy to assume someone else will help. Knowing why that happens makes it easier to be the one who does.

Psychology

John Darley and Bibb Latané’s experiments (1968) found that people were less likely to help when they believed others were also present: responsibility spreads thin. A review by Peter Fischer and colleagues (2011) found the effect is real but weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies. A 2020 study by Richard Philpot and colleagues, using real CCTV footage of public conflicts in three countries, found that in most cases at least one bystander did step in, and the more bystanders there were, the more likely someone helped. So people help more than the old story suggests, and you can be one of them.

Bystander training often teaches “the five Ds,” from the organization Right To Be: distract, delegate (get someone else, like staff), document (if safe, and give the record to the person affected), delay (check in afterward) and direct (speak up, if safe). These give options that don’t require confrontation.

Philosophy

The philosopher Peter Singer (1972) asked whether you would wade into a shallow pond to save a drowning child, even if it ruined your clothes. Almost everyone says yes. He argued that when we can prevent something bad at small cost to ourselves, we ought to. People debate how far that argument reaches, but in everyday life the point is plain: small help matters.

The Stoic Hierocles pictured each of us at the center of circles, with family, neighbors, fellow citizens and all of humanity further out, and urged us to draw the circles inward. The site retells it as The circles of Hierocles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth#circles). The Russian thinker Peter Kropotkin argued in Mutual Aid (1902) that cooperation, not just competition, is a major force in nature and human life.

Through an autistic lens

Unclear public situations can be hard to read for anyone, and some autistic people find it especially hard to know whether, and how, to step in. Having a plan in advance, like one of the five Ds, turns a confusing moment into a known script. Delegating (“I’ll get the driver”) or checking in afterward are good options for people who find confrontation overwhelming.

Autistic people can also be on the receiving end of public hostility for looking or acting differently. Being a quiet ally, like sitting nearby or asking “Are you okay?” can make a big difference.

Putting it into everyday life

Decide now which of the five Ds you’d be most comfortable using. Safety first: you don’t need to put yourself at risk. Even small acts, like asking “Are you okay?” or getting help, break the bystander effect for everyone around you.

Words you could use: “Hey, are you okay?” “You in the blue coat, can you get help? I’ll stay here.”

Let other people help you too

Many good helpers are poor receivers. They feel awkward, indebted or weak when others help them. But giving and receiving are two halves of the same thing.

Psychology

The sociologist Alvin Gouldner (1960) described the “norm of reciprocity”: across cultures, people tend to feel they should return help. Relationships where help flows only one way can start to feel uneven. Francis Flynn and Vanessa Bohns (2008) found that people asking for help greatly underestimated how many others would say yes. In other words, people are more willing to help than we think.

Research by Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton (2008) found that spending money on others was linked with more happiness than spending it on yourself. Studies of volunteering and giving support, such as work by Stephanie Brown and colleagues (2003), have linked giving with better well-being and health, though these are mostly correlations. The upshot: letting someone help you often gives them something good too.

Philosophy

The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre, in Dependent Rational Animals (1999), argued that dependence on others is a normal part of every human life, from infancy to old age, illness and disability, and that we need “virtues of acknowledged dependence”: being able to receive help gracefully as well as give it. Aristotle thought the best friendships were mutual, each person wishing good for the other. The Southern African idea of ubuntu, often summed up as “a person is a person through other people,” sees help as the fabric of community, not a debt.

Through an autistic lens

Asking for help can be especially hard if past requests were dismissed, or if you were told you were “too much.” Many autistic people find it easier to ask in writing, and to ask for something specific: “Could you make the phone call to the dentist for me?” Reasonable adjustments at work or school are a form of help too, and asking for them is a right in many places, not a favor.

The disability rights idea of interdependence fits here: nobody is fully independent, and needing support isn’t a failure. It’s how people live.

Putting it into everyday life

Say yes to small offers. Ask for specific help. Thank people, and let that be enough, without rushing to repay. Notice how it feels to let someone in. And when you’re the helper again, remember how it felt to receive.

Words you could use: “Yes, please. That would really help.” “I’m not good at asking, but could you help me with one thing?”

Putting it together

Good help starts by asking what kind is wanted. Listening is help in itself. Helping someone do it often beats doing it for them. Compassion lasts longer than empathic distress. Limits make help sustainable. Burnout is a signal to share the load, not a failure. In public, small acts break the bystander effect. And receiving help is part of the same circle as giving it.

The three lenses agree. Psychology shows that matched, autonomy-respecting support works best and that helpers need care too. Philosophy, from Maimonides to Tronto to MacIntyre, sees the best help as the kind that leaves people stronger and acknowledges that we all depend on each other. The autistic lens asks for explicit questions, respect for autonomy, and recognition that care has many forms.

This book’s idea: before helping, run through ASK: Ask what kind of help they want; Support their choice rather than replacing it; Keep yourself going, with limits and rest. Then check afterward how it landed.

Worked examples

  • A friend after a breakup: Beatrix asks, “Ideas or venting?” Her friend says venting. Beatrix listens, sums up, and at the end offers one practical thing: “Want me to come with you to get your stuff from his place?” See Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends).
  • Partners with a stressful job: When Ravi has a hard day, his partner sometimes gives “invisible” support: quietly making dinner and taking the dog out, without making a fuss. On other days, Ravi asks to talk, and gets full attention.
  • A parent and a teenager with exam stress: Instead of making a studying schedule for her daughter, a mom asks: “Would a schedule help? Want to make one together?” The daughter makes her own, and sticks to it better.
  • Adult children caring for a parent: Three siblings share care for their dad. One does appointments, one does shopping, one does weekend visits. They meet monthly to check how everyone’s coping, including themselves. See Caring for someone you love.
  • A coworker in distress: A colleague mentions she hasn’t slept in days and feels hopeless. Her teammate asks gently whether she’s thinking about harming herself. She says no, but she’s struggling. They look up the workplace’s employee assistance line together, and the teammate checks in the next day. See At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work).
  • Roommates: When one roommate’s mother dies, the others make a simple schedule for meals and leave a note: “No need to reply. We’re here.” They ask her what would help with the funeral, rather than deciding for her. See Grief (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief).
  • An autistic adult helping a friend: When a friend is upset, Alys’s instinct is to send articles and solutions. She has learned to ask first: “Do you want links, or just company?” Her friend sometimes says “links please,” and loves them.
  • A stranger in trouble: An older man falls in a supermarket. Several people look. Imran says: “You in the red jacket, can you get a staff member? I’ll stay with him.” Within a minute, three people are helping.
  • On your own, receiving help: After surgery, Hazel finally accepts a neighbor’s offer to walk her dog. The neighbor loves it. Six months later, Hazel walks the neighbor’s dog when he’s ill.

Exercises

1. The help menu

Write four kinds of help on a card or in your phone: ideas, listening, practical help, company. Next time someone shares a problem, offer the menu.

2. Two minutes of listening

In one conversation, listen for two minutes without advice or stories of your own. Then sum up what you heard and ask if you got it right. Notice what happens.

3. Do it, or help them do it?

For one week, each time you feel the urge to fix something for someone, ask yourself, and then them, “Would you like me to do this, or help you do it?”

4. Your helping budget

List the people you help regularly and roughly how much time and energy each takes. Mark which feel sustainable and which don’t. For one that doesn’t, plan a smaller, kinder version. This book’s idea.

5. Your early warning signs

Write down three signs that you’re heading toward burnout, like snapping, numbness or dread. Share them with someone you trust, and ask them to tell you if they notice.

7. Your bystander plan

Choose which of the five Ds (distract, delegate, document, delay, direct) you’d feel safest using. Imagine using it in a specific place you often go, like a bus or a store.

8. Say yes

Accept the next offer of help, or ask for one small, specific thing. Notice how it feels, and how the other person responds.

Questions people often ask

What if they don’t know what kind of help they want?

That’s common, especially when someone is overwhelmed. Offer one small, concrete option: “Can I make you a cup of tea and just sit with you?” You can adjust from there.

What if I can see they’re making a mistake?

You can say so once, kindly, if you think it matters: “Can I share a worry?” Then respect their choice. Adults have the right to make choices you wouldn’t, as long as nobody is in danger.

How do I help someone who won’t accept help?

Keep the door open without pushing. “I’m here if you change your mind” matters.

Is it selfish to set limits on helping?

No. Limits are what let you keep helping. A helper who burns out can’t help anyone.

What if I say the wrong thing to someone who is struggling?

Most people worry about this. What matters most is that you showed up and listened. If you’re unsure what to say, “I’m here” is enough.

I’m a professional helper. Does this apply to me?

Yes. Professional helpers face the same risks of empathic distress and burnout. Supervision, peer support and real time off are part of good practice. For counselors, coaches and group leaders (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors) has more.

How do I help a child learn to help others?

Show them: let them see you ask, listen, help and accept help. Notice and name it when they help someone. And teach them to ask “Do you want help?” first.

Limits

  • Much of the research here is from Western countries, and some of it is correlational. Treat it as a guide.
  • The philosophers and traditions are retold in plain words. Their ideas are fuller and more debated than a few sentences can show.
  • The autistic lens is a perspective, not a description of every autistic person, and not a way to diagnose anyone.
  • This chapter isn’t therapy.

Before: Chapter 11, Healing after hurt (page 560). Next: Chapter 13, Anger (page 612). All chapters are in the book’s contents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/).

What to remember

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing a problem for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last, and caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.
