Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterward, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. Putting it together
  11. Worked examples
  12. Exercises
  13. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  14. Helping someone else
  15. Questions people often ask
  16. Limits

At a glance

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed. What you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it. Calming the body, then putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments, helps more.
  • Anger that frightens or hurts someone has become harm. Repair starts with owning it.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 48) works because anger rises in the body first. Slowing the body is what makes the words possible. Big idea: read your state first.
  • “Let a comment land before you react” and “Notice, name, decide” (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) are the step back this chapter describes: look from the outside, then choose.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother texts: “Can’t take Mom to the hospital on Thursday after all. Sorry!!” It’s the third time this month. Your jaw sets and your thumbs start typing fast: “TYPICAL. You never…” Your heart is pounding, your face is hot, and the message is nearly sent.

Why does anger arrive so fast, and feel so right in the moment? Why do we get angriest with the people we love most? Is it better to let it out or hold it in? And when does anger stop being a feeling and start being harm? This chapter looks at anger in full: what it is for, what it does in the body and the mind, what helps in the moment and afterward, and where the line is.

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses. Psychology tells us what researchers have found, and where the evidence is limited. Philosophy shows how thinkers from many traditions have understood the same questions. Through an autistic lens looks at each idea from the point of view of autistic people. It is a perspective, not a diagnosis, and it often shows that the usual advice needs adjusting. Where it matters most, an ADHD lens does the same.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Anger is a signal about something that matters

Anger is one of the most common feelings people have. It tends to show up when something seems unfair, when a goal is blocked, when a line has been crossed, or when something we care about seems under threat. Like other feelings, it is a fast message: “Pay attention. Something here matters.”

Psychology

Many feelings push us away from a problem: fear makes us want to escape, sadness makes us want to withdraw. Anger is different. In a major review, Carver and Harmon-Jones (2009) brought together evidence that anger is an “approach” feeling: it pushes us toward the thing in the way, to change it or remove it. That is why anger can be useful: it gives energy to stand up for yourself or for someone else. It is also why it can go wrong, because the push can land on the wrong target, or be far bigger than the problem.

Anger is also shaped by how we read a situation. The same event (a friend arriving late) can feel annoying or completely fine depending on whether we think they didn’t care, or that the bus broke down. Psychologists call these readings appraisals. We return to them in Step back.

Philosophy

Aristotle did not think anger was simply bad. In the Nicomachean Ethics, he wrote that anyone can become angry, and that is easy; but to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right reason and in the right way is not easy. He thought someone who never got angry, even at real wrongs, was missing something too. Much later, the poet and essayist Audre Lorde, in her 1981 talk “The Uses of Anger,” described anger at injustice as full of information and energy, and argued that it should be listened to rather than silenced.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe a strong sense of fairness and of rules being kept. When rules are broken, promises are changed without warning or someone is treated unjustly, the anger can be strong and long-lasting. That isn’t over-reacting. It often reflects real values: honesty, consistency and fairness. It can help to name the value (“I’m angry because the plan changed and nobody told me, and being told matters to me”), so others hear the reason rather than only the heat.

Thoughts you could try: “What is this anger trying to protect?” “Is this the right person, the right size and the right moment?”

Anger often guards a softer feeling

Anger often arrives first, and loudest. Underneath it, there may be hurt, fear, shame, embarrassment, grief or plain exhaustion. Anger can feel safer than those feelings, because it feels strong rather than exposed.

Psychology

Emotion researchers sometimes distinguish a “primary” feeling (the first reaction) from a “secondary” one (a reaction to the first). Anger is often secondary: we feel hurt, and then angry that we were hurt. Tiredness, hunger, pain and stress also make anger more likely, because they lower the threshold for any strong feeling. Chapter 2 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress) calls this the tank: when it is already full, a small thing makes it overflow. Sleep matters here too. In a daily study, Gordon and Chen (2014) found that people reported more conflict with their partner after nights of poor sleep.

Philosophy

Buddhist teaching names aversion or hatred as one of the “three poisons,” alongside greed and confusion. But many Buddhist teachers also stress gentleness toward our own anger. The Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh, in his book Anger (2001), compared it to a crying baby: not something to fight or throw away, but something to hold, calm and listen to until we understand what it needs.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people find it hard to tell feelings apart, or to know what they are feeling until it is very strong. This is sometimes called alexithymia. A review by Kinnaird and colleagues (2019) found it in about half of autistic participants, compared with a much smaller share of non-autistic people, though it is not universal. If you can’t easily find the hurt or fear under anger, that isn’t a failing. Body clues (“my chest is tight,” “I’m very hot”) and simple scales (“I’m at seven out of ten”) can work better than feeling words.

Words you could use: “I’m angry, and I think underneath I’m scared.” “I don’t know what’s under it yet. I just know I’m at an eight.”

Anger rises in the body fast

Anger is a whole-body event. The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, muscles tense, the face may flush and the voice gets louder. This is the body preparing to act. It can happen within seconds, often before we have had a clear thought.

Psychology

When the stress system is highly activated, careful thinking, listening and seeing another point of view all get harder. Chapter 2 (page 341) calls this being flooded. In this state, people say things they don’t mean and hear things that weren’t said. That is why trying to win an argument while flooded rarely works: the parts of us that would help are temporarily turned down. Learning your own early signs (a clenched jaw, a hot neck, talking faster) gives you a few seconds of warning before you’re fully flooded.

Anger matters for physical health too. In a review of long-term studies, Chida and Steptoe (2009) found that anger and hostility were linked with a higher risk of later heart disease, though the link weakened in studies that took account of habits such as smoking. And in a review of studies by Mostofsky, Penner and Mittleman (2014), the risk of a heart attack or stroke was higher in the two hours after an outburst of anger, especially for people already at risk. These are links, not proof that anger alone causes heart disease, but they are one more reason to learn to settle the body.

Philosophy

William James (1884) argued that the body comes first: we notice our body’s changes, and that noticing is the feeling. Later research suggests it is more of a two-way street, with the mind interpreting what the body is doing. Either way, his insight is useful for anger: if the body is part of the feeling, then changing what the body is doing (breathing, posture, moving away) can change the feeling too.

Through an autistic lens

For some autistic people, sensory overload (noise, light, crowds, an unexpected touch) feels a lot like anger: hot, urgent and hard to think through. What looks like a “temper” may be a body that has had too much input. Turning down the input (a quiet room, headphones, dimmer light, fewer words) often helps more than talking it through. Noticing body signals can also be harder for some autistic people, which makes building a few clear outside cues (“when I start pacing, I need a break”) especially useful.

Through an ADHD lens

Many people with ADHD describe anger that arrives fast and big, then drops away just as fast, sometimes leaving them puzzled that everyone else is still upset. A review by Shaw and colleagues (2014) found that trouble bringing strong feelings back down is common in ADHD at every age. It isn’t a choice or a flaw in character, and it isn’t a free pass either.

What helps is planning for the speed: a pause line short enough to say in three words (“Back in ten”), a rule to wait before sending anything, and fewer sparks in the setup. A forgotten job is a common spark, so a written list with one owner per job takes a lot of heat out of a home. If you live with someone with ADHD, talk on a calm day about how a flash that is over in a minute can feel very different from the person on the receiving end.

Thoughts you could try: “My body is ready for a fight. I don’t have to have one.” “Is this anger, or is it too much noise?”

Professor Puddles

Anger moves faster than words. The Calm-Down Kit is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxhotxminutesqzIn the hot minutes: slow the body first

When anger is high, the most useful thing is usually not to solve the problem, but to settle the body enough to think. Problems wait. Sharp words are hard to take back.

Psychology

A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) compared activities people use to manage anger. Those that calm the body (such as slow breathing, muscle relaxation, mindfulness and yoga) reduced anger and aggression. Those that rev the body up showed little or no benefit for anger. Slow breathing with a longer out-breath, unclenching hands, lowering the shoulders and moving to a quieter place are all simple versions of the same thing.

Taking a break also works best when it isn’t a walk-out. A break with a time to come back (“I’ll come back at eight”) tells the other person you aren’t abandoning the conversation. See time-outs (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict) in the library.

This book’s idea: The Stop, Out, Back plan. Stop talking or typing. Breathe out, long and slow, and step out of the room if you can. Say when you’ll be back. Write your own version on a calm day, with your early sign and your exact words, and keep it somewhere you’ll see it. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) can help.

Philosophy

The Roman Stoic Seneca wrote a whole work, On Anger, in the first century. Unlike Aristotle, he thought anger was almost always harmful and should not be trusted. One of his most practical pieces of advice was that the greatest remedy for anger is delay: wait, and the first rush passes. Many traditions share the advice to count, breathe or sleep on it before acting.

Through an autistic lens

An autistic meltdown is not the same as an angry outburst, although from outside they can look alike. A meltdown is an overwhelming loss of control, often after a build-up of stress, sensory load or change. It isn’t chosen and it isn’t manipulation. In the moment, reasoning, questions and touch usually make it worse. What helps is fewer words, less noise and light, space, and safety for everyone. Talking can come later. A shutdown, where someone goes quiet, still and unable to respond, is another form of overwhelm, and needs the same patience. See Chapter 9 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds).

Words you could use: “I’m too angry to talk well. I’ll come back at eight.” (to someone in a meltdown) “You’re safe. I’ll be right here. No need to talk.”

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxventingqzLetting rip doesn’t empty it

A very old idea says anger builds up like steam, and you have to let it out or it will burst. It is a popular idea, and it feels true in the moment. But when researchers have tested it, it hasn’t held up well.

Psychology

In a well-known experiment by Bushman (2002), people who had been made angry were asked to hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who had annoyed them. Afterward, they felt angrier and acted more aggressively than people who were distracted or simply sat quietly. Going over and over what happened, sometimes called rumination, has a similar effect: it keeps anger switched on long after the moment has passed. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who were made to dwell on a provocation for a while were later more aggressive toward someone who only mildly annoyed them, a pattern called displaced aggression. That doesn’t mean anger should be swallowed. Pushing a feeling down and pretending it isn’t there has its own costs: in research by Gross and John (2003), people who habitually held their feelings in tended to do worse in their relationships and well-being than people who habitually rethought what had happened. The middle path is to calm the body, then think and talk about it, when you can do that without re-heating it.

Philosophy

The Stoic teacher Epictetus said that it is not things themselves that disturb us, but our judgments about them. Rumination is, in a sense, re-making the judgment again and again: “How dare they… how dare they…” Each time, the anger is fed. Stepping out of the loop doesn’t mean deciding the event didn’t matter. It means not letting one moment take over the whole day.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people use stimming (repeated movements or sounds, like rocking, flapping or humming) to settle strong feelings. In interviews by Kapp and colleagues (2019), autistic adults described stimming as a way of managing overwhelming emotions and sensations. That is very different from venting at a person: stimming calms the body, rather than rehearsing the anger. It deserves to be allowed, not stopped. Some autistic people also find their thoughts “loop” on an injustice for a long time. A clear, written plan for what will happen next can help the loop close.

Thoughts you could try: “Going over this again is feeding it.” “I’ll come back to this tomorrow, at a set time.”

Step back and look from the outside

Once the body has settled a little, it helps to see the moment from further away. Not to excuse what happened, but to see it more completely.

Psychology

In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people were provoked by a rude partner and then asked to think about it in one of two ways: by reliving it through their own eyes, or by imagining watching it from a distance, “like a fly on the wall.” The fly-on-the-wall group felt less angry and acted less aggressively. This built on earlier work by Kross, Ayduk and Mischel (2005), who asked people to recall a time they had been angry: asking “why” from a distanced point of view helped people make sense of it without stirring the anger up again, while reliving it through their own eyes did not. Rethinking what happened (“Maybe she was rushed, not rude”) also helps. Gross (1998) described this kind of rethinking, called reappraisal, as a way of changing a feeling early, before it has fully taken hold. Gross and John (2003) found that people who often rethink upsetting moments in this way tend to do better in relationships and well-being.

Seeing the other side matters because anger stories tend to be one-sided. When Baumeister, Stillwell and Wotman (1990) asked people to write about a time they made someone angry and a time someone made them angry, the stories differed in a telling way. As the angry person, people described the harm as more serious and longer-lasting; as the one who caused it, they described it as more understandable and more finished. Both sides are usually leaving something out.

Philosophy

The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, in his private Meditations, often reminded himself that when someone wronged him, he should ask what that person believed was good or bad, and that this would usually bring understanding rather than anger. He also reminded himself how short life is, and how small most quarrels look from far enough away.

Through an autistic lens

Much anger between autistic and non-autistic people comes from misreading, in both directions. A direct comment may be heard as rude when it was meant as help. A hint may be missed and then taken as being ignored. Research such as Crompton and colleagues (2020) suggests that communication can flow well between people who share a way of communicating, and break down more easily across different styles. When you step back, it helps to ask: “Did we just read each other differently?”

Thoughts you could try: “If I were watching this from across the room, what would I see?” “How would they tell this story?”

Say it, don’t throw it

Anger usually carries a message worth hearing. The trouble is the delivery. When we’re calmer, we can keep the message and drop the blow.

Psychology

Communication researchers have long suggested putting a hard feeling into a simple shape: what happened, how it affected you, and what you’re asking for. Thomas Gordon (1970) called these “I-messages”; Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication uses a similar pattern of observation, feeling, need and request. Starting gently matters too. A complaint about one event (“You canceled again”) is easier to hear than a criticism of the whole person (“You always let everyone down”). See Chapter 4 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication) and I-statements (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication) in the library.

Being assertive is different from being aggressive. Assertive means saying clearly what you think and need while respecting the other person. Aggressive means pushing your needs at someone else’s expense. Holding everything in, then exploding, is often a mix of the two.

Philosophy

The philosopher Martha Nussbaum, in Anger and Forgiveness (2016), argues that ordinary anger often contains a wish for payback: for the other person to suffer. She suggests a better kind, which she calls “Transition-Anger”: outrage that quickly turns forward, to “What can be done about this?” rather than “How can they be made to pay?” That forward turn is what a calm, clear request does.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people are sometimes told they sound angry when they aren’t: a flat tone, a direct sentence or a lack of smiling can be misread. It can help both sides to say it plainly: “I’m not angry, I’m just being direct.” And for autistic people who are angry, a written message, sent after a pause, can be easier than a face-to-face talk. That is a fair choice, not avoidance.

Words you could use: “When ___ happened, I felt ___. What I’m asking for is ___.” “I’m not angry, I’m being direct. Can I say it plainly?”

Sugarfoot

Say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it easier for the other person to hear you.

Tool: Cool-down corner: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

After anger, repair

Everyone gets angry, and most people sometimes say or do things in anger that they regret. What happens next matters a great deal.

Psychology

Conflict itself is normal in close relationships. Couples researchers such as John Gottman have long stressed what they call repair: coming back after a rupture and mending it (see repair attempts, spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships, in the library). A good repair after anger is short and specific. It names what you did, without “but,” acknowledges how it landed, and says what you will do differently. If the anger had a fair point in it, you can still make that point, separately and later. Chapter 11 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing) looks at apologies and repair in detail.

For children, repair after a parent’s anger is especially important. It shows them that strong feelings can be survived, that relationships can be mended, and that the anger wasn’t their fault. See Repair after you’ve scared a child (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents).

Philosophy

In Jewish tradition, teshuvah (often translated as “return” or “repentance”) is a path for making amends. As the medieval philosopher Maimonides set it out, it includes recognizing the wrong, regretting it, resolving not to repeat it and, where another person was harmed, going to them to make things right. Many other traditions have similar steps. They share one idea: saying sorry is not the end of repair, but the start.

Through an autistic lens

Clear, specific apologies tend to work well for autistic people: what happened, that it was wrong, and what will happen next time. Vague apologies (“Sorry if you were upset”) can feel confusing or unfair. Autistic people may also need time before they are ready to talk about a conflict. Asking “Would now or later be better to talk about earlier?” respects that.

Words you could use: “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry. Next time I’ll take a break before I answer.”

When anger becomes harm

Anger is a feeling. Some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them. It is important to be clear about the difference, because “I was just angry” can be used to excuse things that should not be excused.

Psychology

Signs that anger has become harmful include: hitting, pushing, grabbing or restraining; throwing or breaking things, especially near people; threats; shouting that leaves others frightened; and using anger, or the fear of it, to control what someone does, wears, spends or who they see. A household where people “walk on eggshells” is a warning sign even if nobody has been hit. Abuse is not only anger: much of it is about control, and some controlling people seem calm.

For people who want to change their own anger, help works for many. In a review of 96 studies, Saini (2009) found that psychological treatments for anger, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy and skills training, were generally effective, though results varied. An earlier review by Del Vecchio and O’Leary (2004), of 23 controlled studies with adults, found medium to large benefits across different anger treatments, with cognitive approaches helping long-standing anger and relaxation helping in-the-moment anger.

Philosophy

John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), argued that the only good reason to limit someone’s freedom is to prevent harm to others. Our feelings, including anger, are our own business. Our actions, when they harm or frighten other people, are not. That is a simple line, and it holds in homes as well as in societies.

Through an autistic lens

A meltdown is overwhelm, not a choice, and an autistic person in meltdown deserves understanding and safety. At the same time, being autistic never makes harm to others acceptable, and plans can be made on calm days to keep everyone safe (a quiet space, a signal, someone to call). Autistic people can also be on the receiving end of other people’s anger and control, and their reports deserve to be believed. Difference never makes someone deserve harm.

Words you could use: “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help.” “I’m frightened of how they get. I need to talk to someone.”

Putting it together

Anger is a fast, physical signal that something matters: fairness, a goal, a boundary, safety. It often guards softer feelings, and it is made more likely by tiredness, stress and too much input. In the hot minutes, the body comes first: slow it, step away with a time to come back. Letting rip and going over it tend to feed anger; calming down, stepping back and seeing the other side tend to ease it. When we’re calmer, we can say what made us angry in words, and repair any harm we did. And when anger frightens or hurts someone, it has become harm.

  • Feel it, don’t follow it. The feeling is allowed. The action is a choice.
  • Body first, words second. Settle, then speak.
  • Keep the message, drop the blow. What happened, how it felt, what you’re asking for.
  • Repair is normal. It’s not a defeat. It’s what keeps relationships going.
  • Safety first, always. If anyone is frightened, getting safe comes before working it out.

Worked examples

Siblings: the canceled hospital trip

Back to the opening. You put the phone face down and walk around the block, breathing out long. You notice what’s under the anger: you’re exhausted, and scared about Mom. Back home you write: “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel alone with Mom’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?” Your brother calls within ten minutes. His shifts have changed and he’s been too embarrassed to say. You agree he’ll take the Saturday appointments and you’ll do weekdays. The anger was right that something needed to change. It needed words, not capitals.

Partners: the same fight about money

Selin and Rhona have the same fight every month about spending. This time, when Selin feels her face getting hot, she says their agreed phrase: “I’m flooding. Back in twenty.” She walks around the yard. When she comes back, she says, “I think I’m scared we won’t manage, not angry at you.” They sit down with the bank statements together. See Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).

Parent and child: the slammed door

A twelve-year-old slams his bedroom door after being told to stop gaming. His mom’s first urge is to shout. She waits ten minutes, then knocks: “You were really angry. I get it, stopping is hard. Slamming doors isn’t okay, though. What would help next time?” He suggests a ten-minute warning. It works most days.

A teenager and a parent: the phone at night

Maisie is 16. The rule at home is phones in the kitchen at ten. Tonight her dad takes hers in the middle of a chat with her friends, who will think she just left. She is furious. It feels like being treated as a child, and like not being trusted. She shouts “You don’t trust me!” and slams the door.

In her room, once her heart stops pounding, she notices what is under the anger: embarrassment, and feeling not trusted. The next morning, when they are both calm and he isn’t rushing, she says: “Last night I was really angry. I was mid-conversation, and it felt like you didn’t trust me. Sorry for slamming the door. Could I have ten minutes’ warning, and keep it till ten thirty on Fridays?” Her dad hadn’t thought about the warning. He says yes to that, and “let’s try it for a month” to Fridays.

Words you could use, as a teenager: “I’m too angry to talk properly right now. Can we talk tomorrow?” “It’s not the rule I mind, it’s how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Being angry with a parent is normal. In a review of many studies, Laursen, Coy and Collins (1998) found that arguments between parents and teenagers get less frequent as the teenage years go on, but feel more intense in the middle teens. That is growing up, not a broken family. A rule given out of care isn’t control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm “can we change it?” works more often than a slammed door.

At work: the credit-taker

A colleague presents Usman’s work as his own in a meeting. Usman is furious, and says nothing at the time. That afternoon, calmer, he emails: “In this morning’s meeting, the analysis was presented without mentioning it was mine. I’d like that corrected with the team.” His colleague apologizes and sends a note. Usman’s anger was useful: it helped him act. The calm gave it a shape that worked.

At work: two teammates, and a manager in the middle

Yusra and Bronwen share a project and have stopped speaking except by email. Each has been to their manager, Cormac, to complain about the other. His first urge is to decide who is right. Instead he meets each of them alone for twenty minutes and asks the same three questions: “What happened, as facts? What did it make hard for you? What would you need to work well together?” He listens, and doesn’t promise either of them anything.

Then he meets them together, with one ground rule: talk about what happened, not about what kind of person the other one is. It turns out the fight is about the setup. Both thought they owned the client updates, so each saw the other as interfering. Cormac gives the updates one owner and a backup, writes it down, and books a ten-minute check in two weeks. They don’t become friends. They do start working together again.

Words you could use, as a manager: “I’m not here to decide who’s right. I want to understand what’s making this hard.” “Let’s talk about what happened, not about each other.” “What would each of you need for the next month to work?”

Follow your workplace’s formal process and involve HR.

Friends: the joke that hurt

At a dinner, a friend makes a joke about Daisy’s weight. She laughs along and goes home furious. The next day, she texts: “That joke last night really hurt. I didn’t say anything at the time, but I wanted you to know.” Her friend replies: “I’m so sorry. That was thoughtless. It won’t happen again.” They’re still close.

On your own: angry at yourself

Ivan forgets an important deadline and spends the evening calling himself an idiot. He notices it’s anger turned inward, and that it isn’t helping. He writes what happened as if to a friend, makes a plan for tomorrow, and goes for a walk. He still feels bad, but he sleeps. See Chapter 7 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-7-worth) on self-compassion.

An autistic adult and a changed plan

Kit, who is autistic, finds out at the last minute that a family lunch has moved to a busy restaurant. She feels a surge of anger and starts to shake. Instead of arguing, she says, “I need fifteen minutes,” puts on headphones and walks. Then she texts her sister: “Changes without notice are really hard for me. Can you tell me as soon as plans change?” Her sister agrees, and saves her a seat by the window.

Exercises

  1. Your anger map. Write down three things that often make you angry. For each, what does it protect: fairness, a plan, a boundary, safety?
  2. Your early signs. List two or three body signs that come before you lose your temper. Ask someone you trust what they notice too.
  3. Stop, Out, Back. Write your own calm-down plan: your early sign, your exact words, where you’ll go, and when you’ll come back. (This book’s idea)
  4. The fly on the wall. Next time you replay an argument, write two lines about it using your own name instead of “I.”
  5. Rewrite the message. Take an angry message you once sent, or nearly sent. Rewrite it as what happened, how you felt and what you’re asking for.
  6. One repair. Think of a recent moment when your anger landed on someone. Make one short, specific repair this week.
  7. What’s underneath? After your next angry moment, when calm, ask: was there hurt, fear, tiredness or too much noise under it?

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, anger takes over in seconds. Words are said that can’t be unsaid. One person shouts and the other freezes or shouts back. Nothing is repaired, so the next fight starts from where the last one left off. Or anger is swallowed for years, until it comes out as coldness or a sudden explosion. In the worst cases, people around the angry person become afraid.

When it goes right, people notice anger early and say so. They take a break and come back at the time they said. They talk about what was underneath. The fair point in the anger gets heard and acted on. Sharp moments are repaired quickly and specifically. Over time, everyone in the home or team learns that anger can be felt, said and survived, and that nobody needs to be afraid.

Helping someone else

You don’t have to stay and calm someone down. When it is safe, the most helpful things are often small: speak slowly and quietly, use few words, don’t argue the point while they’re flooded, and offer space. Later, when they’re calmer, you can ask what was going on, listen for the fair point underneath, and also say clearly if the way they spoke wasn’t okay. If someone tells you they want help with their anger, take it seriously: that is a brave thing to say.

Words you could use: “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Let’s try again at seven.” “I think there’s something fair in what you’re saying. The shouting makes it hard to hear.”

Questions people often ask

Why do I get angriest with the people I love most?

Many people notice this. Close relationships involve the most contact, the most expectations and the most at stake, and we often feel safest letting our guard down with the people closest to us. That doesn’t make it fair on them. Knowing the pattern can help you take more care at home, not less.

Is it better to let anger out or keep it in?

Neither extreme. Venting by shouting or hitting things tends to keep anger going. Swallowing it and pretending it isn’t there has costs too. What usually helps most is calming the body first, then saying what made you angry in words, at a time when you can.

Is it okay to be angry with someone who has died?

Yes. Anger is a common part of grief: at the person, at whoever could have prevented it, at life, at yourself. It doesn’t mean you didn’t love them. See Chapter 8 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-8-loss) and Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief).

My partner says I’m angry when I’m not. What do I do?

Tone, faces and directness can be read very differently. Say what you notice (“I’m not angry, I’m tired and being blunt”), and ask what they heard. It can help to agree on a quick check: “Are you annoyed with me, or just busy?”

Does anger management actually work?

For many people, yes. A review by Saini (2009) found that psychological treatments for anger were generally effective, though results varied between approaches and programs. Those programs teach practical skills and help people understand their own pattern.

What about anger in children and teenagers?

Children’s anger is often about feelings they don’t yet have words for, or about tiredness, hunger and too much input. Staying calm yourself, naming the feeling, and helping them settle their body teaches more than any punishment. See For parents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents#calm) and For teens (spreadloveandacceptance.com/teens).

I was brought up in a home with a lot of anger. Will I be the same?

Not necessarily. Growing up around anger can shape what feels normal, but many people learn very different ways. Noticing your patterns and practicing new ones both make a difference. That you are asking the question is a good sign.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education. It isn’t therapy, and it can’t assess anyone’s safety.

The library’s anger (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions), rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#rumination) and flooding (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict#managing-flooding) entries have more on each idea.

What to remember

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that hurts someone has become harm. The feeling is yours to own, and so is what you do with it.

Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits are sliders, not boxes
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert: energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. Changing on purpose
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Fit, not fault
  9. Putting it together
  10. Worked examples
  11. Exercises
  12. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  13. Helping someone else
  14. Questions people often ask
  15. Limits

At a glance

  • Traits are sliders, not boxes. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are. What happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average, people grow steadier and more organized as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Different isn’t wrong. Most clashes between personalities are about fit, not fault.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • The “How to talk to me” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, page 48) describe how you lean on a few sliders, not which box you are in. Most clashes are about fit, not fault.
  • One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 238) lets people with different temperaments share a home or team without changing who they are: you arrange the jobs around the differences. Big idea: fix the setup, not the person.

Saturday, 3:00pm

It’s your aunt’s seventieth birthday. You’re standing quietly by the cake when she says, loud enough for everyone: “Oh, you were always the shy one!” Everyone laughs. You smile, but something stings. You’re forty-two. You teach thirty children every day. Are you still “the shy one”? Were you ever?

What is personality, really? How much of it are we born with, and how much is shaped by life? Do people change, or do they just get more like themselves? And how do people with very different personalities share a home, a family or a job without driving each other mad? This chapter looks at personality and temperament in full, without putting anyone in a box.

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses. Psychology tells us what researchers have found, and where the evidence is limited. Philosophy shows how thinkers from many traditions have understood the same questions. Through an autistic lens looks at each idea from the point of view of autistic people. It is a perspective, not a diagnosis.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Traits are sliders, not boxes

Personality is the word we use for a person’s usual patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving: the things that make them recognizably themselves across many days and places. Describing it well is harder than it sounds.

Psychology

Over the twentieth century, researchers looked for the broad dimensions that best describe how people differ. A five-part picture, often called the Big Five or five-factor model, became the most widely used. The five are usually named openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (the opposite end is often called emotional stability). In one important study, McCrae and Costa (1987) found the same five factors whether people rated themselves or were rated by peers who knew them well, and found moderate agreement between those views.

Two things matter most for everyday life. First, each trait is a dimension: people are spread along it, and most cluster near the middle. Very few people are at the far end of anything. Second, the model is a description, not an explanation. Saying someone is “high in conscientiousness” describes what they tend to do. It doesn’t say why, or whether they could do otherwise. See the Big Five (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring) in the library.

Philosophy

People have tried to sort personality for a very long time. Around the fourth century BCE, Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle, wrote Characters: short, funny sketches of types such as the flatterer and the chatterbox. Ancient Greek and Roman medicine, from Hippocrates to Galen, described four temperaments (sanguine, choleric, melancholic and phlegmatic), linked to the balance of bodily fluids. The fluids were wrong, but the wish to sort people into a few types has stayed with us, in star signs, color quizzes and four-letter codes. Modern research mostly suggests that sliders describe people better than boxes.

Through an autistic lens

Being autistic is not a personality type. Autistic people have the full range of personalities: outgoing and reserved, organized and chaotic, gentle and fiery. Personality questionnaires can also be tricky for literal readers. A question like “Do you enjoy parties?” may get the answer “It depends which party, how loud, and for how long,” which is a more accurate answer than a number on a scale. If a test result doesn’t feel like you, trust your own knowledge of yourself.

Thoughts you could try: “I’m more of this than that, much of the time.” “A score is a summary, not a sentence.”

A note on this site’s style quiz. The style quiz in How you connect gives you a four-letter “Wave Code” and a nickname, which can look like exactly the kind of type this section says to be careful with. It is meant as four preferences, each a lean along a slider: Pace (Quick Spark or Slow Simmer), Lens (Forest or Trees), Sending (Direct or Nuanced) and Receiving (Explicit or Attuned). The tool says whether you lean or lean strongly, and most people are near the middle on some of them. The letters are shorthand, the nickname is a conversation starter, and your answers can change with the day, the setting and who you’re with. It isn’t a validated personality test, and it doesn’t tell you who you are.

Temperament is the starting point

Anyone who has spent time with babies knows they are not blank slates. From the first months, some are busy and loud, some calm and watchful; some settle into routines easily, others protest every change. This early, largely inborn style is usually called temperament.

Psychology

In the New York Longitudinal Study, which followed children from infancy, Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess described differences in activity level, regularity, adaptability, mood, intensity and how children approached new things. In Thomas and Chess (1977), they described three broad groups that many children fell into: “easy,” “difficult” and “slow to warm up,” with many children not fitting any one group. Their most lasting idea was goodness of fit: problems tend to arise not from a child’s temperament alone, but from a poor match between that temperament and what the people and places around them expect.

Temperament is a starting point, not a script. Genes play a part in personality, and so do relationships, experiences, culture and chance. The same cautious toddler can become a careful, thoughtful adult or an anxious one, depending partly on how that caution was met.

Philosophy

Aristotle wrote that good character is neither simply given by nature nor against nature. We are born able to develop it, and it is completed by habit. On that view, temperament is like the raw material, and what we repeatedly do shapes what it becomes. It is a hopeful idea for parents and for adults: what you were given isn’t the whole story.

Through an autistic lens

Babies and children who are very sensitive to noise, touch or change are sometimes described as “difficult.” For autistic children, these may be sensory and processing differences, not a difficult nature. The goodness-of-fit idea is especially useful here: a quieter room, a warning before change, or clothes without scratchy labels can turn a “difficult” child into a settled one. Many autistic adults look back and recognize that they were labeled for needs that nobody understood at the time.

Words you could use: “You like to watch first. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I was a sensitive child. That wasn’t a flaw. It needed a different setup.”

Situations matter too

If personality were everything, people would act the same everywhere. They don’t. The life and soul of the family party may be silent in meetings; the calm nurse may be impatient in traffic.

Psychology

In his 1968 book Personality and Assessment, Walter Mischel pointed out that how a person behaves in one situation often predicts their behavior in another quite weakly. This started a long “person versus situation” debate. The broad answer most researchers came to is that both matter. Traits describe what someone tends to do across many situations, on average. Situations shape what they do in any single moment. Mischel later suggested thinking of personality as stable “if… then…” patterns: if criticized by a boss, then goes quiet; if criticized by a sibling, then argues back.

Philosophy

Some philosophers, such as John Doris in Lack of Character (2002), have used this research to question whether people have stable character traits at all, or whether situations do most of the work. Others reply that character shows exactly in how we handle different situations. Confucian thought offers another angle: we are always someone’s child, friend, colleague or neighbor, and good character means acting well in each of those roles, which may look different in each.

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people seem very different in different places, often because of masking: hiding autistic traits to fit in. In interviews by Hull and colleagues (2017), autistic adults described camouflaging to fit in and connect, often followed by exhaustion. Someone who seems “outgoing” at work may be using a great deal of energy to appear so, and be very quiet at home. When people say “You’re not like that at work,” it’s worth knowing which version costs more.

Thoughts you could try: “I’ve only seen them in one setting.” “Where am I most myself?”

Introvert and extravert: energy, not liking people

Introversion and extraversion are perhaps the best-known personality words, and among the most misunderstood.

Psychology

Carl Jung brought the words into wide use in Psychological Types (1921). In the modern trait view, extraversion includes sociability, assertiveness, liveliness and a tendency to feel positive emotions strongly. People lower in extraversion (more introverted) aren’t necessarily shy or unfriendly. Many enjoy people a great deal, but prefer smaller groups, quieter settings and more time to recover afterward. Shyness, which involves worry about being judged, is a different thing: there are shy extraverts and confident introverts. Most people sit in the middle and shift with mood, setting and how tired they are. See introversion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring#introversion) in the library.

Philosophy

The French thinker Blaise Pascal wrote in the 1600s that many of humanity’s troubles come from not being able to sit quietly alone in a room. Some cultures and traditions prize quiet reflection; others prize lively company. Neither is the “right” way to be human. Many traditions hold room for both, like the hermit and the host, the monastery and the market.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people can be introverted or extraverted. An autistic extravert may love people and still find social time tiring because of sensory load, unwritten rules and masking. That tiredness isn’t the same as introversion, and it helps to know the difference: an introvert may need quiet; an autistic person may need a quieter, clearer, more predictable kind of company. Many autistic people describe enjoying “parallel play”: being with someone while each does their own thing.

Words you could use: “I loved this, and my social battery (my energy for people) is flat. It’s not about you.” “Could we hang out somewhere quieter?”

Tidbit

Some of us recharge at the park with everyone, and some under a quiet blanket. Both are great. A quiz can show you your own style.

Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

People change across life

It is often said that people don’t change. The research says something more interesting: people change slowly, in fairly predictable directions, all through life, while also staying recognizably themselves.

Psychology

Researchers look at two kinds of stability. Rank-order stability asks whether people keep their place compared with others (does the most outgoing ten-year-old become one of the more outgoing adults?). Mean-level change asks whether people on average shift as they age. Both happen. People’s place compared with others becomes more stable from childhood into adulthood, but it never becomes fixed. And on average, people change. A large review of longitudinal studies by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that people tend to become more socially confident, more conscientious and more emotionally stable as they move through adulthood, with much of the change in young adulthood, between about 20 and 40. A newer review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022), using studies published after 2005, found that emotional stability kept increasing across the whole lifespan, and found less evidence that people “set” at a particular age.

Researchers sometimes call this the “maturity principle”: people tend to grow into the traits that adult roles like work, partnership, caring and community ask of them. These are averages. Individuals vary a great deal, and big life events, relationships and illness can all shift personality in either direction.

Philosophy

The psychologist and philosopher William James wrote in The Principles of Psychology (1890) that by around thirty, character has “set like plaster.” The research above suggests he was partly wrong: personality keeps moving long after thirty. Older traditions said it differently. The Greek thinker Heraclitus is often quoted as saying you cannot step into the same river twice. Buddhist teaching on impermanence holds that everything, including the self, is always changing.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic adults, one of the biggest changes in how they see themselves comes from a late diagnosis. In interviews by Leedham and colleagues (2020), women diagnosed in middle or later life described the process of making sense of themselves anew. Traits they had been told were character flaws (being “difficult,” “too sensitive” or “rigid”) could be understood differently. Personality didn’t change overnight, but the story about it did.

Thoughts you could try: “Who I was at fifteen isn’t who I have to be now.” “The people I knew years ago have probably changed too.”

Changing on purpose

If personality changes anyway, can people change it on purpose? Increasingly, the research says yes, slowly, and mostly through action.

Psychology

In a sixteen-week study, Hudson and Fraley (2015) asked people which traits they wanted to change. Those who set goals to increase a trait tended to show increases in that trait, in how they described themselves and in their daily behavior, over the weeks that followed. A review of 207 studies by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that personality traits changed during interventions such as therapy, most of all emotional stability, and that the changes tended to last after the intervention ended.

The common thread is behavior. People don’t usually change by deciding to “be more confident.” They change by repeatedly doing small, specific things (saying one thing in a meeting, replying to messages the same day) until those things feel normal. Chapter 6 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change) explains how habits form.

Philosophy

Aristotle made this argument more than two thousand years ago: we become just by doing just acts, brave by doing brave acts, and generous by giving. Character, for him, was built through practice, the way a builder becomes a builder by building. The Stoics added that small daily practices matter: reviewing the day each evening, preparing in the morning for what might go wrong.

Through an autistic lens

There is an important difference between change you choose and change forced on you to fit in. Many autistic people have spent years trying to make themselves more “normal”: more chatty, more flexible, less intense. Often that has meant masking, at real cost. Chosen change, toward the life you want, is a different thing. It can also mean changing your surroundings rather than yourself: a quieter job, fewer social events, more time with your interests.

Thoughts you could try: “I don’t have to become a different person. I can practice one different thing.” “Is this a change I want, or one I’ve been told to make?”

Every trait has gifts and costs

It is tempting to think some personalities are simply better. A closer look shows that every trait helps in some settings and gets in the way in others.

Psychology

Each of the Big Five has upsides and downsides. Higher conscientiousness tends to go with reliability and getting things done, and can also bring rigidity and difficulty resting. Higher agreeableness brings warmth and cooperation, and can make saying no hard. Higher neuroticism means feeling worry and sadness more strongly, which is painful, but also means noticing risks others miss. Higher openness brings curiosity and creativity, and can bring restlessness with routine. Higher extraversion brings energy and connection, and can bring risk-taking. There is no single “best” profile. A trait’s value depends on the job, the relationship and the moment.

Philosophy

Aristotle’s “golden mean” describes each virtue as sitting between two extremes: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between meanness and wastefulness. The same quality, turned up too high or too low, becomes a problem. Many traditions share a version of this: the strength and the weakness are often the same thing, seen from different sides.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic traits that are often described only as problems can carry real gifts. Deep, focused interests can bring expertise and joy. In a survey of autistic adults, Grove and colleagues (2018) found that people who were more motivated by their special interests reported higher well-being, though a very high intensity of engagement was linked to lower well-being. Directness can mean honesty and reliability. Love of routine can mean consistency. The same traits can be hard in some settings. That is true of everyone’s traits.

Thoughts you could try: “What is the gift in this trait, and what is the cost?” “What annoys me in them might be the flip side of something I value.”

Professor Puddles

Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

Fit, not fault

When people with different personalities live or work closely together, friction is normal. The question isn’t “Who is wrong?” but “How do we fit?”

Psychology

Thomas and Chess’s idea of goodness of fit applies to adults too. A highly organized person and a relaxed one, a planner and a spontaneous person, a talker and a quiet one, can each be fine on their own and clash together. What helps is naming the difference, without blame, and agreeing on arrangements that work for both: dividing tasks to suit strengths, scheduling some things and leaving others free, building in time alone and time together. Personality differences are also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions; sometimes what looks like a clash of personalities is a mismatch in needs. See Chapter 9 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds).

This book’s idea: The “I like, you like, we’ll try” sentence: “I like ___. You like ___. Let’s try ___.” It names both sides as reasonable before looking for an arrangement.

Philosophy

Michel de Montaigne, writing in the 1500s about his close friendship with Étienne de La Boétie, said that if pressed to say why he loved him, he could only answer: “because it was he, because it was I.” Some fits can’t be fully explained. But Montaigne also wrote with great curiosity about how different people are from one another, and how much we can learn from people unlike ourselves.

Through an autistic lens

The double empathy idea suggests that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run both ways: each finds the other harder to read. Fit, here, means both people adjusting a little: the non-autistic person being more explicit, the autistic person explaining what helps. In mixed homes and teams, small adjustments like written plans, warnings before changes and quiet spaces often help everyone. See Neurodivergent relationships (spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

Words you could use: “I think we’re just made differently here. What would work for both of us?” “I like ___. You like ___. Let’s try ___.”

Putting it together

Personality is best described with sliders, not boxes. Temperament gives us a starting point, which then meets the people, places and events of our lives. Situations shape what we do in any moment; traits describe our patterns across many. People change across the whole of life, on average growing steadier and more organized, and can change on purpose, slowly, through small actions repeated. Every trait has gifts and costs. And when different personalities share a life, the most useful question is about fit, not fault.

  • Describe, don’t define. Traits summarize patterns. They don’t sum up a person.
  • Leave room for change. In yourself and in others, especially people you knew long ago.
  • Change by doing. Small actions, repeated, shape who you become.
  • Look for the gift. And plan for the cost.
  • Fit, not fault. Name differences without blame, then arrange around them.

Worked examples

Family: “the shy one”

Back to the birthday. Later, you sit next to your aunt. “I was the shy one, wasn’t I. I still like quiet. These days I stand in front of thirty children every morning.” She laughs: “I was a terror at your age, and look at me now, doing flower arranging.” You were never only “the shy one.” Neither of you is who you were at ten.

Roommates: the tidy one and the relaxed one

Polly likes the kitchen spotless; Ned doesn’t notice mess. Instead of nagging and sulking, they use “I like, you like”: “I like a clear counter at night. You like to leave dishes till morning.” They agree: counters clear by 10pm, dishes by noon. See Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

Parent and child: the slow-to-warm-up son

Seven-year-old Stanley hides at every birthday party. His dad used to push him in. Now they arrive early, before it gets loud, and Stanley helps put out cups. By the time guests arrive, he feels at home. Same boy, better fit.

At work: the quiet new hire

A team thinks their new analyst is unfriendly. Her manager asks how she likes to work. She says she prefers written questions and hates being put on the spot in meetings. With agendas sent in advance, she becomes one of the team’s most valued contributors.

Partners: the planner and the wanderer

One partner wants every vacation hour planned; the other wants to wander. They agree on one booked thing per day and the rest free. Both enjoy the vacation more, and neither feels they gave in.

On your own: “I’m just not a people person”

After a divorce, Keith tells himself he’s “not a people person.” A friend asks when he last enjoyed company. He remembers his old pickup soccer team. He joins a walking soccer group. He’s still quieter than most, and he has three new friends. The label was too small for him.

An autistic adult, diagnosed at 51

For decades, June was told she was rigid and over-sensitive. After her diagnosis, she rereads her life. Her love of routine kept her family running through hard years. Her sensitivity made her a careful, gentle nurse. She stops trying to be someone else and starts arranging her life to suit who she is.

Exercises

  1. Your five sliders. Mark where you sit on each of the five, from one to ten. Ask someone who knows you well to mark you too. Talk about the differences.
  2. Then and now. Write three words that described you at fifteen, and three that describe you now. What changed? What helped?
  3. Where am I most myself? List the places and people where you feel most like yourself, and least. What’s different?
  4. One practice. Choose one small action that fits who you’d like to be more of. Do it three times a week for a month.
  5. Gift and cost. Pick a trait people sometimes criticize in you. Write one time it helped, and one small plan for its cost.
  6. I like, you like. With someone you clash with, try: “I like ___. You like ___. Let’s try ___.” (This book’s idea)
  7. Retire an old label. Think of someone you still describe as they were years ago. Look for one way they have changed, and tell them.

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, people get stuck in labels: “the difficult one,” “the lazy one,” “the shy one.” Differences are treated as faults, and each person tries to change the other. Quizzes are used as verdicts. People mask to fit in and burn out. Old family roles follow people for decades.

When it goes right, people describe their patterns with curiosity, not judgment. They leave room for each other to grow. They name differences and arrange around them. They notice growth and say it out loud. Each person gets to be more fully themselves, and the home, family or team works better for it.

Helping someone else

If someone you care about feels stuck in a label, or is struggling to fit somewhere that doesn’t suit them, the most useful thing is often to see them as they are now. Notice changes and name them. Ask what helps them work, rest and connect, rather than assuming. Avoid using personality as an insult (“You’re so uptight,” “You’re so lazy”); describe the action instead. And if they want to change something, offer to help with one small practice, not a personality overhaul.

Words you could use: “You’ve really changed in how you handle stress. I’ve noticed.” “What would make this easier for you, given how you like to work?”

Questions people often ask

Are personality tests accurate?

Well-made questionnaires based on the Big Five are reasonably reliable for describing broad patterns. Many popular online tests sort people into types, which is less accurate than placing them along dimensions. Any test is a snapshot. Use results for curiosity and conversation, not as a label.

Is personality genetic?

Partly. Genes play a part, and so do relationships, experiences, culture and chance. Neither genes nor upbringing fix who you become.

Can someone’s personality change after something big happens?

Yes. Big life events, like becoming a parent, a serious illness, a loss or a new role, can shift personality, sometimes in lasting ways.

Are introverts better listeners?

Not necessarily. Listening is a skill anyone can learn. See Chapter 4 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication).

Should couples or friends have similar personalities?

There’s no rule. Some people do well with someone similar, others with someone different. What seems to matter more is how they handle their differences: with curiosity and fair arrangements, or with criticism.

What is a personality disorder?

It is a clinical term for long-lasting patterns that cause significant distress or difficulty, and a diagnosis is a complicated judgment that a short chapter, a test or a stranger on the internet can’t make. It isn’t something to apply to yourself or anyone else from online reading, and it should never be used as an insult.

I’m in my seventies. Is it too late to change?

No. Reviews such as Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found personality keeps changing across the whole of life, and many older people describe becoming calmer and more themselves. Small practices work at any age.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education.
  • Please don’t diagnose yourself or others with a “personality disorder” from what you read online.

The library’s wiring page has more on the Big Five (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring#big-five), introversion and sensitivity (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring#sensory-processing-sensitivity).

What to remember

  • Traits work like sliders. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organized as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.
