Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. When you want different amounts of desire or closeness
  8. Love at every age
  9. Love is something you do
  10. Putting it together
  11. Worked examples
  12. Exercises
  13. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  14. Helping someone else
  15. Questions people often ask
  16. Limits

At a glance

  • Love comes in many forms. Friends, family, partners, chosen family and the love you give yourself are all real love.
  • Closeness grows from being known. You share something real, and the other person responds with understanding and care.
  • Love changes over time. Early excitement often settles, and long love can stay warm, close and even exciting.
  • Love is something you do, in small ways, every day. It never includes fear or control.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • The 90-second daily check-in (Part Two, Chapter I, page 139) has an appreciation line, because closeness grows from small, frequent moments of being seen and known.
  • Who did what (the Preface to Part Two, page 108) matters for love too: work one person never sees slowly wears closeness down. Big idea: see the whole load.

Friday, 10:30pm

You and Charlie have shared a home for eleven years. Tonight you’re both on the couch, both on your phones. You realize you can’t remember the last time you talked about anything except bills, the water heater and whose turn it is to cook. You love Charlie. You just feel, oddly, a little alone in the same room.

What is love? What does it mean to be close to someone? Why can two people who love each other end up feeling far apart, and how do they find their way back? This chapter looks at closeness and love in full: in friendship, family, partnership and every other form, at every age, and for people on their own. It builds on Chapter 5 (page 406), which covers attachment and trust. It is not a guide to sex, though one section looks briefly at different levels of desire. Where physical closeness comes up, it is about comfort, consent and care.

Each section looks at one idea through three lenses. Psychology tells us what researchers have found, and where the evidence is limited. Philosophy shows how thinkers from many traditions have understood the same questions. Through an autistic lens looks at each idea from the point of view of autistic people. It is a perspective, not a diagnosis.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Love comes in many forms

When people say “love,” they often mean romance. But most of the love in most lives is something else: the love of friends, parents, children, siblings, grandparents, chosen family, neighbors and communities.

Psychology

Baumeister and Leary (1995) argued that the need to belong is a basic human motivation: people need frequent, caring contact within a few stable relationships. Nothing in that need says the relationships must be romantic. Friendships, family bonds and close community ties can meet it. People love in many arrangements: partners of any gender, people with more than one partner by agreement, long-distance relationships, people who are asexual (feeling little or no sexual attraction) or aromantic (feeling little or no romantic attraction) and who build deep, committed closeness in other ways, and people who live alone and are richly connected. Research on close relationships has historically focused on young, heterosexual, married couples, so it has a lot less to say about many of these, and that is a limit to keep in mind.

Philosophy

The ancient Greeks had several words that are often translated as love: storge (family affection), philia (friendship), eros (desire and romantic love) and agape (selfless love, later central in Christian thought). C. S. Lewis built his book The Four Loves (1960) around them. Aristotle gave friendship a large part of his Nicomachean Ethics, describing friendships of usefulness, of pleasure, and the deepest kind, between people who love each other for who they are. He called such a friend “another self.”

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people show love in ways that are easy to miss: sharing a deep interest in detail (sometimes called info-dumping), sending a link or a picture of something the other person would like (some autistic people call this “penguin pebbling,” after penguins who give pebbles), doing practical things, or simply being in the same room while each does their own thing. These are real expressions of love. Recognizing them can prevent a lot of hurt on both sides.

Thoughts you could try: “Who do I love, in all the forms it takes?” “How does each person I love show it, in their own way?”

Closeness grows from being known

Intimacy is often used to mean physical closeness. In psychology, it means something broader: the experience of being known, and accepted, by another person.

Psychology

Harry Reis and Phillip Shaver described intimacy as an interpersonal process. One person shares something personal (a thought, feeling or piece of their life). The other responds. If that response leaves the first person feeling understood, accepted and cared for, closeness grows, and the roles can swap. In a diary study, Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998) asked people to record their everyday social interactions, and found that both sharing feelings and feeling that the other person really responded contributed to how intimate the interactions felt. Disclosure alone isn’t enough; the response matters as much.

Philosophy

The philosopher Martin Buber, in I and Thou (1923), distinguished two ways of relating. In an “I–It” relation, we treat the other as an object: useful, interesting, in the way. In an “I–Thou” relation, we meet the other as a whole person, fully present. Buber thought real life happens in those moments of meeting. Most of daily life is I–It, and that’s fine. Intimacy is the moments when it becomes I–Thou.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, being truly known means being able to stop masking: to stim, to talk at length about an interest, to say what they mean without translating. A relationship in which that is safe can feel like a huge relief. Honesty also matters greatly to many autistic people, so being known includes being told the truth kindly, rather than being protected with vague or polite answers.

Words you could use: “Can I tell you something I haven’t said out loud before?” “Thank you for telling me. That makes sense to me.”

Closeness is built a step at a time

Closeness rarely arrives all at once. It tends to grow through a series of small risks: sharing a little more, and seeing what happens.

Psychology

Irwin Altman and Dalmas Taylor’s social penetration theory compared getting to know someone to peeling layers of an onion: from public facts, to opinions, to private hopes and fears. In a well-known study, Aron and colleagues (1997) paired up strangers and gave them a list of questions that became gradually more personal (now often called the “36 questions”). After about 45 minutes, these pairs felt closer than pairs who spent the time on small talk. The authors were clear that this created a temporary feeling of closeness in a lab, not a lasting relationship. But the principle, small, matched steps of sharing, applies to friendships and long relationships too.

Philosophy

Aristotle noted that the wish for friendship can come quickly, but friendship itself does not. He quoted a saying that people cannot know each other until they have “eaten salt together”: shared many meals, over a long time. Trust and closeness need time to be tested.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, small talk is the hardest part of getting close: it feels pointless, tiring and full of hidden rules. Some find it easier to skip straight to a real topic, or to connect through a shared interest or activity. That can be a strength: deeper questions often build closeness faster. It helps to say what works: “I’m not great at small talk. Can I ask you about something I’m actually curious about?” See small talk and social scripts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication) in Chapter 4.

Words you could use: “What’s something you’re looking forward to?” “What’s been on your mind lately?” “What was the best part of your week?”

Tidbit

Closeness grows one small step at a time, a bit like learning a new trick. Need an idea for today’s step?

Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Feeling understood matters most

What makes people feel loved? Often not grand gestures, but the steady sense that the other person sees them, gets them, and cares.

Psychology

Reis, Clark and Holmes (2004) proposed that perceived partner responsiveness, the sense that the other person understands, values and cares for you, sits at the heart of intimacy and closeness. It shows in small moments. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that when people shared good news, responses that were active and enthusiastic (“That’s amazing, tell me everything!”) were linked to more intimacy and satisfaction, while responses that were distracted, flat or deflating were not. Algoe, Gable and Maisel (2010) found that in couples, feeling grateful for a partner’s thoughtful act predicted feeling more connected the next day. See responsiveness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships) and sharing good news (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) in the library.

Philosophy

The French philosopher Simone Weil wrote in a letter that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. To really attend to another person, setting aside our own concerns for a moment to take in theirs, is one of the most loving things we can do. Many contemplative traditions treat this kind of attention as a practice that can be learned.

Through an autistic lens

Responsiveness doesn’t have to look a particular way. An autistic friend or partner may listen best without eye contact, while walking or doing something with their hands, and may show care by remembering every detail of what you said. Equally, an autistic person may need others to respond in clear words rather than looks or hints. Asking “How can I show you I’m listening?” helps both sides.

Words you could use: “Tell me everything!” “That sounds like it really mattered to you.” “How can I show you I’m listening?”

Professor Puddles

Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

Old maps show up in love

The expectations we learned early about closeness, from Chapter 5 (page 409), often come out most strongly with the people we love most.

Psychology

Hazan and Shaver (1987) proposed that adult romantic love uses the same attachment system as the bond between children and caregivers: we seek closeness, feel distress at separation, and use the other as a safe haven and a secure base. Later research, such as Fraley and colleagues (2015), suggests adult attachment is best described along two dimensions, anxiety about being left and discomfort with closeness, rather than as fixed types. The same patterns can appear in close friendships and family relationships. When someone higher in anxiety and someone higher in avoidance love each other, a common cycle is pursue and withdraw: one reaches harder, the other pulls further back. See When one talks and one goes quiet (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw).

Philosophy

In Plato’s Symposium, the comic poet Aristophanes tells a myth: humans were once double beings, split in two by the gods, and love is the search for our missing half. It is a moving story, and it captures how complete a loved one can make us feel. Attachment research suggests a gentler version: we aren’t half-people, but we do feel safest, and most able to explore, when someone has our back.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic behavior is easily mistaken for attachment anxiety or avoidance. Checking plans may be about needing certainty, not fear of being left. Needing time alone after a busy day may be recovery from sensory or social load, not avoiding closeness. Saying what the behavior is for (“I’m checking because certainty helps me relax,” “I need an hour to recharge, then I’m all yours”) can stop a misunderstanding before it starts.

Words you could use: “I’m feeling unsure of us. Can you tell me we’re okay?” “I need some space, and I’m coming back. Let’s talk at eight.”

Love changes over time

Early romantic love can be intense, all-consuming and full of longing. Many people fear that when this fades, love is ending. Often, it is only changing.

Psychology

A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) looked at whether long-term relationships kill romantic love. They distinguished romantic love (intensity, engagement, desire) from the obsessive, anxious edge often found in new love. They concluded that romantic love without obsession can exist in long-term relationships, and that it was linked to greater satisfaction and well-being. Aron and Aron (1986) proposed the self-expansion model: people are drawn to relationships that help them grow, and closeness can fade when life together feels stale. In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who did a new, mildly challenging activity together reported higher relationship quality afterward than couples given a dull task. The same is likely true of friendships: shared new experiences keep them alive.

Philosophy

The psychoanalyst and social philosopher Erich Fromm, in The Art of Loving (1956), argued that love is an art that needs knowledge and practice, like any other. He contrasted the experience of “falling” in love with the lasting state of “standing” in love. Falling happens to us. Standing is something we keep choosing.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, routine and predictability are a form of love: the same Sunday walk, the same goodnight message, the same café. Novelty can be stressful rather than exciting. Keeping love lively doesn’t have to mean big surprises. It can mean small new things chosen together, within a familiar frame: a new walk on the usual day, a new recipe at the usual dinner.

Thoughts you could try: “Calm isn’t the same as cold.” “What small new thing could we try, together?”

Sugarfoot

Little rituals, like a Sunday walk or a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Look after the ones you have.

Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

When you want different amounts of desire or closeness

In long relationships, it is very common for one person to want sex, or physical closeness in general, more often than the other. Desire goes up and down with stress, sleep, illness, pain, medicines, pregnancy and new babies, menopause, grief and age. Different levels of desire are a common reason couples look for help. Neither person is the problem. Wanting more isn’t greedy, and wanting less isn’t cold or broken.

A common trap looks like the pursue–withdraw pattern in Chapter 5 (page 410). One person reaches out more and feels rejected. The other starts avoiding even a hug, in case it leads to pressure. Both end up lonely. What tends to help:

  • Talk about it at a calm time, not in bed and not straight after a “no.” Start with what you both want: to feel close and wanted.
  • Widen what counts as closeness. Touch that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, time alone together, and affection in words can ease the pressure on both sides.
  • A kind “no” is not a rejection of the person, and a “yes” only counts if it is freely given. Nobody owes anybody sex. Pressure, guilt or sulking to get it does harm, even between people who love each other.
  • Check the body. Pain, a sudden change, or problems with arousal can have physical causes, and some medicines, including some antidepressants, can lower desire.
  • Talk about it early. A mismatch that goes unspoken for months tends to turn into hurt and guessing. Saying it as something you want (“I miss us”) lands more softly than saying what the other person never does.

A made-up example. Orla and Rufus have two children under four. Rufus feels turned away most nights; Orla feels that every hug is a question. On a Sunday walk they each say one sentence about what they miss. They agree that hugs and a ten-minute sit-down after the children are asleep are just that, with nothing expected after. A month later, Orla says she feels less hunted and more like reaching out. They also keep the Sunday walk going, so they can keep talking without it turning into a fight.

Words you could use: “I miss being close to you, and I don’t want you to feel pressured.” “Can we have hugs that don’t have to lead anywhere?” “I’m not saying no to you. I’m saying not tonight.”

If you are asexual, or one of you is, differences in desire can still be talked about and worked with. The FAQ below has more. This section is general education, not therapy.

Love at every age

Love is part of every stage of life, and it looks different at each one.

Psychology

Laura Carstensen’s socioemotional selectivity theory, set out in Carstensen, Isaacowitz and Charles (1999), proposes that how much time we feel we have left shapes our goals. When the future feels wide open, as for many young people, we seek new information and new people. When time feels more limited, as for many older people (or anyone facing illness), we focus on fewer, more emotionally meaningful relationships. This helps explain why many older people have smaller social circles and say they are content with them. Love in later life is common and real: long marriages and friendships, new partners after loss, deep bonds with grandchildren. So is love in youth: first loves can be intense and formative, and deserve to be taken seriously.

Philosophy

The Roman statesman Cicero wrote two short works late in life, On Old Age and On Friendship. In the first, he argued that old age brings its own pleasures, including conversation and the company of friends. In the second, he described friendship as one of the greatest gifts life offers. Both were written as he faced loss and danger, and both are still read for comfort.

Through an autistic lens

For autistic adults diagnosed later in life, the diagnosis can change how they see past relationships: why some friendships were exhausting, why some partners misunderstood them, why they always loved in their own particular way. That can bring grief for what was missed, and also relief, and a clearer sense of what kind of closeness suits them now. It is never too late to build relationships that fit.

Thoughts you could try: “It’s never too late to be close to someone.” “Missing someone is a form of love too.”

Love is something you do

Feelings of love come and go, even in the strongest relationships. The actions of love can be steady.

Psychology

John Gottman’s research on “bids for connection” (small reaches like a comment, a question or a touch) found that partners who more often turned toward each other’s bids tended to feel more positive with each other, even in later disagreements, as in work by Driver and Gottman (2004). Small, ordinary acts add up: thank-yous, kept promises, remembering what matters to someone, asking about their day and listening to the answer. See Turning toward (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward).

Physical closeness is part of love for many people: hugs, holding hands, sitting close, and for some relationships, sex. People differ a great deal in how much physical closeness they want, and that can change with age, health, stress and life stage. Neither more nor less is the right amount. What matters is that both people feel comfortable, free to say yes or no, and able to talk about it. Consent is always part of love.

Philosophy

The writer bell hooks, in All About Love (2000), argued that love is best understood as an action, not just a feeling, drawing on the psychiatrist M. Scott Peck’s definition of love as the will to extend oneself to nurture one’s own or another’s spiritual growth. She insisted that love and abuse cannot coexist. Fromm, too, described love as including care, responsibility, respect and knowledge: all things we do, not only things we feel.

Through an autistic lens

Touch can be complicated for autistic people: some love deep pressure hugs, some find light touch unpleasant, some need warning before being touched. Preferences can change from day to day depending on sensory load. Asking (“Hug?” “Is this okay?”) and offering choices (a hand on the shoulder or a wave) is caring for everyone, not only autistic people. Love that respects someone’s body is love that lasts.

Words you could use: “What makes you feel most loved by me?” “Hug, or not today?” “Is this okay for you?”

Putting it together

Love takes many forms, and all of them count. Closeness grows from being known: sharing something real and meeting a response that leaves you feeling understood, accepted and cared for. It is built a step at a time, and kept alive by small, steady acts: attention, enthusiasm for each other’s good news, kept promises, new things tried together. Our old maps of closeness show up most with the people we love most. Love changes over time and across a life, and can deepen rather than fade. And love, whatever its form, never includes fear or control.

  • Every kind of love counts. Friendship, family, partnership and chosen family.
  • Be known, and let others be known. Share a little, and respond well.
  • Attention is a gift. Put the phone down. Ask the second question.
  • Calm isn’t cold. Long love changes. It doesn’t have to fade.
  • Love is safe. If you’re afraid, it isn’t love that’s missing on your side.

Worked examples

Partners: alone on the same sofa

Back to the opening. The next Friday you leave both phones in the kitchen, make two cups of tea and ask: “What’s something you’ve been thinking about lately that you haven’t told me?” Charlie talks about their dad getting older and how scared they are of the phone ringing. You share a worry about work. It’s midnight before you notice. Nothing was fixed. You both feel known again. You agree to make it a Friday habit.

Friends: thirty years of Sundays

Two friends in their sixties have spoken every Sunday for thirty years. When one moves abroad, they keep the call, adjusting for time zones. “She knows me better than anyone,” one says. That is a great love, and it has never been romantic.

Siblings: the drive to the nursing home

Two brothers who mostly talk about football drive to visit their dad. One says, “I find these visits really hard.” The other says, “Me too.” They’ve never said anything like it before. On the way home, they stop for fries and talk for an hour.

Teenagers: a first relationship, and a first breakup

Ines is 16 and has been going out with someone from her year for five months. They message from the moment they wake up, and she has started to feel anxious when a reply takes an hour. Then, on a Tuesday night, it ends by message: “I think we should just be friends.” She cries until two in the morning. The next day, an adult says, “You’re young, you’ll get over it.” It doesn’t help. First heartbreak can hurt as much as any loss, because it is the first.

What helps her is ordinary and slow. She tells her older cousin, who listens without giving advice. She mutes their chats instead of reading them over and over, and makes one rule for herself: no checking their profile after ten at night. She doesn’t post about it. A few weeks later she notices she has gone a whole day without thinking about it. That is how it usually goes: in waves, getting further apart.

Words you could use, as a teenager: “I’m really sad about it. I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we not talk about them for a bit?” If you’re the one ending it: “I don’t want to go out anymore. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

In any relationship, at any age, you get to say no to things you don’t want to do or share, and so do they. Needing an instant reply all day can make love feel like a test. It’s fine to agree “we reply when we can.”

Later life: love after loss

Arthur, 78, meets Winifred at his walking group, three years after his wife died. His children are uneasy. He tells them, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.” Winifred comes to Sunday lunch. Slowly, the family makes room.

More than two partners: time for each

Petra has two partners, Ilan and Keiko. When life gets busy, Petra notices she’s been giving Keiko only tired evenings. They agree on one unhurried evening a week each, and one where all three cook together. See More than two (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two).

On your own: love in many places

Nia, 45, has never wanted a partner. Her life is full of love: her nieces, her book group, her best friend, her dog. When people ask if she’s lonely, she sometimes is, like anyone. Mostly, she’s not. She keeps tending the loves she has.

An autistic couple: pebbles and routines

Two autistic partners rarely say “I love you.” Instead, one sends the other photos of interesting bridges every day, and the other keeps a perfect, quiet routine on Sunday mornings so they can both rest. Each knows exactly what the other’s pebbles mean.

Exercises

  1. Your map of love. Draw yourself in the middle of a page. Add everyone you love, in any form, with how each of you shows it.
  2. One true thing. Share one small, true thing with someone this week: a worry, a hope or a happy moment. Notice how it feels.
  3. The second question. When someone tells you something, ask a second, curious question before you share your own.
  4. Celebrate good news. For a week, respond to every bit of good news with real enthusiasm and a follow-up question.
  5. Something new together. Plan one small new thing with someone you love: new to both of you.
  6. Ask about care. Ask someone: “What’s one small thing that makes you feel cared for?” Then do it.
  7. The Friday question. Once a week, phones away, ask: “What’s on your mind that you haven’t told me?” (This book’s idea)

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, people drift into talking only about jobs and logistics. Bids for attention are missed. Good news meets a flat “nice.” One person reaches harder while the other pulls away. Early excitement fades and both decide love has gone. Sometimes, “love” is used to excuse jealousy, checking and control.

When it goes right, people keep turning toward each other in small ways. They share a little of themselves and respond with care. They celebrate each other’s good news. They name their patterns and agree what helps. They try new things together. Love takes many forms in their lives, and every form is treated as real. And everyone feels safe.

Helping someone else

If someone you care about feels lonely, unloved or distant from the people they love, the most useful things are often simple. Be a person they can tell things to, and respond with warmth. Don’t assume everyone wants a partner, or one kind of relationship. After a breakup or a loss, keep showing up, especially after the first few weeks, when many people drift away.

Words you could use: “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”

Questions people often ask

Is it normal for the spark to fade?

Yes, the early, anxious intensity of new love usually settles. That doesn’t mean love is ending. Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that strong romantic love without the obsessive edge can last in long relationships. Shared new experiences and steady attention help.

Can you love someone and not like them very much at the moment?

Yes. Love and liking can come apart for a while, especially in families and long relationships, and during stress. If it lasts, it’s worth telling a friend you trust, and saying it to each other.

I’m asexual. Can I have a deep relationship?

Yes. Deep, committed, loving relationships don’t need sex. Many asexual people have close partners, friendships and families. What matters is that the relationship suits everyone in it.

Are the 36 questions a way to make someone fall in love?

Not really. Aron and colleagues (1997) used them to create a temporary feeling of closeness between strangers in a lab. They can be a lovely way to get to know someone better, but they aren’t a love spell.

We want different amounts of closeness. Is that a problem?

It’s very common. It helps to talk about it without blame, notice what each of you needs (time, words, touch, space), and look for arrangements that suit you both. For differences in sexual desire, see When you want different amounts of desire or closeness.

Is jealousy a sign of love?

Feeling jealous sometimes is human, and asking for something out of care for the relationship, like not flirting with an ex, is not control. But checking someone’s phone without agreement, controlling who they see or punishing them for time apart is not love. Those take away someone’s freedom.

I’m older and lonely. Is it too late?

No. People find friendship and love at every age. Small steps, like a regular group, class or volunteering, often lead to the closest connections. See Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) and On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Limits

  • This chapter is general education. It isn’t couples therapy, sex therapy or a diagnosis.
  • Much research on love has focused on young, heterosexual, Western couples. Love looks different across cultures, ages and relationship types.

The library’s relationships and connection pages have more on each idea.

What to remember

  • Love comes in many forms.
  • Closeness is built a step at a time.
  • Old maps show up in love.
  • Love changes over time.
  • Love is something you do.

Part Three · Chapter 16

Worry, low mood and trauma

How worry and anxiety work, the difference between a low patch and depression, what trauma is and isn’t, what helps day to day, and how to support someone. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm
  2. Avoiding keeps fear going
  3. Give worry a time and a place
  4. Low mood and depression
  5. Doing often comes before feeling better
  6. Sleep, moving and people
  7. What trauma is, and what it isn’t
  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure
  9. Talk therapies and medicines
  10. Putting it together
  11. Worked examples
  12. Exercises
  13. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  14. Helping someone else
  15. Questions people often ask
  16. Limits

At a glance

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress). Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Telling one person helps, and you don’t need the right words.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • The daily check-in’s “low, medium or high” (Part Two, Chapter I, page 139) works because worry and low mood shrink the room you have. Saying so lets the people around you adjust. Big idea: read your state first.
  • “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, page 205) names a time to come back, because avoiding a thing keeps fear going, and a named time doesn’t.
  • Pick one small goal (Part One, Next, page 81) fits low mood: doing often comes before feeling better.

Sunday, 10:50pm

The house is quiet. You’ve checked the front door twice. Tomorrow is the hospital appointment, and the same three thoughts go around: what if it’s bad, what if I can’t cope, what if there’s nobody to tell. Your chest is tight and your mind won’t stop. You haven’t really wanted to see anyone for a few weeks either. Everything feels like too much effort.

Worry, low mood and the after-effects of frightening events are among the most common human experiences, and among the most misunderstood. People are told to relax, cheer up or move on, as if these were choices. This chapter explains what is known about how they work, what helps day to day, what the research says about treatment, and how to support someone else. It can’t diagnose anyone, and it can’t know your situation.

Each section starts with what research has found, and says where the evidence is strong and where it is thin. Where it adds something, a section also looks at what philosophers have said, or at how things can look different for autistic people. Not every section has every lens. Some ideas simply don’t need one.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm

Fear, anxiety and worry are related but not the same. Fear is the alarm for a danger that is here now: a car swerving toward you. Anxiety is the same alarm ringing about something that might happen: the scan result, the money, the conversation next week. Worry is the thinking side of anxiety, a chain of “What if…?” thoughts that tries to solve a problem in advance.

Psychology

Anxiety runs on the stress system described in Chapter 2 (page 334). The body prepares to deal with a threat: the heart speeds up, breathing quickens, muscles tense, digestion slows, attention narrows onto danger. That is useful for a few minutes. When it switches on often, or stays on for weeks, it is tiring and unpleasant, and it can disturb sleep, concentration and digestion. McEwen (1998) described how the stress system protects us in the short term but wears on the body when it is switched on again and again. See allostatic load (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) in the library.

Anxiety tends to keep itself going through a few predictable loops. We pay more attention to possible threats, so we notice more of them. We read uncertain things as dangerous. We avoid or check (the door, the symptoms, the reassurance), which brings relief now and more anxiety later. And body sensations themselves can become frightening: a racing heart is read as a heart attack, which makes it race more. That last loop is at the heart of a panic attack. Panic attacks are very frightening, but they pass, usually within minutes, and they are not dangerous in themselves.

Anxiety becomes a problem, and may be an anxiety disorder, when it is out of proportion to the situation, hard to control, lasts a long time, and gets in the way of daily life. Anxiety disorders are among the most common mental health conditions, and among the most treatable.

Philosophy

The Roman Stoic Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius that there are more things likely to frighten us than to crush us, and that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, in The Concept of Anxiety (1844), took a different view: he called anxiety “the dizziness of freedom,” the feeling that comes from facing open possibilities. Both are useful. Seneca reminds us that most of what we fear doesn’t happen. Kierkegaard reminds us that anxiety is part of being a person with choices, not a sign that something is broken.

Through an autistic lens

Anxiety is common among autistic people. In a review of 35 studies, Hollocks and colleagues (2019) estimated that about a quarter of autistic adults had an anxiety disorder at the time they were studied, and about four in ten at some point in their lives, though estimates varied a lot between studies. Uncertainty is often a big part of it: a change of plan, a vague instruction or an unclear social rule can set the alarm ringing. Carleton (2016) argued that fear of the unknown may sit underneath many kinds of anxiety, autistic or not. Sensory overload can also feel very like anxiety. It helps to ask, “Is this worry, or is it too much noise and light?” The answers need different help: one needs reassurance or a plan, the other needs a quieter room. See intolerance of uncertainty (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring).

Thoughts you could try: “This is my alarm, not a fact.” “Is this worry, or too much input?” “Panic feels dangerous, and it passes.”

Avoiding keeps fear going

When something makes us anxious, avoiding it brings quick relief. That relief is powerful, and it teaches the brain a lesson: “Escaping kept us safe.” Over time, the avoided things grow in number, and life gets smaller.

Psychology

Avoidance comes in obvious forms (not going to the party, not opening the letter) and subtle ones, sometimes called safety behaviors: sitting near the exit, rehearsing every sentence, carrying medication you never use, asking for reassurance again and again. They all prevent the brain from learning that the feared thing is survivable. The most effective psychological treatments for anxiety include some form of exposure: approaching the feared situation gradually and on purpose. Craske and colleagues (2014) describe how exposure seems to work by building new learning (“I went, and I coped”) that competes with the old fear, rather than by erasing it. They suggest it works best when each step tests a specific prediction, when safety behaviors are dropped, and when practice happens in different places and at different times.

Exposure is not about forcing yourself through terror. It is planned, chosen and gradual.

This book’s idea: The step ladder. Write the thing you’re avoiding at the top of a page. Underneath, list six to eight smaller steps, from “barely uncomfortable” to “nearly there.” Before each step, write what you expect to happen. Afterward, write what did happen. Stay on a step until it feels manageable, then go up one.

Through an ADHD lens

For many people with ADHD, avoidance looks like putting things off: the form that sits unopened for weeks, the email you can’t face. It is often less about laziness and more about a task that feels shapeless, boring or loaded with past failures, and a brain that struggles to start without a deadline. Each day it waits, the dread grows, which is the same loop as any other avoidance. The step ladder works here too, with the first step made almost silly: “open the envelope,” “write the subject line,” then stop if you want. A timer for ten minutes, or doing it with someone else in the room, can help a lot. Worry at night is also common, when the day’s distractions stop. A notebook by the bed for “tomorrow’s worry time” gives the thoughts somewhere to go.

Philosophy

Aristotle thought courage was learned by practice: we become brave by doing brave acts, just as we become builders by building. He also thought courage was not the absence of fear, but acting well while afraid. Exposure is, in a sense, Aristotle’s advice with a step ladder added.

Thoughts you could try: “What do I predict will happen? Let’s find out.” “Uncomfortable isn’t the same as dangerous.” “One step, not the whole staircase.”

zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxworryxtimeqzGive worry a time and a place

Worry feels useful, which is part of why it’s hard to stop. It feels like preparing, or caring, or staying in control. Sometimes it is. Often it goes round in circles without reaching a plan.

Psychology

Telling yourself not to worry rarely works; trying to push thoughts away tends to bring them back. A gentler method is postponement. In an early study, Borkovec and colleagues (1983) taught people who described themselves as worriers to notice when they were worrying, put it off, and give it a set time and place later in the day. Over four weeks, they reported worrying less than people who had no instructions. The study was small, but the idea is now part of many CBT programs for worry.

Worry time works better with a simple sort. For each worry ask: is this a problem I can do something about? If yes, write one next step, with a time. If no, practice noticing the worry and letting it pass, perhaps with slow breathing or by turning to something absorbing. Going over and over a worry without a plan is a kind of rumination, and like the rumination in Chapter 13 (page 622), it tends to feed the feeling rather than settle it. See rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions).

Philosophy

The Stoic teacher Epictetus began his handbook by dividing the world into what is up to us and what is not. Worry time puts that idea into practice: the sorting question (“Can I do anything about this?”) is his question, asked every evening at six. Buddhist teaching offers a related image, the “second arrow.” The first arrow is the painful event. The second is our own reaction to it, the going over and over, which we fire into ourselves.

Thoughts you could try: “Noted. That one’s for six o’clock.” “Is there a next step? If so, what is it? If not, can I put it down for now?”

Low mood and depression

Feeling low is part of life. Sadness after a loss, disappointment after a setback, flatness on a gray week: these are normal and usually pass. Depression is something more lasting and more far-reaching.

Psychology

Depression is usually described as low mood, or loss of interest and pleasure, lasting most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, along with other changes: sleeping much more or less, tiredness, changes in appetite, slowed or restless movement, feeling worthless or excessively guilty, difficulty concentrating, and sometimes thoughts of death or suicide. It ranges from mild to severe, and it can come once or return. It affects the body as well as the mind. Many people with depression first notice tiredness, aches or poor sleep rather than sadness. Some notice irritability, numbness or a sense of running on empty.

Depression has no single cause. Life events (loss, money worries, illness, loneliness, caring for someone), long-term stress, difficult early experiences, physical illness, some medicines, alcohol, and inherited factors can all play a part. A low patch after a hard event isn’t the same as depression, and grief isn’t depression either, though the two can overlap. See Chapter 8 (page 475). Guidelines such as NICE (2022) describe a range of effective help, matched to how severe the depression is and what the person prefers.

Philosophy

Philosophers have long noticed that low mood changes the whole world, not just one’s feelings about it. When depressed, nothing seems worth doing, and the future seems closed. That is part of why depression is so convincing from the inside: it doesn’t feel like a mood, it feels like the truth. Knowing this can help. Hopeless thoughts in depression are symptoms, not forecasts.

Across generations and cultures

In many families, cultures and generations, people talk about low mood mainly through the body (“I’m just tired,” “My back’s bad,” “I can’t sleep”), or not at all. Older people, men, and people from communities where mental illness carries stigma are often less likely to name depression or to talk about it. That doesn’t make their distress less real. Asking about sleep, energy and enjoyment can open a door that “Are you depressed?” would close.

Words you could use: “I haven’t been myself for a few weeks.” “Hopeless thoughts are part of how I feel right now, not the whole truth.” (to someone else) “How have you been sleeping? Are you still enjoying things?”

Doing often comes before feeling better

Depression drains motivation. Most of us wait to feel like doing something before we do it. In depression, that wait can last a very long time.

Psychology

Behavioral activation starts from a simple observation: when people are low, they tend to withdraw from activities and people, which removes sources of pleasure, achievement and connection, which deepens the low. The approach reverses the order. You plan small, specific, doable activities, linked to what matters to you, and do them on schedule, whether or not you feel like it. Mood often follows action rather than leading it. In a review of 26 randomized trials, Ekers and colleagues (2014) found that behavioral activation helped with depression compared with control conditions, and did at least as well as medication in the few trials that compared them. They also noted that many of the studies were small or of low quality, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.

The steps that tend to help: notice what you do in a day and how it affects your mood; choose a few activities that bring pleasure, achievement or closeness; make them small enough to be almost certain to happen; put them at a set time; and treat any doing as a success. A walk around the block counts. A shower counts. A text to a friend counts.

Through an autistic lens

For autistic people, “just get out more” can backfire if the activities are draining. Depression may look different too: losing interest in a special interest, or withdrawing even from safe people, can be an early sign. Behavioral activation can be adapted by choosing restoring activities (a favorite interest, a quiet walk, time with one trusted person) over socially demanding ones, and by planning around energy. Depression is common among autistic adults: Hollocks and colleagues (2019) estimated about a quarter at any one time. It can also be confused with autistic burnout; the two need different kinds of rest and help, though people can have both. See Chapter 9 (page 515).

Thoughts you could try: “I don’t have to feel like it to do it.” “Small counts.” “Did it help a bit, even 5%?”

Professor Puddles

A quick check on how you feel before and after a small activity can show you, in your own words, what lifts your day.

Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

Sleep, moving and people

Sleep, physical activity and contact with other people sound like lifestyle advice, not treatment. But all three have good evidence behind them, and all three tend to slip when people are anxious or low.

Psychology

Sleep. Poor sleep is both a symptom and a cause. In the OASIS trial, Freeman and colleagues (2017) randomly assigned nearly 3,800 university students with insomnia to an online CBT course for sleep or to usual care. The course greatly improved insomnia, and reduced paranoid thoughts and hallucinatory experiences, with the improvement in sleep explaining much of the change. The authors argued that this supports insomnia as one cause of other mental health difficulties, though the sample was students, so it may not apply to everyone. CBT for insomnia, rather than sleeping pills, is usually the first recommended treatment for long-term sleep problems. See Chapter 2 (page 350) on sleep.

Moving. In a large review of 218 trials, Noetel and colleagues (2024) found that exercise reduced depression, with walking or jogging, yoga and strength training showing some of the clearest benefits, and more vigorous exercise doing more. The quality of many studies was low, so the exact size of the effect is uncertain, but the direction was consistent. Exercise also helps many people with anxiety.

People. Strong social ties are linked with better health and longer life (Holt-Lunstad and colleagues, 2010). For depression specifically, Cruwys and colleagues (2013) followed several thousand adults aged 50 and over for up to four years. Belonging to fewer social groups predicted more depression later, and the benefits of groups were stronger for people who were already depressed: among them, joining one group was linked to a 24% lower risk of relapse, and joining three to a 63% lower risk. The study was observational, so it shows a link rather than proof, but it fits a wider pattern. A choir, a club, a faith group or a volunteering team can all be groups in this sense.

None of these fixes everything on its own. They are within reach for most people, even in small doses.

Through an autistic lens

Each of the basics can be harder for autistic people for reasons that are easy to miss. Sleep can be disturbed by sensory discomfort. Gyms, team sports and group exercise can be overwhelming. Social groups may only help if they feel safe, which often means groups built around a shared interest, or autistic-led spaces, rather than general social events. The principle is the same: rest, movement and belonging. The forms need to fit.

Words you could use: “I need help protecting my sleep for a while.” “Would you walk with me? I’m more likely to go if someone’s with me.”

Professor Puddles

Small, steady things help: a walk, a regular bedtime, time with someone kind. Calm sounds can be a soft way to wind down at night.

Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

What trauma is, and what it isn’t

“Trauma” is used in many ways now, from life-threatening events to ordinary disappointments. Being clear about the word helps people get the right help, without making anyone’s pain seem smaller.

Psychology

In the clinical sense, a traumatic event involves actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, experienced directly, witnessed, learned about happening to someone close, or met repeatedly in some jobs. Such events are common. Using surveys from 24 countries, Kessler and colleagues (2017) found that about 70% of adults reported at least one in their lifetime, with interpersonal violence such as sexual assault carrying a particularly high risk of later PTSD.

Most people who go through a traumatic event do not develop PTSD. In an influential review, Bonanno (2004) argued that resilience, a fairly steady return to everyday functioning, is the most common response to loss and potentially traumatic events. In the same World Mental Health surveys, Koenen and colleagues (2017) estimated that about 5.6% of people exposed to trauma developed PTSD at some point. That is still a very large number of people, and the risk is much higher after some kinds of event and with less support.

PTSD involves four main kinds of difficulty: re-experiencing (vivid, intrusive memories, flashbacks or nightmares), avoidance of reminders, negative changes in mood and beliefs (guilt, shame, feeling cut off), and feeling on high alert (jumpy, irritable, poor sleep, scanning for danger). Distress in the first weeks after an event is normal. If it lasts beyond about a month, or is severe at any point, it deserves to be taken seriously.

Repeated or long-lasting harm, especially in childhood or in close relationships, can have wider effects: on trust, on feeling safe in your own body, on managing strong feelings. The Adverse Childhood Experiences study by Felitti and colleagues (1998) found that adults who reported more difficult childhood experiences had higher rates of many later health problems. That is a link across groups, not a prediction about any one person, and many people with hard childhoods live well.

Philosophy

Philosophers who write about trauma often stress that it breaks the sense of a world that makes sense and of a future that can be trusted. Recovery, on this view, is not only about calming symptoms. It is about rebuilding a story you can live inside, and relationships in which you are safe again. That fits closely with what trauma-informed care puts first.

Through an autistic lens

Some autistic people describe events that others might call ordinary, such as repeated bullying, being restrained, or long periods of sensory overload, as having a lasting, trauma-like effect. Whether or not these meet the clinical definition, the effects deserve to be taken seriously. Autistic people can also find ordinary routines hard when they rely on eye contact, vague questions or busy waiting rooms, and these can add to the load. Asking for adjustments, such as written questions, a quieter room or extra time, is fair.

Thoughts you could try: “My reactions make sense after what happened.” “It’s over, even if my body hasn’t caught up yet.” “What happened to me is not who I am.”

After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure

What helps most in the days and weeks after a frightening event is often surprisingly ordinary: safety, practical help, warmth, information, and choice about whether and when to talk.

Psychology

For years, it was common to offer everyone a single “debriefing” session soon after a traumatic event, going over what happened in detail. A Cochrane review by Rose and colleagues (2002) found no good evidence that this prevented PTSD, and some evidence that it might increase the risk for some people. The authors advised that compulsory debriefing should stop. Current approaches tend to offer practical support and information early, watch how people are doing over the following weeks, and offer trauma-focused treatment to those who are still struggling.

Trauma-informed care takes this further, into how services and organizations work. In a widely used framework, SAMHSA (2014) set out six principles: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues. The aim is to realize how common trauma is, recognize its signs, respond in ways that help, and avoid causing harm again. These ideas were written for services, but they translate well into homes, schools and workplaces: explain what’s happening, offer real choices, don’t surprise people, and let them set the pace.

In practice

If someone close to you has been through something frightening: make sure they are safe and have what they need today; stay calm and available; let them talk, or not; avoid pushing for details; help with practical things; and keep in touch over weeks, not just days. Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) are among the treatments recommended for PTSD.

Words you could use: “You don’t have to tell me anything. What would help right now?” “You’re safe. I’m staying.” “Can I check in on you on Thursday?”

Talk therapies and medicines

Many people put off talking about it because they don’t know what treatment involves, or fear being judged or told to “just take a pill.” Knowing what the research says about the options can take some of the fear out.

Psychology

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focuses on the links between thoughts, feelings, body and actions, and teaches practical skills to change unhelpful patterns. It is usually short (often six to twenty sessions), structured and collaborative. In a review of 106 meta-analyses, Hofmann and colleagues (2012) found that the strongest evidence was for anxiety problems and general stress, with support across many other difficulties too. They also noted gaps: few studies looked at specific groups such as ethnic minorities or people on low incomes.

For depression, guidelines such as NICE (2022) describe a range of options, including guided self-help, group or individual CBT, behavioral activation, group exercise, and other talk therapies, as well as antidepressant medicines, and stress that the choice should be made together with the person. For anxiety disorders and PTSD there are similar evidence-based options.

Medicines help many people, especially with moderate or severe depression and some anxiety problems. They also have side effects and take time to work.

Philosophy

Some people worry that talking about it means they’ve failed, or that feelings should be handled alone. Most ethical traditions disagree. Caring for your own health is part of caring for the people who depend on you, and leaning on each other is something we do all the time.

Words you could use: “I’ve been struggling with my mood, and it’s been going on for a while.” “I don’t need you to fix it. I’d like you to hear it.”

Putting it together

Worry, anxiety, low mood and the after-effects of trauma all run through the same stress system. Each has its own loop: anxiety is kept going by avoidance and checking, worry by going around in circles, low mood by withdrawal, trauma reactions by an alarm that hasn’t learned the danger has passed. And each has a way out that starts small: stepping back toward what you fear, giving worry a time and a plan, doing before feeling, protecting the basics, and getting safe, steady support. Talk therapies and medicines help many people.

  • It isn’t your fault, and it isn’t forever. These are common, treatable human experiences.
  • Small steps beat big pushes. One step on the ladder, one activity, one call.
  • The basics are treatment too. Sleep, moving and people.
  • Safety and choice first. Especially after trauma.
  • Ask early. Help works better before things get very bad, and it’s never too late.

Worked examples

These are made-up examples built from common patterns, not real people.

On your own: the night before the appointment

Back to the opening. You write the three worries on an envelope and give them a time: tomorrow, after the appointment. You breathe out slowly at the kitchen window, then text your neighbor, who offers a cup of coffee afterward. Over the coffee you also say that you’ve felt flat for weeks. She says she has had flat stretches of her own, and asks if you’d like to walk together on Thursdays. It isn’t fixed overnight, but you’re not carrying it alone.

Partners: the worrier and the fixer

Gwen worries about money every night; her partner Hugo keeps saying “It’ll be fine,” which makes it worse. They agree a twenty-minute money worry time on Sundays, with a notebook. Problems that can be solved get a next step. The rest go on a “can’t control” list. Gwen still worries, but not every night, and Hugo stops trying to argue her out of it.

A teenager, at 1am

Tolu is 17, with a biology exam on Friday. At 1am the thought arrives again: “What if I fail and don’t get into the course?” She picks up her phone, which makes it worse: everyone in the group chat seems to be revising better. The filled-in “Flip it” example under Give worry a time and a place shows what she did with the worry. She also says it out loud to her mom the next day, which helps more than she expected. If worry is stopping you sleeping, eating or going to school most days for a few weeks, that is more than exam nerves, and it is worth telling someone you trust.

Words you could use, as a teenager: “I keep worrying about the exam at night. Can I talk it through?” “I don’t need you to fix it. I just need to say it.” “Can you help me make a studying plan that’s actually doable?”

Parent and teenager: the stopped football

A fifteen-year-old has stopped going to football, stays in his room, and snaps when asked. His mom resists the urge to lecture. She says, “You’ve seemed really down. I’m not cross. I just want to understand.” Over a few days he tells her about being left out by his friends. She says she is around on Saturday if he wants company, and he does. He starts with one small thing each day, and goes back to football with a different team.

Friends: the friend who keeps canceling

Ama’s friend Femke has canceled four times. Ama is tempted to give up. Instead she texts: “No pressure at all. I miss you. Want to go for a short walk on Saturday, just around the park?” Femke comes, and admits she’s been struggling since her dad’s illness. Ama doesn’t try to fix it. She keeps the walks going, every Saturday.

At work: after the incident

After a frightening incident with a customer, a store team is offered a group session to “talk it all through.” One worker, Deepak, doesn’t want to. His manager, who has read about trauma-informed approaches, makes it optional, offers time off and a check-in a week later. Deepak takes the check-in. A month on, he’s still jumpy at the till, and his manager takes him off late shifts for a few weeks and checks in each Friday.

Later life: the widower

Two years after his wife died, Ted still sets two cups out. He’s stopped going to the bowling league and sleeps badly. His son worries it’s more than grief. Ted agrees to talk about “the sleep.” His son gently asks about mood and enjoyment too. Together they make a plan: a wind-down routine, bowls once a week with his neighbor, and another talk in a month.

An autistic adult and the open-plan office

Celia, who is autistic, has felt anxious and low since her team moved to an open-plan office. She isn’t sure whether it’s depression, burnout or overload. She writes down what she’s noticed, along with a list of what helps: headphones, a quiet room, written instructions. She takes the list to her manager and asks for adjustments, and starts a few restoring activities each week, like her model train club, rather than “getting out more.”

Exercises

  1. Name the alarm. Next time worry rises, write: what is the alarm warning me about? What do I predict will happen? Later, write what actually happened.
  2. The step ladder. Pick one thing you avoid. List six to eight steps from easiest to hardest. Try the first step this week. (This book’s idea)
  3. Worry time. Set fifteen minutes at the same time each day for a week. Note worries as they come, and save them for then. In worry time, sort: can I do something? If yes, write one step.
  4. Three tiny things. Each evening, plan three small activities for tomorrow: one for pleasure, one for connection, one you can finish. Check them off. Notice your mood before and after, out of ten.
  5. The basics check. Rate your sleep, movement and contact with people this week, each out of five. Choose the lowest and make one small change.

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, anxiety and low mood are hidden or dismissed: “Pull yourself together,” “You’ve got nothing to be depressed about.” People avoid more and more, withdraw, sleep badly and stop doing what they enjoyed. Alcohol becomes the way to switch off. After trauma, people are either pressured to talk before they’re ready, or never asked at all. Support comes late, or not at all, and the person feels alone and ashamed.

When it goes right, people notice changes early and say so. Someone close asks, listens and doesn’t try to argue the feeling away. Small steps are taken: a walk, a step on the ladder, a call. Sleep and routine are protected. After a frightening event, people are kept safe, given choice and checked on. When self-help isn’t enough, nobody is ashamed of that, and the next step is chosen together. Over time, the alarm quietens and life grows bigger again.

Helping someone else

You don’t need to be an expert to help someone who is anxious, low or struggling after something frightening. Notice changes, and ask gently and directly: “You’ve not seemed yourself. How are you doing, really?” Listen more than you talk, and resist the urge to fix, cheer up or argue with the feeling. Offer specific, practical help: a ride, a meal, company on a walk, sitting with them in a waiting room. With anxiety, support small steps rather than doing everything for them, which can keep avoidance going. With low mood, keep inviting, with no pressure and no guilt. After trauma, put safety and choice first, and let them set the pace.

If you’re worried someone may be thinking of ending their life, it’s okay to ask them plainly. A review by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found no evidence that asking increases suicidal thoughts. If they say yes, stay with them, listen, and help them tell someone else they trust.

Look after yourself too. Supporting someone through a hard time is tiring, and it’s fine to share the load with others. See Chapter 12 (page 588).

Words you could use: “I’m not trying to fix it. I just want you to know I’m here.” “Would it help if I came with you?”

Questions people often ask

How do I know if it’s anxiety or something physical?

Anxiety causes real physical symptoms: racing heart, chest tightness, dizziness, stomach upset. But physical problems can cause similar feelings, and some conditions (such as thyroid problems) can cause anxiety. Chest pain or sudden breathlessness should always be checked urgently.

Is it depression or just a bad patch?

A bad patch usually lifts within days or a couple of weeks, and good moments still get through. You don’t need to be sure it’s depression to ask.

Is grief the same as depression?

No, though they can overlap. Grief tends to come in waves, with moments of warmth or even laughter, and it is focused on the person or thing lost. Depression is more constant and affects how you see yourself and everything else. If grief stays very intense for a long time, or you feel hopeless or unable to function, it’s worth telling someone you trust. See Chapter 8 (page 475).

Was what happened to me “trauma”?

If you went through, saw or learned about something that threatened life, serious injury or sexual violence, it fits the clinical definition. If not, what happened can still have hurt badly and still deserve care. The label matters less than the effect: if something from the past still shapes your days, nights or relationships, it’s worth telling someone you trust.

Will I have to talk about the worst thing that happened?

Not right away, and not without your choice. Good trauma treatment starts with safety and trust, and goes at a pace you agree. Some trauma-focused therapies do involve carefully revisiting memories, because that is often how the alarm learns the danger has passed, and the pace should always be one you agree to.

Do medicines help?

Research finds that medicines help many people, and so do talk therapies, sometimes both together. Stopping a medicine suddenly can cause problems of its own.

Can these things get better?

Yes. Most people with anxiety, depression or PTSD improve, many fully, especially over time and with support. Recovery isn’t usually a straight line, and setbacks are normal. They don’t mean you’re back at the start.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis or therapy, and it can’t assess anyone’s safety.

The library’s stress response (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#stress-response), window of tolerance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#window-of-tolerance), sleep and mood (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#sleep-and-mood), rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#rumination) and resilience (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#resilience) entries have more on each idea.

What to remember

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2. Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Telling one person helps, and you don’t need the right words.
