Part Three · Chapter 17

Fitting in: groups, influence and culture

Why fitting in pulls so hard, how groups shape what we say and do, how culture and family set the unwritten rules, and how to stay yourself, and disagree kindly, without losing your place, whether the group is a family, a friendship, a team, a faith, a neighborhood or a group chat.

In this chapter

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong
  2. We go along more than we think
  3. Authority can lead people a long way
  4. “Us and them” forms fast
  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down
  6. Culture, with care
  7. Every family is a small culture
  8. Groups online
  9. Teams that are rarely in one room
  10. You can belong and still be yourself
  11. Disagree kindly, and early
  12. Putting it together
  13. Worked examples
  14. Exercises
  15. When it goes wrong, and when it goes right
  16. Helping someone else
  17. Questions people often ask
  18. Limits

At a glance

  • The pull to fit in is old and strong. Being left out hurts, so we bend to stay in. That’s human, not weak.
  • Groups shape us more than we notice: what we say, what we think is normal, and sometimes what we’re willing to do.
  • Cultures and families each have unwritten rules. They differ a lot, and so do the people inside them.
  • You can belong and still be yourself. One calm, kind voice saying “I see it differently” often frees others to say so too.

Why the tools work: this chapter explains the thinking behind these tools from earlier in the book.

  • The rulebook from home (Part One, Then, page 18) and House rules for us (One owner per job) write down the rules nobody wrote down, so a group can choose them instead of just following them. Big idea: notice the quiet incentives.
  • The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, page 271) is “not a review of either person.” That is what lets people speak up early, before the group drifts.

Thursday, 9:20pm

The family group chat is buzzing. Someone has posted a joke about your cousin’s new partner, and the laughing faces are piling up. Your thumb hovers. You don’t find it funny. You also don’t want to be the one who “can’t take a joke.” Everyone else seems fine with it. You start typing a laughing face.

Why do we laugh at jokes we don’t find funny, agree with plans we doubt, and follow rules nobody wrote down? Why do some groups bring out the best in us and others the worst? This chapter looks at the pull of groups: belonging pressure, conformity, obedience, “us and them,” norms, culture, family culture and life online. Then it turns to the practical question: how to stay yourself, and disagree kindly, without losing your place. It follows on from Chapter 5 (page 406), which looked at why we need each other in the first place.

Social psychology has some of the most famous experiments in all of psychology, and some of the most argued about. So this chapter is careful to say what later research found when people tried to repeat them. Where it helps, sections also look at what philosophers have said, at how things look across cultures, or at how they can look for autistic people.

Ideas marked This book’s idea are our own ways of putting things into practice, not established science.

The pull to fit in is old and strong

Humans evolved in small groups where being cast out could be deadly. It is not surprising that being left out still sets off alarm bells, and that we will go to some lengths to avoid it.

Psychology

Baumeister and Leary (1995) argued that the need to belong is a basic human motivation, as described in Chapter 5 (page 408). Exclusion research shows how sensitive that need is. In a series of studies, Williams and colleagues (2000) had people play a simple online ball-throwing game with two other “players,” who were really controlled by a computer. When the others stopped throwing the ball to them, people reported feeling worse and a lower sense of belonging, even though the game was trivial and the other players were strangers on the internet. The first study alone involved nearly 1,500 people from 62 countries. Later studies using the same game found similar effects in many settings.

That sensitivity has a cost. Because exclusion hurts, we often pay to avoid it: by laughing along, keeping quiet, or hiding parts of ourselves. Most of the time this is small and harmless social glue. Sometimes it means going along with things we know are wrong.

Philosophy

The Confucian Analects contains a line often translated as: “The gentleman seeks harmony, not sameness; the small person seeks sameness, not harmony.” It draws a distinction this whole chapter relies on. Harmony means different voices fitting together. Sameness means everyone sounding alike. A group can be close and harmonious without asking its members to be identical.

Thoughts you could try: “Wanting to fit in is human. I still get to choose what I go along with.” “Harmony, not sameness.”

We go along more than we think

Conformity means changing what we say or do to match a group. Sometimes it’s because we think the group knows better. Sometimes it’s because we don’t want to stand out.

Psychology

In Solomon Asch’s line-judging experiments, reported in full by Asch (1956), a participant sat with a group of others who were secretly working with the experimenter. On each trial, everyone said aloud which of three lines matched a target line. On some trials, the whole group gave the same obviously wrong answer. Across these trials, participants went along with the wrong answer on roughly a third of their responses. But the averages hide a lot: about a quarter of people never went along at all, while a few went along nearly every time. When even one other person gave the right answer, conformity fell sharply. Many people who went along said afterward that they had doubted their own eyes, or simply hadn’t wanted to stand out.

How well has this held up? In a review of 133 studies using Asch’s task in 17 countries, Bond and Smith (1996) found that conformity was a reliable effect, but it varied. It had declined in the United States since the 1950s, and it tended to be higher in cultures that place more value on the group. Asch’s findings are best read not as “people are sheep,” but as “social pressure is real, varies with time and place, and is much weaker when you are not alone.”

Through an autistic lens

Many autistic people describe a strong commitment to saying what is true, which can make “just go along with it” feel wrong. At the same time, many have learned to mask, copying others to avoid standing out, at a real cost to energy and well-being (see Chapter 9, page 508). Both can be true for the same person. Groups that value accuracy over agreement, and say so, are often easier places for autistic people to be themselves.

Thoughts you could try: “Would I say this if I were on my own?” “If I’m thinking it, someone else probably is too.”

Authority can lead people a long way

Obedience is going along with an instruction from someone in authority. It keeps hospitals, flights and kitchens running. It can also lead people to do things they would never choose.

Psychology

In Stanley Milgram’s best-known experiment, reported in Milgram (1963), 40 men were told they were taking part in a study of learning. They were asked to give electric shocks of increasing strength to a “learner” in another room each time he got an answer wrong. The learner was an actor and no shocks were real, but the participants didn’t know that. As the learner protested and then fell silent, the experimenter calmly told them to continue. Twenty-six of the forty continued to the highest level on the machine. Many showed great distress while doing so. Milgram later ran many variations, and obedience varied widely: it dropped when the experimenter gave instructions by phone, when the participant had to be close to the learner, or when other “participants” refused.

The studies have been repeated and challenged. For ethical reasons, Burger (2009) stopped his partial replication at the point where the learner first protested. He found that obedience up to that point was only a little lower than in Milgram’s day. But others have questioned what the studies really show. After working through Milgram’s archives, the writer and psychologist Gina Perry (2013) argued that the procedure was less standardized than reported, and that many participants doubted the shocks were real. Haslam and Reicher (2012) argued that people did not follow orders blindly: they were most likely to continue when they identified with the experimenter and believed the work was worthwhile, not simply because they were told to. Their reading is less “people obey anyone” and more “people do harmful things when they’re persuaded the cause is good.”

Philosophy

The philosopher Hannah Arendt, reporting on the trial of the Nazi official Adolf Eichmann, coined the phrase “the banality of evil.” Her point was that great harm can be done by ordinary people who stop thinking for themselves, not only by monsters. Her account has itself been debated by historians. But it sits alongside the research in a useful way: the protection is to keep thinking, keep asking “Is this right?” and keep talking to others who might see it differently.

In practice

Healthcare, aviation and other safety-critical fields now train people to question instructions that look wrong, using phrases like “I need some clarity” or “I have a concern.” They found that respectful challenge saves lives. The same idea works at home and at work: checking isn’t disloyalty. See psychological safety (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/teams) in the library.

Words you could use: “Before I do this, can I check one thing?” “I have a concern about this.” “I’m not comfortable doing that. Can we find another way?”

zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxusxthemqz“Us and them” forms fast

Our groups become part of who we are. That gives us pride, loyalty and support. It also makes it very easy to divide the world into “us” and “them.”

Psychology

Social identity theory, set out by Tajfel and Turner (1979), proposes that part of our self-image comes from the groups we belong to, and that we are motivated to see our groups positively, often by comparing them favorably with others. In earlier “minimal group” experiments, Henri Tajfel and colleagues divided schoolboys into groups on almost meaningless grounds, such as which of two abstract painters they supposedly preferred. Even so, the boys tended to give more rewards to their own group, sometimes even when that meant their group got less in absolute terms, as long as it got more than the other group.

The same research points to ways through. When people share a larger identity (the whole family, the whole team, the whole town), old divisions soften. Seeing members of another group as individuals, and working together on a shared goal, also helps. Chapter 3 (page 369) shows how “us and them” even changes what we see. Social identity can also protect: for people who are often stigmatized, a positive group identity can be a source of strength, as the autistic lens below shows.

Through an autistic lens

For many autistic people, finding other autistic people is a turning point. In a study of over 500 people, Cooper, Smith and Russell (2017) found that autistic adults who identified more strongly with other autistic people tended to have higher self-esteem, and through that, lower anxiety and depression. Identity, here, is not a label put on someone from outside. It is a group to belong to, on your own terms. See Chapter 9 (page 526) on autistic community.

Thoughts you could try: “Am I seeing a person, or a group?” “What larger ‘us’ do we both belong to?”

Norms are the rules nobody wrote down

Norms are a group’s shared sense of what is normal and what is expected. They save effort: you don’t have to work out every situation from scratch. They can also trap a group in habits that nobody actually wants.

Psychology

Psychologists distinguish what people do (descriptive norms) from what people think they should do (injunctive norms). Both shape behavior, and we often misjudge both. In a series of studies, Prentice and Miller (1993) asked university students how comfortable they were with drinking habits on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average student was. Most students thought others were more comfortable than they were themselves. This is called pluralistic ignorance: everyone privately doubts, everyone assumes they’re the only one, and so the norm survives. Over time, some students shifted their own views toward the norm they had wrongly imagined, and those who felt out of step felt more alienated.

The hopeful side is that norms can change quickly once people see what others really think. A single person saying the quiet thing aloud can reveal that many others felt the same.

Philosophy

John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty (1859), warned about a “tyranny of the majority” that works not only through laws, but through opinion and custom: the quiet pressure to think and live like everyone else. He argued that people should be free to live differently, as long as they don’t harm others, and that society gains from “experiments of living.” Norms are useful. Mill’s point is that they shouldn’t be unquestionable.

Thoughts you could try: “Is this what everyone thinks, or just what everyone does?” “What would happen if I asked?”

Culture, with care

Culture is the set of shared habits, values and meanings a group passes on. It shapes how we greet, argue, grieve, raise children and show love. It is also easy to oversimplify.

Psychology

In a large survey of employees of one multinational company across dozens of countries, Hofstede (1980) described differences on several dimensions, the best known being individualism and collectivism: how far people see themselves as independent individuals, or as members of close groups with duties to each other. Markus and Kitayama (1991) developed a related idea: an “independent” self that stresses uniqueness, and an “interdependent” self that stresses relationships and fitting in. These ideas help explain why, for example, speaking up, saying no or showing pride can carry very different meanings in different places.

But the research comes with important caveats. When Oyserman, Coon and Kemmelmeier (2002) pooled many studies, they found the differences were often smaller and less consistent than the textbook picture suggests: for example, European Americans were not more individualistic than African Americans or Latino Americans, and not less collectivistic than Japanese or Korean participants. Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) pointed out a different problem: most psychology research has been done with people from Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic societies, who turn out to be unusual in many ways. What looks like “human nature” in a textbook may be one culture’s habits.

Across cultures

Every culture contains huge variety: by region, class, generation, faith, family and personality. Many people live between cultures, and switch between them. Cultures also change, sometimes fast. So culture is a useful question (“How did you learn to do this?”), but a poor assumption (“People from there are like this”).

Words you could use: “Where I grew up, this was normal. What was normal for you?” “Is this a culture thing, a family thing or a you thing?”

Every family is a small culture

Families have their own languages, jokes, rituals, roles and rules: who decides, who cooks, how loud an argument gets, whether feelings are said or shown, how money is talked about, and what never gets mentioned.

Psychology

Writers on family systems describe “family scripts”: patterns of behavior passed down and repeated, often without anyone choosing them (see family scripts, spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/life, in the library). Families also assign roles, like the responsible one, the funny one or the problem, that can stick long after they fit. We tend to notice our own family’s culture only when we meet another: when we move in with a partner, share a house, or join a family by marriage. What felt like “just how things are” turns out to be one way among many.

In practice

Part One (page 18) looks at the rules you grew up with, and which ones you want to keep. With a partner, roommates or co-parents, it helps to bring the hidden rules into the open and choose new shared ones on purpose, rather than each assuming theirs is the normal one. Old roles can be stepped out of, gently: “I know I’m usually the one who sorts it out. This time, I’d like someone else to.”

Words you could use: “In my family we always… What did yours do?” “Shall we make our own rule for this?”

zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxonlineqzGroups online

Group chats, forums and social media are groups too, with norms, leaders, in-groups and out-groups. They move faster, are more public, and can be harder to leave.

Psychology

Online, the group’s reaction is visible and instant: likes, replies and shares show you the norm within seconds. Brady and colleagues (2017) analyzed over half a million social media posts about divisive political issues and found that each additional moral and emotional word in a message (words like “shame,” “evil” or “disgust”) was linked to it spreading about 20% further, mainly among people who already shared the poster’s views. That helps explain why outrage can run through a group chat in minutes, and why quieter, more nuanced voices are easily drowned out. Many of the same forces in this chapter show up online in stronger form: pressure to agree, “us and them,” and wrong guesses about what most people think.

In practice

A few habits help: pause before reacting to a heated post; take disagreements to a private message; remember that the loudest voices aren’t the whole group; and mute, leave or take a break from groups that leave you feeling worse. If online contact turns into threats, harassment or control, save the evidence and tell someone you trust.

For teenagers, group chats are where a lot of friendship happens, and where a lot of hurt can happen too: being left out of a new chat, a screenshot shared without asking, a joke at one person’s expense that everyone “likes.” If it is happening to you, you don’t have to answer back in the chat. You can screenshot it, leave or mute the chat, and tell an adult you trust. If you see it happening to someone else, a private “that wasn’t okay, are you alright?” helps more than you’d think.

Thoughts you could try: “Would I say this to their face?” “The loudest posts aren’t the whole group.” “I can reply later, privately, or not at all.”

Tidbit

Group chats move fast. Before you send a reply, a helper can read the room with you.

Tool: Chat analyzer spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator

Teams that are rarely in one room

Many teams now work partly or wholly from home. The group is still a group, with norms, in-groups and out-groups, but much of it becomes invisible. People in the office hear the corridor conversation; people at home hear the decision afterward, if at all. Quiet people can disappear on a screen. And nobody sees that a colleague has been struggling for weeks.

Small, written agreements do most of the work:

  • Write decisions down, where everyone can see them, so nobody depends on having been in the room.
  • One person remote means everyone joins from their own screen, so the people at home aren’t watching a meeting from the ceiling.
  • Go around the group before a decision, so silence isn’t taken as agreement.
  • Keep a short daily or weekly check-in: how full is your stress tank (light, medium or high), one thank-you, and one thing that got in the way. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-13) has a team version.
  • Keep a few small rituals alive, like a Friday “one good thing” round. Chapter 10 (page 546) has a filled-in example for a hybrid team.
  • Say when you are offline, and agree what counts as urgent, so being reachable doesn’t become a competition.

Words you could use: “Before we decide, can we hear from everyone on the call?” “Can someone write that decision in the channel?” “I’m logging off at five. If it’s urgent, call me.”

Sugarfoot

Teams that rarely share a room need a small, steady check-in. Ten minutes is plenty.

Tool: Team job list: the 10-minute weekly round spreadloveandacceptance.com/work

You can belong and still be yourself

The aim isn’t to stop being influenced by groups. That’s neither possible nor desirable: groups teach us, support us and make us better. The aim is to stay connected without losing yourself.

Psychology

Several findings point the same way. Allies matter enormously: in Asch’s studies, a single partner who gave the right answer cut conformity sharply. Having more than one group helps: Cruwys and colleagues (2013) found that belonging to more social groups was linked to better mental health, and with several groups, no single one gets to define you. Knowing your own values helps you notice when a group is pulling you away from them (see Chapter 10, page 534). And good groups make room for difference on purpose: teams where people feel safe to speak up and admit mistakes tend to learn and perform better, as Edmondson (1999) found.

The distinction from Chapter 5 (page 419) is worth repeating: fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted; belonging means being accepted as you are. If a group only accepts you when you hide who you are, it may be giving you fitting in, not belonging.

Philosophy

The Southern African idea of ubuntu, often summed up as “a person is a person through other persons,” holds that we become ourselves through our relationships, not in spite of them. It doesn’t ask people to dissolve into the group. It asks communities to make room for each person to become fully human. Seen this way, staying yourself in a group isn’t selfish. It is what a healthy group needs from you.

Thoughts you could try: “Which groups let me be fully myself?” “Who would back me up if I spoke?” “Is this group asking me to fit in, or letting me belong?”

zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxdissentqzDisagree kindly, and early

Disagreeing with a group can feel like risking your place in it. Done well, it usually doesn’t. It often earns respect, and it helps the group make better decisions.

Psychology

The research above suggests what makes dissent work. It is easier with an ally, so look for one, or be one. It is easier early, before a view hardens into a decision. It lands better when it is about the issue, not the people, and when it is calm and short. It is often more effective in private than in public, where people can change their minds without losing face. And, as the norms research shows, you are rarely as alone as you think.

This book’s idea: Notice, name, offer. Notice what you think before the group decides. Name your view briefly and kindly, as yours (“I see it a bit differently”). Offer a way forward: a question, an alternative, or a pause to think. Then let the group respond. You have done your part even if the group goes another way.

Groupthink

The psychologist Irving Janis (1972) gave this pull a name: groupthink. In a close, friendly group under pressure, the wish to agree can crowd out a realistic look at the options. Doubts go unsaid because nobody wants to spoil the mood, silence is read as agreement, and the group feels surer than it should. Janis built the idea from case studies of policy decisions, and later research supports parts of it more than the whole model. The everyday lesson holds: a team that always agrees quickly may not be thinking together.

Leaders can do a lot to prevent it. Share your own view last, not first. Ask for the risks before the benefits. Ask one person to argue the other side on purpose, and rotate the job. Collect concerns in writing before the meeting, so quieter people are heard. In a study of 51 work teams, Edmondson (1999) found that teams who felt it was safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake or asking a naive question, did more of the learning that went with better results.

At work: power, and managing up

Disagreeing with someone who has more power than you is harder, and that is normal. Some things make it easier and kinder:

  • Go early and, where you can, go privately. “Can I flag a risk before Thursday?” gives a manager room to change course without losing face.
  • Bring facts and a suggestion, not only a worry: what you’ve seen, what it might cost, and one thing that would help.
  • Managing up isn’t flattery. It means helping your manager help you: telling them how you like to get updates, what you need to do your best work, and what is getting in the way, before it becomes a problem.
  • If you manage people, remember the gap. Your “just a thought” can land as an order, and your silence as disapproval. Ask what people need from you, and thank people who bring you bad news.

Through an autistic lens

Autistic people are sometimes told their disagreement is “rude” when it is simply direct. It can help to add a short frame (“I’m saying this because I care about getting it right”), and it is also fair to ask a group to take direct feedback as information, not attack. Written dissent, such as a follow-up email or a message after the meeting, is a valid choice for anyone who finds it hard to speak up in the moment.

Words you could use: “I see it a bit differently. Can I say why?” “I might be the only one, but I’d like us to think again.” “Can we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet?” “I’m not comfortable with that joke.” “Can I come back to you on this tomorrow?”

Professor Puddles

Disagreeing early and kindly is easier with the words ready. This workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

Putting it together

We are group animals. The need to belong makes exclusion painful, so we bend to fit in, sometimes in small, harmless ways, sometimes in ways we regret. Asch and Milgram showed how strong social pressure and authority can be, and later work showed that both vary a great deal with the situation, the culture and whether we believe in the cause. Groups become part of who we are, which brings both loyalty and “us and them.” Norms and cultures give us shared rules, and we often guess them wrong. Families are small cultures of their own, and online groups turn everything up. The way through isn’t to stop belonging. It’s to keep thinking, find allies, belong to more than one group, know your values, and disagree kindly and early.

  • Harmony, not sameness. Good groups have room for difference.
  • You’re rarely the only one. Others often share the doubts nobody says.
  • One voice frees others. Be the ally, and look for one.
  • Culture is a question, not an answer. Ask the person.
  • Belonging, not fitting in. You shouldn’t have to hide to be accepted.

Worked examples

These are made-up examples built from common patterns, not real people.

Family: the group chat

Back to the opening. You don’t send the laughing face. You message your aunt privately: “I know it was meant to be funny, but it might hurt if they see it. Could we leave it?” She deletes it. Your cousin thanks you. Nothing dramatic happened. The family’s unwritten rule shifted, a little.

Partners: two family cultures

In Leyla’s family, problems are talked about loudly and at once. In Duncan’s, they are left until everyone has calmed down. Each thinks the other’s way is wrong. They write down both families’ rules, laugh at a few, and agree a new one: say it within a day, at a normal volume, after a cup of tea.

Teenagers: the dare

A group of friends are daring each other to shoplift. Fourteen-year-old Toby doesn’t want to. He says, “Nah, I’m good, I’ll meet you outside,” and walks out. Another boy follows him. Later, two more admit they didn’t want to either.

Teenagers: picked on in the group chat

Rhys is 15. In his class group chat, someone starts posting a photo of him from gym class with jokes underneath. Each one gets more laughing faces. Nobody is exactly cruel to his face, but he starts dreading his phone and makes excuses not to go to school. He thinks, “If I react, it’ll get worse.”

He screenshots the messages, mutes the chat and shows his older sister. Together they tell his homeroom teacher, who deals with it quietly. What surprises Rhys most is a private message from a girl in his class: “That wasn’t funny. Sorry I didn’t say anything.” Most people in a group chat don’t like what is happening. Like the people in the norms research above, they just think everyone else does.

Words you could use, as a teenager: “I’m not okay with this. Please delete it.” To a friend it’s happening to: “That wasn’t okay. Are you alright?” To an adult: “Something’s happening online and I need help with it.”

At work: the meeting

A team is about to approve a plan Rukhsana thinks will overload the newest staff. She has spoken up before and felt ignored, so this time she asks a colleague beforehand whether he sees the same problem. He does. In the meeting she says, “I see a risk for the new hires. Can we look at the workload before we decide?” Her colleague backs her up. The plan is changed.

At work: the plan everyone liked

Gethin leads a team planning a new booking system, and the mood is great. Everyone likes the plan, and the launch date is set. Juno, the newest person, has doubts about the date but doesn’t want to be the one who spoils it. That is groupthink in miniature. This time, Gethin has started a habit: before any big decision, he asks everyone to write down one risk, and he speaks last. Juno writes: “The launch is the week the remote team is off for training.” Two others had noticed the same thing and said nothing. The date moves by a week. Nobody remembers it as a disagreement.

Roommates: the kitchen rules

Four roommates from four different countries keep clashing over cooking smells, doing the dishes and noise. Instead of arguing about whose way is normal, they each describe how things worked at home, then write a short house agreement. The cooking smells stay. The 2am pans go.

Online: the neighborhood group

A neighborhood group turns against a family after a rumor about their dog. Jacqui, who knows them, posts: “I’d want to check this before we decide. I’ll ask them.” She messages the family privately, finds the rumor is wrong, and posts that calmly. The thread goes quiet. A few people message her to say thank you.

An autistic adult and a new group

Rory, who is autistic, has always found social groups exhausting. After a late diagnosis, he joins an online group for autistic adults who like trains. For the first time, he doesn’t have to translate himself. He still sees his old friends, but he feels steadier with them too, because he no longer feels he has to be someone else everywhere.

Exercises

  1. Your groups map. List the groups you belong to: family, friends, work, faith, clubs, online. For each, note: can I be fully myself here? Where can’t I, and why?
  2. Before the group. Before your next group decision, write your own view down first. Afterward, compare it with what you said.
  3. Unwritten rules. Write three unwritten rules from your family, workplace or friendship group. For each, ask: who benefits? Would anyone miss it?
  4. Find the individual. Think of a group you tend to see as “them.” Learn one thing about one person from that group.
  5. Your dissent sentence. Choose one sentence for disagreeing kindly. Practice it out loud until it feels natural.
  6. Be the ally. This week, back up someone who speaks up, even with a quiet “I agree.”

When it goes wrong, and when it goes right

When it goes wrong, nobody says what they think. Everyone assumes they’re the only one with doubts. Jokes that hurt go unchallenged. The loudest voices set the norm, and “us and them” hardens. People who disagree are mocked or pushed out, so others stay quiet. Some people leave, and some stay but hide. In the worst cases, groups do harm that no individual in them would have chosen.

When it goes right, people say what they think, kindly and early. Disagreement is treated as useful information. Leaders ask for other views and thank people who give them. Quieter members are drawn in. Differences in background and culture are talked about with curiosity. People belong to several groups, so no single one has total power. The group stays close, and has room in it for everyone to be themselves.

Helping someone else

If someone you care about is under pressure from a group, the most useful thing you can be is an ally: someone who sees what they see and says so. Ask privately what they really think, and listen without pushing. Help them find words, and other groups where they can be themselves. If you lead a group, make room on purpose: ask quieter people first, invite disagreement, and thank people who give it. Notice who is being left out of chats, plans and jokes, and bring them in.

Words you could use: “I noticed you went quiet when they said that. Are you okay?” “I’d really like to hear what you think, even if it’s different.” “You’re not the only one who feels that way.”

Questions people often ask

Are the Asch and Milgram studies still believed?

Partly. Conformity in Asch’s task has been found many times, though it varies with culture and has declined over time in some places. Milgram’s findings have been partly replicated, but how to interpret them is still debated: many researchers now think people go along most when they believe in the cause, not simply because they’re told to. Both remind us that situations shape behavior more than we expect.

Is conformity always bad?

No. Following shared norms lets groups work: lines, traffic rules, taking turns to speak. Learning from others is often wise. The problem is going along when it conflicts with your values or with the truth, or when it harms someone.

How do I disagree without looking difficult?

Keep it short, calm and about the issue. Say it as your view (“I see it differently”). Offer a way forward. Choose the moment: early, and sometimes privately. Most people respect disagreement made like that.

My partner and I come from very different cultures. Where do we start?

With curiosity rather than judgment. Ask each other how things worked at home, what you each want to keep, and what you’d both like to do differently. Then make your own shared rules. Remember that your partner is a person, not a culture.

How do I help my teenager with peer pressure?

Help them practice a “no” that saves face (“Nah, I’m good”), and agree a code word they can text you for a ride home, no questions asked that night. Encourage friendships in more than one group. And show them, in your own life, that you can disagree and still belong.

Should I leave a group that doesn’t accept me?

Sometimes. It may be worth trying to change it first, especially if you have allies. But if a group keeps asking you to hide who you are, or punishes you for disagreeing, it’s fair to step back and put your energy into groups where you can belong as yourself.

Limits

  • This chapter is general education. It isn’t therapy, and it can’t assess anyone’s safety.

More on the site: Chapter 5: belonging and trust (page 406), psychological safety (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/teams#psychological-safety), family scripts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/life#family-scripts), the false consensus effect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking) and casual ties (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection).

What to remember

  • The pull to fit in is old and strong.
  • Authority can lead people a long way.
  • Norms are the rules nobody wrote down.
  • Online groups pull harder and faster.
  • Disagree kindly, and early.

Afterword

Afterword

What the book adds up to

A short look back at the whole book: what each part was for, the few ideas that run through all of it, and where to go next. For anyone who has read some or all of it, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this afterword

  1. Three parts, one idea
  2. Six threads that run through the book
  3. How the book has used evidence
  4. Why more than one lens
  5. What a book can’t do
  6. Where to go from here

At a glance

  • Part One was about you: where your lens came from, how you work now, and where you want to go.
  • Part Two was about sharing a life: seeing the work, sharing it fairly, and talking about it kindly.
  • Part Three was about people: how feelings, stress, trust, change, loss, minds and groups work.
  • The thread through all of it: notice before you judge, settle before you speak, say it plainly and kindly, take small steps, repair, and keep everyone safe.

This is the expanded version of the afterword. It looks back at what each part of the book was for, the threads that run through all of it, how the book has handled evidence, and where you might go next.

Three parts, one idea

Part One: Self-discovery (page 18) started with you, because the way we see others depends on the lens we see through. It looked back at where that lens came from (family rules, what life taught you, old hurts), at how you work now (your wiring, your weather, your words), and forward to what matters to you and the small steps that get you there. It can be read entirely on your own, and for many readers it is the whole book.

Part Two: Between us (page 108) turned to the shared work of running a life with other people: the visible jobs and the invisible ones, the planning, remembering and worrying that someone always ends up carrying. It offered a way to see that work, give each job one owner, notice how full each person’s stress tank is, agree what fair means, and look back each month. Each chapter came with a worksheet, because understanding only helps when it turns into something you do together.

Part Three: Understanding people (page 306) stepped back to ask how people work at all. It covered feelings and stress, how we see and talk to each other, belonging and trust, change, worth and shame, loss, minds that work differently, values, healing, helping, anger, personality, love, worry and low mood, and the pull of groups. Each chapter was written for any kind of relationship and for people on their own.

Underneath all three parts is one idea: most of what goes wrong between people is understandable, and much of it can be put right. Not by being perfect, and not by one person doing all the adjusting, but by seeing more clearly, settling before we speak, and acting a little more kindly, more often.

Tidbit

You made it to the end. High five. Pick one small thing from the book and try it this week.

Tool: Start in 10 minutes spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes

Six threads that run through the book

The book rests on five big ideas, set out at the front: see the whole load, fix the setup, not the person, read your state first, tune how you send and receive and notice the quiet incentives. The six threads below are the same ideas said as everyday habits. The table after the list shows how they match.

1. Notice before you judge

Again and again, the book has found that behavior has reasons: a full stress tank (Chapter 2, page 332), a different family script (Part One, page 18), a different kind of mind (Chapter 9, page 498), or simply the habit of judging ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions (Chapter 3, page 365). Noticing doesn’t excuse harm. It makes understanding possible.

2. Settle before you speak

A flooded body can’t listen. The hot minutes are for breathing out, stepping away and saying when you’ll come back (Chapter 13, page 612). Words come after.

3. Say it plainly and kindly

What happened, how it felt, what you’re asking for. Hints, sarcasm and silence are easy to misread. Clear is kind, and it helps every kind of mind (Chapter 4, page 379).

4. Small steps beat big pushes

Lasting change is usually small and repeated: one owner per job, one step up the ladder, three tiny things a day (Chapter 6, page 430, Chapter 16, page 677). No streaks, no guilt. Miss a day, start again.

5. Repair is normal

Every relationship has ruptures. What matters is coming back: naming what happened, without “but,” and saying what you’ll do differently (Chapter 11, page 560).

6. Your part, and only your part.

Throughout the book, the advice has been about your part: what you can do, and what isn’t yours to carry. You can change how you act. You can’t make someone else change. When safety is at stake, getting safe comes before working it out.

How the six threads match the five big ideas

ThreadBig idea
Notice before you judgeSee the whole load; fix the setup, not the person
Settle before you speakRead your state first
Say it plainly and kindlyTune how you send and receive
Small steps beat big pushesFix the setup, not the person; notice the quiet incentives
Repair is normalTune how you send and receive
Your part, and only your part.Not one of the five: the frame around all of them

How the book has used evidence

The book draws on a lot of research, and it has tried to be honest about it. Some findings are strong and well replicated: that calming the body helps with anger, that exercise and talk therapies help with depression, that social connection matters for health. Some are useful but debated, like the famous conformity and obedience experiments in Chapter 17 (page 701). Some popular ideas have not held up well, and the book has said so where they come up. And some ideas are the book’s own ways of putting things into practice, marked This book’s idea, not established science.

Every study the book names is listed on The research behind this book, with what it found in plain words, how strong the evidence is, and a link to read more. If something in the book doesn’t match your experience, that matters too. Research describes patterns across many people. You are one person.

Why more than one lens

Many chapters looked at their ideas through more than one lens: what psychology has found, what philosophers from many traditions have said, and how things can look from an autistic point of view, with an ADHD point of view where it matters most. Psychology tells us what tends to happen. Philosophy asks what is worth wanting, and reminds us that people have thought hard about these questions for thousands of years. The autistic and ADHD lenses are a reminder that advice written for “most people” often needs adjusting, and that the adjustments usually help everyone.

What a book can’t do

A book can explain, suggest and encourage. It can’t see your situation, assess your safety, diagnose anything or replace care from someone who knows you.

How the numbers work

Every number in this book is arithmetic you can do with a pencil. None of them is a test, a diagnosis or a verdict on anyone: they describe a week, a load or a way of sharing work. The weights and cut-offs are this book’s own rules of thumb, not research findings, and you are free to disagree with them. The worked examples are the book’s own, so you can check them against the chapters.

Two habits run through all of them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places before their band is read, so the number you see and the words you see always agree. And nobody’s score is ever worked out for them: if someone’s own answer is missing, the total waits.

The stress tank: How much are you carrying?

You score five things from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very true), about the last day or two: sleep debt, workload elsewhere, unresolved conflict, your physical state, and time pressure today.

tank = (sleep + workload + conflict + body + time) ÷ 20

The answer runs from 0 to 1, and higher means fuller. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 medium, and 0.60 or more high. (The worksheet splits each band in two for its words: very light under 0.15, light, medium on the lighter side under 0.45, medium on the heavier side, high under 0.80, and very high from 0.80.) Your battery is the other side of the same thing, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery. The battery is a picture in words, not a second score.

Worked example Rosa, from Part Two, Chapter III, page 205, scores sleep 3, workload 4, conflict 1, body 2 and time 3.

3 + 4 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 13; 13 ÷ 20 = 0.65, which is in the high band.

Two or more of you: each person scores only themselves, and the shared figure is the plain average of everyone’s own scores. If any one person is at 0.60 or more, treat that as the headline, whatever the average says.

Coming back after a pause (the Calm-Down Kit): if you like numbers, take the score again after a calming round. Under 0.50, go back at the time you named. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round. At 0.60 or more after two rounds, put it off to a named time. The kit’s line sits at 0.50 on purpose: you don’t need an empty tank to come back, just one less than half full.

My weather today: the room in your day

My weather today shows words, not numbers: a sky (clear, gusty or fogged in) and how much room you have today. Behind the words sits a rough tally from 0 to 100, where higher means a heavier day. You only see it if you check “Show the numbers behind this.”

What you pickedAdds
The sky: clear, gusty, fogged in0, 26, 34
The pressure: light, building, heavy (skipped: 6)0, 10, 20
Last night’s sleep: properly rested, about enough, short night, barely slept (skipped: 6)0, 2, 10, 18
People load: barely any, a normal amount, a lot, nonstop (skipped: 4)0, 3, 9, 14
Ground conditions (hungry, thirsty, in pain and so on)4 each, up to 14
What’s blowing in (work, money, health and so on)3 each, up to 10

Under 45 reads as lots of room today, 45 to 64 as some room, and 65 or more as very little room.

Worked example Joel, from Part One, Now, page 48, picks gusty, building pressure, a short night, a lot of people time, one ground condition (hungry) and one thing blowing in (work).

26 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 62: some room today, with less than usual, so the forecast says to go gently and settle first.

Workload balance: how evenly the hours are shared

Two people. Work out each person’s share of the logged hours as a percentage.

balance = 1 − (the difference between the two percentages ÷ 100)

50/50 scores 1.00; one person doing everything scores 0.00. It doesn’t matter which of you does more. Balance ignores the total, which is one reason the stress tank sits beside it.

Worked example Rosemary logs 14 hours and Ken 10 (Part Two, Chapter II, page 168). Out of 24 hours, that is 58.3% and 41.7%.

1 − (58.3 − 41.7) ÷ 100 = 1 − 0.167 = 0.83

Three or more people, or an agreed split. The same idea, said more generally: how much of the week would have to change hands to reach the target, compared with the most that ever could.

each share = that person’s hours ÷ everyone’s hours target = an even share (1 ÷ number of people), or the split you agreed moved = ½ × the sum of every |share − target| most = 1 − the smallest target share balance = 1 − moved ÷ most

Worked example Three partners log 15, 9 and 6 hours (Chapter II, page 173): shares 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20, against a third each.

moved = ½ × (0.167 + 0.033 + 0.133) = 0.167, most = 1 − 0.333 = 0.667, and balance = 1 − 0.167 ÷ 0.667 = 0.75. In hours, 0.167 × 30 = 5 hours a week would change hands for an even split.

With an agreed split, use it as the target: co-parents who agreed 60/40 and log 12 and 8 hours score 1.00.

Ownership: does every job have a name?

ownership = jobs with a named owner ÷ all the jobs on the list

The calculator counts a job as owned when it has one named owner. A backstop, the person who notices if it slipped, is a good habit and has its own column, but the score only needs the owner. The starter jobs on the worksheet don’t count until you give them an owner or change them. Never raise the score by deleting the jobs nobody owns: they are exactly what the score is there to show.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken list 12 regular jobs, and 9 have an owner: 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75.

Who carries more of the list. A score of 1.00 can still mean one person owns everything, so One owner per job also shows each person’s share of the list, with each job weighted by how often it comes around and how big it is:

weight of a job = how often × size how often: daily 5, weekly 1, ongoing 1, monthly 0.25, as needed 0.1 size: small 0.5, medium 1 (the default), big 2 (or, where you gave the hours each time: hours ÷ 0.5) share = the weights of that person’s jobs ÷ the weights of all the jobs

A job you decide together counts the same for each of you; on a list for two homes it shows as “Together” instead.

Worked example One person owns the cooking (daily, medium: 5) and the bills (monthly, medium: 0.25). The other owns the laundry (weekly, big: 2) and the car (as needed, medium: 0.1). Each owns two jobs, but 5.25 ÷ 7.35 = 71% of the list’s weight sits with the first person, and 29% with the second.

Who’s carrying more right now. Who did what flags the busiest person when their share of the logged minutes (or of the work done without being asked) is at least half, and at least 20 points over an even share: 70% or more for two people, 53% or more for three. In the example in the Preface, page 108, one partner did 105 of the 115 minutes that were noticed and handled without anyone asking: 91%, so the sheet says so.

The setup score: can the way you share the work last?

setup score = balance × 0.40 + ownership × 0.35 + (1 − the average tank score) × 0.25

The weights add up to 1, so the score runs from 0 to 1, and here higher means the setup is working better, the opposite of the tank score. The tank is the only part that counts against the score, which is why it enters as 1 − tank. 0.70 or more reads as working well (the “Who does what?” page says “holding”). From 0.40 up to 0.70 it reads as needs a look (“drifting”), and below 0.40 as needs a rethink, together. It is a snapshot of the setup, never a probability and never a verdict on anyone.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken (Chapter II, page 168): balance 0.83, ownership 0.75, and their own tank scores are 0.45 and 0.30, an average of 0.375.

0.83 × 0.40 + 0.75 × 0.35 + (1 − 0.375) × 0.25 = 0.333 + 0.263 + 0.156 = 0.75: working well.

The shortfall is what each part could have earned minus what it did earn: balance 0.40 − 0.333 = 0.067, ownership 0.35 − 0.263 = 0.088, and tank 0.25 − 0.156 = 0.094. The biggest shortfall is the tank, which usually eases outside the chore list (more sleep, a lighter week elsewhere). The calculator’s “what would help most” is the single change with the biggest gain: handing about 2 hours a week from Rosemary to Ken would take balance from 0.83 to 1.00, worth 0.067. Naming one more job’s owner would be worth 0.029, and a tank score lower by 0.10 on average 0.025.

The overall score adds a fourth part, retuning: of the moments that landed badly this week, how many you retuned before answering.

overall = balance × 0.35 + ownership × 0.30 + (1 − tank) × 0.20 + retuning × 0.15 (no rough moments this week: leave retuning out, and divide the first three parts by 0.85)

In Chapter II’s first worked example (balance 0.60, ownership 0.80, an average tank score of 0.40, and 3 of 5 rough moments retuned): 0.21 + 0.24 + 0.12 + 0.09 = 0.66.

The 30-day look-back: what shifted this month?

The look-back splits the last 30 days into four weeks (the first takes the first ten days). For each part you filled in (balance, ownership, the stress tank, and last-minute rescues), it compares the start of the month with the end:

start = the average of weeks 1 and 2 end = the average of weeks 3 and 4 it shifted if end − start is 0.10 or more (balance, ownership, tank), or 1 a week or more (rescues); anything smaller didn’t shift

One next step: a part that moved the wrong way comes first (the biggest move for its size). Otherwise, the first of these that is still true at the end: ownership under 0.70, balance under 0.70, 2 or more rescues a week, or anyone’s tank at 0.60 or more. If none is, keep the same rhythm and look again in 30 days.

Hours to change hands over the month: for each person, the hours they did minus their share of everyone’s hours, added up week by week. Half the sum of those gaps (ignoring the minus signs) is how many hours would change hands to make the month even.

Worked example Suppose Rosemary and Ken keep going for a month (made up, like them). Their four weeks look like this. Hours: 14 and 10, 15 and 9, 13 and 11, 12 and 12. Jobs with an owner: 9, 9, 11 and 11 of 12. Rosemary’s tank: 0.45, 0.50, 0.40 and 0.35, and Ken’s 0.30 every week. Rescues: 3, 2, 1 and 1.

PartStart (weeks 1–2)End (weeks 3–4)ChangeReads as
Balance(0.83 + 0.75) ÷ 2 = 0.79(0.92 + 1.00) ÷ 2 = 0.96+0.17Better
Ownership0.750.92+0.17Better
Average tank score0.390.34−0.05About the same
Rosemary’s own tank0.480.38−0.10Lighter
Rescues a week2.51−1.5Fewer

Three of the four parts shifted, all for the better, and nothing is left on the watch list, so the next step is to keep the rhythm. The setup score went from 0.73 to 0.87. Over the month Rosemary did 54 hours and Ken 42, so 6 hours would have changed hands for an even month.

On your own: is your week sustainable?

The “Who does what?” page’s “just me” view adds up the hours your week is spoken for (jobs, the thinking work, care and so on) and compares them with a waking week of about 112 hours (16 waking hours, 7 days).

share = the hours spoken for ÷ 112

Under 50% reads as sustainable, 50% up to 70% as full but workable, and 70% or more as stretched. For example, 50 hours spoken for is 45%, which leaves real room; 80 hours is 71%, a lot to keep up week after week.

All of these are this book’s own ways of putting things into numbers. They have not been tested in research studies, and they shouldn’t be quoted as findings. The free calculators on the website do the arithmetic for you, and each one has a “How is this worked out?” note.

Blank worksheets

Photocopy or print these pages, as many times as you like, and fill them out by hand. Each one is a blank copy of a worksheet in the book. The free fillable versions on the website do the math for you, and keep what you type on your own device.

The printed book has a blank page for each worksheet here. On screen, use the free fillable versions: Who did what, How much are you carrying?, One owner per job, What keeps coming back?, Say it so it lands, the Calm-Down Kit, the 90-second daily check-in, Same moment, different speeds, Is it us, or is it everything else? and Keep your little rituals alive.

Who did what

Fillable version: spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-01.html

Write down what actually happened this week, before anyone starts remembering it as a story. Write down only what you did or saw yourself; never fill in someone else’s side for them.

Person APerson BWeek beginning

Part A: Who did what, this week

One row for each task noticed or done, including the invisible ones: remembering, planning, booking, forms. Time spent only thinking, noticing or planning counts too: log it as “Thinking and planning.”

DayTask noticed or doneWho did itMinutes (rough)How it came up: asked for, noticed, or thinking time?

This week’s totals

Person A: minutes (and %), of which noticed and handled without being askedPerson B: minutes (and %), of which noticed and handled without being asked
Workload balance score: 1 − (A% − B%, ignoring any minus sign) ÷ 100 =

Part B (optional), Kind ways to say no: say why the request is fair, say honestly what you have left, and offer something instead.

Describes how the logged work was split this week, not anyone in it. How the score works: “How the numbers work,” at the back.

How much are you carrying?

Fillable version: spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-02.html

Fill this out on your own, about yourself only. Never fill it out for someone else.

Your nameDate

The checklist

Score each row based on how the last 24–48 hours have actually gone. Circle one: 0 = Not at all, 4 = Very true. Living with a long-term illness? Your physical row may always be high. That fills the tank; it isn’t a mood.

Not at allVery true
Sleep debt (less rested than usual)01234
Workload elsewhere (job, school, caregiving)01234
Recent unresolved conflict (any source)01234
Physical state (hungry, sick, in pain)01234
Time pressure today specifically01234

How full is your stress tank?

Points (add the five circled numbers): ____ out of 20Tank: points ÷ 20 = ____ out of 1.00

Higher means a fuller tank (and a lower battery). Under 0.30: light. 0.30 to 0.59: medium. 0.60 or more: high. Put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour.

Optional

Some of what I’m carrying is caring for someone

Anything you want to name before talking

A high score is a way to press pause, not a way out. It means “let’s come back to this tomorrow,” not “this doesn’t need to happen.”

What keeps coming back?

Fillable version: spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-04.html

A monthly look-back, done together, across four weeks of Who did what and One owner per job. It looks for the tasks that keep slipping. You’re looking for where the setup needs a fix. Nobody is adding up what anyone owes.

Month

Part A: Gather the month’s notes

List every task that was noticed but not done, or done only after being raised more than once. Mark an ✗ for each week it came up.

TaskWeek 1Week 2Week 3Week 4Times flagged

Part B: Sort each gap

Sort every task flagged twice or more. A structural gap has no clear owner (fix One owner per job now). A capacity issue has an owner who can’t keep up (set a time for an honest conversation). A one-off has a temporary cause (note it and move on).

TaskNamed owner on the job list? (Yes / No)ClassificationAction

Part C: Wrap up the audit

Structural gaps foundCapacity issues foundOne-offs

Part D (optional): Thanked, or only noticed when it’s missed?

JobGets thanked (Often / Sometimes / Rarely / Never)Only noticed when missed? (Yes / No)One way to notice it

Not a bill for the past, and not a performance review. A task with no owner is a gap in the setup, not a verdict on the person who kept covering it.

Say it so it lands

Fillable version: spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-09.html

A self-check each of you uses on your own side of a conversation. Use it on one thing that actually stung.

Your nameDate

Before you speak or send: fact, feeling, ask

Raw reaction (optional, and just for you)
What’s the fact underneath this? (One sentence, no adjectives.) For example: “The trash went out late on Tuesday.”
What’s the feeling underneath this? (Frustrated, tired, unseen, rushed…) A feeling about you, not a verdict about them.
What’s the actual ask? (What do you want to happen next, specifically?) Something the other person can say yes to.

Before you react: four quick checks

CheckCircle one
Is this about a specific, nameable task or event?Yes · No
Would I read this the same way if I weren’t already carrying a lot?Yes · No · Not sure
Is there a neutral interpretation that also fits what was said?Yes · No
Am I responding to their words, or to a pattern from a past conversation?Their words · A past pattern

A “No” or “Not sure” on the second check, a “Yes” on the third or “A past pattern” on the fourth are good reasons to pause first. A kind “not right now” and a time to come back keep it honest.

The Calm-Down Kit

Fillable version: spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-11.html

A short plan, made ahead of time, for calming your body down enough to have the conversation, or to put it off honestly. Fill in Part A on an ordinary day, not a hard one. Your kit is yours; only the pause plan is made to share.

Whose kit is this? (your name)Date

Part A: What tends to start it

What tends to start itHow it shows up in my body first

Part A: My two defaults

Pick two calming steps now: asymmetric breathing (breathe in for 4, out for 6) · naming the room (5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you can touch) · weight and pressure (feet pressed firmly into the floor, or something warm held in both hands) · gating (cutting noise and light: lower the lights, step out) · walking it out · a low, steady sound.

First defaultSecond, if the first isn’t available

Part A: My pause line

Say how you are, how long you need, and when you’ll be back: “I’m at capacity. I need ten minutes. I’ll be back at a quarter after.”

Our pause plan (agree it together, and share it)

Our pause word or signalThe shortest break we takeHow we set the time to come backThe first sentence when we come back

Part B, in the moment: say your pause word or line, then do your first calming step.

Part C: Coming back

Still hot? Another round. Twice? Name a new time. Settled enough to listen? Go back at the time you named. (For number fans: your stress tank score, 0 to 1. Under 0.50, go back. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round. At 0.60 or above after two rounds, put it off.)

TimeWhat I didHow I feel now (Still hot / Settled enough)Stress tank before (0–1)Stress tank after (0–1)
Next small actionIf you put the conversation off: when you’ll pick it back up

Where I’ve landed

I’m going with this

Date

Speed: right away · within the hour · later the same day · after a night’s sleep. Talk: quiet time first · a few words, then act · talk it all through. Urgency: low · medium · high.

zqglossaryqz

Words used in this book

The book’s own words, each in one plain sentence. More at spreadloveandacceptance.com/glossary.

Alexithymia
Finding it hard to notice, name or describe your own feelings. It is a trait on a scale, not an illness, and it is more common in some autistic people. Naming body signals first can help.
Backstop
The second name on a job: someone who notices if it slipped and checks in kindly. Not a supervisor. A job counts as owned once it has an owner; the backstop is a good habit on top.
Battery
Your battery is how much energy you have left today. Full means you have room to spare; low means you’re running on empty. “How much are you carrying?” measures the other side of it, how full your stress tank is: a fuller tank means a lower battery. For example: After a poor night and a long workday, your stress tank is nearly full and your battery is low, so a small request feels big.
Calm-Down Kit
Your Calm-Down Kit is your own short list of what settles your body, chosen ahead of time so you don’t have to think when you’re wound up. For example: A glass of cold water, a walk to the corner, and three long breaths out.
Check-in
A check-in is a short, planned talk that keeps small things small. The daily one takes about ninety seconds, with no debating. For example: “Load today: heavy. Thank you for the dishes. One small thing: the car. My ask: could you fill it up?”
Co-regulation
Calming down with the help of someone else’s steady presence: a calm voice, sitting nearby, slow breathing together. Children learn to settle this way first.
Complacency
Complacency is what happens when something has worked for a long time and you stop checking on it. It comes from a setup nobody has looked at lately, and it says nothing about laziness or love. For example: “How was your day?” “Fine.” Months go by and nobody has asked a real question.
Developmental stages
Developmental stages are the phases of growing up, each busy with its own big question, like “Am I capable?” in the school years or “Where do I belong?” in the teen years. For example: A move at 14, right when belonging matters most, can leave a deeper mark than the same move at 4.
Double empathy
The idea, from the autistic researcher Damian Milton, that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run both ways: each finds the other hard to read, so neither side is simply “missing” something.
Drift
Drift is how two people slowly fall out of step when nobody checks in, even when nothing is wrong. For example: Three busy weeks, no real talk, and small things start to feel big.
Flooded
Flooded means being so wound up that listening stops working for a while. The kind thing is a short pause with a time to come back. For example: “I need twenty minutes. Can we talk again at eight?”
Frequency
Your frequency is your natural pace: how fast you decide, talk, reply and recover. For example: One person answers a text in a minute. The other answers at the end of the day. Neither is wrong.
Gatekeeping
Holding on to how a home or child-care job must be done, so the other person steps back. Researchers first described it in mothers (“maternal gatekeeping”), but anyone can do it.
Groupthink
When a close group wants agreement so much that doubts go unsaid and a poor decision goes ahead. Irving Janis named it in 1972.
If-then plan
A small plan written as “If this happens, then I will do that,” which makes a new habit easier to start (Peter Gollwitzer).
Interoception
Your sense of what is happening inside your body: heartbeat, breathing, hunger, tension. Feelings often show up here first.
A kind no
A kind no says what you can and can’t do right now, without blaming anyone. For example: “I can’t take that on this week. I could help on Saturday.”
Kinship care
When a grandparent, aunt, older sibling or family friend raises a child whose parents can’t.
The ladder
Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, running on empty. My weather today calls them clear, gusty and fogged in. A best guess about your state, not a measurement.
Ledger
A notebook where you write down what happened, so you can look at it calmly later. The book works the same way: see what is really going on, without blame, then change one small thing.
The load
The load is all the work of a shared life, including the thinking, planning and remembering that nobody sees. For example: Buying the gift is one job. Remembering the birthday, picking the gift and wrapping it are three more.
Masking
Masking is hiding the way you’re wired to fit in, which can be very tiring over time. For example: Forcing eye contact and rehearsing small talk all day, then needing the evening to recover.
Mental load
The noticing, planning and remembering behind running a shared life: knowing the shoes are too small, booking the appointment, keeping the list. It is real work, even though nobody sees it.
Monotropism
A theory of autistic attention: attention gathers deeply on a few things at a time, rather than spreading thinly across many. Switching away can take real effort.
My weather today
My weather today is a one-minute check on your own conditions today, like sleep, stress and energy: Clear means calm and connected, Gusty means revved up, and Fogged in means running on empty. For example: Short night, busy day: the forecast says to keep big talks for tomorrow.
Owner (one owner per job)
The owner of a job is the one person who makes sure it gets done from start to finish, so nobody has to keep asking. For example: Sam owns the recycling: noticing it’s full, taking it out and buying the bags.
Parallel parenting
Co-parenting with as little direct contact as possible: each home runs its own way, and messages stay short, polite and about the children.
Pluralistic ignorance
When most people in a group privately disagree with something but each thinks they are the only one, so nobody says so.
Pressure
Pressure, in My weather today, is how much you were already carrying today: light, building or heavy. Behind the forecast sits a rough tally from 0 to 100; under 45 leaves room in the day, 65 or more means go gently. It is a reading of what you told it, not a score or a grade. For example: A pressure of 40 leaves room in the day; 75 means go gently and leave big things for later.
Prolonged grief
Grief that stays intense and gets in the way of daily life for a long time after a death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline).
Psychological safety
A shared sense in a group or team that you can speak up, ask a question or admit a mistake without being punished or embarrassed (Amy Edmondson).
Repair
A repair is anything that stops a tense moment from getting worse, like a joke, a softer tone or “Can we start over?” For example: “I said that badly. What I meant was…”
Retune
To retune is to notice you’ve fallen out of step with someone and adjust together: slower, softer, or at a better time. For example: “Can we start that again? I came in too fast.”
The rulebook from home
The rulebook from home is the unwritten set of rules you grew up with, about love, upset, chores and rest, that you may still expect others to follow. For example: “Whoever notices the mess cleans it” was the rule at home, so a messy kitchen feels like “It’s always me.”
Rumination
Going over the same worry or regret again and again without getting closer to an answer.
Second arrow
The extra pain we add on top of a hard moment, such as being angry at ourselves for being sad. The first arrow is the event; the second is what we tell ourselves about it (a Buddhist image).
Setup score
The one number from Is the setup working for everyone?: balance, ownership and stress added up with weights (0.40, 0.35 and 0.25), from 0 to 1. 0.70 and up is working well, 0.40 to 0.69 needs a look, under 0.40 needs a rethink, together. It judges the setup, never a person.
Static
Static is the crackle between two people when the words are fine but the tone, pace or timing doesn’t match. For example: You ask “When will you do it?” calmly. They hear pressure. Nobody meant harm, but it crackles.
Stress tank
How much stress you are already carrying, from How much are you carrying?, scored from 0 (empty) to 1 (full). Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 to 0.59 medium, 0.60 and up high. A fuller tank means less room to take more on. (Your battery is the other side of it: energy left.)
Turning toward
Turning toward means answering someone’s small bids for attention, even briefly, instead of missing or brushing them off. For example: “Oh, that’s a funny one!” instead of scrolling on.
Unbilled debt
Unbilled debt is the work of a shared life that got done but was never noticed or thanked. For example: You remembered the dentist appointment, and nobody knew there was anything to remember.
Wave Code
Four letters from the style quiz in How you connect, one for each of four preferences about how you take in and send words. Each letter shows where you lean on a slider today: a shorthand for preferences, not a personality type.
Window of tolerance
The range in which you can feel strong feelings and still think and talk. Above it you are flooded or revved up; below it you shut down. A phrase from the psychiatrist Dan Siegel.
Wired differently
Being wired differently means your brain works in a less common way, such as being autistic, ADHD, dyslexic or highly sensitive, which changes how words land. For example: A hint like “the trash is full” may be heard as a plain fact, not a request.
Wiring
Your wiring is the way your brain and senses take in words, sound, change and people. It stays the same from day to day. For example: Some people need a plan in writing. Others think best out loud.
Workpaper
A page you fill in, on your own or with someone, about your own week or your own side. Every workpaper is free to print or to fill out on the website. For example: “Who did what” is a week’s log of who did what.
Your lens
Your lens is the set of understandings about yourself, other people and what they owe you that you picked up growing up and still use without noticing. For example: “Rest is earned” can feel like plain fact, until you notice it was your family’s rule.
